# Week 1 Lesson Plan: From DNA to Protein

**Class:** About 25 students · **Schedule:** Four 50-minute periods  
**Driving question:** How does the information in DNA help a cell make a protein that does a job?  
**NGSS connection:** Students work toward **HS-LS1-1** by using evidence to explain how DNA sequence influences protein structure and how a protein contributes to a cellular function. Base pairing, replication, and codon reading are supporting skills. The recurring practice is **Developing and Using Models**.

**Modeling routine:** Give each student a four-panel model sheet: **DNA structure | Replication | Transcription | Translation**. Students build and test models in five groups of five, then record their own version. Have them mark revisions with a star and finish the sentence, “I changed ___ because ___.”

## Day 1 · DNA Structure: How do the strands fit together?

**Objective:** Given one DNA strand, students will build and label a complementary strand and explain how base pairing lets them predict the missing sequence.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–5 min | **Notice and wonder:** Show a DNA diagram with three bases missing from one strand. Ask what students notice and what rule might let them fill the gaps. |
| 5–15 min | **Mini-lesson:** Introduce nucleotides, the sugar-phosphate backbone, and A–T/C–G pairing. Connect the flat ladder diagram to the double helix. |
| 15–32 min | **Build and test:** Groups assemble a short DNA ladder from paper pieces. One student hides a section of one strand; a partner reconstructs it and explains the rule used. Rotate roles. |
| 32–45 min | **Record the model:** Students sketch and label panel 1, then check a partner’s model for correct base pairs and backbone labels. |
| 45–50 min | **Quick check — DNA-only preview of “Copy or transcribe?”** Give a new six-base strand. **Success:** All six complementary bases are correct, and the student explains how the original strand provides the information needed. |

**Materials:** DNA diagram, five sets of paper bases and backbone strips, model sheets, pencils.  
**Homework (5 min):** Draw the complement of a new six-base strand and explain how you knew which bases to use.

## Day 2 · DNA Replication: How does a cell copy its DNA?

**Objective:** Students will model replication and explain why each resulting DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly built strand.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–5 min | **Retrieve:** Correct one mismatched base pair and explain the correction to a partner. |
| 5–15 min | **Mini-lesson:** Model strand separation and complementary copying. Clarify that **both** original strands serve as templates in replication. |
| 15–32 min | **Model it:** Groups separate yesterday’s paper DNA strands and use a second color to build new strands. Partners point to and identify the original and new strands in both products. |
| 32–45 min | **Revise the model:** Students complete panel 2. Show a model with both original strands in one product and both new strands in the other; students correct it and explain the fix. |
| 45–50 min | **Quick check — adapt “Repair the model”:** Students independently fix a flawed replication diagram. **Success:** Both products show correct pairing and one original plus one new strand. |

**Materials:** Day 1 DNA kits, paper bases in a second color, flawed replication diagram, model sheets.  
**Homework (5 min):** Sketch the two products of replication, label original and new strands, and explain why the starting strands must separate.

## Day 3 · Transcription: How does DNA information become an RNA message?

**Objective:** Given a labeled DNA template, students will build a complementary mRNA segment and distinguish it from a DNA copy.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–5 min | **Retrieve:** Ask students what a template does and have them point to one in yesterday’s model. |
| 5–15 min | **Mini-lesson:** Model transcription of a short region from one designated DNA template strand. Introduce uracil and contrast the RNA message with the DNA products of replication. |
| 15–32 min | **Build and compare:** Pairs use the same labeled template to make a complementary DNA strand and an RNA strand. They label each product and explain one difference. |
| 32–46 min | **Revise the model:** Students add panel 3 and label the arrows in panels 2 and 3 with the process and product. Partners use the labels to explain why transcription is not replication. |
| 46–50 min | **Quick check — “Copy or transcribe?”** Given a new labeled template, students write its complementary DNA and RNA strands. **Success:** Both follow the correct pairing rules, and the student identifies which product is RNA and how they can tell. |

**Materials:** Labeled template cards with strand direction shown, RNA base cards including U, model sheets, exit slips.  
**Homework (5–7 min):** Transcribe one short, labeled DNA template and write one sentence comparing the RNA message with a DNA copy.

## Day 4 · Translation: How does an RNA message guide protein building?

**Objective:** Using a codon chart, students will translate a short mRNA segment and use provided evidence to connect a protein to its cellular job.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–5 min | **Retrieve:** Ask students to identify the molecule made in transcription and predict what happens to it next. |
| 5–15 min | **Mini-lesson:** Model how a ribosome reads mRNA in three-base codons, how tRNAs bring amino acids, and how a stop codon ends translation without adding an amino acid. |
| 15–30 min | **Translate and model:** Pairs use a codon chart and a short, pre-labeled mRNA segment to assemble an amino acid chain. Students complete panel 4, then trace **DNA → mRNA → amino acid chain** on their own model. |
| 30–39 min | **Connect to function:** Give groups a fictional case in which a pigment-making enzyme with a changed amino acid shows lower activity. Students annotate where the sequence evidence ends and where the activity data support a prediction about pigment production. |
| 39–45 min | **Quick check — “Repair the model”:** Students fix a diagram that skips mRNA. **Success:** They place mRNA between DNA and the amino acid chain, correctly label transcription and translation, and connect the enzyme to pigment production. |
| 45–50 min | **Quick check — “Sequence evidence or trait evidence?”** Provide two short mRNA sequences and a one-line enzyme-activity result. **Success:** Students say whether the amino acid sequence changed and distinguish measured enzyme activity from a predicted trait effect. |

**Materials:** mRNA strips with a marked start position, codon charts, amino acid cards, fictional enzyme data card, model sheets, exit slips.  
**Homework (8–10 min):** Use the four-panel model to explain how DNA information leads to the pigment-making enzyme. Underline one claim supported by the data and circle one prediction the class has not yet tested.

### Two quick differentiation moves

1. **Scaffold:** Offer a partially labeled model, color-coded strands with text labels, and a word bank. Chunk the task so students check the template and product before moving on. Allow oral rehearsal or a dictated explanation when consistent with the student’s IEP; keep the same science success criteria.
2. **Extend without adding volume:** When a student is ready, replace a repeat practice item with an error-analysis prompt: “A classmate used the DNA strand instead of the mRNA to read the codon chart. Where did the reasoning go wrong?” Students can point to the error on their model and explain the fix orally or in writing.

## RTO vs RPO: Study Notes

**Definitions**
- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** maximum acceptable downtime before the service must be restored.
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** maximum acceptable data loss, measured as the age of the most recent recoverable data.

**How each is used in planning**
- RTO drives architecture choices: failover speed, standby capacity, runbook readiness and staffing.
- RPO drives backup and replication choices: sync vs async replication, backup frequency, log shipping interval and storage costs.
- Both are set by business impact, not by what the technology can do. The architecture must then be designed to meet them.

**Key tradeoffs**
- Tighter RTO means more standby infrastructure, faster failover automation and higher cost.
- Tighter RPO means more frequent backups or synchronous replication, which adds write latency and storage cost.
- You can meet one and miss the other: a fast restore from yesterday's backup hits the RTO but breaches a 15-minute RPO.
- Near-zero RPO (synchronous replication) can slow writes and complicate multi-region design.
- The cost of meeting the target must be weighed against the cost of the outage or data loss it prevents.

**Three examples from our work**

1. **SaaS authentication failover (Runbook 1).** RTO ≤15 min because every application depends on login. RPO <1 min because lost session or credential state causes lockouts. Achieved by active-active regions with synchronous replication and pre-lowered DNS TTL.

2. **Customer transactional database restore (Runbook 2).** RTO 1 to 4 hours because the business can tolerate a short outage with customer communication. RPO 5 to 15 min because transactions are hard to reconstruct and loss may breach regulatory duties. Achieved by PITR with continuous log shipping and cross-region standby.

3. **Internal wiki (generic).** RTO 48 hours because the content is not time-critical. RPO 24 hours because daily backups are sufficient and content can be recreated. Achieved by nightly snapshots with no standby, which is low cost.

**How to pick RTO and RPO for a service (one-line checklist)**

**Question 1: SaaS authentication failover**
Your SaaS authentication service has an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 1 minute. The primary region fails. The secondary region is healthy but replication lag is 8 minutes. You fail over in 12 minutes. Which target is met and which is breached, and why?

**Answer:** RTO is met (12 minutes is within 15). RPO is breached (8-minute lag means up to 8 minutes of session and credential data is lost, which exceeds the 1-minute RPO). The breach means some users may be locked out or have stale MFA state. The root cause is replication lag, not failover speed.

**Question 2: Customer transactional database restore**
Your customer database has an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes. A compromise is detected at 14:00, and the earliest suspected compromise time is 10:30. **Answer:** RTO is met (restore took 3 hours, within the 4-hour target from the 14:00 declaration). RPO is breached (the clean restore point is 10:00, which is 4 hours before detection, so all transactions between 10:00 and 14:00 are lost, far exceeding 15 minutes). The breach occurred because the compromise window pushed the usable restore point back beyond the RPO. Shorter detection time (lower MTTD) would have preserved a closer restore point.

## Third-Party Risk Management Cheat-Sheet

**Vendor risk lifecycle (one line each)**
1. Identify: register the vendor and the data or systems it touches.
2. Classify: tier the vendor by data sensitivity and business criticality.
3. Assess: evaluate security posture against the tier's required controls.
4. Contract: include security clauses matched to the tier.
5. Onboard: provision access with least privilege and monitor from day one.
6. Monitor: review posture, incidents and SLA performance on a set cadence.
7. Reassess: repeat the assessment annually or on material change.
8. Offboard: revoke access, confirm data return or destruction, and close the record.

**Minimum controls by vendor tier**

*Low tier (no access to sensitive data or critical systems)*
- Signed NDA.
- Acceptable use and access policy acknowledgement.
- Annual self-attestation of security practices.
- Incident notification clause in the contract.

*Medium tier (access to internal data or non-critical systems)*
- All low-tier controls.
- Current SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate on file.
- Annual security questionnaire reviewed by the security team.
- MFA required for any access to your systems.
- Data processing agreement if personal data is involved.

*High tier (access to sensitive/regulated data or critical systems)*
- All medium-tier controls.
- Right-to-audit clause exercised at least annually.
- Penetration test report reviewed annually.
- Defined SLAs for incident notification (for example 24 hours) and cooperation.
- Subprocessor controls: prior approval and flow-down of security requirements.
- Business continuity and disaster recovery evidence reviewed.

**Essential contract clauses (one line each)**
- Data ownership: company owns all data; vendor processes on instruction only.
- Incident notification: vendor notifies within [24/48/72] hours of a confirmed or suspected breach.
- Right to audit: company or its agent may audit the vendor's security controls.
- Subprocessor approval: vendor must obtain prior written approval before engaging subprocessors.
- Data return and destruction: vendor returns or certifies destruction within [30] days of termination.
- Insurance: vendor maintains cyber liability coverage of at least [$X].
- Compliance: vendor complies with applicable laws and named standards.
- Termination for breach: company may terminate if vendor fails to remediate a material security deficiency.

**10-question vendor security questionnaire**
1. Do you hold a current SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate? (Y/N, attach report)
2. Do you encrypt data at rest and in transit using AES-256 or equivalent? (Y/N)
3. Do you enforce MFA for all administrative and remote access? (Y/N)
4. Do you perform annual penetration tests by an independent firm? (Y/N, attach summary)
5. What is your incident notification timeline to customers? (hours)
6. Do you use subprocessors for any part of the service? (Y/N, list them)
7. Where is customer data stored and processed? (regions/countries)
8. Do you have a documented business continuity and DR plan? (Y/N, state RTO/RPO)
9. How do you manage employee access on termination? (short answer)
10. Do you perform background checks on staff with access to customer data? (Y/N)

**Scenario exam questions**

**Question 1: Vendor compromise**
Your high-tier SaaS vendor reports a breach affecting your tenant. The vendor's contract requires 24-hour notification, but the vendor waited 10 days. Logs show the attacker accessed your customer records. What are your first three actions, and what contract remedies apply?

**Answer:** First, contain: revoke the vendor's access tokens and API keys to your environment. Second, assess: request the vendor's forensic report and determine the scope of customer data exposed. Third, notify: begin the regulatory notification clock based on your own detection of the exposure, not the vendor's late notice. Contract remedies: the vendor breached the 24-hour notification clause, which supports a claim for damages, triggers the termination-for-breach clause, and should be documented for the regulator as a mitigating factor showing the delay was the vendor's failure.

**Question 2: SLA and data breach**
A medium-tier vendor's SLA guarantees 99.9% uptime. The vendor suffers a 48-hour outage during which your customer-facing reporting service is unavailable. The vendor offers SLA credits. During the outage, the vendor also discovers that an unencrypted backup was exposed. What are your obligations, and is the SLA credit sufficient?

Your obligations are to assess whether personal data was in the backup (if yes, the regulatory notification clock starts), to request the vendor's incident report and evidence of remediation, and to review the vendor's tier and controls since the unencrypted backup breaches the encryption requirement. You already have the RTO vs RPO definitions and the first two examples from earlier in this conversation. I'll keep those concise and add the analytics pipeline as a third.

## RTO vs RPO

**RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** Maximum acceptable downtime before a service must be restored.

**RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** Maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time since the last recoverable point.

**Key difference:** RTO is how long you can be down. RPO is how much data you can lose. You can meet one and miss the other.

## Three examples

**1. SaaS authentication service**
- RTO: 15 min. Every app depends on login, so minutes matter.
- RPO: under 1 min. Lost session or credential state causes lockouts.
- Strategy driver: active-active or hot standby with synchronous cross-region replication and automated failover.

**2. Customer transactional database (sensitive PII)**
- RTO: 1 to 4 hours. Customers tolerate a short outage but not a long one.
- RPO: 5 to 15 min. Transactions are hard to reconstruct and loss triggers regulatory duties.
- Strategy driver: continuous transaction-log shipping or near-synchronous replication, with daily immutable snapshots and quarterly restore tests.

**3. Analytics pipeline (internal reporting)**
- RTO: 24 to 48 hours. Delayed dashboards inconvenience stakeholders but do not block operations.
- RPO: 24 hours. Source data lives upstream, so the pipeline can be reprocessed from the last daily load.
- Strategy driver: daily snapshots are sufficient, with no cross-region replication needed. Store the transformation code in version control so the pipeline can be rebuilt rather than restored.

**Pattern:** as RTO shortens, you move from cold backups to warm standby to active-active. As RPO shortens, you move from daily snapshots to continuous replication to synchronous writes. Cost rises with both, so set targets from business impact, not from what is technically possible.

## RTO vs RPO Quiz

**1.** Which statement best distinguishes RTO from RPO?
- A) RTO measures data loss; RPO measures downtime
- B) RTO measures maximum acceptable downtime; RPO measures maximum acceptable data loss
- C) RTO and RPO both measure backup frequency
- D) RTO applies to databases only; RPO applies to networks only

**2.** A payment gateway has an RPO of 5 minutes but daily backups taken at midnight. A failure occurs at 11:00. Which statement is correct?
- A) The RPO is met because a backup exists
- B) The RPO is breached because up to 11 hours of transactions could be lost
- C) The RPO is irrelevant because the gateway can be restarted
- D) The RPO is met because the RTO has not been tested

**3.** An internal wiki has an RTO of 48 hours and an RPO of 24 hours. Which backup and recovery strategy is most appropriate?
- A) Synchronous cross-region replication with sub-second failover
- B) Daily snapshots stored in a single region with a documented rebuild procedure
- C) No backups because the wiki is internal
- D) Real-time log shipping to a hot standby

**4.** A database restore completes in 2 hours from a backup taken 20 minutes ago. The targets are RTO 4 hours and RPO 15 minutes. Which target is breached?
- A) RTO is breached because 2 hours is too long
- B) RPO is breached because 20 minutes exceeds the 15-minute target
- C) Both are breached
- D) Neither is breached

**5.** A company moves from daily backups to continuous replication for its order management system. Which metric does this most directly improve?
- A) RTO, because replication makes failover faster
- B) RPO, because the gap between the last recoverable point and the failure shrinks
- C) Both equally
- D) Neither, because replication is not a backup

**6.** An authentication service with an RTO of 15 minutes uses a cold standby that takes 45 minutes to provision. Which statement is correct?
- A) The RTO is met because cold standby is a valid strategy
- B) The architecture does not meet the RTO and must be changed to warm or hot standby
- C) The RPO is breached, not the RTO
- D) The RTO only applies during business hours

---

## Answer Key

1. **B.** RTO is maximum acceptable downtime and RPO is maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time back to the last recoverable point.

2. **B.** A daily backup at midnight means up to 11 hours of data loss at 11:00, which far exceeds the 5-minute RPO.

3. **B.** A 48-hour RTO and 24-hour RPO are lenient enough for daily snapshots and a rebuild procedure, making real-time replication unnecessary and costly.

4. **B.** The restore took 2 hours (within the 4-hour RTO), but the backup was 20 minutes old, which exceeds the 15-minute RPO by 5 minutes.

5. **B.** Continuous replication keeps the recoverable point close to the present, directly reducing the RPO gap.

6. **B.** A 45-minute cold standby cannot meet a 15-minute RTO, so the architecture needs upgrading to warm or hot standby with faster failover.

We covered RTO vs RPO earlier in this conversation, so here is the updated version mapped to your two runbooks with the monitoring and recovery-option additions.

## Definitions

**RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** Maximum acceptable downtime, measured from disruption to restored service. Answers "how long can we be down?"

**RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** Maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time back to the last recoverable point. Answers "how much data can we lose?"

## Key differences

RTO is about speed of restoration. RPO is about freshness of the data you restore. You can meet one and miss the other: a fast restore from a stale backup hits the RTO but breaches the RPO.

## Practical examples from your runbooks

**SaaS auth failover (RTO ≤15 min, RPO <1 min)**
- RTO example: primary region fails at 09:00; secondary must serve logins by 09:15.
- RPO example: session and token state must reflect activity up to at most 1 minute before the failure, so a user who logged in at 08:59 is not locked out.

**Transactional DB restore (RTO 1 to 4 h, RPO 5 to 15 min)**
- RTO example: compromise detected at 10:00; restored and validated instance serving traffic by 14:00 at the latest.
- RPO example: restore point is 09:50, so at most 10 minutes of transactions need re-entry or reconciliation.

## How to measure and monitor each

**RTO monitoring**
- Auth service: track time from health-check failure to first successful login on the secondary, using a synthetic login probe that runs every 30 seconds.
- DB restore: track time from incident declaration to application connection string pointing at the validated restore, logged in the incident record.

**RPO monitoring**
- Auth service: alert on cross-region replication lag exceeding 30 seconds, using a CloudWatch, Datadog or equivalent metric on the replication stream.
- DB restore: alert on PITR log-shipping lag exceeding 5 minutes, using the RDS ReplicaLag metric or equivalent, plus a daily check that the latest restorable time is within 15 minutes of now.

## Mapping to recovery options

**DNS failover (Route 53, Traffic Manager, Cloud DNS)**
- Affects RTO: shifts traffic in seconds to minutes once triggered.
- Does not affect RPO: data freshness depends on the replication behind the endpoint.

**Cross-region replica (Aurora Global, Cloud SQL replica, Azure geo-replication)**
- Affects both: reduces RTO (promote the replica) and RPO (continuous replication keeps the replica near-current).
- RPO gap risk: asynchronous replication means the replica can be seconds behind; synchronous replication closes this but adds write latency.

**Point-in-time recovery (PITR, transaction log replay)**
- Primarily affects RPO: lets you choose a precise restore point, so data loss is limited to the gap between the chosen point and the incident.
- RTO cost: PITR restores take longer than promoting a hot replica, so RTO is typically 1 to 4 hours.

**Scheduled backups (daily snapshots, pg_dump, mysqldump)**
- Weakest on both: RPO equals the backup interval (daily = up to 24 hours of loss), and RTO depends on restore time plus validation.
- Use as a last resort or as an immutable safety net behind the other options, not as the primary recovery path.

**Answer: B.** RTO is the time to restore service (12 minutes) and RPO is the data gap at the point of failure (45 seconds of replication lag).

**2.** The transactional DB is compromised at 10:00 but detected at 10:30. The team restores to a PITR point of 09:50 and the application is live again at 13:00. What are the effective RTO and RPO?
- A) RTO 2.5 hours and RPO 10 minutes
- B) RTO 3 hours and RPO 40 minutes
- C) RTO 2.5 hours and RPO 40 minutes
- D) RTO 3 hours and RPO 10 minutes

**Answer: C.** RTO is measured from detection (10:30) to restoration (13:00), which is 2.5 hours. RPO is the gap between the restore point (09:50) and the last good state before compromise (10:00), which is 10 minutes of lost data, but the question asks effective RPO: the data rolled back covers 09:50 to 10:30, so 40 minutes of transactions need re-entry. In exam terms, accept either C or A depending on whether RPO is measured from restore point to compromise or from restore point to detection; flag this for discussion.

**3.** The auth service uses synchronous cross-region replication and DNS failover with a 60-second TTL. The transactional DB uses daily snapshots only. Which conclusion is correct?
- A) Both services have the same RPO
- B) The auth service has a stronger RPO because synchronous replication means near-zero data loss, while the DB could lose up to 24 hours
- C) The DB has a stronger RPO because daily snapshots are more reliable
- D) DNS TTL determines the RPO for the auth service

**Answer: B.** Synchronous replication gives near-zero RPO; daily snapshots give up to 24 hours of potential data loss. DNS TTL affects RTO, not RPO.

**1.** A synthetic login probe runs every 30 seconds against the SaaS auth secondary endpoint. During a failover, the probe starts succeeding at 09:14. The health check failed at 09:00. What does this probe measure?
- A) RPO, because it shows how much session data was lost
- B) RTO, because it shows the time from failure to restored service
- C) Replication lag, because it tests the secondary endpoint
- D) Backup freshness, because the probe runs on a schedule

**Answer: B.** The probe measures elapsed time from outage to successful login, which is the RTO.

**2.** An alert fires when the RDS ReplicaLag metric exceeds 5 minutes for the transactional DB cross-region replica. Which objective does this alert protect?
- A) RTO, because lag slows down failover
- B) RPO, because lag above 5 minutes means more than 5 minutes of data could be lost if a failure occurs now
- C) Both equally, because lag affects everything
- D) Neither, because lag is an infrastructure metric with no business meaning

**Answer: B.** Replication lag directly maps to potential data loss on failure, which is the RPO.

- A) The RTO target was met
- B) The RPO target was met, because the restored data matches the baseline with no unexpected loss or change
- C) The replication lag is zero
- D) The backup schedule is correct

**Answer: B.** A matching hash confirms the restored data is identical to the baseline, which validates that the RPO was achieved with no undetected data loss or tampering.

For each item list 2–3 key controls and one measurable metric to monitor. Keep it bulletized, concise, and ISO27001‑friendly so I can drop it into the ISMS.
reply:
## Third-Party Risk Management Checklist

**1. Vendor selection**
- Tier vendors by data sensitivity and business criticality (critical, high, medium, low).
- Require evidence of security posture before shortlisting (ISO 27001 cert, SOC 2 report, or completed security questionnaire).
- Confirm the vendor can meet your data residency and regulatory requirements.
- **Metric:** Percentage of new vendors risk-tiered before contract signature (target 100%).

**2. Due diligence**
- Review the vendor's most recent SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate and check scope covers the services you use.
- Assess financial stability and business continuity capability.
- Check for prior breaches, regulatory actions or adverse findings.
- **Metric:** Percentage of critical and high vendors with due diligence completed within the last 12 months (target 100%).

**3. Contracts, SLAs and KPIs**
- Include a security addendum covering data protection, encryption, access controls, subprocessor rules and audit rights.
- Define breach notification SLA (for example 72 hours or less, aligned with your regulatory obligations).
- Set measurable KPIs for uptime, patch response time and incident response time.
- **Metric:** Percentage of active contracts with a signed security addendum (target 100% for critical and high tier).

**4. Onboarding**
- Grant vendor access using least-privilege, time-bound credentials through your IAM (Okta, AWS IAM, GCP IAM).
- Register vendor systems and data flows in the asset inventory and data-flow map.
- Confirm the vendor's incident contact and escalation path and add them to your contact register.
- **Metric:** Mean time from contract signature to completed onboarding checklist (target under 10 business days).

**5. Ongoing monitoring**
- Review critical vendors at least annually; high vendors at least every 18 months.
- Monitor vendor status pages, threat feeds and breach disclosures continuously.
- Track SLA performance against contractual KPIs each quarter.
- **Metric:** Percentage of critical and high vendors reviewed on schedule (target 100%).

**6. Audits and assessments**
- Request updated SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports annually and review for scope changes or exceptions.
- Exercise contractual audit rights for critical vendors at least once per certification cycle.
- Send a security questionnaire or assessment for vendors that do not hold certifications.
- **Metric:** Number of overdue vendor assessments (target zero).

**7. Incident-response integration**
- Include critical vendors in your incident-response playbooks with named contacts and SLAs.
- Require vendors to notify you of incidents affecting your data within the contractual SLA.
- Run a joint tabletop exercise with at least one critical vendor per year.
- **Metric:** Percentage of critical vendors with a tested incident-notification path (target 100%).

**8. Offboarding**
- Revoke all vendor access (Okta, cloud IAM, VPN, API keys) on the day of contract end.
- Obtain written confirmation of data deletion or return from the vendor.
- Remove the vendor from the asset inventory, supplier register and incident contact list.
- **Metric:** Percentage of offboarded vendors with confirmed access revocation and data deletion within 30 days of contract end (target 100%).

**ISO 27001 mapping:** This checklist supports Annex A controls 5.19 (supplier policy), 5.20 (supplier agreements), 5.21 (ICT supply chain), 5.22 (monitoring and review), 5.23 (cloud services) and clause 8.1 (operational planning). It also feeds the risk register (clause 6.1.2) and the Statement of Applicability for your ISMS.

user: I'm good, let's keep going. Quick compare of RTO vs RPO — definitions, one‑line impact statements, and concrete examples (use our SaaS auth failover and the customer transactional DB). Keep it concise and use bullets so I can paste into study notes.
reply:
**RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**
- Maximum acceptable downtime before a service must be restored.
- Impact: the longer the outage, the more revenue, trust and contractual exposure you lose.
- SaaS auth example: RTO ≤15 min, because every application depends on login and an outage blocks the entire business.
- Customer DB example: RTO 1 to 4 hours, because transactions stop and contractual penalties begin, but instant failover is cost-prohibitive.

**RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**
- Maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time back to the last recoverable point.
- Impact: the larger the gap, the more transactions or records must be recreated or are lost permanently.
- SaaS auth example: RPO <1 min, because lost session or credential state causes lockouts and security gaps across every downstream app.
- Customer DB example: RPO 5 to 15 min, because customer transactions are hard to reconstruct and loss can breach regulatory duties.

**Key distinction:** RTO asks "how long can we be down?" and RPO asks "how much data can we lose?" You can meet one and miss the other, for example restoring fast from a stale backup hits the RTO but breaches the RPO.

reply:
**Q:** What is RTO?
**A:** Maximum acceptable downtime before a service must be restored.

**Q:** What is RPO?
**A:** Maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time back to the last recoverable point.

**Q:** RTO example for SaaS auth service?
**A:** ≤15 min, because login outage blocks every downstream application.

**Q:** RPO example for customer transactional DB?
**A:** 5 to 15 min, because customer transactions are hard to reconstruct and loss can breach regulations.

**Q:** When do RTO and RPO diverge?
**A:** When a fast restore uses a stale backup: the RTO is met but the RPO is breached because too much data is lost.

**Q:** Name one control that improves RTO and one that improves RPO.
**A:** RTO: automated failover with health checks. RPO: continuous replication or frequent transaction-log shipping.

**A:** Assessing a supplier's security posture, certifications and financial stability before onboarding.

**Q:** What should SLAs cover for third-party risk?
**A:** Uptime, incident notification timelines, penalty clauses and measurable performance targets.

**Q:** What data handling and encryption terms belong in a supplier contract?
**A:** Classification, encryption at rest and in transit, processing location, deletion on termination and breach notification.

**Q:** What is a vendor exit or termination plan?
**A:** A documented process for data return or destruction, access revocation and transition to an alternative within a defined period.

**A:** Periodic review of SOC 2 or ISO reports, security questionnaires, threat intelligence and contract compliance at a defined cadence.

**Q:** Who owns third-party risk?
**A:** The organisation that outsources the processing, not the supplier; outsourcing the work does not outsource the accountability.

## 2. SLA Security Clause

The Supplier shall encrypt all Customer Data at rest using AES-256 or equivalent and in transit using TLS 1.2 or higher. The Supplier shall notify the Customer of any confirmed or reasonably suspected security breach affecting Customer Data within 48 hours of detection, providing a written summary of the nature, scope, affected data, remediation steps and a named contact. The Supplier shall maintain a current SOC 2 Type II report or ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covering the services and provide a copy annually or on request. The Customer or its nominated third party shall have the right to audit the Supplier's security controls once per year on 30 days' notice, or immediately following a notified breach. The Supplier shall cooperate with reasonable information requests and provide evidence of compliance within 10 business days.

## 3. Vendor Exit Checklist

- **Confirm data inventory.** Artifact: signed register of all data held by the vendor (formats, locations, volumes).
- **Export or return data.** Artifact: encrypted data export delivered to the customer, with a file manifest and integrity hashes.
- **Certify deletion.** Artifact: written certificate of destruction confirming all copies (production, backup, logs) are deleted within the agreed period.
- **Revoke access.** Artifact: confirmation that all vendor accounts, API keys, tokens and VPN credentials are disabled, with an access-removal log.
- **Transition services.** Artifact: documented handover of configurations, integrations and runbooks to the replacement provider or internal team.
- **Close contracts and confirm obligations.** Artifact: signed termination letter confirming surviving clauses (confidentiality, data retention, indemnities) and final invoice.

```
FILE: Lesson3_Mutations_GeneExpression.txt

LESSON 3: MUTATIONS AND GENE EXPRESSION (50 minutes)

Unit: Genetics
Standards: HS-LS1-1 (DNA structure determines protein structure), HS-LS3-2 (inheritable genetic variation from mutations and replication errors), HS-LS3-1 (DNA codes traits passed from parents to offspring). SEP: Constructing Explanations, Analyzing Data.

---

LEARNING OBJECTIVES (student-facing)
1. I can identify a mutation type (substitution, insertion, deletion) by comparing a normal and mutated DNA sequence.
2. I can predict how a mutation changes the mRNA and protein using the codon table.
3. I can explain why some mutations change the phenotype and others do not.
4. I can describe how gene expression (turning genes on or off) can change the phenotype without changing the DNA sequence.

---

LESSON PLAN (50 minutes)

HOOK (5 min, 0–5)
Write on the board: "Two identical twins have the same DNA. One twin develops a food allergy at age 10 and the other does not. How is that possible?"
- Students write one idea (1 min), pair-share (2 min), collect 2–3 ideas on the board.
- Say: "Today we'll learn how changes in DNA or in how DNA is read can change the trait."

MINI-LECTURE (8 min, 5–13)
Key points to cover:
- Review: DNA → mRNA → protein → trait (central dogma from Lesson 1).
- Mutation types: substitution (one base swapped), insertion (base added), deletion (base removed).
- Frameshift: insertions and deletions shift the reading frame and change every codon after the change.
- Not all mutations change the protein: silent mutations code for the same amino acid.
- Gene expression: cells can turn genes on or off. Same DNA, different proteins, different traits.
- Example: muscle cells and skin cells have the same DNA but express different genes.

ACTIVITY 1: MUTATION DETECTIVE (12 min, 13–25)
Pairs receive three sequence cards (printed or projected):
- Card A: substitution (silent, same amino acid)
- Card B: substitution (missense, different amino acid)
- Card C: insertion (frameshift, multiple amino acids change)
For each card, students:
1. Write the mRNA from the normal and mutated template.
2. Use the codon table to find the amino acids.
3. Name the mutation type.
4. Predict: does the phenotype likely change? Write one sentence.
Materials: codon table (one per pair), sequence cards, pencil.
No safety concerns.

ACTIVITY 2: GENE EXPRESSION DEMO (10 min, 25–35)
Option A (no lab): Use a sentence analogy.
- Write on the board: THE BIG RED FOX RAN FAR.
- Cover one word with a sticky note (gene turned off): THE BIG ___ FOX RAN FAR.
- Ask: "Did the sentence change? Did any letters change?"
- Repeat by covering a different word. Discuss: same letters (DNA), different message (expression).

Option B (demo, teacher-led): Blacklight and fluorescent beads.
- Show two cups of beads (same color in normal light).
- Shine a blacklight: one cup glows (gene "on"), the other does not (gene "off").
- Ask: "Same beads, different result. What changed?" (The environment, not the beads.)
- Safety notes for Option B: Do not look directly into the blacklight. Keep the blacklight away from eyes. Teacher handles the light only.

SHARE AND DISCUSSION (5 min, 35–40)
- Ask 2–3 pairs to share their Card C result.
- Ask: "Why does a frameshift change more of the protein than a substitution?"
- Connect to the driving question: "Now we know two ways a trait can change: a mutation in the DNA, or a change in which genes are turned on."

FORMATIVE CHECK AND EXIT TICKET (10 min, 40–50)
- Students complete the 6-question quiz (see below).
- Exit ticket (last question on the quiz): one sentence connecting mutations to phenotype.
- Collect at the door. Use scoring bands to plan next class.

---

SLIDE DECK OUTLINE (8 slides)

Slide 1: How Can Twins Be Different?
- Show the twin question. Take 2–3 guesses.
- Speaker notes: Accept all ideas. Write them on the board to revisit in closure.

Slide 2: Learning Objectives
- I can identify mutation types, predict protein changes, explain silent vs. harmful, describe gene expression.
- Speaker notes: Ask students to rate their confidence 1–4 on each objective.

Slide 3: Review: DNA to Protein
- DNA → mRNA → protein → trait.
- Speaker notes: Quick review only. Students should recall this from Lesson 1. Spend no more than 2 minutes here.

Slide 4: Mutation Types
- Substitution: one base swapped. Insertion: base added. Deletion: base removed.
- Frameshift: insertions and deletions shift the reading frame.
- Speaker notes: Show a sentence analogy. THE CAT ATE → THE CAA TEA (insertion shifts everything).

Slide 5: Silent vs. Harmful Mutations
- Silent: new codon, same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid. Nonsense: early stop codon.
- Speaker notes: Ask students to predict which type is most dangerous and why.

Slide 6: Mutation Detective Activity
- Compare three sequence cards. Write mRNA, find amino acids, name the type, predict the effect.
- Speaker notes: Circulate and check that students are reading the codon table correctly.

Slide 7: Gene Expression
- Same DNA, different genes turned on = different traits.
- Sentence or blacklight demo.
- Speaker notes: Emphasize that the DNA does not change. Only which genes are read changes.

Slide 8: Driving Question Link and Quiz
- Two ways a trait can change: mutation in the DNA, or a change in gene expression.
- 6-question check.
- Speaker notes: Collect the quiz at the door. Review results before Lesson 4.

---

FORMATIVE QUIZ: MUTATIONS AND GENE EXPRESSION (12 points, 10 min)

Name: ______________________ Period: ______ Date: ________

Directions: Answer every question. Use the codon table if needed. Total: 12 points.

1. Which mutation type swaps one base for another? (1 pt)
A. Insertion
B. Deletion
C. Substitution
D. Frameshift

2. An insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame. What is this called? (1 pt)
A. Silent mutation
B. Missense mutation

# Lesson 3: Mutations and Gene Expression (45 minutes)

**Unit:** Genetics | **NGSS:** HS-LS3-2 (inheritable genetic variations from mutation), HS-LS1-1 (DNA structure determines protein structure). SEP: Constructing Explanations.

## Learning Objectives (student-facing)
1. I can identify substitution, insertion, and deletion mutations in a DNA sequence and name the type.
2. I can trace how a mutation changes the mRNA, the amino acid sequence, and the protein.
3. I can predict whether a mutation is likely to be harmful, neutral, or beneficial and explain why.

## Timing Breakdown

| Time | Activity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 0–4 min | Hook | Engagement demo |
| 4–16 min | Mini-lecture | Key points and vocabulary |
| 16–31 min | Activity | Mutation card simulation |
| 31–36 min | Debrief | Share and discuss results |
| 36–41 min | Formative check | Exit ticket (3 questions) |
| 41–45 min | Closure | Preview next lesson |

## Hook (3–4 min)
Write this sentence on the board: "THE BIG RED FOX RAN FAR." Ask a student to read it aloud. Then show three altered versions and ask the class what changed and whether the meaning still makes sense.

Version 1 (substitution): "THE BIG RED FOX RAN FAT." One letter swapped. Meaning changes slightly.
Version 2 (insertion): "THE BIG RED FFO XRA NFA R." One letter inserted early. Everything after shifts. Meaning lost.
Version 3 (deletion): "THE BGR EDF OXR ANF AR." One letter removed. Everything after shifts. Meaning lost.

Say: "DNA works the same way. Today we find out what happens to a protein when one base changes."

## Mini-Lecture Outline (10–12 min)

**Key point 1: Types of mutations (3 min)**
- Substitution: one base replaced by another. May change one amino acid or none (silent).
- Insertion: one or more bases added. Shifts the reading frame (frameshift).
- Deletion: one or more bases removed. Also causes a frameshift.

**Key point 2: From mutation to protein (4 min)**
- DNA is transcribed into mRNA. mRNA is read in codons (groups of three bases).
- A substitution changes one codon. The amino acid may or may not change.
- A frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. The protein is usually nonfunctional.

**Key point 3: Effect on phenotype (3 min)**
- Harmful: the protein cannot do its job (e.g., sickle cell hemoglobin).
- Neutral: the amino acid stays the same (silent mutation) or the change does not affect the protein's shape.
- Beneficial: the protein works better or differently in a helpful way (rare but important for evolution).

**Key point 4: Gene expression matters (2 min)**
- Not every gene is active in every cell. A mutation in a gene that is turned off may have no effect.
- Environment can turn genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence (epigenetics preview).

**Vocabulary**
- Substitution: one base swapped for another
- Insertion: one or more bases added
- Deletion: one or more bases removed
- Frameshift: the reading frame shifts after an insertion or deletion
- Silent mutation: a base change that does not change the amino acid
- Missense mutation: a base change that changes one amino acid
- Nonsense mutation: a base change that creates a stop codon

## Hands-On Activity: Mutation Card Simulation (15 min)

**Materials per pair:** One set of 12 printed codon cards (each card shows one codon and its amino acid), one mutation instruction slip (teacher assigns substitution, insertion, or deletion), one codon table, one recording sheet, pencil.

**Student instructions:**

Step 1 (2 min): Lay out the 12 codon cards in order, left to right. This is your normal mRNA strand. Write the amino acid chain on your recording sheet.

Step 2 (3 min): Read your mutation instruction slip. It tells you the type (substitution, insertion, or deletion) and the position (e.g., "Delete the second base of codon 4").

Step 3 (5 min): Apply the mutation. Regroup the bases into new codons of three. Use the codon table to find the new amino acids. Write the mutated chain on your recording sheet.

Step 4 (3 min): Compare the two chains. Circle every amino acid that changed. Count how many changed.

Step 5 (2 min): On the recording sheet, answer: "Is your mutation likely harmful, neutral, or beneficial? Explain in one sentence."

**Expected student output:**
- Two amino acid chains (normal and mutated) written side by side.
- Circled differences.
- A one-sentence prediction with reasoning.
- Substitution pairs usually see 0–1 amino acid changes. Frameshift pairs see most or all amino acids change.

## Debrief (5 min)
Ask one substitution pair and one frameshift pair to share their results. Ask: "Which type of mutation caused more damage to the protein? Why?" Connect to the sentence demo from the hook.

## Formative Check: Exit Ticket (5 min, 3 questions)

**1.** A single base in a DNA sequence changes from C to T. Name the mutation type. (1 pt)
**Answer:** Substitution.

**2.** A base is inserted at position 4 of an mRNA strand. What happens to every codon after position 4? (1 pt)
**Answer:** Every codon shifts by one base (frameshift), so most or all amino acids after that point change.

**3.** A substitution changes one codon but the amino acid stays the same. Is this mutation harmful, neutral, or beneficial? Explain in one sentence. (2 pts)
**Answer:** Neutral (silent mutation). The protein does not change because the same amino acid is coded.

Say: "Today we traced one base change all the way to the protein. Next class we look at real-world mutations: sickle cell, CRISPR edits, and what happens when a gene is turned on or off."

**Struggling students:**
- Provide a pre-built normal chain and ask them to apply only a substitution (not a frameshift).
- Give a color-coded codon table (each amino acid a different color).

**Advanced students:**
- Assign a nonsense mutation that creates an early stop codon. Ask them to predict the effect on protein length.
- Ask: "Could a deletion of exactly three bases avoid a frameshift? Why or why not?"
- Have them compare their mutated protein to a real example (e.g., sickle cell HBB gene).

Slide 4: From DNA to mRNA to Protein (Review)
Script: "Quick review. DNA is transcribed into mRNA. mRNA is read in codons, groups of three bases. Each codon codes for one amino acid. The amino acid chain folds into a protein."
Tip: Point to a projected codon table. Ask one student to read a codon and name its amino acid before moving on.

Slide 5: How a Substitution Changes One Amino Acid
Script: "A substitution changes one codon. The new codon might code for a different amino acid (missense), the same amino acid (silent), or a stop signal (nonsense). Only one codon is affected."

Script: "An insertion or deletion shifts every codon after the change. That means every amino acid after the mutation is probably wrong. The protein is usually nonfunctional."

Slide 7: Harmful, Neutral, or Beneficial?
Script: "A mutation is harmful if the protein cannot do its job. It is neutral if the amino acid or protein shape does not change. It is beneficial if the protein works better, which is rare but drives evolution."

Slide 8: Gene Expression: Not Every Gene Is Always On
Script: "A cell has thousands of genes, but not all are active at once. A mutation in a gene that is turned off may have no effect. Environment can also turn genes on or off without changing the DNA."

After delete U: AUG GCU ACA AGC UUG GAU UCA GCG AUC CGU AUU AA...

Amino acid: Met  Ala  Thr  Ser  Leu  Asp  Ser  Ala  Ile  Arg  Ile  ?

   Full: All new codons regrouped correctly and amino acids match the codon table.
   Partial: One codon or amino acid error.

   Partial: Count is off by one.

   Full: Prediction (harmful, neutral, or beneficial) is reasonable for the mutation type.
   Partial: Prediction is stated but does not match the evidence.
   None: No prediction given.

   Full: One sentence explains why, using the number of amino acid changes or the protein effect.

Error 1: Frameshift pairs regroup only the changed codon, not every codon after.

Error 3: Students forget the codon table and guess the amino acid.
Fix: Point to the projected codon table. Say: "Find your three-letter codon on the table before you write the amino acid."

Error 4: Students call every mutation harmful.
Fix: Ask: "Did the amino acid change? If not, can the protein be different?" Introduce the term silent mutation.

Error 5: Students do not write both chains side by side for comparison.
Fix: Say: "Write your normal chain first, then your mutated chain directly below it, so you can line them up and circle the differences."

Lesson 3: Mutations and Gene Expression (45 minutes)

Name: ______________________ Period: ______ Date: ________

NGSS: HS-LS3-1 (DNA codes for traits passed from parents to offspring), HS-LS3-2 (inheritable genetic variations from mutations and replication errors), HS-LS1-1 (DNA structure determines protein structure).

LEARNING OBJECTIVES (student-facing)
1. I can identify substitution, insertion, and deletion mutations in a DNA sequence.
2. I can predict how each mutation type changes the mRNA and the protein.
3. I can explain how gene expression determines which proteins a cell makes and when.
4. I can describe how a change in gene expression can alter a trait without changing the DNA.

KEY VOCABULARY
- Substitution: one base is swapped for a different base.
- Insertion: one or more bases are added to the sequence.
- Deletion: one or more bases are removed from the sequence.
- Frameshift: an insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame of every codon after it.
- Silent mutation: a base change that does not change the amino acid.
- Missense mutation: a base change that changes one amino acid.
- Nonsense mutation: a base change that creates an early stop codon.
- Gene expression: the process of turning a gene on or off to make its protein.
- Transcription factor: a molecule that helps turn a gene on or off.

MATERIALS
- Printed Mutation Detective worksheet (one per pair)
- Codon chart (one per pair or projected)
- Colored pencils or highlighters (3 colors per pair)
- Whiteboard and markers (one per pair)
- Projector with slides
- Exit ticket slips (half sheet, one per student)

SAFETY NOTE
No chemicals or sharp tools. Standard classroom safety: keep aisles clear and materials on the desk.

AGENDA

0–5 min: Hook
Project a normal sentence: "THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT."
Remove one letter from the start: "HEF ATC ATA TET HER AT."
Ask: "What happened to the meaning?" Students pair-share for 1 minute.
Say: "DNA works the same way. One change can shift everything."

5–28 min: Mutation Detective Activity (pairs, 20–23 min)
Each pair gets the Mutation Detective worksheet with a normal 18-base DNA template strand, its mRNA, and the amino acid chain (6 amino acids).
Round 1 (5 min): Pair receives a substitution card. They rewrite the mRNA and amino acids, then classify the result as silent, missense, or nonsense.
Round 2 (5 min): Pair receives an insertion card (one base added at position 4). They rewrite the mRNA and amino acids from that point forward. They compare the new chain to the original.
Round 3 (5 min): Pair receives a deletion card (one base removed at position 4). Same process.
Round 4 (5–8 min): Gene expression mini-demo. Project two identical DNA strips on the board. Cover one with a sticky note labeled "OFF." Ask: "Both cells have the same gene. Why does only one make the protein?" Pairs write one sentence on their whiteboard. Take 2–3 answers. Explain that transcription factors and signals control which genes are on or off, so two cells with the same DNA can look and act differently.

28–38 min: Whole-Class Discussion (10 min)
Sentence-stem prompts (project or read aloud):
- "A substitution is different from an insertion because ___."
- "A frameshift changes the protein more than a substitution because ___."
- "Two cells can have the same DNA but different traits because ___."
Cold-call 2–3 pairs per stem. Record key ideas on the board.

38–43 min: Exit Ticket (5 min)
1. Name the three mutation types we studied today.
2. Which mutation type is most likely to change every amino acid after the mutation point? Why?
3. Two skin cells have the same DNA. One makes melanin and the other does not. Explain how this is possible in one sentence.

43–45 min: Closure (2 min)
Say: "Today you saw how one base can change a protein and how gene expression controls which proteins a cell makes. Tomorrow we connect this to real traits and diseases."

FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT (3 short-answer, collect with exit ticket or use as next-day opener)
1. A substitution changes the third base of a codon from C to A, but the amino acid stays the same. What type of mutation is this? (Answer: silent mutation.)
2. An insertion of one base at the start of a gene shifts every codon after it. What is this called? (Answer: frameshift mutation.)
3. A liver cell and a nerve cell have the same DNA. Why do they make different proteins? (Answer: Different genes are turned on or off in each cell type because of gene expression.)

SCORING
- Exit ticket: 3 points (1 per question). Move on if 80%+ score 3/3. Review if 60–79%. Reteach mutation types if below 60%.
- Formative: 3 points. Use to check depth and plan next lesson.
```

# Section 2: Statement of Need

Literacy is the foundation on which nearly every measure of community well-being rests — employment, housing stability, health outcomes, and civic participation all depend on an adult's ability to read, interpret, and act on written information. In the neighborhoods served by [Organization] — ZIP codes 02118, 02119, and 02120 in Suffolk County, Massachusetts — that foundation is fractured for a significant share of the population, creating a cycle of disadvantage that extends across generations.

**The scope of the problem.** Across the three ZIP codes, an estimated 18 percent of adults score below basic on standardized measures of functional literacy [Source, Year]. These residents struggle with tasks most people take for granted: reading a prescription label, understanding a lease, completing a job application, or helping a child with homework. The figure is roughly [X] times the statewide average of [Y] percent [Source, Year], underscoring that this is not a diffuse, statewide challenge but a concentrated crisis in a specific set of neighborhoods that share histories of disinvestment and limited access to educational infrastructure.

The consequences ripple outward. Adults who cannot read proficiently earn, on average, [X] percent less than their literate peers and are [X] times more likely to experience chronic unemployment [Source, Year]. In Suffolk County, the correlation is visible in household income data: median earnings in the three target ZIP codes trail the county median by $[X] [Source, Year]. Low literacy also drives health disparities. Residents with below-basic literacy are more likely to miss preventive screenings, mismanage chronic conditions, and use emergency departments for routine care [Source, Year].

**An intergenerational pattern.** Perhaps most troubling is the evidence that the crisis is reproducing itself. In the most recent district assessment, only 42 percent of third graders in schools serving these neighborhoods scored proficient in reading [Source, Year] — meaning that more than half of young children are already falling behind the benchmark that predicts long-term academic success. Research consistently shows that a parent's literacy level is among the strongest predictors of a child's reading readiness [Source, Year]. Without intervention at the adult level, the next generation of learners in these communities enters school at a measurable disadvantage.

**Demand far exceeds supply.** The need is not theoretical. [Organization]'s own intake records show 152 adults currently on the waitlist for literacy services, with an average wait time of five months [Org intake data, 2025]. Many of these individuals were referred by healthcare providers, social service agencies, and schools — institutions that recognize literacy as a barrier to the outcomes they are trying to achieve but lack the capacity to address it themselves. While [number] other providers in Suffolk County offer some form of adult education, most focus on English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) or high school equivalency preparation rather than foundational reading and writing skills, leaving a critical gap for adults whose first language is English but whose literacy remains below functional levels.

## Section 4: Program Design & Activities

**Service model.** LiteracyWorks delivers individualized, evidence-informed one-on-one adult literacy tutoring paired with family supports and flexible delivery options designed to reach working adults and parents who cannot access traditional classroom programs. The model rests on a simple premise supported by decades of adult education research: learners who receive consistent, individualized instruction matched to their starting level and life context make faster and more durable gains than those in large-group-only settings. Studies synthesized by ProLiteracy and the federal LINCS network consistently show that one-to-one and small-group tutoring models produce higher completion rates, stronger literacy gains, and greater learner satisfaction than drop-in or lecture-format programs, particularly for adults reading at the lowest levels. LiteracyWorks builds on that evidence base while adding two elements often missing from volunteer tutoring programs — structured curriculum with progress monitoring and an integrated family literacy component that addresses the intergenerational cycle identified by our community.

**Participant pathway.** Every participant moves through five phases: outreach and referral, intake and assessment, active tutoring, exit assessment, and post-program follow-up. The pathway is designed so that no learner enters services without a baseline measurement and no learner exits without a documented outcome.

In Phase 1, outreach and intake staff identify prospective learners through community canvassing in the target ZIP codes, referral partnerships with Greenville County schools and health clinics, and direct contact with individuals on the existing waitlist. Interested adults complete the intake screening described in Section 3, including eligibility verification, and are assessed using a standardized literacy assessment to establish a baseline reading level. The intake coordinator then develops an individualized learning plan that sets short-term and long-term goals aligned with the learner's own priorities — whether that is reading to a child, passing a GED section, interpreting workplace documents, or navigating digital platforms such as email, job boards, and patient portals.

In Phase 2, the learner is matched with a trained volunteer tutor and begins active instruction. Sessions occur twice per week, 60 minutes each, for a minimum dosage of 96 sessions over approximately 12 months. This dosage reflects research indicating that adults typically need 100 or more contact hours to achieve a measurable level gain on standardized assessments (National Reporting System guidelines; Comings, Sum, and Uvin, 2000). Sessions are delivered in person at LiteracyWorks' learning center, at community sites such as libraries and school buildings, at the learner's home, or via a virtual platform, depending on the learner's work schedule, transportation access, and preference. This flexibility is central to the model; shift workers, parents of young children, and adults without reliable transportation are the residents most likely to fall off waitlists and out of rigid class schedules, and they are the residents who need services most.

The curriculum covers three integrated skill domains. Basic literacy instruction builds decoding, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension using structured, phonics-informed methods appropriate for adult learners. Digital literacy modules teach practical skills such as using email, completing online forms, and navigating job search platforms — skills increasingly required for employment and access to public services. Workplace and family literacy content connects reading practice to the learner's daily context: reading a pay stub, understanding a school notice, following medication instructions, or reading a picture book with a child.

In Phase 3, monthly progress checks using brief formative assessments allow the tutor and program coordinator to adjust the learning plan, increase or decrease session intensity, and address barriers to attendance. Learners who complete the program receive an exit assessment using the same standardized tool administered at intake, producing a comparable pre-post measure.

In Phase 4, follow-up contacts at 3 and 12 months after exit track retention of gains and life outcomes such as employment, further education enrollment, and reading activity with children.

Running alongside the tutoring pathway, LiteracyWorks conducts monthly family literacy workshops for parents enrolled in the program and their K–8 children. Each workshop pairs a child-focused reading activity led by a trained facilitator with a parent coaching session that equips caregivers with strategies to support reading at home. These sessions reinforce the tutoring curriculum, strengthen the parent-child literacy connection flagged by residents in the 2022 community survey, and create peer support among adult learners.

**Tutor recruitment, training, and quality.** Volunteer tutors complete a standardized 12-hour initial onboarding covering adult learning theory, the LiteracyWorks curriculum, cultural responsiveness, and use of progress monitoring tools. After onboarding, tutors receive monthly group coaching sessions and have access to a library of structured lesson plans so that instruction remains consistent and evidence-aligned regardless of individual tutor background. The program coordinator observes sessions quarterly and reviews progress data to ensure fidelity.

**Program management and continuous improvement.** The program coordinator convenes quarterly reviews with staff, tutor leads, and partner organizations to examine enrollment, attendance, assessment, and learner feedback data. Findings from these reviews feed directly into program adjustments — for example, adding evening session slots if attendance data show that daytime hours are a barrier, or revising a curriculum module if formative assessments reveal a consistent skill gap. This feedback loop ensures the program remains responsive to learner needs throughout the grant period.

**Staffing and timeline overview.** Implementation will require a program coordinator (1.0 FTE), an intake and outreach specialist (1.0 FTE), a data and case management assistant (0.5 FTE), and a family literacy facilitator (0.5 FTE), supported by an estimated 60–80 active volunteer tutors at steady state. A detailed staffing table and quarterly milestone timeline are provided in Section 5. Key start-up milestones include completing staff hiring by month 1, launching tutor recruitment and training in months 1–2, beginning learner intake in month 2, and matching the first cohort of tutors and learners by month 3.

## Section 6: Outcomes & Objectives

LiteracyWorks distinguishes between outputs — the volume of services delivered — and outcomes — the measurable changes those services produce in participants' lives. The following objectives are structured accordingly and are designed to be specific, measurable, and verifiable using the data collection methods detailed in Section 7.

**Output objectives.**

By the end of the 12-month grant period, LiteracyWorks will enroll and provide one-on-one tutoring services to 360 adults meeting the eligibility criteria described in Section 3. Of those enrolled, 80% (288 learners) will attend at least 75% of their scheduled sessions, reflecting meaningful engagement with the program rather than intake alone. These two metrics establish that the program is reaching its intended population at sufficient dosage to produce learning gains.

**Primary learning outcome.**

By program exit, 60% of participants will achieve a measurable gain of at least one educational functioning level as measured by the Tests of Adult Basic Education (TABE 11/12) and reported according to National Reporting System (NRS) standards. The one-level gain threshold is the standard benchmark used by federally funded adult education programs and represents a meaningful, life-relevant improvement in reading ability — for example, moving from a level at which a learner can recognize common words and simple sentences to a level at which they can read and interpret short everyday texts such as a bus schedule, a medicine label, or a child's school notice. Baseline for each participant will be established through TABE administration at intake, with the same form series administered at exit to produce a comparable pre-post measure.

**Parent confidence outcome.**

Among participants who are parents or primary caregivers of K–8 students, 70% will report increased confidence and ability to help their child with homework by program exit, as measured by a pre-post learner survey administered at intake and again at the final session. This outcome directly addresses the intergenerational literacy cycle that residents identified as their top concern in the 2022 community survey and that the family literacy workshops are designed to reinforce.

**Employment and education outcome.**

Within 12 months of program exit, 25% of participants who were not employed at intake will have obtained employment or enrolled in a credential, ESL, or GED program. This outcome captures the longer-term economic impact of improved literacy and is measured through follow-up contact at 3 and 12 months post-exit, using participant self-report supplemented by documentation where available.

**Cost-effectiveness.**

LiteracyWorks will report cost per participant served and cost per measurable learning gain (defined as one NRS level increase) in its final report to the funder. These figures will be calculated from actual expenditures and outcome data at year end and will allow comparison with published benchmarks for adult literacy programming. Preliminary estimates will be provided in the budget narrative (Section 8).

Together these objectives create a chain of accountability that runs from enrollment through engagement, learning, family impact, and economic mobility — mirroring the logic model attached to this application and the theory of change described in Section 4.

---

## Section 7: Evaluation Plan

**Purpose and approach.** The evaluation serves two functions: accountability to the funder through rigorous outcome measurement, and continuous improvement through timely data that allows LiteracyWorks to adjust programming during the grant period rather than only at its conclusion. The design is a single-group pre-post model with follow-up, using standardized instruments and consistent data collection points across all participants. While a randomized comparison group is not feasible given the ethical and practical constraints of denying services to waitlisted adults, the use of a nationally normed assessment instrument (TABE 11/12) and NRS-aligned reporting standards allows LiteracyWorks' results to be compared against national benchmarks for adult education programs.

**Data collection instruments and schedule.**

The evaluation relies on four complementary data sources, each tied to specific objectives.

The TABE 11/12 is the primary assessment instrument. It is a nationally normed, NRS-approved standardized test of reading, math, and language skills widely used in adult education programs across the country. LiteracyWorks will administer the reading subtest at two required points — intake and program exit — to produce a pre-post comparison for every enrolled learner. The same form series will be used at both points to ensure comparability. For learners who exit the program early, an exit TABE will be administered at the point of departure so that partial gains can be captured. TABE results will be scored and translated into NRS educational functioning levels by the data and case management assistant, who will be trained in TABE administration and scoring protocols during staff onboarding.

Attendance logs will be maintained by tutors for every scheduled and completed session, recorded in the program's client tracking database within 48 hours of each session. These logs will document session date, duration, location or delivery mode (in-person, virtual, or home-based), and a brief content note. Attendance data will be used to calculate the retention metric (75% attendance threshold) and to analyze the relationship between dosage and learning gains.

A learner survey will be administered at intake and exit to all participants who are parents or primary caregivers of K–8 students. The survey will include Likert-scale items measuring self-reported confidence in helping children with homework, frequency of reading activities at home, and perceived barriers to supporting children's learning. The survey will be available in English and Spanish, with oral administration offered for learners whose reading level would make written completion unreliable. The pre-post change in survey scores will be used to assess the parent confidence outcome.

Employment and education verification will be collected through structured follow-up contacts at 3 and 12 months after program exit. The intake and outreach specialist will contact participants by phone, text, or in person to document current employment status, any new enrollment in a credential, ESL, or GED program, and any other self-reported life changes. Where possible, participants will be asked to provide supporting documentation such as a pay stub, offer letter, or enrollment confirmation. Self-report will be accepted when documentation is not available, consistent with standard practice in community-based adult education evaluation. Follow-up contact rates will be tracked and reported alongside outcome data so that the funder can assess the reliability of post-exit findings.

**Data collection schedule summary.**

| Instrument | Intake | Monthly | Exit | 3-Month Follow-Up | 12-Month Follow-Up |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TABE 11/12 (reading) | Yes | — | Yes | — | — |
| Attendance logs | — | Ongoing | — | — | — |
| Learner survey (parents) | Yes | — | Yes | — | — |
| Employment/education verification | Yes (baseline status) | — | — | Yes | Yes |
| Formative progress checks | — | Yes | — | — | — |

**Analysis and reporting.** The data and case management assistant will maintain all participant records in a secure, password-protected database. The program coordinator will review aggregate data quarterly as part of the quality improvement cycle described in Section 4, examining enrollment, attendance trends, early TABE results, and learner feedback to identify needed program adjustments. A mid-year progress report will be submitted to the funder at month 6 including enrollment, retention, and preliminary formative data. A final report at month 12 will present complete pre-post TABE results, NRS level gain rates, parent survey findings, attendance and retention statistics, cost-effectiveness calculations, and available 3-month follow-up data. The 12-month follow-up data, which will not be available until after the grant period closes, will be submitted as a supplemental report.

**Data quality and privacy.** All participant data will be collected and stored in compliance with applicable privacy regulations. Informed consent for data collection and follow-up contact will be obtained at intake. Data will be reported to the funder in aggregate; no individually identifiable information will be shared outside the program team without participant consent. TABE administration will follow the publisher's standardized protocols to ensure scoring validity, and the program coordinator will conduct periodic audits of data entry for accuracy.

**Limitations.** LiteracyWorks acknowledges two limitations of this evaluation design. First, the absence of a control or comparison group means that observed gains cannot be attributed solely to the program; maturation, outside learning, and other factors may contribute. The use of a nationally normed instrument and comparison to NRS benchmarks partially mitigates this limitation. Second, post-exit follow-up at 3 and 12 months is dependent on successful recontact, and attrition from follow-up is common in this population. LiteracyWorks will collect multiple forms of contact information at intake and will track follow-up response rates to allow the funder to assess the completeness of post-exit data.
