## Evaluation Plan (~400 words)

**Design.** The program uses a single-group pre/post design as its primary evaluation framework. We will use pre/post TABE scores and employer-verified employment checks at 30/60/90 days to assess impact. Every participant is assessed at intake, mid-cycle, and exit using the same instrument and scoring protocol, producing three measurement points per learner from which individual and cohort-level gains are calculated. Where feasible, we will pursue a quasi-experimental comparison by requesting de-identified aggregate outcome data from [City/County adult education consortium or partner provider] for learners of similar demographics and baseline reading levels served during the same period. This comparison would allow us to contextualize our gain and employment rates against a non-equivalent control group. We acknowledge the limitations of this approach—selection bias and differing dosage—and will report any comparison findings with appropriate caveats. If a comparison dataset cannot be secured, we will benchmark results against National Reporting System state averages and published outcome data from comparable workforce-literacy programs ([Citation]).

**Data sources and tools.** Each outcome objective maps to a specific instrument. Literacy gain (Objective 1) is measured by the TABE or CASAS reading assessment, administered at Weeks 1, 12, and 24. Workforce document proficiency (Objective 2) is measured by the employer-co-developed workshop rubric, scored at each of six workshops. Employment placement (Objective 3) is measured by participant self-report at 30-, 60-, and 90-day follow-up, verified by pay stub or written employer confirmation. Learner persistence (Objective 4) is measured by session-level attendance logs recorded in [database]. Output indicators—enrollment counts, contact hours, workshops delivered, tutors trained—are captured through intake forms, sign-in sheets, and training rosters.

**Analysis approach.** Literacy gain rates will be calculated as the percentage of completers achieving at least one educational functioning level increase on TABE/CASAS, using matched pre/post scores. Employment placement rates will be calculated as the percentage of participants unemployed at intake who report verified employment within 90 days of exit. We will use an intent-to-treat frame for transparency, reporting outcomes for all enrollees and separately for the completer subgroup (those meeting the 80% attendance threshold defined in Objective 4). For attrition and missing data, participants who exit before Week 24 without a post-test will be counted as non-gainers in the intent-to-treat calculation; the Site Coordinator will attempt to administer an abbreviated exit assessment for any learner who withdraws after Week 12. Follow-up non-response will be addressed through up to three contact attempts by phone, text, and email before a case is coded as "unable to verify."

**Sample size considerations.** With a Year 1 enrollment target of [number] adults across two cohorts, we anticipate [number] completers based on our 65% persistence target. This completer sample is sufficient to detect meaningful descriptive patterns in gain rates and employment placement and to report outcomes with confidence to the funder, though it is not large enough to support complex inferential statistics. We will note this limitation in all reports and use effect-size estimates rather than statistical significance as the primary indicator of program impact. If the program scales in subsequent years, we will revisit the feasibility of a more rigorous evaluation design with a larger sample.

**Data quality, privacy, and storage.** The Site Coordinator enters participant data into [database/system] within 48 hours of each assessment or follow-up contact. The Data and Evaluation Assistant conducts monthly audits, checking a random 20% of records against source documents (paper assessments, sign-in sheets, verification letters) and flagging discrepancies for correction. All participant data are stored in a password-protected, encrypted system accessible only to authorized program staff. Participants provide written informed consent at intake, covering data collection, use for evaluation and funder reporting, and the option to withdraw consent at any time without affecting services. No personally identifiable information is included in external reports; all data are reported in aggregate or with de-identified case examples.

**Roles and reporting cadence.** The Data and Evaluation Assistant prepares quarterly data summaries. The Program Director reviews them with the full team and submits required reports to the funder on [funder's schedule, e.g., quarterly and annually]. If the budget permits, [Organization] will contract with [external evaluator or university partner] to conduct an independent year-end review of data quality and outcome findings, adding a layer of credibility for the funder and for future proposals. That determination will be finalized during Month 1 budget reconciliation.

**Continuous improvement loop.** Evaluation is not an end-of-year exercise. The monthly all-staff data review described in Section 5 serves as the primary learning loop: if attendance trends, mid-cycle assessment results, or follow-up employment rates fall below quarterly benchmarks, the team identifies root causes and implements adjustments—schedule changes, additional tutor support, revised workshop content—within 30 days. Mid-cycle reassessment at Week 12 functions as a built-in course correction for individual learners and for the program as a whole. Findings from each cohort cycle directly inform tutor training content, employer workshop design, and outreach strategy for the next cohort, creating a structured rhythm of reflection and adaptation across the full grant period.

---

**Program Design & Activities** (~800 words)

The program is grounded in a simple theory of change: when early-elementary students who are reading below grade level receive consistent, individualized literacy instruction during the school year and summer, supported by family engagement that extends reading practice into the home, they will reach grade-level proficiency at higher rates and sustain those gains over time. A one-page logic model is included as Attachment [X] and summarizes the relationship among inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes described below.

**How the program works**

The program operates on a continuous, year-round cycle with three interconnected components — weekly one-to-one tutoring, family literacy nights, and a six-week summer boost — each designed to address a specific barrier identified in the Statement of Need.

*Weekly one-to-one tutoring* is the program's core instructional activity. Each of the 120 enrolled students is matched with a trained tutor for one 45-minute session per week during the 36-week school year, held in dedicated space at Westside Elementary immediately after dismissal. Sessions follow a structured, evidence-based curriculum aligned with the Science of Reading framework, emphasizing phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension (Scarborough, 2001; National Reading Panel, 2000). Tutors use each student's MAP Growth diagnostic data to set individualized learning targets and adjust instruction on a six-week cycle. The Program Coordinator builds tutor-student matches and schedules, the Lead Literacy Specialist trains and supervises all tutors, and a team of 10 part-time tutors — recruited from local university education programs and required to hold or be pursuing at least a bachelor's degree in education or a related field — delivers the sessions. This model mirrors the dosage and structure used by proven programs such as Reading Partners, which has demonstrated statistically significant gains in fluency and comprehension in randomized controlled trials (MDRC, 2016).

*Family literacy nights* address the home-environment barriers documented in our needs assessment, particularly the finding that only 29% of Westside households report having more than five age-appropriate books at home. These events are held once per month during the school year (nine sessions total) in the Westside Elementary cafeteria, each running 90 minutes on a weekday evening. Every session includes three elements: a 20-minute parent/caregiver workshop on a practical reading strategy (for example, dialogic reading or vocabulary-building during daily routines), 40 minutes of guided parent-child reading practice, and distribution of two free, culturally relevant books for the family to take home. Light dinner and on-site childcare for siblings are provided to remove attendance barriers. The Family Engagement Specialist plans and facilitates these events with support from the Program Coordinator and two volunteers. Research on family literacy programming shows that when caregivers learn specific techniques for shared reading, children's oral language and print awareness improve significantly beyond what tutoring alone achieves (Sénéchal & Young, 2008).

*The six-week summer boost* directly targets the 2.8-month average summer reading loss documented among Westside students. Running Monday through Thursday for six weeks in June and July at Westside Elementary, the program serves all 120 enrolled students in two rotating cohorts of 60. Each day includes 90 minutes of small-group literacy instruction (groups of six, led by tutors) and 60 minutes of enrichment activities — read-alouds, creative writing, library visits — designed to build motivation and reading identity. The Lead Literacy Specialist oversees curriculum and instruction, the Program Coordinator manages logistics and attendance tracking, and the same tutor team delivers instruction, providing continuity of relationships from the school-year component. Meta-analytic evidence indicates that structured summer literacy programs of at least five weeks can eliminate summer loss and produce net gains for low-income elementary students (Kim & Quinn, 2013).

**Participant pathway**

Each student's journey follows four stages. At intake (September), the Program Coordinator reviews MAP Growth scores, confirms eligibility, and conducts a family orientation. During active programming (October through May), the student attends weekly tutoring while the family is invited to monthly literacy nights. At the summer bridge (June through July), the student participates in the six-week boost. At year-end review (August), the team administers a post-assessment, reviews progress, and determines whether the student continues into the next program year or transitions out at grade level. Students who reach proficiency mid-year are celebrated and may shift to a maintenance schedule of biweekly sessions, freeing slots for waitlisted peers.

**Quarterly implementation timeline**

In Quarter 1 (July–September of Year 1), we will finalize the data-sharing agreement with Springfield School District, hire and onboard the Lead Literacy Specialist and tutor team, procure curriculum materials, and conduct student intake and family orientation. In Quarter 2 (October–December), weekly tutoring and monthly family literacy nights will launch at full enrollment of 120 students, with the first six-week progress check completed in November. In Quarter 3 (January–March), programming continues, mid-year MAP Growth assessments are administered and reviewed, and tutor learning plans are adjusted based on results. In Quarter 4 (April–June), school-year tutoring and literacy nights conclude, end-of-year assessments are administered, and the summer boost begins in June. This quarterly cycle repeats in Years 2 and 3, with start-up activities replaced by returning-student re-enrollment and continuous improvement based on evaluation findings from the prior year.

**Outcomes & Evaluation** (~800 words)

This section presents three measurable objectives that correspond directly to the program's three core activities, followed by an evaluation plan describing how we will collect, analyze, and use data to track progress and improve programming.

**Objectives**

All three objectives use the same measurement structure: a specific target population, a quantified outcome, a defined timeframe, a baseline, and a named assessment instrument. Objectives are set for Year 1; targets for Years 2 and 3 will be adjusted upward based on findings, with proposed benchmarks of 55% and 65% for Objective 1, respectively.

*Objective 1 — Reading proficiency (tutoring).* By the end of Year 1, 45% of enrolled K–3 students (n=54 of 120) will reach at-or-above grade-level reading on the MAP Growth Reading assessment, up from a baseline of 0% of enrolled students at program entry (measured at intake and year-end by district MAP tests).

*Objective 2 — Summer learning retention (summer boost).* By August of Year 1, 70% of students who complete the six-week summer boost (n=84, assuming 100 of 120 complete) will maintain or improve their spring MAP Growth Reading score, compared with a district-documented average summer loss of 2.8 months among Westside peers not enrolled in summer programming (measured by spring and late-summer MAP Growth administrations).

*Objective 3 — Family engagement and home reading practice (family literacy nights).* By the end of Year 1, 60% of participating families (n=72 of 120) will report reading with their child at home at least four times per week, up from a baseline established at program entry through a family reading habits survey (measured at intake and year-end by the same survey instrument).

Together, these three objectives capture the program's intended impact across its core theory of change: direct skill-building through tutoring, loss prevention through summer programming, and home-environment change through family engagement. Outputs — number of tutoring sessions delivered, family literacy nights held, summer boost days completed, and books distributed — will be tracked alongside outcomes but are reported separately in quarterly progress reports.

**Evaluation Plan**

*Design.* The evaluation uses a pre-post design with repeated measures at three points during each program year: intake (September), mid-year (January), and year-end (May/August). Where feasible, we will also employ a quasi-experimental comparison to strengthen causal claims, described below.

*Baseline sources.* Baseline reading proficiency for each student will be drawn from the MAP Growth Reading assessment administered by Springfield School District at the start of the school year, obtained under the existing data-sharing agreement. Baseline family reading habits will be established through a brief intake survey (12 items, available in English and Spanish) administered by the Family Engagement Specialist during family orientation in September. These two sources — one standardized and externally administered, one program-collected — provide both a validated academic measure and a self-reported behavioral measure at entry.

*Data collection tools and frequency.* Reading proficiency will be measured three times per year using MAP Growth, which is already administered district-wide in fall, winter, and spring windows; a fourth administration in late summer will capture summer boost effects and will be coordinated with the school district. Family reading habits will be measured twice per year — at intake and year-end — via the family survey, with a short mid-year pulse check (four items) distributed at the January family literacy night. Tutoring session attendance, dosage, and fidelity will be tracked weekly by tutors in a shared program database. Family literacy night attendance will be recorded at each event by the Family Engagement Specialist.

*Responsibility.* The Program Coordinator holds primary responsibility for data collection, entry, and reporting. The Lead Literacy Specialist reviews MAP Growth results and translates them into instructional adjustments. The Family Engagement Specialist administers and collects family surveys. An external evaluator, contracted on a part-time basis (budgeted in Section 8), will conduct the annual analysis, produce a year-end evaluation report, and present findings to staff and the board.

*Comparison-group approach.* Because all eligible students at Westside Elementary are invited to participate, a randomized control group is not ethical or practical. Instead, the external evaluator will construct a matched comparison group using de-identified MAP Growth data from students in demographically similar elementary schools within Springfield School District who are not receiving comparable programming. Matching criteria will include grade level, baseline MAP score, free/reduced-price lunch status, and English Learner classification. This quasi-experimental approach allows us to estimate program effects above and beyond typical growth, while acknowledging its limitations relative to a randomized design.

*Using findings for improvement.* Data will feed a continuous improvement cycle. After each MAP Growth administration, the Lead Literacy Specialist will convene a tutor review meeting to examine student-level progress, identify students who are not on track, and adjust learning plans. Mid-year family survey results will inform changes to literacy night content and scheduling. The external evaluator's annual report will include actionable recommendations, which the Program Coordinator will incorporate into a written improvement plan shared with the funder in each annual progress report.

*Dashboard metrics.* Staff and leadership will monitor program health through a quarterly dashboard tracking seven indicators: number of students actively enrolled, average tutoring attendance rate, percentage of students on track to meet Objective 1 at year-end, number of family literacy nights held, average family literacy night attendance, percentage of families meeting the four-times-per-week home reading target, and summer boost completion rate. The dashboard will be maintained by the Program Coordinator and reviewed monthly by the Program Director.

# Outcomes & Objectives

## Outputs vs. Outcomes

Before presenting objectives, it is important to distinguish outputs from outcomes, as reviewers weight them differently. Outputs measure what the program delivers — the number of learners enrolled, instructional hours provided, workshops held. Outcomes measure what changes for learners as a result — skill gains, employment, continued education. The objectives below are outcome-focused. Output targets (e.g., [X] learners enrolled per year, [X] instructional hours delivered per cohort, [X] digital literacy labs completed) are tracked internally and reported in progress narratives but are not substitutes for evidence of learner change.

---

## SMART Objectives

### Objective 1: Literacy Skill Gain

By the end of each [X]-week cohort cycle, at least [X]% of participants who complete the program will improve their reading level by a minimum of [X] grade levels, as measured by pre- and post-administration of the [TABE/CASAS/OTHER], compared with a baseline average intake reading level of [X] grade equivalent ([YEAR program data or pilot results]).

**Why this matters:** The Statement of Need documented that [X]% of adults in [TARGET NEIGHBORHOOD(S)] lack functional literacy skills. A [X]-grade-level gain moves learners across the threshold from survival-level reading into functional literacy, enabling them to navigate employment applications, health information, and educational materials independently.

### Objective 2: Digital Competency

By the end of each cohort cycle, at least [X]% of participants will demonstrate basic digital competency — defined as the ability to use email, conduct a web search, and complete an online form — as measured by the [Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment / OTHER TOOL] post-test, up from a baseline of [X]% at intake ([YEAR program data]).

**Why this matters:** Workforce data cited in the Statement of Need show that [X]% of entry-level positions in [CITY/COUNTY] require digital skills that our learners currently lack ([SOURCE, YEAR]). This objective directly targets the digital barrier that locks residents out of available employment.

### Objective 3: Employment, Education, or Training Placement

Within [X] months of program completion, at least [X]% of program completers will have obtained employment, enrolled in a GED or vocational training program, or enrolled in a next-level adult education course, up from a baseline placement rate of [X]% among similar learners not receiving transition support ([YEAR internal data or comparable program data, SOURCE]).

**Why this matters:** Instruction without a structured bridge to next steps produces skill gains that often stall. This objective measures whether the Transition Navigator pathway described in Activity 3 converts literacy improvement into tangible economic or educational progress.

### Objective 4: Learner Confidence and Self-Efficacy

By program exit, at least [X]% of completers will report increased confidence in managing daily literacy and digital tasks (e.g., reading mail, helping children with schoolwork, using public benefits portals), as measured by a pre/post self-efficacy survey using a validated [X]-point Likert scale, compared with baseline scores collected at intake.

**Why this matters:** Community voice data from our [YEAR] needs survey showed that [X]% of respondents identified low confidence — not just low skill — as a barrier to pursuing employment and education. Sustainable change requires that learners internalize their own capability, and capturing this dimension ensures the program addresses the whole person rather than a test score alone.

---

|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Literacy Skill Gain | [TABE / CASAS / OTHER] — standardized, nationally normed | Lead Literacy Instructor | Pre: intake week. Post: final week of cohort cycle. Optional midpoint at week [X] for formative use. |
| 2. Digital Competency | [Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment / OTHER] | Digital Literacy Facilitator | Pre: first lab session. Post: final lab session. |

All data are entered into [DATA SYSTEM — e.g., Salesforce, ETO, Apricot, internal database] within [X] business days of collection. **Change Management Policy (8.32)** — Defines change types (standard, normal, emergency), risk-assessment and approval process, security-impact assessment for relevant changes, back-out planning, and post-implementation review.

**Vulnerability Management Policy (8.8)** — Specifies scan cadence, severity-based remediation SLAs, exception and risk-acceptance process, and reporting requirements.

### Tier 3 — Supporting Policies

**Human Resource Security Policy (6.1–6.8)** — Covers pre-employment screening, security responsibilities in employment terms, awareness and training requirements, and disciplinary and termination processes.

**Secure Development Policy (8.25–8.31)** — Defines SDLC requirements, secure-coding standards, code-review and testing gates (SAST/DAST), environment separation, and test-data management.

**Logging and Monitoring Policy (8.15–8.16)** — Specifies which events must be logged, log-protection and integrity controls, retention periods, monitoring responsibilities, and alert-response expectations.

**Remote and Mobile Working Policy (6.7, 8.1)** — Covers approved devices and connectivity (VPN, ZTNA), home-working security requirements, public-network restrictions, and lost/stolen device procedures.

**Privacy and Personal Data Policy** — Aligns with GDPR or applicable data-protection law, defines lawful bases, data-subject rights procedures, breach notification, and DPIA triggers. (Not an Annex A requirement but auditors expect it in fintech.)

**Information Transfer Policy (5.14)** — Covers approved methods for transferring sensitive information internally and externally, encryption in transit, and use of secure file-sharing platforms.

**Audit and Compliance Policy (Clause 9.2)** — Defines the internal-audit programme, auditor independence, audit-cycle cadence, findings classification, corrective-action tracking, and management-review inputs.

## 2. SIEM Detection Use-Cases

### UC-01: Credential Compromise — Impossible Travel

**Source:** Azure Entra ID sign-in logs

**Trigger logic:** Two successful authentications for the same UPN from geolocations that are physically impossible to traverse within the time elapsed between events. Threshold: locations more than 500 km apart within 60 minutes. Exclude known VPN egress IPs and expected travel patterns stored in a whitelist.

**Severity:** High

**Required fields:** Timestamp, UPN, source IP, geolocation (derived), authentication result, client application, MFA status.

**Response playbook:** Validate whether the user has an active VPN session or corporate travel scheduled. If neither, disable the account and revoke active sessions within 30 minutes. Notify the user via out-of-band channel (phone). Review sign-in logs for the previous 72 hours for the same UPN. Check for mailbox-rule changes, MFA-method registration, or OAuth-app consent grants that may indicate session hijack. Escalate to incident management if compromise is confirmed.

---

### UC-02: Privilege Escalation — Unexpected Role Assignment

**Source:** Azure Entra ID audit logs and AWS CloudTrail

**Trigger logic (Azure):** A directory-role assignment event (`Add member to role`) for any privileged role (Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Security Administrator, Exchange Administrator) where the assigning principal is not a member of the approved PAM group, or where the assignment occurs outside a valid Privileged Identity Management (PIM) activation window.

**Trigger logic (AWS):** `AttachUserPolicy`, `AttachRolePolicy`, `PutUserPolicy`, or `AddUserToGroup` events granting `AdministratorAccess`, `IAMFullAccess`, or any policy containing `"Effect":"Allow","Action":"*"`, performed by a principal not in the approved break-glass or platform-team role.

**Severity:** Critical

**Required fields:** Timestamp, acting principal (UPN or ARN), target principal, role or policy name, source IP, event name, correlation/request ID.

**Response playbook:** Immediately verify with the acting principal whether the change was authorised and has an approved change request. If unauthorised, revert the role or policy assignment, disable the acting principal's account, and preserve CloudTrail or audit-log evidence. Review all actions taken by the target principal since the assignment. Check for lateral movement, resource creation, or data access. Escalate to incident management and notify the CISO.

---

### UC-03: Suspicious Infrastructure Change — Unscheduled Security-Group or Firewall Modification

**Source:** AWS CloudTrail and MSP infrastructure logs (firewall)

**Trigger logic:** `AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress`, `CreateSecurityGroup`, `ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute`, or firewall-rule changes (permit rules added) that expose ports or protocols not in the approved baseline, or any such change that does not have a matching approved RFC in the ITSM tool within a one-hour correlation window. Alert specifically on ingress rules opening SSH (22), RDP (3389), or database ports (1433, 3306, 5432) to 0.0.0.0/0 or broad CIDR ranges.

**Severity:** Critical

**Required fields:** Timestamp, principal ARN or MSP operator ID, event name, security-group or firewall-rule ID, protocol, port range, source CIDR, associated resource (instance/subnet), source IP of the actor.

**Response playbook:** Immediately check the ITSM tool for a correlated RFC. If no matching change exists, revert the rule within 15 minutes and block the acting principal pending investigation. If an RFC exists but scope differs, flag for CAB review. Scan the affected resource for indicators of compromise. Inspect CloudTrail for other actions by the same principal in the preceding 24 hours. For MSP-initiated changes, escalate via the MSP incident path and request a root-cause statement within 24 hours.

---

### UC-04: Credential Stuffing or Brute Force Against Payment-Facing Services

**Source:** WAF logs and Azure Entra ID sign-in logs

**Trigger logic (WAF):** More than 50 HTTP 401 or 403 responses from a single source IP within a 10-minute window targeting authentication endpoints (e.g., `/auth`, `/login`, `/token`, `/oauth2`). Alternatively, more than 20 distinct usernames attempted from a single source IP within 5 minutes.

**Trigger logic (Azure Entra ID):** More than 30 failed sign-in events (error code 50126 — invalid password) for a single UPN within 10 minutes, or more than 10 failed sign-ins across more than 5 distinct UPNs from a single IP within 5 minutes.

**Severity:** High

**Required fields:** Timestamp, source IP, target URI or UPN, HTTP response code or sign-in error code, user-agent string, geolocation, request count (aggregated).

**Response playbook:** Confirm whether the source IP is a known corporate or partner address. If external, block the IP at the WAF and Azure conditional-access level for a minimum of 24 hours. Check whether any attempts succeeded by correlating with successful-auth events from the same IP or for the targeted accounts. If any succeeded, treat as UC-01 (credential compromise). Review for password-spray patterns across multiple accounts. Notify the security team on-call for after-hours events. Update threat-intelligence block lists.

---

### UC-05: Data-Exfiltration Indicator — Anomalous Outbound Data Volume

**Source:** AWS VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs, and MSP infrastructure logs (firewall/proxy)

**Trigger logic:** An internal resource (EC2 instance, container, database) transmits more than 1 GB of outbound data to a single external IP within a one-hour window, where that destination IP has not appeared in the previous 30 days of baseline traffic. Alternatively, any outbound transfer exceeding 5 GB in a single session regardless of destination, excluding known backup, CDN, and SaaS endpoints maintained in an allow list.

**Severity:** Critical

**Required fields:** Timestamp, source IP and port, destination IP and port, bytes transferred, flow direction, protocol, associated resource ID (instance, ENI), destination geolocation, DNS resolution of destination (if available).

**Response playbook:** Immediately isolate the source resource from the network (security-group change or NSG block) while preserving volatile evidence. Identify the process or service generating the traffic. Check for recent compromise indicators on the resource: unauthorised access, new cron jobs or scheduled tasks, unexpected software installations. Correlate with UC-02 and UC-03 to determine whether privilege escalation or firewall changes preceded the transfer. If cardholder or merchant data may be involved, invoke the data-breach notification procedure and notify legal within one hour. Preserve all logs and disk images for forensic analysis.

---

### UC-06: MSP Operator Anomaly — Out-of-Hours or Out-of-Pattern Administrative Access

**Source:** MSP infrastructure logs (OS authentication, RDP/SSH, privileged-command execution)

**Trigger logic:** An MSP operator account authenticates to an in-scope system outside the agreed maintenance windows (defined in Schedule [X] of the MSP contract) and the session is not associated with an open RFC or declared incident ticket. Alternatively, an MSP operator account executes a command or accesses a system that falls outside their normal 30-day behavioural baseline (e.g., first-time access to a database server, use of data-export utilities, access to payment-processing hosts not in their usual scope).

**Severity:** High

**Required fields:** Timestamp, MSP operator username, source IP, destination host, authentication method, session duration, commands executed (if audit logging is enabled), associated RFC or incident ticket number.

**Response playbook:** Contact the MSP's designated security point of contact and request immediate justification. If no valid ticket or authorisation is confirmed within 30 minutes, terminate the session and disable the operator account. Audit all actions performed during the session. Review whether any data was accessed or exported. Cross-reference with UC-03 and UC-05 for related infrastructure changes or outbound data transfers. Document the incident and raise it in the next quarterly MSP review. If malicious activity is confirmed, invoke the incident-management process and consider contractual remedies.

---

### Quick-Reference Summary

| Use-case | Source | Threat | Severity | Key threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UC-01 Impossible travel | Azure Entra ID | Credential compromise | High | >500 km in <60 min |
| UC-02 Privilege escalation | Azure Entra ID + CloudTrail | Privilege misuse | Critical | Unplanned privileged-role or policy assignment |
| UC-03 Unscheduled infra change | CloudTrail + MSP firewall | Unauthorised access, persistence | Critical | No matching RFC within 1 hr |
| UC-04 Credential stuffing | WAF + Azure Entra ID | Credential compromise | High | >50 failures / 10 min (WAF) or >30 / 10 min (Entra) |
| UC-05 Anomalous outbound data | VPC Flow Logs + MSP firewall | Data exfiltration | Critical | >1 GB to new external IP / hr |
| UC-06 MSP operator anomaly | MSP infra logs | Insider / supply-chain threat | High | Activity outside maintenance window or behavioural baseline |

Each use-case should be reviewed and tuned quarterly against false-positive rates and updated threat intelligence. Document tuning decisions in your detection use-case register — auditors will ask for evidence that you actively maintain these rules, not just that they exist.

### Tier 2 — Continued

**Release and Deployment Management (ITIL) → 8.25, 8.26, 8.28, 8.29**

**Monitoring and Event Management (ITIL) → 8.15, 8.16, 5.7**

Centralize logs from cloud infrastructure, application layer, identity provider, endpoint agents, and network devices into a SIEM or managed detection platform. Define use cases and alert rules covering failed authentication spikes, privilege escalation, data exfiltration indicators, anomalous API usage, and changes to security configurations. Establish a triage workflow that routes security alerts into your incident management process with appropriate SLAs.

Evidence: SIEM deployment records and log-source inventory, alert rule documentation, triage runbooks, monthly detection metrics (alerts generated, investigated, escalated), log retention configuration showing at least 12 months.

**Service Request Management (ITIL) → 5.15, 5.18, 8.2**

Use your existing service request catalogue to create standardized, auditable request types for new user access, elevated or privileged access, firewall rule changes, and exception requests against security policy. Each request type should have a defined approval chain that includes security review for sensitive requests.

Evidence: service catalogue entries, completed request tickets with approval timestamps, exception request register with risk acceptance sign-off.

**Risk Management → Clause 6.1.2, 5.7, 8.8**

Establish a formal risk assessment methodology (likelihood × impact, qualitative or semi-quantitative), build a risk register seeded from your gap analysis and threat intelligence, define risk acceptance criteria approved by leadership, and perform a full risk assessment at least annually and after significant changes. Vulnerability management should feed directly into this process: scan results generate risk entries, and patching SLAs are derived from risk ratings.

Evidence: risk assessment methodology document, risk register with owner, rating, treatment plan, and status for each risk, risk acceptance records signed by appropriate management level, management review minutes discussing the risk register.

You can use internal staff (trained and independent of the area being audited) or an external consultant. Produce an audit programme, individual audit plans, findings, and corrective action records.

**Management Review → 9.3**

## 3. Prioritized 12-Month Project Plan

### Phase 0: Foundations (Months 1–2)

**Objective**: Secure commitment, define scope, and establish the ISMS framework.

Milestone 0.1 — Executive sponsorship and project launch (Week 2). Obtain board or executive committee approval, appoint an ISMS owner (likely your CISO or IT Director), allocate budget for tooling, training, consultancy, and certification body fees, and form a cross-functional ISMS steering group (IT, security, dev, HR, legal, operations). Deliverables: signed project charter, ISMS owner appointment letter, budget approval.

Milestone 0.2 — ISMS scope and context (Week 4). Document the scope (your healthcare SaaS platform, supporting infrastructure, hybrid cloud, on-prem, corporate IT, and third-party SaaS), identify interested parties and their requirements (customers, regulators, healthcare bodies), and document the internal and external context (Clause 4). Deliverables: scope statement, context of the organization document, interested parties register.

Milestone 0.3 — Risk methodology and initial gap assessment (Week 8). Define your risk assessment methodology and acceptance criteria, conduct the full gap analysis using the checklist in this document, and produce the initial risk register seeded from gap findings. Deliverables: risk assessment methodology, completed gap-analysis checklist, initial risk register with ~40–60 risks prioritized by severity.

### Phase 1: Core Policy and High-Priority Controls (Months 3–5)

**Objective**: Close the highest-risk gaps, build the policy framework, and start the vulnerability management overhaul.

Milestone 1.1 — Information security policy suite (Month 3). Write and approve the top-level information security policy plus supporting policies for access control, data classification, acceptable use, cryptography, supplier security, secure development, and incident response. Assign document owners and set review cycles. Deliverables: approved policy documents, document register.

Milestone 1.2 — Data classification and asset inventory (Month 3–4). Implement a classification scheme (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted–PHI), extend the CMDB to cover data assets, cloud resources, and SaaS subscriptions, and produce data-flow diagrams showing where PHI is stored, processed, and transmitted. Deliverables: classification policy, updated CMDB, data-flow diagrams.

Milestone 1.3 — Vulnerability management programme (Month 3–5). Deploy or configure vulnerability scanning across infrastructure, cloud workloads, and applications, define scanning cadence (infrastructure weekly, application DAST weekly, dependency SCA on every build), establish remediation SLAs (critical: 72 hours, high: 7 days, medium: 30 days, low: 90 days), assign ownership for remediation tracking, and integrate scan findings into the risk register. Deliverables: vulnerability management policy and procedure, scanner deployment records, first scan reports, remediation tracking dashboard.

Milestone 1.4 — Privileged access and authentication hardening (Month 4–5). Implement PAM tooling for cloud admin, database, and production access, enforce MFA on all user and admin accounts across all systems, review and document role-based access matrices, and schedule first quarterly access review. Deliverables: PAM deployment records, MFA enforcement reports, RBAC matrices, access review schedule.

Milestone 1.5 — Secure development lifecycle (Month 4–5). Integrate SAST and SCA into CI/CD pipelines with blocking policies, document secure coding standards, train developers, establish a threat modelling process for new features, and schedule first annual penetration test. Deliverables: pipeline configuration evidence, secure coding standard, developer training records, threat model template, pen test contract.

### Phase 2: Extend Controls and Operationalize (Months 5–8)

**Objective**: Build out remaining controls, embed processes, and start generating evidence.

Milestone 2.1 — Supplier security programme (Month 5–6). Build the vendor risk register covering all third-party SaaS vendors, classify vendors by data access tier, collect current SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates, review and update contracts for security clauses and DPAs, and define an annual vendor review cycle. Deliverables: vendor risk register, contract amendment tracker, vendor evidence library.

Milestone 2.2 — Logging, monitoring, and detection (Month 5–7). Deploy or configure centralized logging with at least 12 months retention, implement SIEM or managed detection with use cases covering your top risks, integrate security alert triage into your ITIL incident process, and document monitoring procedures. Deliverables: log-source inventory, SIEM deployment records, alert rule documentation, triage runbook, first monthly detection metrics report.

Milestone 2.3 — Business continuity and DR (Month 6–7). Update BCP/DR plans to include security scenarios (ransomware, cloud provider failure, insider threat), validate RTO and RPO for the SaaS platform, and schedule a DR test. Deliverables: updated BCP/DR plan, DR test plan.

Milestone 2.4 — Security awareness and training (Month 6–7). Deploy a security awareness platform with healthcare-specific content (PHI handling, phishing, social engineering), run a baseline phishing simulation, establish quarterly training cadence, and ensure all staff complete initial training. Deliverables: training platform records, phishing simulation results, completion reports.

Milestone 2.5 — Remaining control implementation (Month 7–8). Close medium and low-priority gaps from the checklist: physical controls review, data masking in non-production, DLP for email and cloud storage, network segmentation review, information transfer procedures, and remote working security. Deliverables: control implementation evidence per item.

### Phase 3: Assurance and Readiness (Months 8–10)

**Objective**: Prove the ISMS works, refine, and prepare for audit.

Milestone 3.1 — Statement of Applicability finalized (Month 8). Complete the SoA using the template below, covering all 93 Annex A controls with justification for inclusion or exclusion and implementation status. Deliverables: approved SoA.

Milestone 3.2 — Full risk assessment review (Month 8). Re-assess the risk register with updated control status, document residual risk and risk treatment plans, and obtain management sign-off on risk acceptance. Deliverables: updated risk register, risk treatment plan, risk acceptance records.

Milestone 3.3 — Internal audit cycle (Month 8–10). Execute internal audits covering all ISMS clauses and all applicable Annex A controls, document findings and assign corrective actions, and track corrective actions to closure. Deliverables: internal audit programme, audit reports, corrective action log.

Milestone 3.4 — Management review (Month 10). Conduct a formal management review with all clause 9.3 inputs (audit results, risk status, incident trends, metrics, corrective actions, changes in context), and document decisions and resource commitments. Deliverables: management review minutes.

Milestone 3.5 — DR test execution (Month 9–10). Execute the DR test, document results and lessons learned, and feed findings into corrective actions. Deliverables: DR test report, corrective actions.

Milestone 3.6 — Penetration test (Month 9). Execute the annual penetration test, remediate critical and high findings before Stage 1, and document remediation evidence. Deliverables: pen test report, remediation records.

### Phase 4: Certification (Months 10–12)

**Objective**: Pass Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits.

Milestone 4.1 — Stage 1 audit (Month 10–11). The certification body reviews ISMS documentation: scope, policies, SoA, risk assessment, internal audit results, and management review minutes. They assess readiness for Stage 2 and may raise observations. Address any Stage 1 findings immediately. Deliverables: Stage 1 audit report, corrective actions for any findings.

Milestone 4.2 — Remediate Stage 1 findings (Month 11). Close any nonconformities or observations raised at Stage 1. Deliverables: evidence of corrective actions.

Milestone 4.3 — Stage 2 audit (Month 11–12). On-site (or hybrid) audit assessing implementation effectiveness. Auditors will interview staff, sample evidence, observe processes, and test controls. For a 350-person healthcare SaaS organization, expect 8–12 auditor-days. Deliverables: Stage 2 audit report, certificate (assuming no major nonconformities).

Milestone 4.4 — Post-certification actions (Month 12 and ongoing). Close any minor nonconformities from Stage 2 within the agreed timeframe, establish the surveillance audit schedule (typically every 6 or 12 months), and transition the ISMS into business-as-usual with continual improvement. Deliverables: corrective action closure, surveillance audit calendar, ISMS continual improvement plan.

| 1–2 | 0: Foundations | Charter, scope, risk methodology, gap analysis, initial risk register |
| 3–5 | 1: Core policies and high-priority controls | Policy suite, classification, vulnerability management, PAM/MFA, SDLC security |

| 8–10 | 3: Assurance and readiness | SoA, risk re-assessment, internal audits, management review, pen test, DR test |
| 10–12 | 4: Certification | Stage 1 audit, remediation, Stage 2 audit, certificate |

Glad it's all in one place now. A few practical suggestions as you kick off:

**Engage your certification body early.** Contact an accredited CB in Month 1 or 2 and book a Stage 1 slot for around Month 10. Availability can be tight, especially for healthcare, and locking the date creates a firm deadline that keeps the project honest.

**Don't underestimate the documentation effort.** The policies, procedures, and risk register are where most teams lose time. Assign a dedicated ISMS coordinator — even part-time — to own document drafting, version control, and evidence collection. This person saves the CISO and control owners enormous time.

**Leverage what you already have.** Your ITIL-aligned incident, change, and CMDB processes are a real advantage. In many organizations those take months to build from scratch. Focus your energy on the genuine gaps — vulnerability management, supplier security, secure development, and monitoring — rather than rebuilding what works.

**Budget items people forget:** penetration testing (plan for two rounds if you want one before Stage 1 and one annual), security awareness platform licensing, PAM tooling, SIEM or MDR service, and the certification body fees themselves (Stage 1 plus Stage 2 for a 350-person scope can run $15,000–$30,000 depending on the CB and region).

Feel free to come back when you need help drafting specific policies, building the risk register, or preparing for the internal audit cycle.

# ISO 27001 Certification Gap Analysis — Fintech Payment Processor (250 Staff, Hybrid Cloud)

---

## How to read this checklist

Each item is assigned a priority tier based on certification risk and regulatory exposure. **Tier 1** items are foundational — an auditor cannot proceed without them. **Tier 2** items are high-value controls that close your biggest operational gaps. **Tier 3** items mature your programme and strengthen governance reporting. Within each tier, items are roughly ordered by dependency (do the earlier ones first).

For each item I note the ISO 27001 clause or Annex A control, the gap based on what you've described, the required action, which ITIL 4 practice supplies evidence, and where COBIT or NIST CSF adds value. PCI-DSS overlap is flagged where relevant so you can reuse evidence across both programmes.

---

## Tier 1 — Mandatory foundations (target: months 1–3)

### 1.1 Establish the ISMS scope and context

**ISO ref:** Clauses 4.1–4.3

**Gap:** No formal ISMS exists. PCI scope is defined for card systems but the broader information security boundary is not documented.

**Actions:** Document the organisation's internal and external context, identify interested parties (regulators, card schemes, customers, cloud providers), and define the ISMS scope boundary. Explicitly note which systems fall inside PCI scope and which are ISO-only. The scope statement must cover your hybrid cloud environment and name the IaaS and SaaS providers.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS requires a documented cardholder data environment (CDE) scope and network segmentation validation. Build the ISMS scope document so it nests around the CDE scope rather than duplicating it.

**COBIT/NIST value:** NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC (Organisational Context) provides a structured way to identify and document the external environment, regulatory landscape, and stakeholder expectations. This feeds directly into Clause 4.

---

### 1.2 Leadership commitment and security roles

**ISO ref:** Clause 5.1–5.3, Annex A 5.2 (Information security roles and responsibilities)

**Gap:** No board-level security reporting cadence; CISO/security-owner accountability is not formalised.

**Actions:** Obtain a signed information security policy from senior management. Define and communicate the CISO or equivalent role with authority over the ISMS. Establish a management review cadence (at least annually, quarterly recommended for a first cycle). Assign control owners for every Annex A control in the Statement of Applicability.

**ITIL evidence:** The ITIL 4 "Strategy management" and "Workforce and talent management" practices document roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths. If you have a RACI for incident and change already, extend it to cover all ISMS roles.

**COBIT/NIST value:** This is where COBIT adds the most value early on. EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting) and EDM05 (Ensured Stakeholder Engagement) give you a template for board-level reporting structure, KPIs, and escalation. Use COBIT's governance objective structure to design a quarterly security dashboard for the board.

---

### 1.3 Risk assessment and risk treatment plan

**ISO ref:** Clauses 6.1.2, 6.1.3, 8.2, 8.3

**Gap:** No formal risk treatment programme.

**Actions:** Select a risk methodology (ISO 27005 or a lightweight likelihood-×-impact matrix is fine for 250 people). Identify information assets, threats, and vulnerabilities. Assess and score risks. Produce a risk treatment plan that maps each unacceptable risk to one or more Annex A controls. Document risk acceptance criteria approved by management. This process directly produces your Statement of Applicability.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS v4.0 Requirement 12.3.1 now mandates a formal targeted risk analysis for controls with flexible implementation. Align your risk methodology so a single risk register serves both ISO and PCI.

**NIST value:** NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA (Risk Assessment) and GV.RM (Risk Management Strategy) provide a mature outcome taxonomy you can use to validate your risk categories. The CSF's "Profile" concept (current state vs. target state) is a useful communication tool for presenting the risk treatment plan to the board.

---

### 1.4 Statement of Applicability (SoA)

**ISO ref:** Clause 6.1.3 d)

**Gap:** Does not exist.

**Actions:** For each of the 93 Annex A controls (2022 version), document whether it is applicable or excluded, the justification, the current implementation status, and the control owner. This is the single most important audit document — the Stage 1 auditor will review it before anything else.

**PCI overlap:** Map each applicable Annex A control to its PCI-DSS v4.0 requirement counterpart. Many map one-to-many. Maintaining this cross-reference in the SoA itself saves significant effort during PCI assessments.

---

### 1.5 Complete the asset inventory

**ISO ref:** Annex A 5.9 (Inventory of information and other associated assets), 5.10 (Acceptable use), 5.12 (Classification)

**Gap:** Asset inventory is incomplete; CMDB is partial.

**Actions:** Enumerate all information assets (data stores, databases, file shares, SaaS tenancies), supporting assets (servers, endpoints, network devices, cloud instances), and personnel assets (roles with privileged access). Classify each by confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Assign an owner.

**ITIL evidence:** The ITIL 4 "Service configuration management" practice is the natural home for this. Your partial CMDB is the starting artefact — extend it with classification labels, data-owner fields, and PCI-scope flags. The auditor wants to see a living register, not a perfect one, so prioritise coverage over precision in the first pass.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 12.5.1 requires an inventory of system components in scope. Requirement 9.4.1 extends to media. A unified asset register with a "PCI in-scope" flag avoids maintaining two separate inventories.

---

## Tier 2 — Close the major operational gaps (target: months 3–6)

### 2.1 Formalise vulnerability and patch management

**ISO ref:** Annex A 8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities), 8.32 (Change management)

**Gap:** Patching is ad-hoc.

**Actions:** Implement a vulnerability management policy with defined scan cadence (at least monthly for infrastructure, continuous for internet-facing), severity-based SLAs for remediation (e.g., critical within 14 days, high within 30), and exception/risk-acceptance workflow. Integrate patching into the existing ITIL change process so every patch is a standard or pre-approved change with a record.

**ITIL evidence:** "Deployment management" and "Change enablement" practices. Each patch cycle becomes a change record with test evidence and rollback plan. This is strong audit evidence because it shows both the control (vulnerability management) and the operational discipline (change management) working together.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 6.3.3 mandates critical and high patches within one month. Aligning your ISO SLA to the same window means one patching cadence satisfies both.

---

### 2.2 Access control and privileged access management

**ISO ref:** Annex A 5.15 (Access control), 5.16 (Identity management), 5.17 (Authentication), 5.18 (Access rights), 8.2 (Privileged access rights), 8.5 (Secure authentication)

**Gap:** Not described in detail, but with 250 staff, hybrid cloud, and PCI systems, this is almost certainly under-documented.

**Actions:** Document an access control policy covering least privilege, segregation of duties, and joiners/movers/leavers process. Inventory all privileged accounts across cloud consoles, databases, and payment systems. Implement periodic access reviews (quarterly for privileged, six-monthly for standard). Enforce MFA on all administrative and remote access.

**ITIL evidence:** "Access management" practice. Each access request, change, and review should produce a ticket or log entry. These tickets are your primary audit evidence.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirements 7 and 8 are detailed and prescriptive on access. If you meet PCI requirements for in-scope systems, extending the same controls to out-of-scope systems generally satisfies Annex A with minimal additional effort.

---

### 2.3 Incident management and security event handling

**ISO ref:** Annex A 5.24–5.28 (Incident management, assessment, response, learning, evidence collection)

**Gap:** Basic ITIL incident process exists but likely does not distinguish security incidents or mandate evidence preservation.

**Actions:** Extend the existing incident process with a security incident classification scheme, escalation path to the CISO/security owner, evidence preservation procedure (chain of custody for forensics), mandatory root-cause analysis for security incidents, and a lessons-learned process that feeds back into the risk register.

**ITIL evidence:** "Incident management" and "Problem management" practices. The key audit expectation is that you can show a sample of security incidents handled end-to-end with timestamps, decisions, and post-incident reviews.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 12.10 requires an incident response plan with specific card-brand notification obligations. Build one incident process with a PCI-specific playbook appendix rather than two separate processes.

---

### 2.4 Supplier and cloud provider security

**ISO ref:** Annex A 5.19–5.23 (Supplier relationships, cloud services)

**Gap:** Occasional vendor security questionnaires, no formal programme.

**Actions:** Create a supplier register with risk tiering (critical, high, medium, low) based on data access and service dependency. For critical suppliers (your IaaS provider, SaaS platforms, payment processors), document security requirements in contracts, obtain SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates annually, and perform periodic reviews. Annex A 5.23 specifically addresses cloud services — document shared responsibility models for each IaaS/SaaS provider.

**ITIL evidence:** "Supplier management" practice. Maintain a supplier review calendar with evidence of annual reviews.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 12.8 requires maintaining a list of service providers, written agreements, and monitoring. A unified supplier register with a "PCI service provider" flag and annual review evidence satisfies both.

---

### 2.5 Logging, monitoring, and detection

**ISO ref:** Annex A 8.15 (Logging), 8.16 (Monitoring activities)

**Gap:** Not described, but typically weak before a formal ISMS.

**Actions:** Define what events must be logged (authentication, privilege use, access to sensitive data, system changes, security events). Centralise logs (SIEM or log aggregation), set retention periods (at least 12 months is a safe default; PCI requires 12 months with 3 months immediately available), protect logs from tampering, and implement alerting rules for critical security events.

**ITIL evidence:** "Monitoring and event management" practice. Alert-to-incident workflows demonstrate that monitoring feeds the incident process.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 10 is very specific about log contents, integrity, and review cadence. Meet PCI Requirement 10 first, then extend to non-PCI systems for ISO coverage.

---

### 2.6 Business continuity and backup

**ISO ref:** Annex A 5.29 (Information security during disruption), 5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity), 8.13 (Information backup), 8.14 (Redundancy of information processing facilities)

**Gap:** Not described; likely informal.

**Actions:** Conduct a business impact analysis. Define RTOs and RPOs for critical systems (especially payment processing). Document backup procedures, test restores at least annually (quarterly for critical systems), and develop and test an ICT continuity plan.

**ITIL evidence:** "Service continuity management" and "Availability management" practices. Test records and restore logs are the key evidence.

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 12.10.2 covers incident response testing. Align continuity tests with PCI's annual testing requirement.

---

## Tier 3 — Governance maturity and continuous improvement (target: months 6–9)

### 3.1 Security awareness and training programme

**ISO ref:** Clause 7.2–7.3, Annex A 6.3

**Actions:** Implement role-based security awareness training (general staff annually, developers on secure coding, privileged users on elevated responsibilities). Track completion rates and test effectiveness (phishing simulations are a practical measure).

**PCI overlap:** PCI-DSS Requirement 12.6 requires annual security awareness training with specific content. One programme with a PCI module satisfies both.

---

### 3.2 Documented information and document control

**ISO ref:** Clauses 7.5.1–7.5.3

**Actions:** Establish a document control process covering version control, review cycles, approval, and access restrictions. This applies to all ISMS documentation: policies, procedures, risk registers, SoA, meeting minutes, and audit reports. The Stage 1 auditor will check this early.

**ITIL evidence:** "Knowledge management" practice.

---

### 3.3 Internal audit programme

**ISO ref:** Clause 9.2

**Actions:** Plan and conduct at least one full internal audit cycle before the certification audit. Use an independent auditor (internal staff not responsible for the area being audited, or an external consultant). Document findings, corrective actions, and closure evidence.

**COBIT value:** APO11 (Managed Quality) and MEA02 (Managed System of Internal Control) provide a structured approach to internal assurance if you want to build a repeatable audit function beyond ISO.

---

### 3.4 Management review

**ISO ref:** Clause 9.3

**Actions:** Conduct a formal management review with minutes covering all inputs specified in Clause 9.3.2 (audit results, risk status, nonconformities, metrics, opportunities for improvement). This must happen at least once before certification and should become a recurring event (quarterly is recommended in year one).

**COBIT value:** EDM01 and MEA01 (Managed Performance and Conformance Monitoring) give you a KPI and reporting structure to feed into management review. This is the mechanism for establishing the board-level reporting cadence you currently lack.

**NIST value:** Use NIST CSF Profiles (current vs. target) as a visual executive summary in the management review pack. A simple heat map of the six CSF functions is easier for non-technical board members to absorb than a control-by-control status report.

---

### 3.5 Corrective action and continual improvement

**ISO ref:** Clause 10.1–10.2

**Actions:** Implement a nonconformity and corrective action process. Every internal audit finding, security incident lesson, and management review action should enter a corrective action tracker with root-cause analysis, action owner, deadline, and closure evidence. This demonstrates the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle the auditor expects.

**ITIL evidence:** "Continual improvement" practice and the continual improvement register.

---

## Cross-reference summary

| Framework | Where it helps you most given your current state |
|---|---|
| **ISO 27001** | The certifiable spine — every item above maps to it |
| **ITIL 4** | You already have change and incident processes; extend them to supply audit evidence for roughly 40% of Annex A controls without building new processes from scratch |
| **COBIT** | Fills your board-reporting gap — use EDM01/EDM05/MEA01 to design the quarterly security dashboard and governance structure (Tier 1.2 and Tier 3.4) |
| **NIST CSF 2.0** | Use Profiles and the six-function model as a communication layer for executives and customers; also useful for US-facing customer security questionnaires |
| **PCI-DSS v4.0** | Already required — reuse evidence by maintaining cross-reference flags in the SoA, asset register, and supplier register rather than running parallel programmes |

---

## Suggested timeline at a glance

**Months 1–3:** Tier 1 — scope, leadership, risk assessment, SoA, asset inventory. Engage a certification body for a Stage 1 readiness review at the end of this phase.

**Months 3–6:** Tier 2 — patch management

---

## 1. Workstream Plan (26-Week ISO-Readiness Path)

The plan is divided into six workstreams. Each contains discrete tasks with a recommended owner, effort size (S = under 3 person-days, M = 3–10 person-days, L = 10+ person-days), and a target week window. Dependencies flow top to bottom — later tasks assume earlier ones are substantially complete.

**Column definitions:**

"Control_ID" is the Annex A reference, e.g., 5.1, 8.8. "Control_Title" is the control name from the standard. "Annex_A_Theme" is one of Organisational, People, Physical, or Technological. ## 5. PCI-DSS Quirks to Flag for the Project Manager

These are the issues that most commonly trip up organisations running ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS in parallel. Print this list and hand it to your PM.

**Scope creep is the number-one PCI audit killer.** Every time you add a system to the CMDB, ask whether it stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, or whether it is connected to a system that does. If the answer is yes and it is not already in PCI scope, your CDE boundary document is wrong. Task 3.4 must be treated as a living activity, not a one-time exercise. Flag any scope changes to the QSA immediately.

**PCI v4.0 "customised approach" traps.** PCI-DSS v4.0 allows a customised approach for meeting certain requirements, but each customised control requires a documented targeted risk analysis and the QSA must validate it. If your team plans to use the customised approach for any requirement, budget extra time for the documentation and expect QSA pushback. For a first ISO+PCI programme, the defined approach is almost always faster.

**SAQ vs. ROC confusion.** Make sure the PM knows whether your organisation requires a Self-Assessment Questionnaire or a Report on Compliance. At 250 staff doing payment processing, you likely need an ROC with a QSA assessment. This is a separate engagement from the ISO certification body and has its own timeline. Coordinate the two audit windows so they do not overlap — your control owners cannot support both simultaneously.

**Compensating controls require formal documentation.** If any PCI requirement is met with a compensating control, PCI-DSS requires a completed Compensating Controls Worksheet per control. These are often forgotten until the QSA asks for them. Identify any compensating controls during task 2.4 and document the worksheets at that point.

**Key management is easy to under-document.** PCI Requirement 3.6–3.7 requires detailed documentation of cryptographic key management procedures — key generation, distribution, storage, rotation, retirement, and replacement of compromised keys. ISO Annex A 8.24 (Use of cryptography) is less prescriptive. If you document to PCI's level of detail, you automatically satisfy ISO, but not the reverse. Write the key management procedure to PCI's standard first.

**Network segmentation testing must be performed every six months for the segments that isolate the CDE, not annually.** This is PCI-DSS Requirement 11.4.5. Many teams schedule it annually and get a finding. Put two test windows into the project plan (approximately weeks 9 and 22) so the evidence is fresh for both the QSA and the ISO auditor.

**Evidence timestamps matter more than you expect.** Both auditors will check that evidence is from the current review period. A vulnerability scan report from six months ago is stale. A change record without a timestamp is useless. Ensure every process produces dated artefacts, and brief the ops leads that "we did it but didn't record it" is functionally equivalent to "we didn't do it" in an audit context.

### ISMS-001: Define ISMS Scope Boundary Document

**Summary:** Define and document the ISMS scope boundary including CDE, cloud providers, and office locations

**Description:** Create the ISMS scope boundary document required by ISO 27001 Clauses 4.1–4.3. The document must define the organisational context (internal and external issues affecting information security), identify all interested parties and their requirements (regulators including FCA/PSD2 as applicable, card schemes, customers, cloud providers), and draw the ISMS boundary. The scope must explicitly reference the existing PCI CDE scope document and explain how the ISMS boundary nests around it. All IaaS and SaaS providers must be named. Remote workforce and hybrid working arrangements must be addressed. The document must be version-controlled under the document control process established in task 1.4.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Scope document covers Clauses 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 with no gaps.
- CDE boundary is referenced and consistent with current PCI scope documentation.
- Every IaaS and SaaS provider is named with service description.
- Document has been reviewed by IT Ops Lead and approved by CISO.
- Document is stored in the controlled document repository with version number and approval date.
- Certification body has confirmed the scope is auditable (can be validated at Stage 1).

**Assignee:** CISO + IT Ops Lead

**Due:** Week 3

**Description:** Identify at least two certification bodies accredited by UKAS, ANAB, or equivalent national accreditation body for ISO/IEC 27001:2022. Request quotes covering Stage 1 (documentation review), Stage 2 (certification audit), and the three-year surveillance cycle. Evaluate based on fintech/payment-processing sector experience, auditor availability for weeks 13–14 and 24–26, and cost. Execute the contract and obtain written confirmation of the Stage 1 date. - Selected CB is accredited for ISO/IEC 27001:2022.
- Contract signed and Stage 1 date confirmed in writing for no later than week 14.

### ISMS-005: Centralise Logging and Onboard All Sources to SIEM

**Summary:** Onboard all in-scope log sources to Splunk Cloud, define mandatory event types, configure retention, and validate log integrity

**Description:** The current Splunk deployment ingests logs from firewalls, WAF, payment database, and Linux hosts. This task extends coverage to all remaining sources required for ISO 27001 Annex A 8.15 and PCI-DSS Requirement 10 compliance. Sources to onboard: Windows server and endpoint event logs, cloud control-plane logs (AWS CloudTrail, and equivalent for any other cloud provider), SaaS audit logs (identity provider, collaboration tools, CI/CD platform), container and orchestration platform logs, database audit logs for non-PCI databases, and VPN/remote access logs. For each source, configure log forwarding, validate event parsing, confirm required fields are captured (timestamp, user identity, event type, source, outcome), and verify ingestion in Splunk. Set retention to 12 months with 3 months immediately searchable (hot/warm). Confirm log integrity controls: RBAC restricting log deletion, daily integrity verification checks, and alerting on log source dropout (no events received within expected interval). Document the full log source inventory as a living register linked to the CMDB, with a quarterly review process to catch new or decommissioned systems. If a SIEM contractor has been engaged, they should lead the onboarding and build the correlation rules while SecOps and IT Ops provide access and environment knowledge.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Every production system in the CMDB has a corresponding log source entry in Splunk with validated event ingestion.
- Mandatory event types are documented and confirmed for each source: authentication events, privilege use, access to sensitive data, configuration changes, and security-relevant system events.
- Retention is verified at 12 months total with 3 months hot/warm, meeting PCI 10.5.1.
- Log integrity controls are operational: RBAC confirmed, daily integrity checks running, log source dropout alerts tested and routed to SecOps.
- Log source register is created, linked to the CMDB, and assigned a quarterly review cycle.
- PCI-scoped sources satisfy all sub-requirements of PCI-DSS 10.2.1–10.2.2 and 10.3.1–10.3.4 as confirmed by cross-reference in the SoA.

### ISMS-006: Document Access Control Policy and Privileged Account Inventory

**Summary:** Create the access control policy covering least privilege, segregation of duties, JML lifecycle, MFA, and produce a complete privileged account inventory

**Description:** Document an access control policy that meets ISO 27001 Annex A controls 5.15, 5.16, 5.17, 5.18, 8.2, and 8.5, and aligns with PCI-DSS Requirements 7 and 8. The policy must define the principle of least privilege as the default, specify segregation of duties rules (at minimum separating development, deployment, and production administration), and establish the joiners/movers/leavers (JML) process with defined SLAs for provisioning, role-change, and de-provisioning (target: same-day disable on termination, within 3 business days for role changes). Mandate MFA for all administrative access, remote access, and access to CDE systems. Produce a complete inventory of all privileged accounts across cloud consoles (AWS IAM, Azure AD), databases (including payment DB), CI/CD pipelines, network devices, and operating systems. Identify and flag all shared or service accounts. For each shared account, document a remediation plan to convert to individual named accounts or implement compensating controls (session recording, break-glass procedures) with a target date. Define the quarterly privileged access review process and six-monthly standard access review process that will be executed under task 4.4.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Access control policy document is approved by CISO and version-controlled.
- Policy explicitly addresses least privilege, SoD, JML with SLAs, and MFA requirements.
- Privileged account inventory is complete across all platforms, with each account attributed to a named individual or documented as a service account with justification.
- All shared accounts are identified with a documented remediation plan and target date.
- MFA is confirmed as enforced on all administrative and remote access to CDE systems, satisfying PCI 8.3.1 and 8.3.6.
- Quarterly privileged access review procedure is documented with template, reviewer assignment, and evidence-capture process ready for first execution in task 4.4.
- Policy maps to PCI-DSS Requirements 7.2.1, 7.2.2, 8.2.1–8.2.8, 8.3.1, 8.3.6, and 8.6.1 with cross-references noted in the SoA.

**Assignee:** IAM Specialist

**Due:** Week 9

### ISMS-007: Extend Incident Management Process with Security Classification and PCI Playbook

**Summary:** Extend the existing ITIL incident process to handle security incidents with formal classification, evidence preservation, post-incident review, and a PCI-specific notification playbook

**Description:** The current ITIL incident management process handles service disruptions but does not distinguish security incidents, mandate evidence preservation, or include card-brand notification procedures. This task extends the process rather than replacing it. Add a security incident classification tier (Critical / High / Medium / Low) with clear definitions and examples. Define the escalation path: service desk performs initial triage, SecOps confirms whether the incident is security-related, CISO is notified for all High and Critical security incidents. Document an evidence preservation procedure covering chain of custody, forensic image requirements, log snapshot procedures, and rules on what must not be altered (no rebooting compromised systems before imaging, no deleting logs). Add a mandatory post-incident review for all High and Critical security incidents, with output feeding the risk register (new risks) and the corrective action tracker (process improvements). Create a PCI-specific playbook appendix covering: identification of whether cardholder data is confirmed or suspected to be compromised, card-brand notification timelines (Visa and Mastercard require notification within 24–72 hours depending on the brand), acquirer notification procedure, PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI) engagement criteria, and evidence preservation requirements specific to PCI forensics. Integrate the playbook into the existing ticketing system so that selecting "Security Incident" as a category triggers the correct workflow and mandatory fields.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Security incident classification scheme is documented with definitions, examples, and escalation paths.
- Evidence preservation procedure is documented and reviewed by CISO.
- Post-incident review template is created with fields for root cause, risk register updates, and corrective actions.
- PCI playbook appendix covers card-brand notification timelines, acquirer contact details, PFI engagement criteria, and forensic evidence requirements.
- Ticketing system is configured so that "Security Incident" category triggers the security workflow with mandatory fields for classification, evidence preservation confirmation, and CISO notification.
- At least one tabletop exercise has been conducted using a simulated CDE breach scenario, with the exercise record filed as evidence.
- Process satisfies ISO 27001 Annex A 5.24–5.28 and PCI-DSS Requirement 12.10.1 as confirmed by cross-reference in the SoA.

**Assignee:** CISO + Service Desk Lead

**Due:** Week 10

---

### ISMS-008: Conduct Full Internal Audit of the ISMS

**Summary:** Plan and execute a comprehensive internal audit covering all ISMS clauses and applicable Annex A controls, and deliver a formal audit report with findings

**Description:** ISO 27001 Clause 9.2 requires at least one complete internal audit cycle before the certification audit. The audit must cover all mandatory clauses (4–10) and sample evidence across all applicable Annex A controls in the Statement of Applicability. The auditor must be independent — they cannot audit controls they own or implemented. Given the team size (one CISO, one GRC Analyst, both of whom own controls), an external consultant is strongly recommended for this task. The audit should be planned with an audit programme and schedule shared with all control owners at least two weeks in advance. Each audit session should review documented procedures, interview control owners, and examine evidence artefacts (tickets, logs, review records, meeting minutes). Findings should be classified as Major Nonconformity (control is absent or fundamentally failing), Minor Nonconformity (control exists but has an implementation gap), or Observation (improvement opportunity). The audit report must be formally issued to the CISO and executive sponsor and must feed directly into task 6.4 (corrective actions). Pay particular attention to areas that were still in progress at Stage 1, as the Stage 2 auditor will probe these for evidence of closure. Schedule the audit so that control owners have at least four weeks after the report to close findings before the management review in week 22–23.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Audit programme and schedule are documented and distributed to all control owners at least two weeks before the audit begins.
- Auditor independence is confirmed and documented (external consultant or internal staff with no ownership of audited controls).
- All mandatory clauses (4–10) are audited with evidence of review documented.
- A representative sample of applicable Annex A controls is audited (minimum 50% of controls, 100% of controls flagged as findings in Stage 1).
- Formal audit report is issued with each finding classified as Major, Minor, or Observation.
- All findings are entered into the corrective action tracker with assigned owners and deadlines, ready for task 6.4.
- Audit evidence pack (programme, schedule, working papers, report) is filed in the evidence repository for Stage 2 auditor review.

**Assignee:** External Audit Consultant (independent)

**Due:** Week 20
