# ISO 27001 Gap Analysis & 9-Month Certification Roadmap

## Your starting position

You're in better shape than many orgs at this stage. SOC 2 Type II work gives you partial coverage of roughly 30–40% of ISO 27001 Annex A controls, and your existing ITIL practices (change board, incident management) provide ready-made evidence. The biggest gaps are likely the ISMS governance layer (Clauses 4–10), formal risk assessment, asset inventory completeness, and vulnerability management maturity.

---

## Part 1: Prioritized Gap Analysis Checklist

I've organized this by priority tier rather than sequential Annex A numbering, because auditors care most about whether your ISMS is coherent and risk-driven, not whether you tackled controls in numerical order.

### Tier 1 — Foundational (do these first; everything else depends on them)

**ISMS governance framework (Clauses 4–6, 9–10)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Context of the organization (Clause 4) | Informal understanding | Documented scope statement, interested parties register, internal/external issues | Scope document with clear boundaries (AWS accounts, services, locations, exclusions) |
| Leadership and policy (Clause 5) | Possibly ad hoc security policies | Board-endorsed ISMS policy, defined roles (ISMS owner, risk owner), management commitment | Signed ISMS policy, RACI matrix, board/exec meeting minutes showing security agenda items |
| Risk assessment and treatment (Clause 6.1.2–6.1.3) | SOC 2 risk register (partial) | Formal methodology, consistent criteria for likelihood/impact, risk treatment plan, Statement of Applicability | Risk assessment methodology document, risk register with scored risks, treatment plan linked to Annex A controls, SoA with justifications for every included/excluded control |
| Performance evaluation (Clause 9) | SOC 2 monitoring | ISMS internal audit programme, management review process | Internal audit schedule and reports, management review meeting minutes with defined agenda per Clause 9.3 |
| Continual improvement (Clause 10) | Incident post-mortems | Formal corrective action process, nonconformity tracking | Corrective action log with root cause analysis, evidence of closure |

**Asset management and classification (Annex A 5.9–5.13)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Information asset inventory | Partial inventory, AWS resource tags | Comprehensive register covering data assets, software, cloud services, people, physical assets | Asset register with owners assigned, classification labels, review dates |
| Information classification | Possibly informal | Classification scheme (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), handling procedures | Classification policy, labelling evidence in repos and storage, handling matrix |
| Media and asset disposal | Ad hoc | Documented disposal/return procedures | Disposal logs, AWS resource decommissioning records, offboarding checklists |

**Risk assessment and vulnerability management (Annex A 8.8, 5.7, 8.34)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vulnerability management | Ad hoc scanning | Formal policy with defined scan frequency, SLAs for remediation by severity, coverage of infra and application layers | Policy document, scan reports (e.g., AWS Inspector, Qualys, Snyk), remediation tickets with timestamps showing SLA compliance, exception/risk-acceptance records |
| Threat intelligence (5.7) | Possibly AWS GuardDuty alerts | Documented process for consuming and acting on threat intel | Procedure document, evidence of feed subscriptions, examples of threat intel leading to action |
| Audit logging and monitoring (8.15–8.16) | EDR, some CloudWatch/CloudTrail | Centralized logging with retention policy, defined alert thresholds, review cadence | Log retention configuration, SIEM or log platform dashboards, alert triage records |

### Tier 2 — Strengthen existing controls (leverage your ITIL and SOC 2 work)

**Access control (Annex A 5.15–5.18, 8.2–8.5)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access control policy | MFA deployed, likely role-based access | Documented access control policy covering need-to-know, least privilege, segregation of duties | Policy document, evidence of periodic access reviews (quarterly recommended), recertification records |
| Privileged access (8.2) | Likely some AWS IAM controls | Formal privileged access management (PAM) process, break-glass procedures | PAM tool logs or documented procedure, list of privileged accounts with justification, session recording or audit trail |
| Identity provisioning and deprovisioning | HR/IT onboarding process | Automated joiner-mover-leaver process tied to HR system, timely deprovisioning evidence | Onboarding/offboarding checklists with timestamps, access removal within defined SLA (e.g., 24 hours of termination) |

**Change management (Annex A 8.32, 8.25–8.31)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Change enablement | Change board (ITIL), CI/CD pipelines | Link between change board approvals and deployment evidence, emergency change procedure, rollback criteria | CAB meeting minutes or Jira/ServiceNow tickets showing approval before deployment, CI/CD pipeline logs showing gate checks (tests, security scans, approval steps), emergency change records with post-implementation review |
| Secure development lifecycle (8.25–8.27) | CI/CD with some testing | Documented SDLC security policy, SAST/DAST in pipeline, code review requirements, separation of dev/test/prod | SDLC policy, pipeline configuration showing security scan stages (e.g., Snyk, SonarQube, OWASP ZAP), PR merge rules requiring review, environment separation evidence in AWS accounts or VPCs |
| Configuration management (8.9) | Likely Terraform/IaC | Formal baseline configurations, drift detection | IaC repos with version history, AWS Config rules or similar drift detection, hardening standards (CIS benchmarks) |

**Incident management (Annex A 5.24–5.28)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incident response process | ITIL incident management, PagerDuty or similar | Formal information security incident classification (vs. operational incidents), escalation matrix, breach notification procedure, evidence preservation | Incident response plan document, classification matrix, tabletop exercise records, post-incident reports with root cause and corrective actions, breach notification procedure aligned with GDPR/contractual obligations |

### Tier 3 — Fill remaining gaps

**Supplier management (Annex A 5.19–5.22)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supplier security | AWS shared responsibility awareness, possibly some vendor questionnaires for SOC 2 | Supplier register with risk ratings, security clauses in contracts, periodic reassessment | Supplier register, contract clauses or DPAs, evidence of annual review (e.g., requesting SOC 2 reports from critical vendors), AWS shared responsibility documentation |

**People security (Annex A 6.1–6.8)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Background screening (6.1) | Possibly for some roles | Policy covering all roles proportionate to risk | Screening policy, evidence of checks completed (redacted records) |
| Awareness and training (6.3) | Possibly phishing simulations | Formal security awareness programme with annual training, role-based training for developers and admins | Training platform records showing completion rates, training content, phishing simulation results with trend data |
| Disciplinary process (6.4) | HR policy | Link between security violations and disciplinary procedures | Policy cross-reference, ideally in acceptable use policy |

**Business continuity and backup (Annex A 5.29–5.30, 8.13–8.14)**

| Gap area | What you likely have | What's missing | Evidence auditors expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backup (8.13) | AWS snapshots, RDS backups | Documented backup policy with RTOs/RPOs, tested restore procedures | Backup policy, backup configuration evidence, restore test records (at least annual) |
| ICT readiness for business continuity (5.30) | AWS multi-AZ or similar | Documented BCP/DR plan, tested failover | BCP/DR plan, test results, lessons learned |
| Redundancy (8.14) | AWS infrastructure redundancy | Documentation linking redundancy design to availability requirements | Architecture diagrams, availability SLAs, failover evidence |

**Physical and environmental (Annex A 7.1–7.14)**

For a SaaS company on AWS, most physical controls are inherited from AWS (reference their SOC 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate). You still need to cover your own offices: visitor logs, clean desk, physical access controls for any on-premises equipment.

## Part 2: 9-Month Certification Roadmap

### Months 1–2: Establish the ISMS and assess risk

**Governance setup**: Draft and get executive sign-off on the ISMS policy, scope document, and roles/responsibilities. Appoint an ISMS manager or owner. Set up an information security steering committee (can be monthly, 30 minutes, with CTO/CISO/VP Eng/Head of IT).

**Risk assessment**: Choose and document a methodology (e.g., ISO 27005-aligned, qualitative 5×5 matrix). Identify information assets by working through your AWS accounts, data stores, SaaS tools, and repositories. Score risks and produce a treatment plan. Draft the Statement of Applicability — this is the single most important document for your audit.

**Quick wins**: Formalize your existing ITIL incident and change processes as ISO 27001 evidence. Map SOC 2 controls to Annex A — your SOC 2 auditor may have a mapping or you can use the AICPA-to-ISO mapping as a starting point.

**DevOps evidence tip**: Export your Jira/ServiceNow change tickets, CI/CD pipeline configurations, and PagerDuty incident timelines now. These become Annex A evidence with minimal reformatting.

**Deliverables**: ISMS scope, ISMS policy, risk assessment methodology, asset register (v1), risk register, treatment plan, Statement of Applicability (draft).

### Months 3–4: Build core policies and close Tier 1 gaps

**Documentation sprint**: Write or formalize the core policy set. At minimum you need policies covering access control, acceptable use, classification, cryptography, backup, vulnerability management, supplier security, secure development, and incident response. Keep them concise — auditors prefer short, enforceable policies over 50-page documents nobody reads.

**Vulnerability management programme**: Deploy or configure automated scanning across infrastructure (AWS Inspector, Qualys, Nessus) and application code (Snyk, Dependabot, SonarQube). Define remediation SLAs (e.g., Critical: 72 hours, High: 7 days, Medium: 30 days, Low: 90 days). Integrate scan results into your ticketing system so you have timestamped evidence of remediation.

**Asset inventory completion**: Use AWS resource tagging, a CMDB, or even a well-maintained spreadsheet. Every asset needs an owner and a classification label.

**Security awareness**: Launch a formal programme. Platforms like KnowBe4 or Proofpoint give you completion dashboards auditors love.

**Deliverables**: Policy library (10–15 policies), vulnerability management procedure with SLAs, complete asset register, awareness training launched.

### Months 5–6: Operationalize controls and generate evidence

**Access reviews**: Run your first formal access recertification across critical systems (AWS IAM, source code repos, production databases, SaaS admin consoles). Document results and remediation of any excess access.

**Supplier register**: Build a register of all third parties with access to your data or systems. Rate them by risk. Collect SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates from critical vendors. Ensure contracts contain appropriate security clauses.

**Secure SDLC hardening**: Ensure CI/CD pipelines have mandatory security scan stages that block deployment on critical findings. Document branch protection rules, PR review requirements, and environment separation. Auditors will want to see a pipeline run showing a security gate in action.

**Backup and DR testing**: Run and document a restore test and, if possible, a failover test. Record RTOs achieved versus targets.

**Logging and monitoring**: Ensure CloudTrail, CloudWatch, and your EDR feed into a centralized platform with defined retention (12 months is a common auditor expectation). Document alert rules and triage procedures.

**Deliverables**: Access review records, supplier register, SDLC security evidence, backup/DR test results, logging architecture documentation.

### Months 7–8: Internal audit, management review, and remediation

**Internal audit**: Conduct a full internal audit against Clauses 4–10 and all applicable Annex A controls. Use an independent auditor if possible (external consultant, or at least someone not responsible for the controls being audited). Document findings as nonconformities or observations.

**Management review**: Hold a formal management review meeting covering the agenda items required by Clause 9.3: audit results, risk treatment status, interested party feedback, improvement opportunities. Produce minutes and action items.

**Remediation**: Close nonconformities from the internal audit. Each one needs root cause analysis, corrective action, and evidence of closure. This corrective action cycle is itself evidence that your ISMS works.

**Mock audit (optional but recommended)**: Engage your chosen certification body or an independent consultant for a pre-assessment. This surfaces issues before the real audit.

**Deliverables**: Internal audit report, management review minutes, corrective action log, remediation evidence.

### Month 9: Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits

**Stage 1 (documentation review)**: The certification body reviews your ISMS documentation, SoA, risk assessment, and policies. This is typically a 1–2 day remote or on-site review. They confirm you're ready for Stage 2 and flag any areas of concern. For a 250-person SaaS company, expect roughly 2–3 auditor-days.

**Gap between Stage 1 and Stage 2**: Typically 4–8 weeks. Use this time to address any Stage 1 findings.

**Stage 2 (implementation audit)**: The auditor verifies that controls are implemented and operating effectively. They interview staff, review evidence, and sample records. For your org size, expect roughly 8–12 auditor-days. They will sample change tickets, incident records, access reviews, vulnerability scans, training records, and risk treatment evidence.

**Deliverables**: Stage 1 report clearance, Stage 2 audit passed, certificate issued (typically 4–6 weeks after Stage 2).

## Controls to tackle first (priority order and reasoning)

The sequence matters because auditors evaluate your ISMS as a system, not a checklist. The first three items create the structure that makes everything else coherent.

1. **Risk assessment and SoA** — every control decision must trace back to a risk. Without this, nothing else has justification.
2. **ISMS governance documents** — scope, policy, roles. These take days to write but are hard prerequisites for audit.
3. **Asset inventory** — you can't protect what you don't know about, and your risk assessment is hollow without it.
4. **Vulnerability management** — your biggest operational gap. Moving from ad hoc to SLA-driven scanning gives you high-value evidence quickly.
5. **Access control formalization** — you have MFA, so you're ahead. Add periodic reviews and privileged access documentation.
6. **Change and SDLC security** — your DevOps pipeline is an asset here. Add security gates and document what you already do.
7. **Incident response formalization** — extend your ITIL process to cover security-specific classification and breach notification.
8. **Supplier management** — often overlooked and time-consuming because it depends on third parties responding.
9. **Training and awareness** — easy to implement, slow to generate trend data, so start early.
10. **Internal audit and management review** — these prove the ISMS is a living system, not shelfware.

## Finishing the cut-off section: What specific evidence auditors sample most heavily

Auditors at Stage 2 will typically ask for live demonstrations and samples across these areas, roughly in order of how much time they spend on each.

**Risk assessment and treatment trail.** They will pick a risk from your register and trace it end to end: from identification, through scoring, to the treatment decision, to the specific Annex A control(s) it maps to in the SoA, to evidence that the control is operating. If this chain breaks at any point, it is a major nonconformity. They may do this three to five times with different risks.

**Change and deployment records.** They will ask you to pull up recent change tickets (often five to ten samples) and show the approval, testing evidence, security scan results, and deployment log. For a DevOps shop, expect them to ask you to walk through a CI/CD pipeline run on screen, showing gate checks, test results, and who approved the merge/deploy.

**Incident records.** They will sample two to four incidents and check for classification, escalation, root cause analysis, corrective actions, and evidence that lessons learned fed back into the ISMS. If you had a security incident, they will examine it in detail. If you had none, they will probe how you would know — which leads to your monitoring and detection evidence.

**Access reviews.** They want to see a completed recertification cycle: who reviewed, what access was found, what was revoked, and when. They will also sample joiner and leaver records to check provisioning and deprovisioning timeliness.

**Vulnerability scan reports and remediation.** They will pull scan reports, pick critical or high findings, and check your ticketing system for evidence that remediation met your SLA. Exceptions or risk acceptances need to be formally documented and approved — ad hoc "we decided to leave it" is a finding.

**Training completion records.** They want dashboards or reports showing completion rates, ideally above 95%, and evidence that new joiners are trained within a defined window.

**Supplier due diligence.** They will pick two to three critical suppliers and ask for the contract security clauses, the last assessment or SOC 2 report you collected, and evidence of periodic review.

**Management review minutes.** They will read these carefully. The minutes must show that the agenda covered the items in Clause 9.3 (risk status, audit results, interested party feedback, opportunities for improvement) and that actions were assigned and tracked.

**Internal audit report.** They will check scope coverage, auditor independence, findings, and corrective actions. If your internal audit found zero nonconformities, they will be skeptical — a mature ISMS always finds something to improve.

**Corrective action records.** For every nonconformity from internal audit or previous external audits, they want root cause analysis, the corrective action taken, evidence of implementation, and evidence of effectiveness verification.

Can you produce a prioritized gap-analysis checklist mapped to ISO/IEC 27001 (including Annex A controls), show which ITIL practices already cover each control, and call out quick wins to get certification-ready?
reply:
# ISO 27001 Gap Analysis Checklist

## Context and assumptions

You're a 250-person SaaS company, AWS-hosted, serving EU and US customers, mid-flight on SOC 2 Type II, with ITIL-based change, incident, and configuration management already running. That gives you a meaningful head start. SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria overlap roughly 60–70% with ISO 27001 Annex A, and your ITIL processes will produce much of the documentary evidence auditors expect. The biggest gaps will likely be in formal ISMS governance (Clauses 4–10), complete asset inventory, supplier security, and business continuity testing.

I've organized everything into three priority tiers: foundational work that must come first, core controls where you likely have partial coverage, and advanced or specialized controls you can tackle last. Within each tier, items are roughly ordered by dependency and audit impact.

---

## Tier 1 — Foundational (do first, months 1–3)

These are the mandatory ISMS clauses (4–10) plus the Annex A controls that underpin everything else. Without these, a Stage 1 auditor will stop the process.

**1.1 — Establish the ISMS scope and context (Clauses 4.1–4.3)**

Define your organizational context, interested parties (EU customers, US customers, regulators, staff), and ISMS boundaries. For a SaaS provider your scope will likely be "the design, development, delivery, and support of [product] hosted on AWS, including all supporting infrastructure, people, and processes." Document this in a one- to two-page scope statement. Your SOC 2 scoping work is directly reusable here.

ITIL coverage: None directly, but your service catalogue and configuration management system (CMS) will help define the boundary.

Quick win: Reuse your SOC 2 system description as the starting point.

**1.2 — Leadership commitment and roles (Clauses 5.1–5.3)**

You need documented executive commitment (a signed information security policy), a named ISMS owner (typically the CISO or head of security), and defined roles and responsibilities. The policy must be communicated to all employees.

Annex A: 5.1 (Policies for information security), 5.2 (Information security roles and responsibilities).

ITIL coverage: ITIL's organizational structure helps but doesn't produce the ISO-required policy or role assignments.

Quick win: Draft and sign the top-level information security policy — it can be two pages. Assign ISMS ownership formally.

**1.3 — Risk assessment and treatment (Clause 6.1.2, 6.1.3)**

This is the engine of the ISMS. You need a documented risk assessment methodology (likelihood × impact is fine), a risk register, defined risk acceptance criteria approved by management, and a risk treatment plan that maps each unacceptable risk to Annex A controls. The output feeds directly into the Statement of Applicability.

Annex A: 5.7 (Threat intelligence — feeds risk identification).

ITIL coverage: ITIL's risk management practice provides a process skeleton, but you need a formal, security-specific risk register.

Quick win: If your SOC 2 readiness included a risk assessment, adapt it. Add likelihood/impact scoring and map findings to Annex A controls.

**1.4 — Statement of Applicability (SoA)**

A mandatory document listing all 93 Annex A controls, stating whether each is applicable or not (with justification for exclusions), and noting implementation status. This is the single most important audit artifact.

Quick win: Start with a spreadsheet of all 93 controls, pre-populate "implemented" for controls your ITIL processes and SOC 2 work already cover, and mark gaps.

**1.5 — Asset inventory completion (Annex A 5.9, 5.10, 5.11, 5.12, 5.13)**

You flagged this as partial. The auditor will want a complete inventory of information assets (data stores, databases, S3 buckets), supporting assets (servers, SaaS tools, endpoints, network devices), software assets, and people/roles with classified ownership, classification labels (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), and acceptable use rules. Controls 5.10 (acceptable use), 5.12 (classification), and 5.13 (labelling) all depend on a finished inventory.

ITIL coverage: Your configuration management practice and CMS should already track CIs. Extend it to cover data assets and apply classification.

Quick win: Export your AWS resource inventory (AWS Config, AWS Organizations), merge with your CMS, and add ownership and classification columns. This can close the gap fast.

**1.6 — Documented information and document control (Clauses 7.5, Annex A 5.1, 5.37)**

ISO 27001 requires controlled documents with version history, approval, and distribution. You need a document control procedure and a central repository.

ITIL coverage: ITIL's knowledge management practice covers some of this.

Quick win: If you use Confluence, SharePoint, or similar, create an ISMS space with a naming convention, version control, and an approval workflow. Many orgs overthink this.

---

## Tier 2 — Core controls (months 2–5, many already partially covered)

These are the Annex A controls most relevant to a SaaS company on AWS with ITIL processes. I've grouped them by theme and flagged where your existing processes likely give you coverage.

**2.1 — People security (Annex A 6.1–6.8)**

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 Screening | Background checks before employment | None | Partial (check HR) | Formalize screening policy, ensure it covers contractors |
| 6.2 Terms and conditions | Security obligations in contracts | None | Likely in place | Verify employment contracts include confidentiality and security clauses |
| 6.3 Awareness and training | Security awareness program | Workforce and talent mgmt | Partial if SOC 2 required it | Implement annual training with tracked completion; add role-specific training for devs |
| 6.4 Disciplinary process | Consequences for violations | None | Likely in HR policy | Document and reference in security policy |
| 6.5 After termination | Obligations survive departure | None | Check contracts | Ensure NDAs and IP clauses survive termination |
| 6.6 Confidentiality agreements | NDAs | None | Likely partial | Extend to contractors and third parties |
| 6.7 Remote working | Security for remote work | None | Likely informal | Document remote work security requirements (VPN, endpoint, screen lock) |
| 6.8 Security event reporting | Staff report incidents | Incident management | Covered if incident process includes reporting channel | Ensure all staff know how to report; test annually |

Quick win: If SOC 2 required security awareness training, you already have it — just document the program and ensure completion records exist.

**2.2 — Access control (Annex A 5.15–5.18, 8.2–8.5)**

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.15 Access control policy | Documented policy | Access management | Likely informal | Write a one-page access control policy (need-to-know, least privilege) |
| 5.16 Identity management | Unique IDs, lifecycle | Access management | Likely via IdP (Okta, Azure AD) | Document identity lifecycle (joiner/mover/leaver) |
| 5.17 Authentication | MFA, password policy | Access management | Likely in place for SOC 2 | Verify MFA on all production, admin, and SaaS accounts |
| 5.18 Access rights | Provisioning and review | Access management | Likely partial | Implement quarterly access reviews with evidence |
| 8.2 Privileged access | Admin account controls | Access management | Likely partial | Document privileged access procedure, enforce just-in-time or break-glass |
| 8.3 Information access restriction | App-level controls | None | Likely in product | Document RBAC model in application |
| 8.5 Secure authentication | Hardened auth mechanisms | None | Likely in place | Verify password hashing, session management, brute-force protection |

Quick win: If you use an IdP with SSO and MFA, your evidence is largely in the IdP's logs and config. Export and document.

**2.3 — Change, incident, and configuration management (Annex A 5.24–5.28, 8.9, 8.32, 8.33)**

This is where your ITIL maturity pays off.

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.32 Change management | Controlled changes | Change enablement | **Covered** | Map ITIL change process to this control in SoA; ensure security review is a gate |
| 8.9 Configuration management | Secure baselines | Service config mgmt | **Covered** | Document baseline configs for AWS (use AWS Config rules or CIS benchmarks) |
| 5.24 Incident mgmt planning | Process exists | Incident management | **Covered** | Verify process includes security-specific classification and escalation |
| 5.25 Assessment and decision | Classify severity | Incident management | **Covered** | Ensure classification criteria distinguish security incidents |
| 5.26 Response to incidents | Containment, eradication | Incident management | **Mostly covered** | Add forensic preservation and communication steps |
| 5.27 Learning from incidents | Post-incident review | Problem management | Likely in place | Ensure PIRs are documented and feed back into risk register |
| 5.28 Evidence collection | Chain of custody | None | Likely gap | Write a short evidence collection procedure (log preservation, timestamps, chain of custody) |
| 8.33 Test information | Protect test data | None | Unknown | Ensure production data is anonymized/masked in non-prod environments |

Quick win: Your ITIL change and incident processes probably need only light annotation ("this process satisfies Annex A 8.32") and a security gate added to the change workflow.

**2.4 — Cryptography, network, and infrastructure security (Annex A 8.24, 8.20–8.23, 8.26, 8.7, 8.1, 8.8)**

| Control | Description | Likely status (AWS SaaS) | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.24 Use of cryptography | TLS, encryption at rest | Likely in place (ACM, KMS, RDS encryption) | Document cryptographic standards (algorithms, key lengths, key management via KMS) |
| 8.20 Network security | VPC segmentation, security groups | Likely in place | Document network architecture diagram with security controls |
| 8.21 Security of network services | Managed services, WAF | Likely partial | Verify WAF, DDoS protection (Shield), and document |
| 8.22 Segregation of networks | Prod/dev/staging separation | Likely in place | Document VPC/account separation; verify no prod-to-dev bridging |
| 8.23 Web filtering | Outbound filtering | May be a gap | Assess need; can use DNS filtering or proxy for corporate endpoints |
| 8.26 Application security requirements | Secure SDLC | Likely partial (SOC 2 often requires this) | Document SDLC with security gates (threat modelling, code review, SAST/DAST) |
| 8.7 Malware protection | Endpoint and server AV/EDR | Likely in place | Verify EDR on all endpoints and document |
| 8.1 User endpoint devices | Device management | Likely partial | Formalize MDM or endpoint policy (encryption, screen lock, patching) |
| 8.8 Vulnerability management | Scanning and patching | Likely in place for SOC 2 | Document scan cadence, SLAs for remediation by severity, and evidence |

Quick win: Most of these are AWS-native. Export your AWS Config compliance dashboard, Security Hub findings, and KMS key policies as evidence.

**2.5 — Logging and monitoring (Annex A 8.15, 8.16, 8.17)**

| Control | Description | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.15 Logging | Audit trails for access, changes, errors | Likely in place (CloudTrail, application logs) | Document what is logged, retention periods (align with legal/contractual), and tamper protection |
| 8.16 Monitoring activities | SIEM or alerting | Likely partial | Ensure alerts for security-relevant events (failed logins, privilege escalation, config changes); document monitoring procedures |
| 8.17 Clock synchronization | NTP across systems | Covered by AWS | Document; trivial for cloud |

Quick win: If you have CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty enabled, document and reference them.

**2.6 — Backup and continuity (Annex A 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30)**

| Control | Description | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.13 Information backup | Backup policy and testing | Likely in place (RDS snapshots, S3 versioning) | Document backup schedule, retention, and **test restores** quarterly with evidence |
| 8.14 Redundancy | HA design | Likely in place (multi-AZ) | Document architecture and failover procedures |
| 5.29 Disruption planning | Business continuity | May be a gap | Write a business continuity plan covering key scenarios (AWS region failure, key person loss, ransomware) |
| 5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity | DR testing | Likely partial | Conduct and document a DR test; define RTO/RPO per service tier |

Quick win: If you already have multi-AZ and automated snapshots, document them and run one verified restore test.

---

## Tier 3 — Specialized and advanced (months 4–6+)

**3.1 — Supplier and third-party security (Annex A 5.19–5.23)**

Critical for a SaaS company using AWS and likely dozens of sub-processors.

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|
| 5.19 Supplier security policy | Write a supplier security management policy |
| 5.20 Addressing security in supplier agreements | Ensure contracts include security clauses, audit rights, breach notification |
| 5.21 Managing security in the ICT supply chain | Assess supply chain risk (AWS, CI/CD tools, monitoring SaaS) |
| 5.22 Monitoring and review of supplier services | Implement annual supplier reviews (collect SOC 2 reports, ISO certs) |
| 5.23 Cloud service security | Document AWS shared responsibility model, your responsibilities, and how you verify AWS controls |

Quick win: Collect SOC 2/ISO 27001 reports from your top 10 suppliers now. Many (AWS, Datadog, PagerDuty, etc.) publish them. Create a supplier register with risk ratings.

**3.2 — Privacy and data protection (Annex A 5.34, 5.35, 5.36)**

With EU customers you're subject to GDPR, so these controls are non-negotiable.

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|
| 5.34 Privacy and PII protection | Document how you identify and protect PII; align with GDPR obligations |
| 5.35 Independent review | Plan for internal audit or external review of the ISMS (Clause 9.2 requirement too) |
| 5.36 Compliance with policies and standards | Implement compliance checking (can be part of internal audit) |

Quick win: If you have a GDPR data processing agreement template and a data processing register, reference them.

**3.3 — Physical security (Annex A 7.1–7.14)**

Since production is on AWS, most physical controls apply only to your offices. The auditor will verify that AWS's physical controls are addressed via the shared responsibility model and AWS's own ISO 27001 certificate.

For offices: ensure visitor logs, clean desk policy, secure disposal of media, and physical access controls to server rooms (if any) are documented. This is usually low effort.

**3.4 — Secure development (Annex A 8.25–8.31, 8.33, 8.34)**

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|

>
> **Version:** 1.0 | **Classification:** Internal | **Owner:** [CISO Name] | **Approved by:** [CEO Name] | **Date:** [Date] | **Review:** Annual
>
> ---
>
> **Purpose**
>
> This policy establishes management's direction and commitment to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information entrusted to [Company Name] by its customers, employees, and partners.
>
> **Scope**
>
> This policy applies to all employees, contractors, and third parties who access [Company Name] information, systems, or facilities. It covers all information assets within the ISMS scope as defined in the ISMS Scope Statement.
>
> **Principles**
>
> [Company Name] commits to the following principles. First, we will protect customer data and company information commensurate with its sensitivity and value, applying controls proportionate to assessed risk. Second, we will comply with all applicable legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations, including the EU General Data Protection Regulation and customer contractual commitments. Third, we will manage information security risk through a systematic process of identification, assessment, treatment, and ongoing monitoring, documented in our risk register and Statement of Applicability. Fourth, we will grant access to information and systems on a need-to-know and least-privilege basis, verifying identity through strong authentication. Fifth, we will prepare for, detect, respond to, and recover from information security incidents in a timely manner, learning from each event to improve our defences. Sixth, we will foster a culture of security awareness through regular training and clear communication of responsibilities. Seventh, we will continually improve the effectiveness of our Information Security Management System through internal audit, management review, corrective action, and measurement against defined objectives.
>
> **Responsibilities**
>
> The Chief Executive Officer bears overall accountability for information security. The [CISO / Head of Security] is responsible for maintaining the ISMS, conducting risk assessments, reporting to senior management, and coordinating security activities. All managers are responsible for ensuring their teams understand and comply with this policy and supporting policies. All employees and contractors are responsible for complying with security policies, completing required training, and reporting security events promptly.
>
> **Information security objectives**
>
> Management will define measurable information security objectives annually, aligned with business strategy and risk appetite, and will review progress during management reviews. >
> **Enforcement**
>
> Violations of this policy or its supporting policies may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment or contract, and may also result in legal action where applicable.
>
> **Review**
>
> This policy is reviewed at least annually and updated whenever significant changes occur to the organisation, its risk environment, or applicable regulations. All changes require approval by the CEO or delegated authority.

# Remediation Plans for the Two Critical Gaps

---

## Plan A — Asset Inventory and CMDB Completeness

### Objective, ownership, and scope

Your draft is solid. One adjustment: extend the target to 14 weeks to allow a realistic validation and governance phase at the end. The objective should be stated as an auditable outcome: "Establish and maintain a complete, classified, and owner-assigned inventory of all information assets that store, process, or transmit PHI and other sensitive data, across AWS and on-premises environments, within 14 weeks."

**Ownership:**

The ITSM Manager owns day-to-day execution. The CISO sponsors and removes blockers. You also need a Clinical Systems Lead (or Biomedical Engineering representative) accountable for medical devices and clinical application assets, because IT discovery tools often miss or misidentify them. Each asset must have a named Business Owner (typically a department head) who accepts risk and approves classification, distinct from the Technical Owner (the IT person who maintains it).

### Phase 1 — Discovery and baselining (weeks 1–4)

**Task 1.1: Define the asset taxonomy and classification scheme (week 1).** Before scanning anything, agree on asset types (server, endpoint, network device, medical device, cloud resource, SaaS application, data store), data-classification tiers (e.g., PHI/restricted, confidential, internal, public), and the minimum attribute set every CMDB record must carry. For ISO 27001 you need at minimum: unique asset ID, asset type, description, technical owner, business owner, data classification, location/environment (AWS region, on-prem site, hybrid), network zone, and last-verified date. Document this in a CMDB policy or standard. This is audit evidence in its own right.

**Task 1.2: AWS automated discovery (weeks 1–2).** Enable AWS Config across all accounts and regions with a conformance pack. Use AWS Systems Manager Inventory to pull OS-level detail (installed software, patches, services) from every EC2 instance. Use AWS Organizations and resource-tagging policies to enforce mandatory tags: data-classification, owner, cost-centre, and CMDB-CI-ID. Run AWS Config advanced queries to produce a full resource list (EC2, RDS, S3 buckets, Lambda functions, ELB, VPC endpoints) and export it. For S3 specifically, enable Amazon Macie to flag buckets containing PHI — this feeds your data-classification effort. The output of this phase is a raw AWS asset register in a format your CMDB can ingest.

**Task 1.3: On-premises automated discovery (weeks 1–3).** Deploy or configure a network discovery scanner. If you are already on ServiceNow, its Discovery module with MID servers is the most natural choice because CIs populate directly into the CMDB without a reconciliation step. Alternatives include Lansweeper or Qualys asset inventory (which doubles as your vulnerability scanner, relevant to Plan B). Scan all subnets, including clinical VLANs and medical-device segments. Coordinate with Biomedical Engineering for segments that may be sensitive to active scanning — some legacy medical devices do not tolerate aggressive probes, so use passive discovery or manual enumeration for those. The output is a raw on-prem asset register.

**Task 1.4: Manual enumeration of shadow assets (weeks 2–4).** Automated tools miss SaaS applications, departmental databases, paper-based PHI stores, and assets behind firewalls that block discovery. Send a brief questionnaire to each department head asking them to list systems, applications, and data stores their team uses. Cross-reference against SSO/IdP application lists, DNS records, firewall rules, and procurement/contract records. This is unglamorous but essential — auditors love to find assets that exist in procurement records but not in the CMDB.

### Phase 2 — Reconciliation and enrichment (weeks 5–8)

**Task 2.1: Merge and deduplicate (weeks 5–6).** Import the AWS register, on-prem register, and manual list into ServiceNow. Reconcile duplicates using hostname, IP, serial number, or cloud resource ID as matching keys. ServiceNow's Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE) handles most of this if you configure reconciliation rules. Flag orphan CIs (discovered but no known owner) and ghost CIs (in CMDB but not found by discovery). Orphans need an owner assigned; ghosts need investigation and either reactivation or retirement.

**Task 2.2: Assign owners and classify data (weeks 5–8).** This is the most labour-intensive step. For each CI, assign a Technical Owner (from IT) and a Business Owner (from the business unit). For data classification, start with the systems you already know hold PHI (EHR, PACS, lab, pharmacy, billing) and tag them as restricted. Use the Macie output for AWS. For everything else, work through the list with department heads. Where you are unsure, classify up (treat it as restricted until proven otherwise). Record the classification decision and the person who made it — this is direct audit evidence for Annex A 5.12.

**Task 2.3: Map data flows for PHI (weeks 6–8).** Produce a data-flow diagram showing how PHI moves between systems, networks, and third parties. This is not strictly a CMDB task but auditors expect it and it falls out naturally from the inventory work. Tools like AWS VPC flow logs, firewall logs, and application integration documentation feed this. The diagram supports your risk assessment (ISO 27001 Clause 6.1.2) and your network segmentation controls (Annex A 8.20).

### Phase 3 — Governance and continuous accuracy (weeks 9–14)

**Task 3.1: Automate ongoing discovery (weeks 9–10).** Schedule ServiceNow Discovery to run weekly for on-prem. Configure AWS Config to stream resource-change events into ServiceNow via an integration (ServiceNow's AWS Service Management Connector or a lightweight Lambda-to-API integration). The goal is that no asset exists for more than seven days without appearing in the CMDB.

**Task 3.2: Establish a CMDB governance process (weeks 9–11).** Appoint a Configuration Manager (can be part of the ITSM Manager's remit) responsible for CMDB accuracy. Define a verification cycle: every CI must be reviewed by its Technical Owner at least every six months (quarterly for PHI systems). Tie CMDB accuracy to change enablement — no RFC should be approved unless the affected CIs exist in the CMDB and are verified. This creates a self-reinforcing loop.

**Task 3.3: Validation and audit-readiness review (weeks 12–14).** Run a sample audit: pull 30 random CIs and verify that they physically or logically exist, that their attributes are correct, and that the owner can confirm their classification. Run the reverse: pick 30 assets from a fresh discovery scan and confirm they are in the CMDB. Document the results. This is exactly what an ISO 27001 auditor will do, so doing it first lets you fix problems before Stage 1.

### Tooling summary for Plan A

| Layer | Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| AWS | AWS Config, Systems Manager Inventory, Organizations tag policies, Macie | Automated cloud asset and data discovery |
| On-prem | ServiceNow Discovery + MID servers (or Lansweeper/Qualys) | Automated network and OS-level discovery |
| Medical devices | Passive discovery or Biomedical Engineering manual register | Safe enumeration of sensitive clinical devices |
| CMDB | ServiceNow CMDB with IRE | Single source of truth, reconciliation, governance |
| Data flows | VPC flow logs, firewall logs, integration docs | PHI data-flow diagrams |

### KPIs

Track these monthly and report to the CISO:

**CMDB completeness** — percentage of assets found by discovery scan that have a matching, verified CI in the CMDB. Target: 95% by week 14, 98% steady state.

**Classification coverage** — percentage of CIs with a data-classification tag assigned. Target: 100% for all CIs in PHI-bearing network zones.

**Owner assignment** — percentage of CIs with both a Technical Owner and a Business Owner. Target: 100%.

**Stale CI rate** — percentage of CIs not verified within the defined cycle (six months general, three months PHI). Target: below 5%.

**Ghost CI rate** — CIs in CMDB not found by any discovery source. Target: below 2%.

### Audit evidence to collect and retain

The auditor will ask for the following, so file these as controlled documents or exportable reports:

CMDB policy/standard (taxonomy, minimum attributes, governance process). Full CMDB export with classification and owner fields. AWS Config resource inventory snapshots. Discovery scan logs and schedules. Data-flow diagrams for PHI. Owner-assignment records with sign-off dates. Verification/sample-audit results from Phase 3. CMDB accuracy KPI dashboard or report history. Evidence that CMDB is integrated into the change process (e.g., RFC records referencing CIs). Meeting minutes from CMDB governance reviews.

## Plan B — Patching and Vulnerability Management

### Objective, ownership, and scope

"Implement a risk-rated vulnerability management programme covering all in-scope assets (AWS and on-premises), with defined patching SLAs, compensating controls for unpatchable systems, and auditable tracking, within 16 weeks."

**Ownership:**

A Vulnerability Management Lead (new role or assigned within the security team) owns the programme. The CISO sponsors. The Infrastructure Manager and Clinical Systems Lead are accountable for patching execution in their respective domains. Change enablement (your existing ITIL process) governs patch deployment approvals.

### Phase 1 — Foundations (weeks 1–4)

**Task 1.1: Define the vulnerability management policy and patching SLAs (week 1–2).** Write a policy that covers scope (every asset in the CMDB — this is why Plan A matters), scanning cadence, risk-rating methodology, and remediation SLAs. Recommended SLAs for healthcare, calibrated to CVSS base score and exploitability, with adjustments for PHI exposure:

Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0 or actively exploited in the wild): remediate within 72 hours, or apply a compensating control within 24 hours and patch within 14 days. High (CVSS 7.0–8.9): remediate within 14 days. Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9): remediate within 30 days. Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9): remediate within 90 days or accept risk with documented justification.

These SLAs should be tighter for internet-facing assets and systems that directly handle PHI. Document exceptions for medical devices separately (see Task 3.3 below).

**Task 1.2: Select and deploy scanning tooling (weeks 1–4).**

For AWS: enable Amazon Inspector across all accounts. Inspector v2 continuously scans EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and ECR container images for software vulnerabilities and network-reachability issues. It integrates with AWS Security Hub, which gives you a single-pane view alongside Config findings. For EC2 instances, Inspector uses the SSM agent (already deployed if you followed Plan A's Systems Manager Inventory step), so there is minimal additional deployment.

For on-premises: deploy a credentialed vulnerability scanner. Tenable Nessus (or Tenable.sc for central management) and Qualys VMDR are the two most common in healthcare. If you chose Qualys for asset discovery in Plan A, using Qualys VMDR here avoids a second agent and unifies asset and vulnerability data. Ensure credentialed scanning is configured — uncredentialed scans miss a large percentage of vulnerabilities, and auditors know this.

For medical devices: coordinate with Biomedical Engineering. Many medical devices cannot tolerate active scanning. Use passive scanning (network traffic analysis) or rely on vendor-published vulnerability disclosures and the FDA's medical device safety communications. Tools like Claroty or Medigate are purpose-built for this if budget allows; otherwise, maintain a manual register of known vulnerabilities per device model.

**Task 1.3: Run the first full scan and establish the baseline (weeks 3–4).** Scan everything. Export the results and categorise by severity, asset type, and owner. This baseline becomes your "before" measurement. Expect the numbers to be large and alarming — this is normal for a first scan in an organisation without an established programme. Present the baseline to the CISO and IT leadership as a risk-rated summary, not a raw vulnerability count, to avoid panic and to focus attention on what matters.

### Phase 2 — Operationalise patching (weeks 5–10)

**Task 2.1: Establish patch-deployment pipelines (weeks 5–7).**

For AWS EC2: use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager. Define patch baselines (approved patch classifications and severities), maintenance windows (aligned to clinical low-activity periods — typically late-night or early morning, coordinated with clinical operations), and patch groups (by environment: dev/test/staging/prod). Patch dev and test first, validate for 24–48 hours, then promote to prod. Use SSM Compliance to report patch status.

For on-premises Windows: use WSUS or SCCM/MECM if already in place, integrated with your ITIL change process. Define deployment rings (pilot group of non-critical systems, then broader rollout). For on-premises Linux: use your existing configuration management tool (Ansible, Puppet, Chef) or native package managers with a central repository.

For third-party applications: tools like ManageEngine Patch Manager Plus, Ivanti, or PDQ Deploy handle non-OS patches (Java, Adobe, browsers, clinical application middleware). These are often the most exploited and the most neglected.

**Task 2.2: Integrate with change enablement (weeks 5–6).** Every patch deployment to production must follow your existing ITIL change process. Create a standard change template for routine, low-risk patches (e.g., monthly OS security updates to non-PHI systems) so they can be pre-approved and do not bottleneck the CAB. Emergency changes cover critical/actively-exploited vulnerabilities. Normal changes cover everything else. The change record must reference the vulnerability ID(s), affected CIs (from the CMDB), test results, back-out plan, and post-implementation verification. This generates the audit evidence the ISO 27001 auditor needs for both Annex A 8.8 (vulnerability management) and 8.32 (change management) in a single artefact.

**Task 2.3: Remediate the baseline backlog (weeks 5–10).** Prioritise the backlog from the baseline scan. Work through critical and high findings first, focusing on internet-facing systems, PHI-bearing systems, and anything with a known exploit in the wild. Track remediation as a burn-down. Do not try to reach zero — the goal is to reach a steady state where new vulnerabilities are remediated within SLA and the residual backlog contains only accepted risks with documented justification.

### Phase 3 — Continuous operations and exceptions (weeks 11–16)

**Task 3.1: Set the ongoing scanning cadence (week 11).** Amazon Inspector and Qualys/Tenable can scan continuously or near-continuously. At minimum, run authenticated scans weekly for critical assets and monthly for everything else. Run ad-hoc scans after any major change or when a new critical CVE is published (CISA KEV catalogue is a good trigger).

**Task 3.2: Build the reporting and escalation cycle (weeks 11–12).** Produce a monthly vulnerability management report for the CISO and IT leadership that includes: total open vulnerabilities by severity, percentage remediated within SLA, overdue items with owners, trend over time, and risk-accepted exceptions. This report is audit evidence for Annex A 5.35 (independent review) and ISO 27001 Clause 9 (performance evaluation). Automate it from your scanner's dashboard if possible.

**Task 3.3: Document compensating controls for unpatchable systems (weeks 11–14).** Healthcare always has systems that cannot be patched: legacy medical devices with vendor-locked OS, end-of-life clinical applications awaiting replacement, and devices under FDA premarket approval where vendor patches lag. For each, document a risk acceptance signed by the Business Owner and CISO, the compensating controls in place (network segmentation into an isolated VLAN, application-layer firewall rules, disabled unnecessary services, enhanced monitoring, restricted access), and a review date (at least every six months or when the vendor releases an update). Store these in a risk-treatment register. Auditors do not expect you to have zero unpatchable systems — they expect you to know what they are and to have treated the risk formally.

---

### Justification for emergency classification

CVE-2026-41738 is an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in PostgreSQL's SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication handler. A specially crafted authentication packet allows an unauthenticated attacker on a network path to the database listener to execute arbitrary code as the postgres OS user. CVSS 3.1 base score: 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released an emergency patch on 2026-11-19. CISA added CVE-2026-41738 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-19 with a federal remediation deadline of 2026-11-26. H-ISAC issued alert TLP:AMBER AA-2026-323A on 2026-11-19 at 09:14 ET confirming active exploitation against US hospital systems, with at least two confirmed intrusions involving data exfiltration from PostgreSQL-backed EHR databases. The affected service, app-ehr-db-01, is the primary EHR database containing PHI for approximately 487,000 active patient records. It listens on port 5432 and, while not directly internet-facing, is reachable from the application tier which is exposed through the EHR web front end. Exploitation could result in full database compromise, PHI exfiltration, ransomware deployment, and disruption of clinical operations. This change cannot wait for the next scheduled maintenance window or the standard CAB cycle.

- [ ] 3 changes of clothes, pajamas, underwear, socks

reply:
# ROOM-BY-ROOM PACKING CHECKLIST

**Labeling scheme:** Every box gets three things written on two sides and the top in thick marker: (1) the room name, (2) a short contents description, and (3) a priority tag. Use three priority tags: **OPEN FIRST** for things you need the first night, **SOON** for the first week, and **LATER** for everything else. Example: *"KITCHEN — coffee maker, mugs, filters — OPEN FIRST."* Number boxes sequentially within each room (Kitchen 1 of 8, Kitchen 2 of 8, etc.) so you can spot a missing box immediately.

---

## KITCHEN

**Estimated time:** 6–10 hours across two sessions (pack rarely used items first, daily items last)
**Estimated boxes:** 8–15 (kitchens are deceptively box-heavy because of fragile items)

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Specialty appliances you rarely use (bread maker, food processor, waffle iron)
- [ ] Bakeware, roasting pans, holiday dishes
- [ ] Cookbooks, decorative items, vases
- [ ] Extra utensils, duplicate tools, gadgets you forgot you had
- [ ] Entertaining supplies (platters, punch bowls, candles, table linens)

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most pots, pans, and mixing bowls (keep one pot, one pan, one spatula out)
- [ ] Plates, glasses, mugs (wrap each individually in packing paper — never newspaper, the ink transfers)
- [ ] Knives in blade guards or wrapped in towels and taped
- [ ] Small appliances (toaster, blender)
- [ ] Pantry dry goods that are sealed and worth moving (spices, oils, canned goods)

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The one pot, one pan, one spatula you kept out
- [ ] Coffee maker, last two mugs, dish soap, sponge, hand towel
- [ ] Trash bags, paper towels, cleaning spray (keep these accessible until the very end)

**Declutter tips:** Toss or donate anything chipped, warped, missing lids, or duplicated. Spices older than a year have lost most of their flavor. Half-empty condiments and open pantry items aren't worth moving 2,400 miles. If you haven't used a gadget in a year, donate it.

---

## LIVING ROOM

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours
**Estimated boxes:** 5–10

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Books, DVDs, games, board games (use small boxes — book boxes get brutally heavy)
- [ ] Decorative items, picture frames, wall art (wrap frames in bubble wrap or towels; label FRAGILE)
- [ ] Throw pillows, blankets you don't use daily
- [ ] Candles, coasters, shelf decor, plants you're not bringing

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Electronics: TV, gaming console, speakers, streaming devices. Photograph cable setups before unplugging. Coil cords and label them or put each device's cables in a labeled zip-lock bag taped to the device.
- [ ] Lamps (remove bulbs, wrap shades separately — they crush easily)
- [ ] Remaining blankets and throw pillows
- [ ] Curtains and rods if you're taking them

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The one blanket and pillow you used last night
- [ ] Remote controls, charging cables you used overnight
- [ ] Any cleaning supplies you used for the final wipe-down

**Declutter tips:** Books are the single heaviest category per cubic foot. Be ruthless. If you won't re-read it and it's not sentimental, donate it. Old cables, remotes for devices you no longer own, and dead batteries can go.

---

## BEDROOM(S)

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours per bedroom
**Estimated boxes:** 5–8 per bedroom

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Off-season clothing, formal wear, costumes
- [ ] Extra bedding sets, decorative pillows, spare blankets
- [ ] Jewelry you don't wear daily (carry valuable jewelry with you, not in the truck)
- [ ] Nightstand clutter: old magazines, books you've finished, random chargers
- [ ] Under-bed storage items

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most clothing. Wardrobe boxes (tall, with a hanging rod) are worth the extra cost for nice clothes. For everything else, leave clothes in dresser drawers and wrap the dresser in moving blankets; the weight is usually fine.
- [ ] Shoes (stuff socks inside to save space and hold shape)
- [ ] Remaining bedding except what you'll sleep on the last night
- [ ] Mirrors and artwork (wrap in bubble wrap, stand upright, label FRAGILE and THIS SIDE UP)

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The sheets, pillows, and blanket you slept on. Roll them into a trash bag and toss them in the car for the first night at the new place.
- [ ] Phone charger, alarm clock, bedside lamp
- [ ] Air mattress or sleeping bag if you used one the last night

**Declutter tips:** Try everything on. If it doesn't fit, isn't flattering, or hasn't been worn in a year, donate it. Shoes with worn soles aren't worth the box space. Old pillows that have lost their loft should be replaced, not moved.

---

## BATHROOM(S)

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per bathroom
**Estimated boxes:** 2–4 per bathroom

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Guest bathroom entirely (if you have one)
- [ ] Backup toiletries, bulk supplies, extra towels
- [ ] Medicine cabinet: expired medications (dispose safely at a pharmacy drop-off), first aid supplies, rarely used items
- [ ] Hair tools you don't use daily
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink (seal lids with tape and bag them upright in a plastic bin)

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most towels (keep two per person)
- [ ] Most toiletries (keep daily essentials in a zip-lock bag)
- [ ] Shower curtain, bath mat, wastebasket

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Toothbrushes, toothpaste, deodorant, face wash, contacts solution — straight into your personal bag
- [ ] Last two towels — damp is fine, stuff them in a plastic bag
- [ ] Toilet paper (keep one roll accessible until the very end, and put a fresh roll in the car for the new place)

**Declutter tips:** Expired medications and sunscreen go. Mostly-empty bottles, old razors, travel-sized products from hotels, and stained towels can all be tossed. If you have seven half-used shampoo bottles, consolidate into one.

---

## HOME OFFICE

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours
**Estimated boxes:** 4–8

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Books, reference materials, old notebooks
- [ ] Supplies you rarely use (extra printer ink, envelopes, old stationery)
- [ ] Filing cabinet contents: shred anything older than 7 years for taxes, or anything you don't need. Keep the last 3 years of tax returns, contracts, and legal documents.
- [ ] Spare cables, old hard drives, peripherals you don't use

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Printer (remove ink cartridges, bag them separately)
- [ ] Monitor (original box is best; otherwise wrap in a moving blanket and stand upright)
- [ ] Desk accessories, desk lamp, bulletin board contents
- [ ] Photograph your desk and cable setup before dismantling

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Laptop, charger, mouse — these go in your personal bag, not a box
- [ ] Any external drives or USB sticks with important data — carry these with you
- [ ] Desk phone or headset if you're working remotely during the transition

**Declutter tips:** Old manuals for products you no longer own, dead pens, dried-out markers, and broken office chairs aren't worth moving. Scan important papers and save them to cloud storage before shredding the originals if you're comfortable with digital-only copies.

---

## GARAGE / STORAGE / UTILITY AREAS

**Estimated time:** 4–8 hours (this is usually the worst room because it's been ignored the longest)
**Estimated boxes / bins:** 5–15 depending on how much you've accumulated

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out — start here if you can)**
- [ ] Seasonal items (holiday decorations, camping gear, sports equipment)
- [ ] Tools: keep a basic toolkit out (screwdriver, pliers, hammer, tape measure, box cutter) for disassembling furniture. Pack the rest.
- [ ] Lawn and garden tools — decide what's worth moving vs. selling or donating
- [ ] Paint cans, solvents, propane, aerosols — these cannot go on a moving truck. Use them up, give them away, or dispose of them through your local hazardous waste program.
- [ ] Bikes, strollers, large toys

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Remaining tools except the basic toolkit
- [ ] Cleaning supplies you're bringing (seal and bag them)
- [ ] Extension cords, flashlights, batteries

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Basic toolkit (last thing in, first thing out — you'll need it to reassemble furniture)
- [ ] Broom and dustpan for the final sweep
- [ ] Remaining cleaning supplies

**Declutter tips:** This room has the highest percentage of things that aren't worth moving. Broken items, rusty tools, dried-out paint, mystery hardware, and furniture you've been meaning to fix for two years can go. If you wouldn't buy it again, don't pay to move it.

---

## CLOSETS (hall, coat, linen, entry)

**Estimated time:** 1–3 hours total
**Estimated boxes:** 2–5

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Linen closet: extra sheet sets, tablecloths, towels beyond what you've kept out
- [ ] Coat closet: off-season jackets, scarves, hats, gloves, umbrellas
- [ ] Hall closet: board games, crafts, luggage (use luggage as packing containers for soft items)
- [ ] Entry closet: shoes, bags, reusable shopping bags

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Remaining coats and jackets
- [ ] Vacuum cleaner (but keep it accessible for the final clean)
- [ ] Ironing board, iron, hangers you're keeping

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Vacuum cleaner after the final pass
- [ ] Last coats or jackets

**Declutter tips:** Wire hangers can go back to the dry cleaner. Mismatched sheet sets, threadbare towels, and broken umbrellas aren't worth packing. If you have more luggage than you use on your most ambitious trip, donate the extras.

---

## BOX COUNT SUMMARY (1–2 bedroom apartment, two adults)

| Room | Estimated Boxes |
|---|---|
| Kitchen | 8–15 |
| Living Room | 5–10 |
| Bedroom 1 (primary) | 5–8 |
| Bedroom 2 (guest/spare) | 3–6 |
| Bathroom(s) | 2–4 each |
| Home Office | 4–8 |
| Garage / Storage | 5–15 |
| Closets (all) | 2–5 |
| **Total estimate** | **34–71** |

Order 10–15% more boxes than you think you'll need. You'll use them. Small boxes for heavy things (books, tools, cans), medium for general items, large for light bulky things (pillows, lampshades, linens). Never put heavy items in large boxes.

---

**General rule:** Cancel Ohio services for the day *after* you leave (so you have service on your last full day). Start Oregon services for the day *before* you arrive (so they're live when you walk in). Confirm everything in writing or by email, and screenshot the confirmations.

## HOW TO TRACK CANCELLATIONS

Create a simple spreadsheet or note with four columns: **Service Name, Date Notified, Confirmation Number, Final Bill Date.** Check each one off as you get written confirmation. Screenshot every cancellation confirmation email or chat transcript. Services that don't confirm in writing should be followed up with a phone call.

---
---

# COPY-PASTE TEMPLATES

Each template below is meant to be edited with your real details. Brackets [ ] mark the parts you fill in. Keep the tone short and professional — these aren't negotiation letters, they're notifications.

---

## 1. LANDLORD NOTICE — Written Notice to Vacate

**Who sends:** J (both names on the lease should sign or be named)
**How to send:** Email and printed letter if your lease requires written notice. Send both to be safe. Keep a copy.
**When to send:** Check your lease for the required notice period (usually 30 or 60 days). Send on or before that deadline.

**Subject line:** Notice to Vacate — [Your Address] — Effective [Date]

```
Dear [Landlord Name / Property Management Company],

This letter serves as our formal [30/60]-day notice to vacate the property at [full address, including unit number]. Our intended move-out date is [date]. We request a move-out inspection and ask that our security deposit be returned to our forwarding address: [new Oregon address or a reliable forwarding address].

Please let us know if you need anything else from us to complete the move-out process.

Sincerely,
[Your Name] and [Partner's Name]
[Phone number]
[Email]
```

---

## 2. CABLE / INTERNET — Cancellation Request

**Who sends:** P
**How to send:** Phone is fastest, but follow up with email or chat so you have a written record. Ask for a confirmation number.
**When to send:** 1–2 weeks before move-out date.

**Subject line:** Account Cancellation Request — Account #[number] — Effective [Date]

```
Hello,

I'd like to cancel our internet/cable service at [full address] effective [last day of service, ideally the day after you move out]. Our account number is [number] under the name [name on the account].

Please confirm the cancellation, the final bill amount, and instructions for returning any equipment (modem, router, cable box). I'd like written confirmation of this cancellation by email.

Thank you,
[Name]
[Phone number]
```

---

## 3. ELECTRICITY / GAS — Stop Service

**Who sends:** M
**How to send:** Most utilities let you do this online or by phone. Follow up with email if possible.
**When to send:** 5–7 business days before move-out.

**Subject line:** Request to Disconnect Service — Account #[number] — [Address]

```
Hello,

Please schedule a final meter read and disconnect service at [full address] effective [date, the day after move-out]. Our account number is [number] under [name on the account].

Please send the final bill to our new address: [Oregon address]. If a deposit refund is due, please send it to the same address.

Thank you,
[Name]
[Phone number]
```

- New Oregon address (the one you're moving to)

# OHIO → OREGON DRIVE ROUTE PLANNER

**Route:** I-80 West across Ohio, Indiana, Iowa, Nebraska, Wyoming → I-84 West through Idaho and into Oregon. This is roughly 2,300–2,500 miles depending on your starting city in Ohio and destination in Oregon. The I-80/I-84 corridor is the most common and well-serviced route for this move.

**Important caveat:** Drive times below assume decent weather and no major construction. Check road conditions before each day's departure, especially through Wyoming and the Blue Mountains in Oregon. In late fall or winter, carry chains and check WYDOT and TripCheck.com (Oregon) for pass conditions. Summer is generally clear but can be very hot through Nebraska and Wyoming.

---

## 3-DAY OPTION (long days, not ideal with a dog)

| Day | Start → End | Miles | Drive Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ohio → Lincoln/Omaha, NE | ~750–800 | ~11–12 hrs | Very long. Only do this if you leave at dawn. |
| 2 | Lincoln/Omaha → Salt Lake City, UT | ~850 | ~12–13 hrs | Brutal. Wyoming is beautiful but empty. |
| 3 | Salt Lake City → Oregon destination | ~600–750 | ~9–11 hrs | Through Boise and into Oregon on I-84. |

This pace is hard on you and harder on the dog. Not recommended unless you're under a strict deadline.

---

## 4-DAY OPTION (recommended with a dog)

This is the pace I'd suggest. Days are manageable, the dog gets real breaks, and you arrive without being wrecked.

**Day 1: Ohio → Des Moines or Omaha area**
- Miles: ~550–650 depending on where in Ohio you start
- Drive time: ~8–9 hours with stops
- Terrain: flat, easy, Interstate the whole way
- Dog stops: rest areas every 60–90 miles along I-80 through Indiana and Iowa are plentiful and usually have grass
- Overnight: Des Moines or Omaha. Both have plenty of dog-friendly hotels and restaurants with patios.

**Day 2: Des Moines/Omaha → Cheyenne or Rawlins, WY**
- Miles: ~500–550
- Drive time: ~7–8 hours with stops
- Terrain: Nebraska is flat and long. Western Nebraska gets more scenic. Wyoming starts climbing.
- Dog stops: rest areas thin out in western Nebraska. Plan fuel and bathroom stops at exits with truck stops. Bring water for the dog at every stop.
- Overnight: Cheyenne is a bigger town with more hotel options. Rawlins is smaller but puts you further west and shortens Day 3. Either works.

**Day 3: Cheyenne/Rawlins → Boise, ID**
- Miles: ~550–650
- Drive time: ~8–10 hours with stops
- Terrain: across Wyoming on I-80, then north on US-30 or I-15 through Pocatello to I-84 near Twin Falls, then west to Boise. Alternatively, continue I-80 to I-84 through Ogden/Salt Lake City if you prefer that junction. The SLC route adds ~30 min but is better-serviced.
- Dog stops: Wyoming has long empty stretches. Fill up on gas whenever you're below half a tank. Rest areas exist but are spaced out. Idaho is better.
- Overnight: Boise. Good city with dog-friendly parks, restaurants, and hotels. The Boise River Greenbelt is a great place to let the dog stretch.

**Day 4: Boise → Oregon destination**
- Miles: ~350–450 to Portland metro, ~250–350 to Bend area, ~400–500 to Eugene area
- Drive time: ~5–8 hours depending on destination
- Terrain: I-84 follows the Snake River, then climbs through the Blue Mountains near La Grande and Pendleton, then descends along the Columbia River Gorge into Portland. If your destination is south of Portland, you'll peel off onto US-97 or other routes.
- Dog stops: good rest areas along I-84. The Columbia Gorge is stunning — if you have time, stop at a viewpoint.
- Arrival: aim to arrive by mid-afternoon so you have daylight to unload essentials and set up the dog's space.

---

## DOG TRAVEL TIPS FOR THE DRIVE

Stop every 2–3 hours for 15–20 minutes. Let the dog walk, sniff, drink water, and go to the bathroom. Bring a gallon jug of water from home so the dog's stomach doesn't react to changing water sources along the route.

Never leave the dog in a parked car, even with windows cracked. Summer temps in Nebraska and Wyoming can push a parked car past 120°F in minutes.

Feed the dog a light meal in the morning and a normal meal at the hotel in the evening. Some dogs get carsick if they eat a full meal before driving. Keep treats small and infrequent.

A crate or crash-tested harness is safer than letting the dog roam the car. If the dog is anxious, a Thundershirt, calming chews, or a vet-prescribed mild sedative can help. Test any medication on a short drive before the trip so you know how the dog reacts.

Bring a lint roller and a seat cover. You'll thank yourself.

---

## DOG-FRIENDLY HOTEL CHAINS AND TYPICAL PET FEES

Call ahead or check the specific location's pet policy before booking. Policies vary by franchise location even within the same chain. Fees listed are typical ranges as of 2024–2025 and may have changed.

| Chain | Typical Pet Fee | Weight Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| La Quinta by Wyndham | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit | One of the most consistently dog-friendly chains. No deposit at most locations. Two pets max at most locations. |
| Motel 6 / Studio 6 | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit | Budget option. Quality varies. Call ahead to confirm. |
| Red Roof Inn | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit (one pet) | Similar to Motel 6 in price and variability. |
| Best Western | $10–$50/night per pet | Varies by location, often 80 lbs | Some locations don't accept pets. Always call. |
| Holiday Inn / IHG brands | $25–$75/night or per stay | Varies, often 50–80 lbs | Pet fees and weight limits vary significantly by location. |
| Drury Inn & Suites | $35–$50/night per room | Usually 80 lbs | Includes free hot breakfast, which helps the budget. |
| Marriott (select brands) | $25–$150 per stay or per night | Varies widely by brand and location | Residence Inn and TownePlace Suites tend to be more pet-friendly than full-service Marriotts. |
| Kimpton Hotels | Usually no fee | No weight limit | Upscale option, not everywhere along I-80. |

**Booking tip:** BringFido.com lets you filter by pet-friendly hotels along a route. Book refundable rates when possible since your driving pace might change.

---

## EMERGENCY VET CLINICS ALONG THE ROUTE

**Important:** Verify hours, availability, and addresses before you travel. Emergency vet clinics change ownership, hours, and locations. Save these as contacts in your phone before you leave, and do a quick Google Maps search the morning of each driving day to confirm the nearest 24-hour option along that day's stretch.

**Salt Lake City area (Day 2 or 3, depending on route)**
- Search for "24 hour emergency vet Salt Lake City" the morning you'll be in that area
- The SLC metro area generally has multiple 24-hour emergency veterinary hospitals. Look near I-15 and I-80 interchange area for quick highway access.
- There are also emergency vet options in Ogden (north of SLC) and Provo (south) if you're passing through those areas instead.

**Boise, ID (Day 3 overnight)**
- Search for "24 hour emergency vet Boise Idaho" before you arrive
- Boise is a mid-size metro and typically has at least one or two 24-hour emergency vet hospitals. Your hotel front desk can also help in a pinch.
- If you're stopping in Twin Falls earlier in the day, search for emergency vet options there as well, though options are more limited in smaller Idaho cities.

**Pendleton / La Grande, OR (Day 4, mid-route)**
- These are small towns. 24-hour emergency vet availability is limited and may not exist locally.
- Search for "emergency vet Pendleton Oregon" and "emergency vet La Grande Oregon" before entering this stretch. Identify the nearest option and save the number.
- If this stretch concerns you, consider stopping in La Grande for a break and assessing the dog's condition. The next well-serviced area is the Tri-Cities in Washington (Kennewick/Richland, about 45 minutes north of I-84 via US-395) or The Dalles and Hood River further west along I-84.
- Once you reach the Portland metro area, multiple 24-hour emergency veterinary hospitals are available.

**General advice for emergencies on the road:** Keep your dog's medical records, medications, and your home vet's phone number accessible. If the dog has a known condition (seizures, allergies, heart issues), write a one-page medical summary with the dog's name, breed, weight, conditions, medications, and your vet's contact info. Keep it in the dog travel kit. Any emergency vet will appreciate having that information immediately.
