# FIRST-WEEK UNPACK PRIORITY CHECKLIST

Don't try to unpack everything in the first week. Unpack what you need to function, sleep, eat, and work. Everything else can wait.

---

**BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE (arrival day, first 30 minutes)**

- [ ] Walk through every room and photograph existing damage before anything is unloaded
- [ ] Confirm water, electricity, gas, and heat/AC are working
- [ ] Locate the breaker box, water shutoff valve, and gas shutoff
- [ ] Set up the dog's space first: water bowl, food bowl, bed or blanket, one toy, in a quiet room away from the chaos. Close the door or use a baby gate so the dog has a safe retreat.
- [ ] Unload your personal overnight bags and the moving day car kit

**DAY 1 EVENING — sleep and basic function**

- [ ] Set up beds or air mattresses. Put on sheets and pillows. This is the single most important unpack task — a bad first night makes everything harder.
- [ ] Unpack the bathroom OPEN FIRST box: toilet paper, towels, soap, toothbrushes, shower curtain
- [ ] Unpack the kitchen OPEN FIRST box: coffee maker, mugs, one pot, one pan, dish soap, sponge, paper towels, trash bags
- [ ] Set up one lamp or light source in each room you'll use tonight
- [ ] Plug in and charge all phones and laptops
- [ ] Take the dog for a walk around the neighborhood. Let them sniff and start learning the new territory.
- [ ] Order food or eat something simple. You are not cooking tonight.

**DAY 2 — kitchen and living room basics**

- [ ] Unpack remaining kitchen boxes marked OPEN FIRST and SOON
- [ ] Put away dishes, utensils, pots, and pans. Don't worry about optimizing cabinet layout yet.
- [ ] Set up the coffee station properly. Morale matters.
- [ ] Unpack the living room seating area: couch, chairs, TV if you want it. You need a place to sit and decompress.
- [ ] Break down empty boxes as you go and stack them in the garage or a closet. They pile up fast.

**DAY 3 — bedrooms and closets**

- [ ] Unpack clothing into closets and dressers. Hang what you can; stack the rest.
- [ ] Set up nightstands, lamps, alarm clocks
- [ ] Make the bed properly — this is now home, not a campsite
- [ ] Unpack the linen closet: towels, sheets, blankets

**DAY 4 — home office and connectivity**

- [ ] Set up your desk, monitor, keyboard, and chair

**DAY 5 — bathrooms, remaining kitchen, and dog admin**

- [ ] Walk to or drive by the nearest grocery store, pharmacy, and gas station. Learn the neighborhood basics.
- [ ] Update the dog's microchip with the new address

**DAYS 6–7 — garage, storage, decor, and settling in**

- [ ] Unpack garage and storage boxes. Set up tools, cleaning supplies, outdoor gear.
- [ ] Hang pictures and artwork. This is when a place starts feeling like home.
- [ ] Unpack remaining decor, books, and personal items
- [ ] Do a full grocery shop for the week ahead
- [ ] Take the dog to explore a local park or trail
- [ ] Sit down together and make a list of anything you still need to buy, fix, or handle in week two

**WEEK 2 AND BEYOND**

- [ ] Oregon DMV: driver's license and vehicle registration
- [ ] Oregon dog license from your county or city
- [ ] Emissions test if required
- [ ] Find a dentist, doctor, and pharmacy
- [ ] Update remaining subscriptions and memberships with new address
- [ ] Explore your neighborhood for real. Find the coffee shop, the hardware store, the good takeout place, the dog-friendly spots.

## SPREADSHEET TIPS

**Column-by-column guidance:**

"Box ID" uses the room abbreviation scheme above (KIT-01, BED1-03, etc.). Keep it consistent.

"Box # / Total" is the count within that room. You won't know the total until you're done packing that room, so leave the total blank and fill it in at the end. Write it on the labels at the same time.

"Contents (short)" is what goes on the physical label — a quick 3–5 word description you can read from across the room.

"Contents (detailed)" is the full list of what's inside. This is what you'll search when you're in Oregon wondering which box has the can opener.

"Est. Weight" helps movers and helps you decide what goes on the truck first (heavy on the bottom). Don't overthink it. "Light," "medium," and "heavy" work too if you don't want to guess pounds.

"Fragile" matches the checkbox on the label.

"Priority" matches the label: OPEN FIRST, SOON, or LATER.

"Destination" is where the box goes in the new home. This matches the "Destination" line on the label and aligns with the furniture placement worksheets you're taping to each door.

"Mover Notes" is anything special: "keep upright," "do not stack," "unload last," "this box is weirdly heavy."

"Packed By" is M, P, or J. Useful when one of you is looking for something and the other one packed it.

"Packed Date" and "Opened Date" help you track progress and notice if any box never got opened, which probably means you didn't need what was inside.

"Photo" is optional but useful. Snap a photo of the box contents before you seal it, name the file to match the Box ID, and save to a shared folder (Google Photos album or Google Drive folder). If you file a claim for damage, you'll have photographic proof of condition and contents.

---

## SHARING THE SPREADSHEET

Create the sheet in Google Sheets and share it with your partner so both of you can update it in real time from your phones. Bookmark it on both phones. As you pack each box, one person fills in the row while the other tapes the label. It takes about 60 seconds per box once you're in a rhythm.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Kitchen & Living Room

---

## KITCHEN

The kitchen takes the longest and breaks the most stuff. Start here early — you use fewer kitchen items daily than you think.

**Estimated total time:** 8–12 hours across multiple sessions

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Go through every drawer and cabinet once before you touch a box. For each item, ask: *Have we used this in the last year? Can we replace it for under $20 in Oregon? Are we keeping duplicates?*

Common kitchen cuts that save real weight and box space: mismatched tupperware and lids (keep only nesting sets), chipped mugs and glasses, duplicate spatulas and wooden spoons, expired spices and pantry items (check the shelf — most people find 10–15 expired items), single-use gadgets you bought optimistically (bread maker, fondue pot, spiralizer), old cookbooks you haven't opened (photograph favorite recipes instead), and cleaning supplies that are cheaper to rebuy than to move.

Donate or sell anything in good shape. Most Goodwills and Habitat ReStores take kitchen items. Post bigger items on your local Buy Nothing group or Facebook Marketplace. For hazardous items like propane, lighter fluid, and certain cleaners, check your Ohio county's household hazardous waste drop-off — movers won't take them and they can't go in a truck safely.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Rarely used items (Weeks 6–5)** — **P**, 3–4 hrs

- [ ] Baking dishes, specialty pans, cake pans, muffin tins
- [ ] Holiday and entertaining dishes, serving platters, punch bowls
- [ ] Small appliances you won't use before the move (stand mixer, blender, food processor, slow cooker, waffle iron)
- [ ] Fine china or fragile glassware (wine glasses, stemware)
- [ ] Cookbooks (keep 1–2 favorites out if you cook from them)
- [ ] Vases, candles, decorative items stored in the kitchen
- [ ] Extra dish towels, tablecloths, cloth napkins

*Packing tip:* Wrap each plate individually in packing paper (not newspaper — the ink transfers). Stack plates vertically like records, not flat. They're stronger on edge. Nest bowls with paper between them. Put a "FRAGILE — THIS SIDE UP" note on every dish box and don't stack heavy boxes on top.

**Wave 2: Most of the kitchen (Week 3–2)** — **P**, 3–4 hrs

- [ ] Most pots and pans (keep one skillet, one saucepan out)
- [ ] Most utensils (keep one chef's knife, one spatula, one wooden spoon, tongs)
- [ ] Most cups and mugs (keep 2 each)
- [ ] Toaster, coffee maker (switch to pour-over or instant for the last week if you can stand it)
- [ ] Cutting boards beyond one
- [ ] Spice rack (tape lids, bag them in a zip-lock in case of leaks, pack upright)
- [ ] Pantry items you're keeping (dry goods, canned items — these are heavy, use small boxes)
- [ ] Drawer organizers, junk drawer contents, rubber bands, twist ties

*Packing tip:* Small boxes for heavy items. A large box full of canned goods can hit 60–70 lbs and will tear or hurt someone. Keep each kitchen box under 30–35 lbs. Fill gaps with dish towels or packing paper so nothing shifts.

**Wave 3: Last-day kitchen (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Remaining skillet, saucepan, spatula, knife, tongs
- [ ] Last 2 mugs and 2 plates
- [ ] Dish soap, sponge, one hand towel
- [ ] Trash bags (keep a few out — you'll need them on moving day)
- [ ] Paper towels (last roll stays out until the truck is loaded)
- [ ] Remaining cleaning supplies for the final wipe-down

*Label this box "OPEN FIRST — KITCHEN" and put it in the car or last on the truck.*

---

## LIVING ROOM

The living room is usually faster than people expect because so much of it is furniture the movers handle. The real work is the stuff *on* and *around* the furniture.

**Estimated total time:** 5–8 hours across sessions (longer because of your 200 books and the bike)

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Books are the big decision here. At roughly 200 volumes, you're looking at 10–13 medium boxes weighing 30–40 lbs each. That's real truck space and real weight on a moving estimate. Some options to consider together: keep the ones that matter to you emotionally, professionally, or that you'll reread; sell or donate the rest. Half Price Books buys in bulk and gives you a quote on the spot. Little Free Libraries, local library donation programs, and Buy Nothing groups move books fast. If you're on the fence about a title, take a photo of the spine and let it go — you can rebuy or borrow later.

Beyond books, common living room cuts include old magazines, dead remotes, cables and chargers for devices you no longer own, board games with missing pieces, DVDs and CDs you've replaced with streaming, throw pillows and blankets that are worn, and decor that doesn't fit the new space.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Shelves and storage (Weeks 5–4)** — **M**, 3–4 hrs (books take time)

- [ ] **Books:** Pack in small or medium boxes only — a large box of books is a back injury. Stand hardcovers upright, spine down. Lay paperbacks flat in alternating directions. Fill gaps with packing paper so they don't shift. Label each box "BOOKS — HEAVY" and number them (Books 1 of 13, etc.) so you know if one goes missing.
- [ ] DVDs, CDs, vinyl records, video games
- [ ] Photo albums and framed photos (wrap frames in bubble wrap or towels; put cardboard corners on anything with glass)
- [ ] Board games and puzzles (rubber-band the lids shut)
- [ ] Decorative objects, candles, bookends, sculptures
- [ ] Seasonal items stored in living room closets

**Wave 2: Surfaces and electronics (Week 3–2)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Lamps (remove bulbs and shades separately; wrap shades in large bags or pillowcases)
- [ ] Electronics: TV, gaming console, speakers, router, streaming devices. Photograph the cable setup behind each device before you unplug anything — you'll thank yourself later. Coil each cable and label it or bag it with the device it belongs to. If you still have original TV or console boxes, use them. If not, get a TV box from a moving supply store or U-Haul — TVs are expensive to replace.
- [ ] Remotes (bag them together, label "LIVING ROOM REMOTES")
- [ ] Throw blankets, decorative pillows you're keeping
- [ ] Side table and coffee table contents (coasters, trays, magazines)
- [ ] Area rugs (roll tightly, secure with packing tape or rope; if they'll be in the truck more than a few days, wrap in plastic to prevent moisture damage)

**Wave 3: Furniture prep (Week 1 / Moving day)** — **J**, 1–2 hrs (or movers handle)

- [ ] **Queen mattress:** Get a mattress bag (around $10–$15 at any moving supply store). Slide it on before it goes in the truck. If you're using movers, they usually provide one — confirm ahead of time. Transport the mattress on its side if possible so it doesn't get crushed under boxes.
- [ ] **Bike:** Remove the front wheel and pedals if you can (5 min with a wrench). Wrap the frame in moving blankets or bubble wrap and secure with tape. If you have a bike box from a shop, use it. If the bike is going in a truck with movers, point it out and ask them to strap it — bikes get damaged easily when they shift. If it's going on a car rack, make sure the rack is rated for highway speeds and cross-country distance.
- [ ] Couch cushions (bag them in large trash bags to keep them clean)
- [ ] Disassemble shelving, media console, and tables if needed. Bag all hardware in a zip-lock and tape it to the furniture piece it belongs to. Keep the Allen wrenches with the hardware.
- [ ] Vacuum and wipe down the empty room before the walk-through

---

## Quick-Reference: Box Counts (Estimates)

| Category | Approx. Boxes | Box Size | Weight per Box |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kitchen dishes and glassware | 4–6 | Medium | 25–35 lbs |
| Kitchen pantry and dry goods | 2–4 | Small | 30–40 lbs |
| Kitchen appliances | 2–3 | Medium/Large | 15–30 lbs |
| Kitchen misc (utensils, towels, etc.) | 2–3 | Medium | 15–25 lbs |
| Books (200 volumes) | 10–13 | Small/Medium | 30–40 lbs |
| Living room decor and media | 3–5 | Medium | 15–25 lbs |
| Electronics | 2–3 | Varies | Varies |
| Lamps and shades | 1–2 | Large | 10–15 lbs |

---

Ready for bedrooms, bathroom, and garage/storage whenever you are. The garage section will also cover general outdoor gear, tools, and anything that movers won't transport (fuel, paint, propane, etc.).

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Bedrooms, Bathroom & Garage/Storage

---

## MASTER BEDROOM

The bedroom feels simple until you open the closets. Clothes and linens are bulky, not heavy, so the challenge is volume, not weight. Your queen mattress is already bagged from the living room prep — good.

**Estimated total time:** 6–9 hours across sessions

---

### Declutter First (Week 7–6) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Closets are where moves get expensive because you're paying by space or truck footage to haul things you forgot you owned. Pull everything out of both closets and sort into four piles: keep, donate, sell, trash. Some guidelines that help: if you haven't worn it in a year and it doesn't have sentimental or seasonal value, let it go. Shoes you don't love walking in won't improve in Oregon. Stretched-out basics like old t-shirts and underwear are cheaper to replace than to move. Coats and heavy winter gear still matter — Oregon's winters are milder than Ohio's in the valleys but you'll want layers, especially if you're near the mountains or the coast.

For linens, most households have 2–3x more bedding than they use. Keep one set per bed plus one backup. Donate flat or stained pillows, mismatched sheet sets, and the guest bedding you never actually put on a guest bed. Old comforters and blankets in decent shape go fast at donation centers.

Nightstand drawers tend to accumulate cables, old glasses, random batteries, receipts, and half-read books. Empty them completely and only put back what you'd actually set up on a nightstand in the new place.

---

### Pack in Three Waves

**Wave 1: Off-season and storage (Weeks 5–4)** — **P**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Off-season clothes (heavy coats if moving in summer, shorts and sandals if winter). Use wardrobe boxes if the budget allows — they keep hanging clothes clean and wrinkle-free and cost about $10–$15 each. You'll need roughly 2–4 depending on how much you kept.
- [ ] Formal wear, suits, dresses you won't wear before the move
- [ ] Extra shoes and boots (stuff socks or packing paper inside each shoe to hold its shape, then pair them in bags)
- [ ] Spare bedding sets, extra pillows, quilts
- [ ] Luggage and duffel bags (pack soft items inside them — they're free boxes)
- [ ] Memorabilia, keepsakes, jewelry you don't wear daily (wrap fine jewelry individually and keep it in your car documents pouch, not the truck)
- [ ] Under-bed storage bins and their contents (sort before repacking)
- [ ] Seasonal decor stored in bedroom closets

*Packing tip:* Dresser drawers full of folded clothes can sometimes stay in the dresser if you're using movers — ask them. If DIY, pull the drawers out and wrap them in stretch wrap to keep the clothes in place, then stack them. This saves boxes and time.

**Wave 2: Most of the closet and surfaces (Week 3–2)** — **P**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Most hanging clothes (leave 4–5 days of outfits out). Wardrobe boxes or the trash-bag-over-hangers trick: punch a small hole in the bottom of a large trash bag, slide 8–10 hangers through the hole so the hooks poke out, and tie the bag loosely at the bottom. Keeps clothes clean and together.
- [ ] Most folded clothes from dressers (keep 2 outfits per person out)
- [ ] Most shoes (keep one everyday pair and one weather-appropriate pair out)
- [ ] Mirrors and wall art (wrap in bubble wrap, then sandwich between two pieces of cardboard taped together; label "GLASS" and store vertically in the truck)
- [ ] Alarm clock, fan, humidifier, white noise machine
- [ ] Hamper and iron/ironing board
- [ ] Curtains and rods (if you're taking them — measure the new windows first)
- [ ] Rugs

**Wave 3: Bedside kits and final strip (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 1–1.5 hrs

- [ ] Strip the bed. The mattress is already bagged. Roll sheets and the last pillowcase into a bag.
- [ ] **Keep one bedside kit per person — do not pack these. They go in the car:**
  - Phone charger and backup battery
  - Current medications and vitamins (with original labels)
  - 2 changes of clothes (one for travel, one for arrival day)
  - Toothbrush, deodorant, face wash (small bag)
  - Glasses or contacts and solution
  - Sleep essentials if you're staying in hotels: earplugs, eye mask, melatonin if you use it
- [ ] Pack the last pillow per person into the car for road-trip naps — not the truck
- [ ] Disassemble the bed frame. Bag all bolts, screws, and slats hardware in a zip-lock and tape it directly to the frame rail. Keep the Allen key or wrench with it. Photograph the assembly if the frame is complicated.
- [ ] Nightstands: empty the last drawer, wipe down, done
- [ ] Final vacuum and wipe

---

### Guest Bedroom / Office (if applicable)

If you have a second bedroom used as a guest room or office, it usually packs in a single session because there's less daily-use stuff.

**Estimated total time:** 2–4 hours — **M**, all in one session during Week 4–3

- [ ] Desk contents: sort paperwork (shred what you don't need, file what you do into the car documents folder)
- [ ] Computer, monitor, keyboard, mouse (photograph cable setup, coil and label each cable, use original boxes if you have them)
- [ ] Printer (remove ink cartridges and bag them separately — they leak in transit)
- [ ] Office supplies: keep a pen, a notepad, tape, and a marker out until moving day, pack the rest
- [ ] Guest bedding and pillows (donate if worn)
- [ ] Closet overflow: often this is where the random storage lives — holiday decor, luggage, old hobby supplies. Declutter hard here.
- [ ] Bookshelf contents (most books should already be packed from the living room wave)

---

## BATHROOM(S)

Bathrooms are small but deceptively time-consuming because of liquids, sharps, and the sheer number of tiny items crammed under the sink.

**Estimated total time:** 2–3 hours per bathroom

---

### Declutter First (Week 6–5) — **J**, 1 hr per bathroom

The medicine cabinet and under-sink area are the two biggest purge zones in any home. Check expiration dates on everything. Most people find medications, sunscreen, and skincare products that expired 1–3 years ago. Expired medications should go to a pharmacy take-back program or an FDA-approved disposal location, not down the drain or in the trash (some exceptions exist — check FDA guidelines or ask your pharmacist). Expired cosmetics and skincare can go in the trash.

Other common bathroom cuts: hotel shampoo and lotion collections, hair products that didn't work for you, duplicate razors and toothbrushes still in packaging (donate unopened toiletries to a local shelter — they always need them), ratty towels and washcloths beyond what you actually use (keep 2 per person plus 2 for the dog), cleaning supplies that are nearly empty, and the curling iron or styling tool you haven't plugged in since 2021.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Cabinets and storage (Week 3–2)** — **M**, 1.5–2 hrs per bathroom

- [ ] Backup toiletries and bulk items (extra shampoo, soap, toothpaste)
- [ ] First aid kit (restock anything missing before you move — you'll want a full kit in the car)
- [ ] Medications you aren't currently taking (keep current prescriptions in your bedside kit)
- [ ] Hair tools you won't use in the next 2 weeks (wrap cords around each tool and rubber-band them)
- [ ] Towels and washcloths beyond your daily set (use them as packing material for fragile items — dual purpose)
- [ ] Bathroom decor, extra mirrors, soap dishes, organizers
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink (see the movers-won't-transport list at the end — some cleaners are restricted)
- [ ] Scale, step stool, trash can

*Packing tip:* Liquids leak. Put every bottle in a zip-lock bag or wrap it in cling wrap with a rubber band over the cap. Pack liquids upright in a small box lined with a trash bag. Label it "LIQUIDS — UPRIGHT" on all sides. Even with precautions, consider whether a half-empty bottle of conditioner is worth the risk to the box of towels beneath it.

**Wave 2: Daily-use strip (Moving day minus 1)** — **J**, 30–45 min

- [ ] Last towels (1 per person for the final shower)
- [ ] Shower curtain and rings (if you're taking them)
- [ ] Toilet paper — keep 2 rolls out until the last moment, then toss them in the car
- [ ] Hand soap
- [ ] Toothbrush, toothpaste, face wash, deodorant, razor — these go in your bedside travel bag, not a box
- [ ] Prescription medications — bedside kit, not a box
- [ ] Final wipe-down of counters, toilet, mirror, floor
- [ ] Plunger and toilet brush: honestly, consider leaving these and buying new ones in Oregon. If keeping, bag them in trash bags.

---

## GARAGE / STORAGE / OUTDOOR

This is where moves stall. Garages accumulate years of "I'll deal with it later" items, and a surprising number of common garage contents are prohibited from moving trucks. Start the garage early and treat it as a major declutter event, not just a packing task.

**Estimated total time:** 8–14 hours (the widest range because garage contents vary enormously)

---

### Declutter First (Week 8–6) — **J**, 3–5 hrs

Walk through the entire garage and sort everything into zones: tools, automotive, sports and outdoor, holiday, chemicals and paint, and "why do we have this." Be ruthless. You're paying per pound or per cubic foot to haul this across the country.

Specific declutter targets: partially used paint cans (take the lids to a paint store and get color-match codes saved to your phone, then dispose of the paint properly through your county's hazardous waste program), old motor oil and automotive fluids (auto parts stores like AutoZone accept used oil for free), broken tools and duplicates, garden hoses and sprinklers that are cracked or leaking, pots with no plants and soil bags, rusty or wobbly shelving, holiday lights that are half-burnt-out, that box of random screws and nails and hardware — keep it if it's organized, dump it if it's chaos.

The bike is already prepped from the living room section (front wheel and pedals removed, frame wrapped).

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Stored and seasonal items (Weeks 5–4)** — **M**, 3–5 hrs

- [ ] Holiday decorations (consolidate into fewer bins if possible — ornaments get their own small box with dividers or egg-carton-style packing)
- [ ] Camping and outdoor gear: tent, sleeping bags, camp stove (empty fuel canisters completely and do not pack them — see prohibited list), coolers, hiking packs
- [ ] Sports equipment: balls, rackets, golf clubs, skis, snowboard. Wrap heads and blades individually. Golf bags can stay assembled.
- [ ] Lawn and garden tools you're keeping: shovels, rakes, pruners. Bundle long-handled tools together with rope or bungee cords. Clean soil off everything — Oregon has agricultural inspection stations and dirty tools can cause delays or questions.
- [ ] Power tools: drain all fuel from gas-powered tools (mower, leaf blower, chainsaw, trimmer) completely. Even fumes can be a hazard in an enclosed truck. Wrap blades and bits. Coil cords and label.
- [ ] Hand tools: wrenches, screwdrivers, hammer, pliers, socket set. A tool bag or small toolbox keeps these together. Keep one basic set out until moving day (screwdriver, pliers, adjustable wrench, box cutter, tape measure) for furniture disassembly.
- [ ] Workbench contents: sort hardware into labeled bags. Throw away rusted or unidentified fasteners.
- [ ] Luggage and storage bins you didn't already pack from the bedroom
- [ ] Ladders: if full-size, consider whether it's worth moving vs. buying in Oregon. Extension ladders eat truck space.
- [ ] Bike accessories: helmet, pump, lock, lights, panniers — bag together and label

**Wave 2: Final garage items (Week 1)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Remaining tools (the set you kept out for disassembly goes in the car for reassembly at the new place)
- [ ] Broom and dustpan (last items — you'll sweep the garage floor)
- [ ] Trash cans and recycling bins (empty, clean, usually not worth moving unless they're nice)
- [ ] Garden hose (drain completely, coil, and secure)
- [ ] Grill: clean it out, remove and properly dispose of the propane tank (see below), wrap grates
- [ ] Shelving units: disassemble, bag hardware, label
- [ ] Sweep and photograph the empty garage

---

## ITEMS MOVERS WON'T TRANSPORT

Federal and carrier regulations prohibit these from commercial moving trucks. If you're driving a DIY truck, some of these are still illegal or dangerous to transport. Dispose of them properly before the move.

**Flammable Liquids and Gases**
- Propane tanks (even "empty" ones — exchange or return to a Blue Rhino or AmeriGas location, or check your local fire department's disposal program)
- Gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid
- Paint thinner, turpentine, mineral spirits, acetone
- Lamp oil

**Paints and Chemicals**
- Latex and oil-based paints (dry latex paint can go in regular trash in many municipalities — mix with cat litter and let it harden, then check local rules)
- Stains and varnishes
- Pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers with chemicals
- Pool chemicals
- Household cleaners containing bleach, ammonia, or acid (some movers allow sealed, consumer-size cleaners — ask yours specifically)

**Automotive**
- Motor oil and transmission fluid (AutoZone, O'Reilly, and similar stores accept used oil)
- Antifreeze
- Brake fluid
- Car batteries (auto parts stores often accept these for recycling)

**Pressurized Containers**
- Aerosol cans of any kind (spray paint, hairspray, cooking spray, WD-40, compressed air dusters)
- Fire extinguishers (some movers accept these — ask, but don't assume)
- CO2 cartridges
- Scuba tanks

**Batteries and Electronics**
- Car batteries (see above)
- Loose lithium batteries (tape terminals and keep them with you if you need to transport them)
- Damaged or swollen lithium batteries (do not transport — take to a battery recycling drop-off like Call2Recycle locations at Lowe's, Home Depot, or Best Buy)

**Explosives and Ammunition**
- Firearms ammunition (transport in your personal vehicle following federal and state laws for each state you pass through — research Ohio, Indiana/Illinois/Iowa or whichever route you take, Nebraska/Wyoming, and Oregon laws individually, or ship via a licensed dealer)
- Fireworks
- Flares

**Perishable and Living**
- Perishable food (opened, refrigerated, or frozen — eat it, give it away, or toss it)
- Plants (many movers won't take them, and Oregon has border agricultural inspection that may confiscate certain plants, soil, or produce — check the Oregon Department of Agriculture's guidelines)
- Live animals (obviously — the dog rides with you)

**Other**
- Nail polish and nail polish remover (flammable)
- Rubbing alcohol in large quantities
- Charcoal and charcoal lighter
- Oxygen tanks

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist: Office, Attic/Basement, Outdoor & Misc Storage

---

## HOME OFFICE

The office is where your most valuable and irreplaceable items live — not in dollar terms necessarily, but in data, documents, and devices that can't be re-bought at a store in Oregon. The packing itself is straightforward; the preparation and backup work is what takes time.

**Estimated total time:** 5–8 hours (including digital backup and document sorting)

---

### Electronics Backup Protocol (Week 6–5) — **J**, 2–3 hrs

Do this before you pack a single cable. Moving is the highest-risk moment for electronics — drops, temperature swings, vibration, and moisture all threaten data. Assume anything could arrive damaged and prepare accordingly.

**Computers (desktop and laptops)**

- [ ] Run a full backup of each computer to an external hard drive. If you already use Time Machine, Windows Backup, or a similar tool, run a fresh one. If you don't, this is the moment to start. Plug in an external drive, run the backup, verify it completed, and label the drive.
- [ ] Run a second backup to a cloud service. If you already use iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox, confirm your most important folders are synced and up to date. If you don't use cloud backup, consider a one-month subscription to Backblaze or similar — it's about $7–$9 and covers unlimited data from one computer. The goal is redundancy: one local copy on a drive you carry in the car, one cloud copy that survives even if the drive and the computer are both lost.
- [ ] Photograph your desktop setup from multiple angles: front, back (showing every cable connection), and any peripherals. When you reassemble in Oregon, these photos save an hour of "where did this USB go."
- [ ] Write down or screenshot your Wi-Fi network name, passwords for any network-attached devices (printer, NAS, smart home hub), and any software license keys stored locally. Save this to a note on your phone and to the cloud.

**Phones and tablets**

- [ ] Confirm iCloud or Google backup is current on each phone. Check settings and verify the last backup date.
- [ ] Download offline maps for your driving route in Google Maps or Apple Maps. Cell coverage is spotty in parts of Wyoming, Idaho, and rural Oregon.

**External drives, USBs, and memory cards**

- [ ] Gather all of them in one place. Label each one with its contents if you haven't already. These ride in the car with you, never in the truck.

**Serial numbers and warranty info**

- [ ] Photograph the serial number sticker on the back or bottom of every piece of electronics worth more than $200: computers, monitors, TV (if not already done in living room), gaming consoles, tablets, cameras, printers. Save the photos to a dedicated album on your phone called "Move — Serial Numbers." If anything is lost, damaged, or stolen during the move, you'll need serial numbers for insurance claims and police reports.
- [ ] If you have receipts or warranty documents for major electronics, photograph those too and add them to the same album.

---

### Declutter First (Week 5–4) — **M**, 1–2 hrs

Office clutter tends to be paper and cables. Go through every drawer and shelf and pull out old manuals for products you no longer own, cables and adapters you can't identify (the "mystery cable" drawer is universal — if you can't name what it connects to in 10 seconds, recycle it at a Best Buy or Staples e-waste bin), dried-out pens and markers, old business cards, outdated reference materials, and printed documents you have digital copies of.

For paper files: you'll sort these in detail during the document packing step below. For now, pull out anything that's clearly trash — old bank statements from 5+ years ago that you have digital access to, expired insurance cards, junk mail that migrated into a file folder.

Shred anything with personal information before you toss it. If you don't have a shredder, many UPS Stores and FedEx offices offer shredding by the pound.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Non-daily office contents (Week 4–3)** — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Reference books and binders (small boxes — these are heavy like the living room books)
- [ ] Printer: remove ink or toner cartridges and bag them in a zip-lock (they leak under pressure and temperature changes). If the printer is more than 3–4 years old and was under $150, consider recycling it and buying new in Oregon — printers are cheap, and old ones often don't survive moves well. Staples and Best Buy accept printers for recycling.
- [ ] Scanner, shredder, label maker, and other peripheral devices
- [ ] Desk lamp (remove bulb, wrap shade)
- [ ] Office supplies: stapler, tape dispenser, paper clips, sticky notes, envelopes, stamps. Consolidate into one box. Keep a pen, a Sharpie, packing tape, scissors, and a notepad out until moving day.
- [ ] Filing cabinet contents: see the document sorting section below. The cabinet itself can go empty — bag the drawer hardware if you're disassembling it.
- [ ] Wall art, diplomas, certificates, bulletin board (wrap framed items as described in bedroom section — cardboard sandwich for glass)
- [ ] Surge protectors and power strips (coil cords and rubber-band them, but do not pack these in the same box as anything fragile — the cords tangle and shift)
- [ ] Networking gear you're replacing (old routers, range extenders, outdated modems — recycle or donate)

**Wave 2: Daily-use electronics and desk (Week 1 / Moving day minus 1)** — **M**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Desktop computer: shut it down properly (don't just unplug). If it's a tower, transport it upright if possible, and remove the GPU if it's a heavy aftermarket card — GPUs mounted horizontally in a tower can snap off their PCIe slot during truck vibration. Wrap the tower in a moving blanket. If you have the original box and foam, use them. The monitor gets its own wrap and should be treated like a TV — face it toward a padded surface, never lay it screen-down on a hard box.
- [ ] Laptop: goes in your bag in the car, fully charged, not the truck.
- [ ] Monitor, keyboard, mouse, webcam (label each cable and bag with its device)

## ATTIC / BASEMENT / CRAWL SPACE

These spaces are where things go to be forgotten, so approach this as an archaeological dig first and a packing job second. If you haven't opened a box since you moved into this house, there's a strong chance you don't need what's inside it.

**Estimated total time:** 4–10 hours (wildly dependent on how much is stored)

---

### Declutter First (Week 8–6) — **J**, 2–4 hrs

This is the highest-impact declutter session of the entire move. Bring trash bags, a donation bin, and your phone (for listing items to sell). Go through everything and ask one question per item: "Would I pay $50 to have this shipped to Oregon?" If the answer is no, it goes.

Common attic and basement cuts: old furniture you replaced and stored "just in case," broken holiday decorations, outgrown clothing in storage bins, old textbooks and school papers (photograph anything sentimental, recycle the rest), luggage with broken wheels or zippers, exercise equipment you haven't used in a year (treadmills and ellipticals are expensive to move and cheap to find used in Oregon on Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace), boxes from previous moves that you never unpacked (if you survived this long without opening them, you don't need what's inside — open them one last time to confirm, then donate or toss), and old electronics like VCRs, ancient laptops, and CRT monitors (e-waste recycling).

**Moisture and pest check:** Before you pack anything from a basement or attic, inspect it. Look for water damage, mold, mildew, mouse droppings, or insect damage. If a box is water-stained, the contents may be compromised. If you find mold on fabric or paper, it's usually not worth saving — mold spores will travel with the item and colonize your new space. If in doubt, photograph the item, discard it, and file an insurance claim on your renter's or homeowner's policy if it's valuable.

---

### Pack in Two Waves

**Wave 1: Keep-and-repack (Weeks 5–4)** — **J**, 2–4 hrs

- [ ] Holiday and seasonal decorations (consolidate — if you have 6 bins of Christmas decorations, can it be 3?)
- [ ] Keepsakes and memorabilia: family photos, yearbooks, heirlooms. Wrap fragile items individually. These go in clearly labeled boxes — "KEEPSAKES — FRAGILE — DO NOT STACK." Consider putting irreplaceable photos and documents in a waterproof bin or bag.
- [ ] Seasonal clothing not already packed from bedroom wave 1
- [ ] Stored luggage and bags (pack soft items inside them)
- [ ] Craft and hobby supplies: sewing machine, fabric, yarn, woodworking project stock. Be selective — raw materials are heavy and cheap to replace.
- [ ] Stored kitchenware and dishes you're keeping (china sets, inherited pieces)
- [ ] Archived paperwork and tax records: keep 3–7 years of tax returns depending on your situation (the IRS generally recommends 3 years minimum, but some advisors suggest 7 for safety). Shred older documents with personal information. See the documents section below for what to carry with you vs. what can go in the truck.
- [ ] Tools and hardware that didn't live in the garage

**Wave 2: Large and awkward items (Week 2–1)** — **M**, 1–2 hrs

- [ ] Folding tables, spare furniture, shelving units (disassemble, bag hardware)
- [ ] Storage racks and bins (empty, nest, and stack)
- [ ] Dehumidifier, space heater, window AC unit (drain all water, coil cords). Note: Oregon's climate may mean you no longer need a dehumidifier or window AC depending on where you're moving — the Willamette Valley is mild, and many homes have central air or don't need it.
- [ ] Washer and dryer connections: if you own them and are moving them, disconnect water lines (shut off water first), drain hoses, and secure the washer drum with transit bolts (check your model's manual — running a washer without transit bolts during a move can destroy the drum suspension). If you don't have the transit bolts, a moving company can sometimes source them, or check the manufacturer's website.
- [ ] Final sweep: flashlight check every corner, shelf, rafter, and crawl space. It's very common to leave things in attic eaves and basement utility closets.

## OUTDOOR GEAR & MISCELLANEOUS STORAGE

This covers the porch, patio, shed, balcony, car trunk, and anywhere else items accumulate outside the main rooms.

**Estimated total time:** 3–5 hours

---

### Declutter First (Week 6–5) — **M**, 1–2 hrs

Outdoor items take a beating from weather and are often the least worth moving. Inspect everything for rust, rot, UV damage, and broken parts. Plastic patio furniture that's become brittle and faded is not worth truck space. Clay pots crack easily in transit and are cheap to replace. Garden soil and mulch stay behind — the weight isn't worth it and Oregon's agricultural inspection may flag out-of-state soil anyway.

Keep things that are expensive, in good condition, and that you'll use in Oregon: quality patio set, grill (propane tank disposed of separately — see the prohibited items list in the garage section), good garden tools, outdoor recreation gear.

---

### Pack in One Wave (Weeks 4–3) — **M**, 2–3 hrs

- [ ] Patio furniture: clean, dry, and disassemble if possible. Wrap cushions in plastic bags to protect from moisture in the truck. Stack chairs and bag hardware.
- [ ] Grill: deep clean the grates and interior. Remove and properly dispose of the propane tank. Wrap grates in newspaper or packing paper. Tape the lid shut.
- [ ] Outdoor recreation: kayak, paddleboard, ski gear, fishing rods, camping chairs. Fishing rods should be transported in a hard case or PVC tube — they snap easily. Ski edges can cut other items, so wrap them in moving blankets.
- [ ] Hoses, sprinklers, watering cans: drain completely. Coil hoses tightly and secure with a bungee.
- [ ] Potted plants you want to bring: repot into plastic (not clay) for the trip. Research Oregon's plant import rules — the Oregon Department of Agriculture runs inspection stations on major highways entering the state. Generally, healthy houseplants in commercial potting soil are fine, but plants in outdoor soil, plants with visible pests, and certain species may be flagged. When in doubt, check ODA's website or call them. Many people find it simpler to give plants away and start fresh.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

## Labeling System

Before you pack a single box, grab a thick marker and use this format on the top and at least one side of every box:

**ROOM — Contents — Priority — Fragile?**

Example: **KITCHEN — Coffee maker, mugs, spices — OPEN FIRST — FRAGILE**

Use three priority levels: **OPEN FIRST** (things you need within hours of arrival), **OPEN SOON** (within the first few days), and **OPEN LATER** (seasonal, decorative, rarely used). If you want to go further, number each box and keep a running list in your phone's notes app — "Kitchen #4: blender, mixing bowls, baking sheets" — so you can find anything without opening every box.

Color-coding with colored tape or stickers works well too. Pick one color per room and slap it on. The movers or your future selves will thank you.

---

## Fragile-Packing Rules (apply everywhere)

These apply to every room, so internalize them before you start.

Dishes, glasses, and ceramics go on their edges (not flat) inside cells or wrapped individually in packing paper. Never use newspaper directly on anything you eat from — the ink transfers. Nest bowls with paper between each one. Fill every gap in the box with crumpled paper or towels so nothing shifts. If you can shake the box and hear movement, add more fill.

Mirrors, frames, and glass art get an X of painter's tape across the glass (limits shatter spread), then get wrapped in bubble wrap and placed in a flat mirror box or between two pieces of cardboard taped together. Mark FRAGILE and THIS SIDE UP.

Electronics get wrapped in anti-static bubble wrap if you have it, or soft cloths. If you saved the original box, use it. Photograph the cable setup behind TVs and entertainment centers before unplugging. Put all cords and remotes in a labeled zip-lock bag taped to the device or its box.

Lamps get disassembled: remove the shade, wrap it in a large garbage bag to keep it clean, and pack it upright in a tall box with paper around it. Wrap the base separately.

Liquids always get a strip of plastic wrap under the cap, then cap tightened, then placed upright in a zip-lock bag inside the box. Pack liquids in small boxes so weight stays manageable and leaks stay contained.

---

## Kitchen

**Responsibility:** J
**Estimated time:** 4–6 hours total (split across 2 sessions)
**Priority:** Pack non-essentials 3–4 weeks out. Pack daily-use items last, the day before or morning of the move.
**Suggested boxes:** 8–15 medium, 3–5 small (for heavy items like cans and ceramics), 1–2 large (for lightweight bulky items like plastic containers)

**Non-essentials (pack first, OPEN LATER or OPEN SOON):**

- [ ] Specialty appliances: stand mixer, food processor, blender, waffle maker, slow cooker, instant pot, bread maker
- [ ] Baking supplies: cake pans, muffin tins, cookie sheets, rolling pin, decorating tools
- [ ] Serving ware: platters, punch bowls, gravy boats, holiday dishes, entertaining pieces
- [ ] Extra dish sets and glassware beyond daily use
- [ ] Cookbooks and recipe binders
- [ ] Table linens: tablecloths, cloth napkins, placemats
- [ ] Wine and bar supplies: bottles (wrap individually, pack upright in small boxes), cocktail tools, bar glasses
- [ ] Vases, decorative bowls, and countertop decor
- [ ] Rarely used utensils and gadgets: melon baller, mandoline, spiralizer, fondue set

**Daily essentials (pack last, OPEN FIRST):**

- [ ] One pot, one pan, one baking sheet
- [ ] One plate, one bowl, one mug per person
- [ ] One set of utensils per person plus one sharp knife
- [ ] Can opener, bottle opener, corkscrew
- [ ] Coffee maker or French press, coffee, filters, sugar, creamer
- [ ] Dish soap, one sponge, one dish towel
- [ ] Paper towels, paper plates, and plastic utensils for moving day and the first night
- [ ] Trash bags
- [ ] Snacks and water bottles for the road

**Declutter tips:** Open every drawer and cabinet. If you have duplicate whisks, three sets of measuring cups, or a panini press you used once in 2019, let it go. Spices expire — check dates and toss anything older than 2–3 years. Mismatched food storage containers without lids go in recycling. Chipped or cracked dishes get tossed. Donate usable items to a local kitchen supply thrift shop or community kitchen.

---

## Living Room

**Responsibility:** J
**Estimated time:** 3–4 hours
**Priority:** Pack 2–3 weeks out, keeping one entertainment setup for the final days if you want.
**Suggested boxes:** 4–8 medium, 2–3 small (for heavy books or media), 1–2 large (for throw pillows, blankets, lampshades), specialty boxes for TV or mirrors if applicable

**Items:**

- [ ] Books: pack in small boxes, spine-down, fill gaps with packing paper. These get heavy fast — never fill a large box with only books
- [ ] DVDs, games, vinyl records: small boxes, upright like files
- [ ] TV: original box if you have it, otherwise wrap in a moving blanket and use a TV box. Photograph cable setup first. Put remote in a labeled zip-lock bag
- [ ] Sound system, speakers, streaming devices: wrap each piece, label cords
- [ ] Gaming consoles and controllers: wrap individually, keep cords bundled and labeled
- [ ] Decorative items: picture frames (see fragile rules), candles, figurines, sculptures, vases
- [ ] Lamps: disassemble, pack shades separately upright, wrap bases
- [ ] Throw pillows, blankets, curtains: use these as padding inside boxes or pack in large trash bags (not for trash — label them clearly)
- [ ] Rugs: roll tightly, secure with twine or stretch wrap, stand upright in the truck
- [ ] Shelving and small furniture: disassemble if possible, bag hardware in a zip-lock taped to the piece, wrap corners in bubble wrap
- [ ] Coffee table books, magazines, coasters
- [ ] Remotes and batteries: one labeled zip-lock bag for all remotes

**Declutter tips:** Books are one of the heaviest things to move per cubic foot. Be ruthless. If you won't reread it, donate it. Same goes for DVDs and CDs in a streaming era. Old magazines, catalogs, and dead remotes go. If you have decorative items you've been displaying out of obligation rather than love, this is the moment to pass them on.

---

## Primary Bedroom

**Responsibility:** P
**Estimated time:** 2–3 hours
**Priority:** Pack non-essentials 2–3 weeks out. Pack daily clothes and bedding the morning of the move.
**Suggested boxes:** 4–8 medium, 1–2 wardrobe boxes (if you have hanging clothes worth protecting), 2–3 large (for bedding and pillows if not using bags)

**Non-essentials (pack first):**

- [ ] Off-season clothing: winter coats in summer, etc.
- [ ] Shoes beyond daily wear: wrap each pair in packing paper or keep in shoe boxes
- [ ] Extra bedding sets, quilts, and decorative pillows
- [ ] Jewelry: carry valuable jewelry with you in the car, not on the truck. Use a small zip-lock or jewelry roll
- [ ] Dresser contents: you can leave clothes in dresser drawers if the movers allow it and the dresser is light enough — ask. Otherwise, pack drawer contents into bags and label by drawer
- [ ] Nightstand contents: books, journals, chargers, personal items
- [ ] Under-bed storage items
- [ ] Wall art, mirrors, and photos (see fragile rules)
- [ ] Hamper, iron, ironing board, hangers (bundle hangers with a rubber band)

**Daily essentials (pack last, OPEN FIRST):**

- [ ] 3 days of clothes, underwear, socks (into overnight bag for the car)
- [ ] Pajamas
- [ ] Shoes you'll wear during the move and drive
- [ ] Phone charger and bedside essentials
- [ ] One set of sheets, one set of pillowcases, pillows — carry pillows in the car
- [ ] Alarm clock or confirm phone alarm is set

**Declutter tips:** Try everything on. If it doesn't fit, you don't love it, or you haven't worn it in a year, donate it. Worn-out socks and underwear get tossed, not donated. Old pillows that have lost their shape get replaced — they're cheap and not worth shipping 2,400 miles. This is the single best room for reducing box count because clothing and bedding are bulky.

---

## Guest Room / Spare Room

**Responsibility:** M
**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours
**Priority:** Pack first — 4+ weeks out. This room usually has the least essential items.
**Suggested boxes:** 2–5 medium, 1 large

**Items:**

- [ ] Guest bedding and pillows
- [ ] Extra towels stored here
- [ ] Hobby supplies and craft materials
- [ ] Exercise equipment: disassemble if needed, wipe down
- [ ] Stored luggage: use suitcases as packing containers for soft items — this saves box count
- [ ] Board games, puzzles, card games
- [ ] Gift wrapping supplies
- [ ] Seasonal decorations (holiday items)
- [ ] Anything in the closet that's been in there since the last move

**Declutter tips:** This room is typically the declutter gold mine. If you stored it here because you didn't know where else to put it, ask yourself whether you actually need it in Oregon. Holiday decorations can be trimmed to favorites only. Broken exercise equipment, dusty craft projects you'll never finish, and guest bedding for a guest room you might not have — all fair game.

---

## Bathroom(s)

**Responsibility:** P
**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per bathroom
**Priority:** Pack non-essentials 2 weeks out. Pack daily toiletries the morning of the move.
**Suggested boxes:** 1–3 small (liquids are heavy), 1 medium

**Non-essentials (pack first):**

- [ ] Extra towels and washcloths beyond one set per person
- [ ] Backup toiletries and bulk supplies
- [ ] Hair tools: straightener, curling iron, dryer (wrap cords, let cool completely before packing)
- [ ] Medicine cabinet overflow: first aid supplies, bandages, cold medicine, vitamins
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink: seal all lids with plastic wrap, pack upright in a small box lined with a trash bag
- [ ] Bathroom decor: shower curtain (wash first or replace at destination), bath mat, wastebasket
- [ ] Rarely used items: nail kits, face masks, travel-size bottles

**Daily essentials (pack morning of, OPEN FIRST):**

- [ ] Toothbrushes, toothpaste, floss
- [ ] Deodorant, soap, shampoo, conditioner
- [ ] Contact lenses, solution, glasses
- [ ] Daily medications and prescriptions
- [ ] Razor
- [ ] One towel per person
- [ ] Toilet paper (at least 2 rolls for the first night at the new place)
- [ ] Hand soap

**Declutter tips:** Check expiration dates on every medication, sunscreen, and product. Most people have a bathroom cabinet full of expired items. Travel-size bottles from hotels you'll never use, old makeup, dried-out nail polish, and that half-used bottle of something you didn't like all get tossed. Consolidate duplicate products.

---

## Home Office / Desk Area

**Responsibility:** M
**Estimated time:** 2–3 hours
**Priority:** Pack non-essentials 2–3 weeks out. Keep your computer and work setup running until the last possible day.
**Suggested boxes:** 3–5 medium, 2 small (for heavy files and supplies)

**Non-essentials (pack first):**

- [ ] Books and reference materials
- [ ] File cabinet contents: sort, shred anything you don't need, keep 2–3 years of tax records and anything you can't replace
- [ ] Office supplies: staplers, tape, pens, paper (be honest about how many pens you actually need)
- [ ] Printers, scanners, shredders: original boxes if available, otherwise wrap well and pack cords in labeled bags
- [ ] Extra cables, adapters, and chargers: label every one with what it goes to
- [ ] Desk accessories and decor

**Daily essentials (pack last):**

- [ ] Laptop and charger — this goes in the car, not on the truck
- [ ] External hard drives and USB drives with backups — car, not truck
- [ ] Webcam, headset, and anything needed for remote work
- [ ] A notepad and pen for moving-day notes and phone numbers

**Declutter tips:** Shred old bank statements, expired warranties, old manuals (most are online now), and junk mail that piled up. Recycle dead pens. Old tech — the drawer full of phone cases for phones you no longer own, ancient chargers, broken headphones — recycle it through an e-waste program, don't move it.

---

## Garage / Storage / Utility Areas

**Responsibility:** J
**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours
**Priority:** Pack first — 4+ weeks out. This is where the biggest declutter gains happen.
**Suggested boxes:** Varies widely — 3–10 boxes plus loose items. Use original packaging for power tools when possible.

**Items:**

- [ ] Tools: consolidate into a toolbox or tool bag. Wrap sharp edges in cardboard and tape
- [ ] Garden tools and outdoor furniture: clean soil off everything. Drain fuel from gas-powered equipment — movers won't transport fuel or propane
- [ ] Holiday and seasonal decorations
- [ ] Sporting equipment: bikes, skis, camping gear
- [ ] Automotive supplies: drain or dispose of fluids. Movers won't take flammable or hazardous items (oil, paint, gasoline, propane, pesticides, pool chemicals). Check your mover's prohibited items list
- [ ] Luggage and storage bins
- [ ] Paint cans: unless you need them for touch-up at the new place, leave them. Take a photo of the label for color-matching later
- [ ] Ladders, shelving units: disassemble, bag hardware
- [ ] Laundry supplies: partially used detergent and bleach are often not worth moving. Seal anything you do bring

**Declutter tips:** This is the room where people move things they never use from house to house for decades. Broken items waiting to be fixed, duplicate tools, old paint, mystery hardware, and furniture stored "just in case" should all be evaluated hard. If you haven't touched it in 2+ years, let it go. Dispose of hazardous materials at a local collection event or drop-off — don't put them in the trash.

---

## Dining Room

**Responsibility:** P
**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours
**Priority:** Pack 2–3 weeks out.
**Suggested boxes:** 2–5 medium, 1–2 small for heavy items like china

**Items:**

- [ ] China, fine glassware, crystal: individually wrap each piece, pack on edge, fill all gaps, mark FRAGILE
- [ ] Serving dishes, platters, centerpieces
- [ ] Table linens and cloth napkins
- [ ] Candlesticks and candles
- [ ] Buffet or hutch contents: pack contents, then disassemble furniture if needed
- [ ] Chair cushions: stuff into large trash bags, label NOT TRASH
- [ ] Dining table: if it disassembles, bag all hardware in a zip-lock taped to the underside

**Declutter tips:** Formal dining sets that only come out at holidays are heavy and expensive to move. If you use them and love them, pack carefully and move them. If you've inherited a set out of obligation and never use it, this may be the time to pass it on to a family member or consign it.

---

## Laundry Area

**Responsibility:** P
**Estimated time:** 30–60 minutes
**Priority:** Pack

# 10-Week Packing Timeline

This is designed to be printed on one page. Adjust box counts based on your actual household size. These are estimates for a 1–2 bedroom apartment or small house for two people.

---

**WEEKS 1–2: Gather and declutter only. No packing yet.**

Who: J | Est. boxes packed: 0

Sort every room into Keep, Sell, Donate, Trash. Focus on the garage, storage areas, guest room, and closets first. List items for sale online. Schedule donation pickups. Order packing supplies at the end of Week 2.

---

**WEEK 3: Garage, storage, and guest room**

Who: M leads garage/storage, M leads guest room | Est. boxes: 5–12

Pack everything in the garage that's coming with you. Pack the entire guest room. These are your least-used spaces and the easiest place to start. Use suitcases and storage bins as packing containers for soft items.

---

**WEEK 4: Dining room, holiday/seasonal items, and outdoor/patio**

Who: P leads dining room, J leads outdoor | Est. boxes: 5–10

Wrap china and glassware carefully. Pack all seasonal decorations. Clean and pack outdoor furniture and grill. Sell or give away the propane tank.

---

**WEEK 5: Home office, books, and media**

Who: M leads office, J leads books/media | Est. boxes: 5–10

Shred old files. Pack reference books, supplies, and non-essential electronics. Keep your daily work computer and setup running. Pack all DVDs, games, vinyl, and books from every room this week. Books go in small boxes only.

---

**WEEK 6: Living room non-essentials**

Who: J | Est. boxes: 5–10

Pack decor, art, lamps, extra blankets, and throw pillows. Leave one entertainment setup if you want it for the final two weeks. Roll and secure rugs. Photograph cable setups before unplugging anything.

---

**WEEK 7: Kitchen non-essentials and laundry area**

Who: J leads kitchen, P leads laundry | Est. boxes: 6–12

Pack specialty appliances, baking supplies, serving ware, extra dish sets, bar supplies, cookbooks, and table linens. Pack all laundry area items except one load's worth of detergent. Keep daily kitchen essentials out: one pot, one pan, one plate and bowl per person, utensils, coffee maker, and dish soap.

---

**WEEK 8: Bedrooms (non-essentials) and closets**

Who: P leads primary bedroom, M leads closets and entryway | Est. boxes: 6–12

Pack off-season clothes, extra shoes, spare bedding, jewelry (goes in the car), nightstand contents, wall art, and closet overflow. Leave out 3 days of clothes per person, one set of sheets, pillows, and daily shoes. Pack the entryway and coat closet.

---

**WEEK 9: Bathrooms (non-essentials), remaining living room, final kitchen items**

Who: P leads bathrooms, J leads the rest | Est. boxes: 4–8

Pack extra towels, medicine cabinet overflow, cleaning supplies, and hair tools. Pack the last of the living room (remaining electronics, the TV, final decor). Pack remaining kitchen items down to your moving-day essentials. Each person keeps a toiletry bag with daily items. Leave out two rolls of toilet paper, hand soap, and one towel per person.

---

**WEEK 10: Final packing, moving day, and go**

Who: J | Est. boxes: 2–5

Monday through Thursday: Pack the final toiletries, bedding, cleaning supplies, and remaining daily items. Defrost the fridge. Do a final cleaning pass. Pack the OPEN FIRST boxes and the car essentials box. Load overnight bags, dog kit, documents, and car survival kit into the car.

Moving day: Movers or truck gets loaded. Walk-through photos. Return keys. Drive to Oregon.

---

**Estimated total box count: 40–80 boxes**

This varies widely by household. A minimalist couple might use 30. A couple with a full garage, home office, and lots of kitchen gear could hit 80 or more. When in doubt, order 10–15 extra boxes — most suppliers take back unused ones.

---

**Quick box-size guide for reference:**

Small boxes (16×12×12 or similar) are for heavy things: books, canned goods, tools, ceramics, files, and liquids. Medium boxes (18×18×16 or similar) are your workhorse — most items go here. Large boxes (18×18×24 or similar) are only for lightweight bulky items: pillows, lampshades, plastic containers, linens, and stuffed animals. If a large box is heavy enough that you can't comfortably lift it, you've packed it wrong.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

**How to use this:** Work through rooms in the order listed. Earlier rooms contain things you use least, so they can be packed first. Each room has a declutter pass built in — do it before you pack, not during, or you'll slow down. Label every box with the room name and a 1–3 word content summary (e.g., "Kitchen — baking tools").

---

## 1. Storage / Garage / Attic

**Responsible:** J | **Priority:** Start first (weeks 6–5) | **Estimated time:** 4–8 hours depending on volume

**Declutter first:**
This is where the most cuttable weight lives. Be aggressive. If you haven't touched it since the last move, it probably shouldn't survive this one. Seasonal gear you won't need in Oregon's climate (heavy snow blower, for instance) can go. Rusty or duplicate tools, old paint cans, and broken items should be tossed, donated, or recycled. Take photos of anything you're unsure about — if you wouldn't buy it again today for half its price, let it go.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Seasonal decorations (holiday, outdoor)
- [ ] Camping, hiking, and outdoor gear
- [ ] Tools and hardware (wrap sharp edges, bag small parts and label them)
- [ ] Sporting equipment
- [ ] Luggage and travel bags (use suitcases as packing containers for heavy items like books)
- [ ] Stored furniture, shelving, or bins
- [ ] Lawn and garden tools — decide what's worth the weight
- [ ] Car supplies (jumper cables, emergency kit — set the emergency kit aside for the drive)

---

## 2. Guest Room / Spare Room / Office

**Responsible:** P (office items), J (guest room) | **Priority:** Weeks 5–4 | **Estimated time:** 3–5 hours

**Declutter first:**
Shred old paperwork you don't need (keep tax returns for 7 years, vital records forever). Recycle old magazines, manuals for products you no longer own, and outdated tech cables. Donate books you won't reread. Old electronics can go to an e-waste drop-off.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Books (small boxes, spines down, fill gaps with packing paper)
- [ ] Desk supplies, stationery, and office equipment
- [ ] Computer peripherals and cables (label both ends of each cable or take a photo of the back of your setup before unplugging)
- [ ] Files and documents — separate "carry with us" documents (see the master list) from "ship" files
- [ ] Guest bedding, pillows, and towels (use vacuum bags to compress)
- [ ] Art, frames, and wall décor (cardboard corner protectors, wrap in bubble wrap, pack upright)
- [ ] Printer, scanner, monitor (original boxes if you have them; otherwise double-wrap and mark FRAGILE)

---

## 3. Living Room / Family Room

**Responsible:** J | **Priority:** Weeks 4–3 | **Estimated time:** 4–6 hours

**Declutter first:**
DVDs, CDs, and games you've replaced digitally can be donated or sold. Old remotes, dead batteries, mystery chargers, and tangled cables in the junk drawer — toss them. Decorative items you don't love enough to wrap, protect, and carry 2,400 miles should stay behind.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Books and media (small boxes)
- [ ] Decorative items, vases, candles, and knickknacks (wrap individually)
- [ ] Throw pillows, blankets, and curtains (vacuum bags or garbage bags)
- [ ] Electronics: TV, sound bar, gaming consoles, streaming devices. Take photos of cable setups. Wrap screens in moving blankets or towels, not bubble wrap (it can leave marks on warm screens)
- [ ] Lamps (remove bulbs and shades, wrap shades in paper, pack bulbs separately)
- [ ] Board games, puzzles, and hobby items
- [ ] Small furniture drawers — if the mover allows it, leave clothes in dresser drawers and wrap the dresser. If DIY, tape drawers shut
- [ ] Area rugs (roll tightly, secure with rope or stretch wrap)

---

## 4. Dining Room

**Responsible:** P | **Priority:** Weeks 4–3 | **Estimated time:** 2–3 hours

**Declutter first:**
Chipped dishes, mismatched glasses, placemats you never use, and the fondue set from 2016 can all go. Keep only the servingware you actually put on a table in the last year.

**Pack:**
- [ ] China, glassware, and stemware (pack vertically like records, not flat-stacked; use cell dividers or wrap each piece in paper)
- [ ] Serving dishes and platters (paper between each layer)
- [ ] Table linens, placemats, napkins
- [ ] Candlesticks and centerpieces
- [ ] Buffet or hutch contents
- [ ] Small appliances stored in the dining area (wrap cords, bag accessories)

---

## 5. Kitchen

**Responsible:** J | **Priority:** Weeks 3–2 (non-essentials) and final 2 days (essentials) | **Estimated time:** 6–10 hours total — this is usually the longest room

**Declutter first:**
The kitchen is the single best place to cut weight and box count. Duplicate spatulas, novelty mugs, stained plastic containers without lids, expired spices and food, single-use gadgets (melon baller, avocado slicer), and anything you bought "just in case" — donate or discard. Keep one good version of each tool. If you have more than 8 mugs for a 2-person household, choose your favorites.

**Pack in two waves:**

*Wave 1 — weeks 3–2 (things you won't need):*
- [ ] Baking supplies and specialty pans
- [ ] Entertaining dishes, punch bowls, extra serving ware
- [ ] Cookbooks
- [ ] Small appliances you won't use in the next 2 weeks (stand mixer, blender, food processor, waffle maker)
- [ ] Vases, decorative items on top of cabinets
- [ ] Spice duplicates and pantry overflow

*Wave 2 — last 2 days:*
- [ ] Everyday dishes, cups, and silverware (keep one set per person until the last meal)
- [ ] Pots, pans, and cooking utensils
- [ ] Coffeemaker (pack the morning of moving day, right after the last pot)
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink — keep a small kit out for final cleanup
- [ ] Refrigerator and freezer contents: use coolers for the drive, donate or toss the rest
- [ ] Trash bags, paper towels, and hand soap — these go in the car, not the truck

---

## 6. Bedrooms (Master and Any Others)

**Responsible:** Each person packs their own; J for shared items | **Priority:** Weeks 3–2 (off-season and extras), last 2 days (daily use) | **Estimated time:** 3–5 hours per bedroom

**Declutter first:**
Clothes are heavy and take up enormous space. Try the "reverse hanger" trick if time allows: turn all hangers backward and only flip them when you wear something. Anything still backward in two weeks gets donated. Worn-out shoes, old undergarments, and clothes that don't fit can go now. Under-bed storage often holds forgotten items — sort before you pack.

**Pack in two waves:**

*Wave 1 — weeks 3–2:*
- [ ] Off-season clothing (vacuum bags save a lot of space)
- [ ] Shoes you won't wear in the next 2 weeks (stuff shoes with socks to hold shape, pack in original boxes or wrap in paper)
- [ ] Extra bedding, pillows, and linens
- [ ] Jewelry and accessories (carry valuables with you, not in the truck)
- [ ] Dresser décor, bedside items you don't use daily
- [ ] Luggage (use as packing containers)

*Wave 2 — last 2 days:*
- [ ] Daily clothes, sleepwear, and shoes (pack enough for 3–4 days of travel in a suitcase that stays in the car)
- [ ] Bedding you're sleeping on (strip and pack the morning of)
- [ ] Alarm clocks, phone chargers, and bedside essentials
- [ ] Hangers (bundle with rubber bands or pack in wardrobe boxes)

---

## 7. Bathrooms

**Responsible:** Each person handles their own toiletries; J for shared/linen closet | **Priority:** Last 3 days (non-essentials), morning of (daily items) | **Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per bathroom

**Declutter first:**
Expired medications (take to a pharmacy drop-off, don't flush), nearly-empty bottles, old makeup and skincare, ratty towels, and hotel shampoo collections. Medicine cabinets are graveyards — clear them out.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Towels and washcloths (keep 1 per person plus 1 for the dog; use extras as packing material for fragile items)
- [ ] Linen closet overflow (sheets, first aid supplies, extra TP — toss what's nearly gone)
- [ ] Hair tools, styling products (bag liquids in zip-lock bags to prevent leaks)
- [ ] Medications and vitamins (carry current prescriptions in the car, not the truck)
- [ ] Shower curtain, rings, bath mat (pack the morning of after final showers)
- [ ] Toiletries bag for the drive (toothbrushes, toothpaste, deodorant, face wash, contacts, glasses — this goes in the car)

---

## 8. Laundry Room / Mudroom / Entry

**Responsible:** M | **Priority:** Last 3 days | **Estimated time:** 1–2 hours

**Declutter first:**
Old cleaning products, dried-up supplies, wire hangers, single gloves, and broken umbrellas.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Washer and dryer: run a cleaning cycle, disconnect hoses, let the washer drum dry 24 hours. Tape the drum (some models need shipping bolts reinstalled — check your manual or search your model number online)
- [ ] Iron, ironing board, drying rack
- [ ] Coats, boots, rain gear (keep what you need for travel weather)
- [ ] Cleaning supplies: keep a small "last clean" kit (all-purpose cleaner, paper towels, broom, dustpan, trash bags, toilet cleaner). This is the very last thing packed
- [ ] Pet leashes, harnesses, and outdoor gear stored here (set aside travel items for the car)

---

## 9. Outdoor / Patio / Balcony

**Responsible:** M | **Priority:** Weeks 3–2 | **Estimated time:** 1–3 hours

**Declutter first:**
Cheap resin furniture, rusty grills, cracked planters, and hose attachments that leak are not worth moving cross-country. Sell or give away patio furniture if you can replace it for less than the shipping weight cost.

**Pack:**
- [ ] Patio furniture (clean, fold, wrap cushions in plastic)
- [ ] Grill (clean, disconnect propane — propane tanks cannot go in a moving truck; dispose or give away). Pack grill tools separately
- [ ] Planters and garden décor
- [ ] Hoses, sprinklers, garden tools worth keeping
- [ ] Outdoor toys, bikes (deflate tires slightly for altitude changes on the drive)

# Services Cancellation and Startup Checklist

For each service below I've included who to notify, the typical lead time, who's responsible, the priority level, and a sample script or talking point you can use on the phone or in a chat window. Adapt the scripts to your situation.

---

## Ohio — Cancel or Transfer

**Electric (e.g., AEP Ohio, Duke Energy, Ohio Edison)**
Responsible: J | Priority: HIGH | Lead time: 3–7 business days
Request a final meter read for February 14, 2026 (the day after the move). Ask for the final bill to be sent to your Oregon address or emailed.

Sample script: "I'm moving out of [address] on February 13, 2026. I'd like to schedule a final meter read for February 14 and close my account. Please send the final bill to [Oregon address or email]. Can you confirm there are no early termination fees or deposits to be refunded?"

**Natural gas (e.g., Columbia Gas, Dominion Energy)**
Responsible: J | Priority: HIGH | Lead time: 3–7 business days
Same process as electric. If you have a deposit on file, ask how and when it will be refunded.

Sample script: Same structure as electric. Add: "I believe I have a deposit on file. Can you confirm the amount and how it will be returned?"

**Water and sewer (typically your city or county)**
Responsible: J | Priority: HIGH | Lead time: 3–5 business days
Some municipalities require an in-person visit or a written request. Ask whether the final bill will be deducted from your deposit or mailed.

Sample script: "I'd like to close my water and sewer account at [address] effective February 14, 2026. What's the process for the final bill and any deposit refund?"

**Trash and recycling (city service or private hauler)**
Responsible: J | Priority: MED | Lead time: 1–2 weeks
If it's a private hauler, check your contract for cancellation terms. City services usually end when you notify the utility office.

Sample script: "I'm canceling trash and recycling service at [address] effective February 13, 2026. Are there any final charges or equipment returns needed?"

**Internet and cable (e.g., Spectrum, AT&T, WOW)**
Responsible: J | Priority: HIGH | Lead time: 1–2 weeks, but call early to avoid auto-renewal
Ask about equipment return (modem, router). Most providers have a UPS drop-off option. Get a return receipt. Check for early termination fees on contracts.

Sample script: "I'm moving out of state on February 13, 2026, and need to cancel my service at [address]. Is there an early termination fee? What equipment do I need to return, and can I drop it at a UPS store? Please email me a confirmation of the cancellation date and any final charges."

**Home security or monitoring (e.g., ADT, SimpliSafe, Ring)**
