reply:
# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

**How to use this:** Work through each room in the order listed. The priority levels tell you when to pack each category relative to your move date. "Early" means 4–6 weeks out, "Mid" means 2–3 weeks out, and "Late" means the final week. Box counts assume standard medium (18×18×16) and small (16×12×12) boxes. Adjust for your actual volume. Time estimates assume two people working together at a steady pace without major interruptions.

---

## KITCHEN

**Estimated totals:** 12–20 boxes, 4–6 hours across two sessions

**Who:** Joint (this room has the most stuff and the most fragile items — do it together)

**Declutter first (1–2 hours, do this 4+ weeks out):**
Go through every drawer and cabinet before you pack a single box. Pull out everything you haven't used in the past year. That garlic press you forgot you owned, the chipped mugs, the duplicate spatulas, the novelty shot glasses from a road trip five years ago — let them go. Expired spices and food get tossed. Donate functioning appliances you won't miss. If you have more than two of something (can openers, colanders, cutting boards), keep the one you like best and pass the rest along. Be ruthless here because kitchen boxes are heavy and fragile, which means they're expensive to move and annoying to unpack.

**Early (4–6 weeks out) — Priority: Medium**

Category: Baking supplies and specialty cookware (bundt pans, roasting pans, pie dishes, cookie sheets you won't use before the move). Also pack cookbooks, entertaining dishes, serving platters, holiday dishware, fondue sets, and anything aspirational you haven't touched recently. Estimated boxes: 2–4 medium. Time: 45 min.

Category: Small appliances you won't use in the next month (bread maker, food processor, stand mixer, waffle iron, blender if you have a backup). Wrap cords around each appliance and secure with a rubber band. If you kept the original box, use it. Otherwise wrap in dish towels and bubble wrap. Estimated boxes: 1–3 medium. Time: 30 min.

**Mid (2–3 weeks out) — Priority: High**

Category: Most dishes, glasses, and mugs. Keep out 2 plates, 2 bowls, 2 mugs, and 2 glasses per person. Pack everything else. Wrap each glass and plate individually in packing paper or newsprint. Stand plates on edge in the box like records, not flat. Put glasses in cell dividers if you have them. Estimated boxes: 3–5 medium. Time: 1–1.5 hrs (this is the slowest part because of wrapping).

Category: Most utensils, tools, and gadgets. Keep out one chef's knife, one spatula, one wooden spoon, one can opener, tongs, and a peeler. Bundle silverware in rubber bands by type. Wrap sharp knives in cardboard sleeves or towels. Estimated boxes: 1–2 small. Time: 20 min.

Category: Pots and pans (keep out one pot and one skillet). Nest pans with paper between them to prevent scratching. Lids can go in a separate box or on top. Estimated boxes: 1–2 medium. Time: 20 min.

Category: Pantry food. Discard anything expired, opened and stale, or not worth the weight. Seal open packages in zip-lock bags. Pack cans and jars in small boxes (they get heavy fast — do not use large boxes for canned goods). Wrap glass bottles and jars individually. Estimated boxes: 2–4 small. Time: 30 min.

**Late (final week) — Priority: Critical**

Category: Last-use kitchen items. On the last full day in the house, pack the remaining plates, mugs, pot, skillet, utensils, dish soap, sponge, hand towel, trash bags, and paper towels. Put the dish soap and sponge in a zip-lock bag and tuck them into your moving-day essentials box so you can clean up at the new place on arrival. Estimated boxes: 1 small. Time: 15 min.

Category: Cleaning supplies under the sink. Pack or discard. Check which items movers won't transport (flammable or hazardous — lighter fluid, certain cleaners). If driving yourself, keep these in a separate clearly labeled box and transport upright. Estimated boxes: 1 small. Time: 15 min.

**Kitchen tips:** Line the bottom of every kitchen box with crumpled paper for cushion. Mark all kitchen boxes "FRAGILE — KITCHEN" on the top and two sides. Pack a "first meal" zip-lock in your essentials box with paper plates, plastic utensils, napkins, a corkscrew, and a couple of snack bars so you don't have to dig through boxes your first night.

---

## LIVING ROOM

**Estimated totals:** 6–12 boxes plus furniture, 2–4 hours across two sessions

**Who:** Joint for packing, P takes point on electronics and cables, M handles wall art and decor

**Declutter first (1 hour, do this 4+ weeks out):**
Take everything off the shelves and surfaces and sort it on the floor. Old magazines, DVDs you'll never rewatch, board games with missing pieces, candles burned down to nubs, decorative items you've stopped noticing — donate or discard. Books are the biggest trap: be honest about which ones you'll reread. If you haven't opened it since you moved in here, it probably shouldn't make the trip to Oregon. A box of books weighs 30–50 pounds, and you'll feel every one of them on that truck or invoice.

**Early (4–6 weeks out) — Priority: Low to Medium**

Category: Books. Use small boxes only. A medium box full of books will weigh 50+ pounds and the bottom will blow out. Fill small boxes about three-quarters full and use packing paper or a towel to fill the gap at the top. Alternate spine-in and spine-out for a tighter fit. Estimated boxes: 2–6 small. Time: 30–60 min depending on your collection.

Category: Decorative items, photo frames, vases, candles, knickknacks. Wrap frames in bubble wrap or towels. Put glass items in packing paper. Stand frames upright in the box, not flat. Estimated boxes: 1–3 medium. Time: 30 min.

Category: Media (CDs, DVDs, vinyl, games). If you've gone fully digital, now is the time to sell or donate physical media. Pack what you're keeping in small boxes. Estimated boxes: 1–2 small. Time: 20 min.

**Mid (2–3 weeks out) — Priority: High**

Category: Wall art, mirrors, and hanging decor. Take photos of your arrangement if you want to recreate it. Use picture boxes or make a cardboard sandwich (two pieces of cardboard taped around the frame). Mark "FRAGILE — DO NOT LAY FLAT" on each one. Remove nails and hooks from the walls and spackle the holes. Estimated boxes: 1–3 flat or specialty. Time: 30–45 min. (Who: M)

Category: Throw pillows, blankets, and curtains. These are great box fillers but can also go in large trash bags or vacuum-seal bags if you have them. Remove curtain rods and bundle the hardware in a labeled zip-lock taped to the rod. Estimated boxes: 1–2 large bags or boxes. Time: 15 min.

Category: Board games and puzzles. Rubber-band game boxes shut so lids don't pop off. Bag loose pieces. Estimated boxes: 1 medium. Time: 10 min.

**Late (final week) — Priority: Critical**

Category: Electronics. Photograph the back of your TV, router, and any entertainment setup so you know exactly which cable goes where. Coil each cable and label it with a small piece of tape. Pack remotes in a zip-lock bag labeled "LIVING ROOM REMOTES." If you still have original boxes for the TV or console, use them. Otherwise, wrap the TV in a moving blanket and transport it upright, never flat. If movers are handling it, ask them to use a TV box. Estimated boxes: 1–3 medium (not counting TV). Time: 30–45 min. (Who: P)

Category: Lamps. Remove bulbs and shades. Wrap shades in packing paper (don't use newsprint — the ink transfers). Wrap bases in bubble wrap. If the lamp is tall, consider whether it's worth moving or replacing in Oregon. Estimated boxes: 1–2 medium. Time: 15 min.

Category: Rugs. Roll, don't fold. Secure with twine or packing tape. If they're large, the movers can handle them or they can go on the truck floor. Estimated boxes: 0 (they're rolled). Time: 10 min.

**Living room tips:** Keep the couch, one lamp, and the TV set up until the last week if you need a place to relax after packing sessions. Disassemble furniture on the last day or let the movers do it. Put all hardware (screws, bolts, brackets) for each piece of furniture in a labeled zip-lock bag and tape it to the furniture itself.

---

## HOME OFFICE

**Estimated totals:** 5–10 boxes, 2–3 hours

**Who:** Whichever of you uses the office most takes the lead. Assign M or P based on whose workspace it primarily is. The other person helps with furniture and filing.

**Declutter first (1–2 hours, do this 4+ weeks out):**
Shred old documents you no longer need (bank statements older than 7 years unless relevant to taxes, old utility bills, expired warranties, old pay stubs if you have digital copies). Recycle old notebooks, dried-out pens, broken supplies, and tangled cables you can't identify. If you have old electronics (phones, tablets, laptops) collecting dust, wipe them and recycle them at a local e-waste drop-off. Test every pen and marker — throw away the dead ones.

**Early (4–6 weeks out) — Priority: Medium**

Category: Reference books, manuals, and binders you won't need before the move. Small boxes for books, medium for binders. Estimated boxes: 1–3 small. Time: 20 min.

Category: Archived files and tax records. Keep the last 3 years of tax returns accessible in your documents folder. Pack older records in a clearly labeled box. Consider scanning anything you're keeping purely for reference and storing it in the cloud. Estimated boxes: 1 medium file box. Time: 30 min (longer if you're scanning).

**Mid (2–3 weeks out) — Priority: High**

Category: Office supplies (staplers, tape, paper clips, sticky notes, printer paper, ink). Put small loose items in zip-lock bags. Estimated boxes: 1–2 small. Time: 15 min.

## GARAGE

**Estimated totals:** 5–15 boxes plus loose items and large tools, 4–8 hours (this room takes the longest because of sorting)

**Who:** M takes the lead (or whoever uses the garage more). P assists with heavy lifting and sorting decisions.

**Declutter first (2–3 hours, do this 5–6 weeks out — start here before any other room if possible):**
The garage is where moves go to die. It's full of things you kept because you "might need them someday" and that day has not come. Be aggressive. Get four zones set up: keep and move, keep and sell, donate, and trash. Work through one section at a time — don't try to do the whole garage in one pass or you'll burn out.

Things to seriously consider not moving: half-used paint cans (movers won't take them and they're not worth the weight — note the color codes and buy new in Oregon), old lumber scraps, rusty tools that have better replacements available for $15 at a hardware store, broken holiday lights, that exercise bike you haven't touched, dried-out garden chemicals, and anything you've been meaning to fix for more than a year. Gasoline, propane tanks, motor oil, pesticides, and other hazardous materials cannot go on a moving truck and are often not worth transporting yourself. Dispose of them at your local hazardous waste facility and replace them in Oregon.

If you have power tools with value (table saw, miter saw, drill press), decide now whether to sell or move them. They're heavy and expensive to ship, but also expensive to replace. Price it out both ways.

**Early (4–6 weeks out) — Priority: High**

Category: Seasonal items you won't use before the move (holiday decorations, camping gear out of season, ski equipment). Estimated boxes: 2–4 large. Time: 30–45 min.

Category: Sporting goods and outdoor recreation (bikes, kayak accessories, fishing gear, golf clubs). Clean them before packing. Bikes can ride in the truck unboxed if the movers allow it, or disassemble the front wheel and pedals and wrap the frame. Estimated boxes: 1–3 medium plus loose items. Time: 30 min.

**Mid (2–3 weeks out) — Priority: High**

Category: Hand tools and hardware. Sort screws, nails, and small hardware into labeled zip-lock bags. Wrap sharp tools (saws, chisels) in cardboard or towels. Put hand tools in a sturdy box or a tool bag. Estimated boxes: 1–2 medium (heavy — keep them small). Time: 30–45 min.

Category: Power tools. Wrap cords, remove batteries, and pack in original boxes if available. If not, wrap in moving blankets and box. Transport lithium batteries in the car if possible, as extreme heat in a truck can be a concern. Estimated boxes: 1–3 medium. Time: 30 min.

Category: Garden tools (rakes, shovels, hoe, pruners). Bundle long-handled tools with twine or bungee cords. Wrap blades in cardboard. These often ride loose in the truck. Consider whether your Oregon yard will need the same tools — if you're moving from a house with a big lot to an apartment, you may not need them. Estimated boxes: 0 (bundled). Time: 15 min.

Category: Lawn mower. Drain the gas and oil before the move (movers require this, and it's safer for a DIY truck too). If the mower is old or low-value, it may cost more to move than to replace. Estimated boxes: 0 (loose). Time: 20 min.

**Late (final week) — Priority: Medium**

Category: Workbench items, shelving contents, last-pass sweep. By this point the garage should be mostly clear. Do a final pass for anything tucked behind shelves, in rafters, or on high hooks. Estimated boxes: 1–2 medium. Time: 20 min.

Category: Car supplies (jumper cables, tire inflator, emergency kit, ice scraper). The emergency kit goes in the car for the drive. The rest gets boxed. Estimated boxes: 1 small. Time: 10 min.

**Garage tips:** Photograph your garage before you start so you can see the progress. It's motivating. Rent a dumpster for a weekend if you have a lot to toss — it's usually $200–$400 and saves a dozen trips to the dump. Schedule a Habitat for Humanity ReStore pickup for large donated items like workbenches and shelving.

## STORAGE UNIT

**Estimated totals:** Varies wildly. Budget 3–6 hours for sorting and 2–4 hours for packing what you keep.

**Who:** Joint (block out a full Saturday for this)

**Declutter first (this is the whole point):**
If you're paying monthly for a storage unit, the move is the perfect reason to empty it completely. Here's the uncomfortable math: if you've been paying $75–$150 a month and the stuff has been in there for a year or more, you've already spent $900–$1,800 storing it. Is it worth that much? For most people, the answer is no for at least half of what's in there.

Pull everything out into the daylight. Make the same four piles as the garage: move, sell, donate, trash. Anything you forgot was in there is a strong candidate for not making the trip. Furniture you replaced, boxes from your last move you never opened, old electronics, duplicate kitchen items from when you combined households — let it go. If you find items with genuine sentimental or financial value, great, those go on the truck. Everything else should leave your life before you leave Ohio.

**Packing what survives the purge:**

Re-box anything in damaged or water-stained boxes. Check for mold or pest damage on soft goods like clothes and upholstery. If something smells musty, it's not going to improve in a truck for three days. Label everything clearly since these boxes tend to get shoved in last and opened last. Estimated boxes: 3–10 medium depending on what you keep. Time for packing: 2–4 hrs.

**Cancel the unit.** Give written notice per your rental agreement (often 30 days) and schedule a walk-through. Clean the unit and return the lock. Get your deposit back in writing. Add "cancel storage unit" to your calendar at the right time.

## FINAL NOTES ON THE ROOM-BY-ROOM PROCESS

**Labeling system that actually works:** Write three things on every box in large marker on the top and at least one side. First, the room it's going to in the new house (not where it came from — this is for the movers or for you on unload day). Second, a one-line summary of contents ("kitchen — plates and bowls, fragile"). Third, a number. Keep a running list on your phone with the box number and a quick note of what's inside. This sounds tedious but it takes five seconds per box and will save you an hour of opening and re-closing boxes when you're looking for the coffee maker at 7 AM on your first morning in Oregon.

**The "open first" boxes:** Pack one per room, labeled clearly with "OPEN FIRST" in a different color marker. These contain the things you'll need within the first hour of unloading: kitchen gets the coffee maker, dish soap, paper towels, and a few mugs; bedroom gets the sheets, pillows, and phone chargers; bathroom gets the toilet paper, hand soap, towels, and shower curtain.

**A word on pacing:** You don't have to do this in marathon sessions. Two focused hours in the evening, three or four times a week, will get a 2-bedroom packed in about 3 weeks without destroying your quality of life. Put on a podcast, work through one category at a time, and stop when the energy drops. Packing while exhausted leads to bad labeling, broken items, and fights about whose job it was to wrap the wine glasses.

reply:
# Room-by-Room Packing & Declutter Plan

**Before you start:** Set up a simple labeling system. Every box gets a label with three things: a room code, a sequential number, and a priority tag. Write it on two sides and the top with a thick marker.

**Room codes:** KIT (kitchen), LR (living room), BR1 (primary bedroom), BR2 (second bedroom/office), BA1 (primary bath), BA2 (second bath), GAR (garage), ATT (attic), BSM (basement), OUT (outdoor), LAU (laundry), CLO (hall closet/coat closet).

**Format:** KIT-04 / FRAGILE / OPEN FIRST — meaning kitchen box number 4, fragile contents, unpack this one immediately.

**Priority tags:** OPEN FIRST (essentials for night one), FRAGILE, HEAVY (keep small and under 50 lbs), DONATE, and SELL.

Keep a running inventory on your phone. A shared Google Sheet or Apple Note works fine: box number, room, short contents list, priority tag. Photograph the inside of each box before taping it shut. It takes five seconds and saves twenty minutes of searching later.

---

## KITCHEN — Pack weeks 3–2, finish week 1

**Estimated time:** 6–10 hours total across multiple sessions. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] Pull everything out of cabinets one section at a time. Group into keep, donate, toss.
- [ ] Purge duplicates: how many spatulas, can openers, and mugs do you actually use? Keep the ones you reach for. The rest go.
- [ ] Toss expired spices, food, and anything sticky or stale. Check the backs of cabinets.
- [ ] Donate small appliances you haven't used in a year (bread maker, fondue pot, spare blender).
- [ ] Recycle takeout containers, mismatched lids, and chipped dishes.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Entertaining and holiday items, baking supplies you won't use, cookbooks, decorative items, bar tools, vases.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Most dishes, glasses, pots, pans, and small appliances. Keep one pot, one pan, one cutting board, one knife, two plates, two bowls, two mugs, two forks/knives/spoons, a can opener, and a dish towel unpacked until moving day.
- [ ] **Last (day before or morning of):** The survival set above, cleaning supplies, trash bags, paper towels.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap each plate individually in packing paper. Stack plates vertically on edge like records — they're stronger that way and less likely to crack.
- [ ] Wrap glasses and mugs with packing paper stuffed inside the cup. Nest them upside down in cells or in a box with cardboard dividers.
- [ ] Put a 2-inch cushion of crumpled paper on the bottom and top of every fragile box.
- [ ] Never let fragile items touch each other or the box walls.
- [ ] Use dish towels and oven mitts as padding — they're free and they're coming with you anyway.
- [ ] Mark FRAGILE and THIS SIDE UP on two sides and the top. Draw an arrow.

---

## LIVING ROOM — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 4–6 hours. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Sort books: keep favorites, donate the rest to a Little Free Library or used bookstore. Books are the heaviest thing you own per cubic foot.
- [ ] Assess decor honestly. If you haven't noticed it in six months, donate it.
- [ ] Check media: DVDs, CDs, and games you've replaced digitally can go.
- [ ] Test electronics. If it's broken and you haven't fixed it yet, you won't fix it after the move.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Books (small boxes — never fill a large box with books), DVDs/games, wall art, decorative objects, photo frames, candles.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Lamps (remove bulbs and shades, wrap separately), electronics (see fragile tips), throw pillows and blankets, curtains and rods.
- [ ] **Last (week 1):** TV, gaming console, router/modem, streaming devices. Photograph the cable setup on the back of your TV and router before unplugging.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap framed art and mirrors in bubble wrap, then sandwich between two pieces of cardboard taped together. Mark GLASS.
- [ ] If you have original boxes for electronics, use them. If not, wrap in bubble wrap and pack snugly so nothing shifts.
- [ ] Zip cables into labeled bags (write what they connect to). Tape the bag to the device or put it in the same box.
- [ ] Remove batteries from remotes to prevent corrosion.
- [ ] Lamp shades dent easily. Wrap in paper, never in bubble wrap (it leaves marks). Pack in a separate box, top only, nothing on top of them.

---

## PRIMARY BEDROOM (BR1) — Pack weeks 2–1

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Clothing: try the reverse-hanger trick if you have a few weeks — turn all hangers backward, and anything you don't wear stays turned and gets donated.
- [ ] Shoes: if they're worn out or uncomfortable, they go.
- [ ] Nightstand junk drawer: sort, toss, keep.
- [ ] Under the bed: pull everything out. Be honest.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Off-season clothing, formal wear, shoes you won't need. Use wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes if your mover offers them, or leave clothes on hangers and drape a trash bag over a bundle with a hole for the hooks.
- [ ] **Second (end of week 2):** Most dresser contents, extra bedding, decorative pillows, nightstand items.
- [ ] **Last (morning of move):** The sheets you slept on, the pillow you used, the clothes you're wearing tomorrow, and the phone charger. These go in the car, not the truck.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Jewelry: carry it with you in the car. Use a small ziplock or travel case.
- [ ] Use clothing (socks, t-shirts) to wrap small fragile items like picture frames. It saves paper and packs two things at once.

---

## SECOND BEDROOM / OFFICE (BR2) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours. **Who:** P

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Shred old documents you no longer need (see the document list for what to keep).
- [ ] Recycle old magazines, catalogs, and junk mail piles.
- [ ] Sort office supplies — donate excess pens, binders, and notebooks to a school or thrift store.
- [ ] Old tech (chargers for devices you don't own, dead hard drives, tangled mystery cables): e-waste recycling.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Books, files you're keeping, craft supplies, decorative items, guest bedding.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Desk contents, office supplies, monitor, printer. Photograph cable setups.
- [ ] **Last (week 1):** Laptop and work essentials. If you're working remotely up to the move, this may be the very last thing packed. Keep it in the car.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Monitors: wrap the screen face with a soft cloth, then bubble wrap. Pack upright, never flat, and mark which side is the screen.
- [ ] Hard drives and backup drives: carry in the car. They're irreplaceable.

---

## BATHROOMS (BA1, BA2) — Pack week 1

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours total. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (30 min per bathroom)**

- [ ] Check expiration dates on medications, sunscreen, and first aid supplies. Toss expired items safely (many pharmacies accept old meds).
- [ ] Discard nearly empty bottles, dried-out products, and hotel toiletries you'll never use.
- [ ] Old towels that are threadbare: donate to an animal shelter, they always need them.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Guest towels, extra supplies, medicine cabinet overflow, cleaning products you won't need again.
- [ ] **Second (day before):** Most toiletries, towels, bath mat, shower curtain.
- [ ] **Last (morning of):** Toothbrushes, deodorant, face wash, prescription meds, one towel per person. These go in your toiletry bag in the car.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Put caps on liquids and seal them in individual ziplock bags in case they leak. Group the bags in one box.
- [ ] Mirrors: wrap and pack like art (see living room).

---

## LAUNDRY ROOM — Pack week 1

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours. **Who:** P

**Declutter (20 min)**

- [ ] Toss nearly empty detergent bottles and stained rags.
- [ ] Donate surplus cleaning supplies rather than moving them 2,400 miles.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 2):** Iron, ironing board, drying rack, extra supplies.
- [ ] **Second (day before):** Do a final load of laundry. Pack detergent, hamper, and remaining supplies.
- [ ] **Last:** Leave the washer and dryer doors open overnight after the final load to prevent mildew (if you own them and they're staying, wipe them down).

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Seal all liquids in ziplock bags. Transport upright.

---

## HALL CLOSETS / COAT CLOSETS (CLO) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per closet. **Who:** J

**Declutter (30 min per closet)**

- [ ] Off-season coats you haven't worn in two years: donate.
- [ ] Board games missing pieces, old umbrellas, random bags: toss or donate.
- [ ] Luggage: empty it, check every pocket, then use it as a packing container for soft items.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Seasonal gear, luggage (packed with soft items inside), board games, extra linens.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Coats, shoes, vacuum, miscellaneous.
- [ ] **Last:** Keep one coat per person accessible if traveling through mountain weather (you will be).

---

## GARAGE (GAR) — Pack weeks 4–3

**Estimated time:** 4–8 hours depending on volume. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (2–3 hours — this is usually the biggest purge)**

- [ ] Sort tools: keep one good set, donate or sell duplicates. A cross-country move is not worth it for a rusty rake.
- [ ] Chemicals, paint, propane, fertilizer, pesticides: movers cannot transport these and you should not put them in a moving truck. Dispose of them at your county hazardous waste facility or give them to a neighbor.
- [ ] Old furniture, broken items, and "I'll fix it someday" projects: be ruthless. Sell, donate, or curb alert.
- [ ] Sports equipment nobody uses: donate.
- [ ] Holiday decorations: keep only what you love. Donate the rest.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 4):** Holiday decorations, seasonal items, rarely used tools.
- [ ] **Second (week 3):** Remaining tools, workbench contents, bikes, sports gear. Disassemble what you can.
- [ ] **Last (week 2):** Items you use regularly — lawn equipment (if bringing it), car supplies, step ladder.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap power tool blades and sharp edges in cardboard secured with tape.
- [ ] Drain fuel from all gas-powered equipment (mower, trimmer, chainsaw). Movers and truck rental companies prohibit fuel.

---

## ATTIC (ATT) — Pack weeks 5–4

**Estimated time:** 2–6 hours depending on what's up there. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] If you haven't opened a box since the last move, seriously consider donating it unopened or at least opening it and deciding quickly.
- [ ] Check for water damage and pest damage. Damaged items are not worth moving.
- [ ] Sentimental items: keep what matters, photograph the rest and let it go.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 5):** Since attic items are by definition not in daily use, pack everything early. Re-box items in deteriorated boxes.
- [ ] **Last:** Nothing should remain in the attic by week 3.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Old photos and documents: pack flat in a sealed plastic bin to protect from moisture during transport. Carry irreplaceable photos in the car.

---

## BASEMENT (BSM) — Pack weeks 5–3

**Estimated time:** 3–6 hours. **Who:** J

**Declutter first (1–2 hours)**

- [ ] Same rules as attic: if it's been down there untouched for years, question its value.
- [ ] Check for mold or mildew on stored items. Don't bring it to the new home.
- [ ] Old paint cans, solvents, and chemicals: hazardous waste disposal, same as garage.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 5):** Storage items, seasonal decor, archived boxes.
- [ ] **Second (week 4):** Furniture, exercise equipment (disassemble what you can and bag the hardware in labeled ziplock bags taped to the item).
- [ ] **Last (week 3):** Anything you're still using regularly.

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Wrap exercise equipment screens and panels in bubble wrap. Tape loose cables to the frame.

---

## OUTDOOR SPACES (OUT) — Pack weeks 3–2

**Estimated time:** 2–4 hours. **Who:** M

**Declutter first (1 hour)**

- [ ] Decide what patio furniture is worth moving. Resin chairs cost less to replace than to ship.
- [ ] Garden tools: keep the good ones, donate the rest.
- [ ] Potted plants: movers generally will not transport live plants across state lines (and Oregon has agricultural restrictions). Give them to friends or neighbors. Research Oregon's plant import rules if you want to bring something specific.
- [ ] Hoses, sprinklers, and yard chemicals: usually cheaper to replace than to move.

**Pack in this order**

- [ ] **First (week 3):** Decor, string lights, bird feeders, small garden tools.
- [ ] **Second (week 2):** Patio furniture (disassemble if possible), grill (clean it, remove the propane tank, do not transport propane).
- [ ] **Last:** Door mats, welcome signs, house numbers (if yours).

**Fragile tips**

- [ ] Ceramic pots break easily. Wrap in bubble wrap and pack in boxes with crumpled paper. If the pot isn't special, leave it.

---

## GENERAL PACKING RULES

**The heavy-light rule:** Heavy items (books, tools, cans) go in small boxes. Light items (linens, pillows, clothes) go in large boxes. Never make a box heavier than you can comfortably lift.

**The 50-pound rule:** No box should exceed roughly 50 lbs. Your back, your movers, and your boxes will all thank you.

**Fill every box completely.** Half-empty boxes collapse when stacked. Use packing paper, towels, or clothing to fill gaps.

**Tape matters.** Use quality packing tape, not masking tape or duct tape. Tape the bottom of every box with an H-pattern (one strip down the center seam, one strip across each edge).

**One room per box.** Don't mix rooms. It makes unpacking chaotic.

**Color coding (optional upgrade):** Buy colored dot stickers — one color per room

# DELIVERABLE 2B: Declutter-for-Sale Plan (One Page)

**Responsibility: P** leads listings and communication. **M** handles photos and staging. **J** for pricing decisions.

---

## Where to Sell

**Facebook Marketplace** is the strongest platform for furniture, appliances, and household goods in most Ohio markets. It's free to list, has local reach, and buyers expect to pick up. **Craigslist** still works for tools, electronics, and niche items but has a smaller audience than it used to. **OfferUp** is a decent backup, especially in suburban areas. **Nextdoor** is good for small items and "curb alert" free-stuff posts. **Mercari or eBay** are worth it only for items worth $40+ that are easy to ship (electronics, collectibles, brand-name goods), because they take fees and require shipping logistics you don't have time for right now.

**Recommended default:** List everything on Facebook Marketplace first. Cross-post to Craigslist if it doesn't sell in 3 days.

## Pricing Guidance

The goal is speed, not maximum profit. You're on a 4–6 week sell-off window. Price to move, not to negotiate.

A reasonable starting point for used household goods in good condition is roughly 25–40% of what it costs new. For furniture, 30–50% of retail if it's in good shape and from a recognizable brand, and 15–25% if it's flat-pack or heavily used. For electronics, check the same item's "sold" listings on eBay or Facebook to see what people actually paid, not what others are asking. For free stuff, post it on your curb with a "FREE" sign and a Nextdoor post. It will disappear in hours.

**The two-week rule:** If it hasn't sold in a week, drop the price by 25–30%. If it still hasn't sold after two weeks, donate it, give it away, or leave it curbside. You do not have time for a third week.

## Sample Listings

**Version 1: Quick Sell (priced to go fast)**

Title: `IKEA KALLAX shelf 4x2 — white — $30 OBO — must pick up by Saturday`

Description: `IKEA KALLAX 4x2 shelf unit in white. Good condition, some minor scratches on top. We're moving and need it gone this week. $30 or best offer. Pickup only — [your neighborhood or cross streets]. Available evenings and Saturday morning. Cash or Venmo.`

**Version 2: Better Price (for items worth more patience)**

Title: `West Elm Mid-Century Media Console — Acorn — 56" — $275`

Description: `West Elm mid-century media console in Acorn finish, 56 inches wide. Bought in 2022 for $600. Excellent condition — no scratches, stains, or damage. Holds a 55" TV comfortably. Solid wood legs, two cabinets with adjustable shelves. We're relocating out of state; available for pickup in [neighborhood] anytime in the next two weeks. I can help load if you bring a truck or SUV. $275 firm for the first week; after that I'll consider offers. Cash, Venmo, or Zelle.`

## Photo Tips

Take photos in daylight, not under overhead lamps. Open the curtains or move the item near a window. Clear clutter from the background — buyers are looking at your item, but a messy room makes everything look worse. Shoot one wide shot showing the full item, one close-up of the brand label or any notable detail, and one close-up of any flaws (scratches, stains). Showing flaws builds trust and prevents time-wasting arguments at pickup. Shoot at the item's level, not looking down at it. Five photos is enough for most items.

## Pickup and Safety

Meet buyers at your front door or driveway, not inside the house. Daytime pickups only. If the item is small and you're uncomfortable with a home address, meet at a well-lit public spot (many police stations have designated safe-trade zones in the parking lot). Tell someone in your household when a buyer is coming and roughly when. Cash is king, but Venmo and Zelle work. Don't accept personal checks. If a buyer asks you to ship something, says they'll send a courier, or offers to overpay with a cashier's check, it's a scam — ignore and move on. Don't hold items without a deposit; "I'll come tomorrow" often means never. First person with cash in hand wins.

## Declutter-for-Sale Timeline

Weeks 6–5: List the big-ticket items (furniture, appliances, electronics) while you still have time to wait for a fair price. Weeks 4–3: Drop prices on anything unsold, list medium items (kitchen gear, tools, decor). Weeks 2–1: Everything remaining either gets donated, given away on Nextdoor/curb alert, or goes in the trash. Do not let unsold items delay your packing. The last week is for packing and cleaning, not negotiating with buyers.

# Ohio → Oregon Vehicle & DMV Action Plan

**Important caveat:** DMV rules, fees, and timelines change. Everything below reflects information current as of early-to-mid 2025. Verify details at the official Oregon DMV site (oregon.gov/odot/dmv) and Ohio BMV site before you act. Call ahead to confirm document requirements, especially for financed vehicles, because individual DMV offices sometimes ask for additional paperwork.

---

## TIMELINE AT A GLANCE

Oregon law generally requires new residents to get an Oregon driver's license and register their vehicles within 30 days of establishing residency. "Establishing residency" typically means the date you move in, start working, or enroll kids in school — whichever comes first. In practice, you want to start the process in your first two weeks so you aren't scrambling at the deadline.

| When | What | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Before you leave Ohio | Gather documents, contact lienholder, do NOT cancel Ohio registration yet | M |
| Days 1–3 in Oregon | Settle in, locate nearest DMV, book appointments online | M |
| Days 4–10 | Get Oregon driver's licenses (both of you) | M and P separately |
| Days 7–14 | Get emissions test if required in your county | M |
| Days 10–20 | Register vehicle(s) and title in Oregon | M |
| Days 20–30 | Confirm everything is complete, update insurance, cancel Ohio registration and return plates | M |

---

## STEP 1: BEFORE YOU LEAVE OHIO

**Who:** M leads, P gathers their own license documents.

**Timeline:** Weeks 3–1 before move.

**1a. Gather documents for each vehicle**

- [ ] Ohio certificate of title. If you have a paper title in hand with no lien, you're set. Bring the original.
- [ ] Current Ohio registration card.
- [ ] Proof of insurance (your current policy is fine for now as long as it covers you in Oregon — call your insurer to confirm).
- [ ] Odometer reading (write it down; you'll need it for the Oregon title application).

**1b. If the vehicle is financed or leased**

This is the step most people underestimate. If there's a lien on the title, the lienholder (bank, credit union, or lease company) holds the title or is listed on it. Oregon DMV needs the title or proof of lien to register.

- [ ] Call your lienholder now, at least 2–3 weeks before the move. Tell them you're moving to Oregon and need to register the vehicle there.
- [ ] Ask the lienholder to send the title directly to the Oregon DMV, or ask them to send you a letter of authorization (sometimes called a "letter of lien" or "lienholder authorization") that Oregon DMV can accept in lieu of the physical title.
- [ ] Some lienholders will send an electronic lien (ELT) directly to Oregon. Ask if they participate in Oregon's ELT program.
- [ ] If the lienholder mails a physical title, have them send it to your new Oregon address or to the Oregon DMV office you plan to visit. Do not have it sent to your old Ohio address after you've left.
- [ ] Get the lienholder's exact legal name and address as it appears on the title — Oregon DMV will need this.
- [ ] If you're leasing, contact the leasing company. Some lease agreements restrict out-of-state registration. Get written confirmation that you're allowed to register in Oregon.

**1c. Contact your auto insurance company**

- [ ] Tell them your move date and new address.
- [ ] Confirm your policy covers you in Oregon effective on your arrival date.
- [ ] Ask about updating the policy to Oregon after you register. Some insurers handle this as a simple address change; others require you to start a new policy with Oregon-specific coverage.
- [ ] Get a new insurance card or digital proof showing Oregon coverage. You'll need proof of insurance at the Oregon DMV.

**1d. Do NOT cancel Ohio registration or return Ohio plates yet**

You need valid registration to legally drive the car to Oregon. Keep Ohio plates on the vehicle until Oregon plates are in hand. Cancel Ohio registration after Oregon registration is complete.

---

## STEP 2: DAYS 1–3 IN OREGON — SET UP APPOINTMENTS

**Who:** M

Oregon DMV offices are appointment-preferred. Walk-ins are possible but wait times can be very long, especially in the Portland metro area.

- [ ] Go to oregon.gov/odot/dmv and book appointments for driver's license and vehicle registration. You can sometimes combine them into one visit, but it depends on the office. Book the earliest slots available.
- [ ] Identify which DMV office serves your area. Major offices include Portland (multiple locations), Salem, Eugene, Bend, and Medford.
- [ ] Check the specific office's hours and whether they handle titling (most full-service offices do, but some smaller ones have limited services).

---

## STEP 3: DAYS 4–10 — GET OREGON DRIVER'S LICENSES

**Who:** M and P each do this individually. You can go together but each person completes their own application.

**What to bring (each person)**

- [ ] Your current valid Ohio driver's license.
- [ ] Proof of legal presence (U.S. passport, birth certificate, or permanent resident card). If you want a Real ID–compliant license, you'll need one of these plus proof of Social Security number (SSN card or W-2) and two proofs of Oregon residency (lease agreement, utility bill in your name, bank statement with Oregon address). Check the Real ID document requirements on the Oregon DMV site for the current list.
- [ ] If you don't need Real ID, the requirements may be simpler, but Oregon has been issuing Real ID–compliant licenses by default. Verify what your specific situation requires.
- [ ] Payment (see fees below).

**What happens at the DMV**

Oregon generally does not require a written knowledge test if you hold a valid license from another state, but policies can vary and this may have changed. Check the DMV site or call ahead to confirm. You will not need a driving test. You will get a vision screening. You will get a new photo taken. You'll surrender your Ohio license (they'll punch a hole in it and may let you keep it, or they may keep it).

**Fees (ballpark, verify current amounts)**

Oregon driver's license for a standard license is typically around $40–$60 for an 8-year license. Real ID–compliant licenses may cost slightly more. Check the current fee schedule on the Oregon DMV site.

---

## STEP 4: DAYS 7–14 — EMISSIONS TESTING (IF REQUIRED)

**Who:** M

This is the step that depends entirely on where in Oregon you're living. Oregon's DEQ (Department of Environmental Quality) requires emissions testing in specific areas. Here's the breakdown by major region:

**Portland Metro (Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties)**

Required. This is the most common scenario for new residents. You need a DEQ emissions test before you can register a vehicle that is new to Oregon (meaning it wasn't previously registered here). The test is called a "Clean Air Station" test. Stations are located throughout the metro area. The test is a tailpipe or OBD-II scan depending on the vehicle's year. Cost is approximately $25 as of recent years. You can find station locations and hours at oregon.gov/deq. Some stations accept walk-ins; some require appointments. Go early in the day for shorter lines.

**Eugene / Springfield (Lane County, parts of)**

Required in the Eugene-Springfield urban growth boundary. Same DEQ test, same approximate cost. Fewer stations than Portland, so book early or go at off-peak times.

**Medford / Ashland (Jackson County, parts of)**

Required in the Medford-Ashland area and Rogue Valley. Same DEQ test.

**Bend (Deschutes County)**

Not required. Bend and Central Oregon are outside the DEQ testing area. No emissions test needed to register.

**Salem, Corvallis, coast cities, rural Oregon**

Not required in most of these areas. If you're unsure, check the DEQ boundary maps on the DEQ website or call them.

**What to bring to the emissions test**

- [ ] The vehicle.
- [ ] Your Ohio registration (to prove it's your car).
- [ ] Payment (cash or card, approximately $25).
- [ ] You'll receive a certificate or receipt. Keep it — you'll need it at the DMV for registration.

**Common issue:** If your car fails the emissions test, you'll need to get it repaired and retested before you can register. If you suspect your car might have an emissions issue (check engine light on, old catalytic converter), consider getting it checked before the move.

---

## STEP 5: DAYS 10–20 — REGISTER AND TITLE THE VEHICLE IN OREGON

**Who:** M

**What to bring**

- [ ] Oregon driver's license (get this first, it makes everything smoother).
- [ ] Ohio certificate of title (original). If financed, bring the lienholder authorization letter, or confirm the lienholder has sent the title or ELT to Oregon DMV.
- [ ] Current Ohio registration card.
- [ ] Proof of Oregon insurance (updated card or printout showing the vehicle, your name, and Oregon address).
- [ ] DEQ emissions certificate (if your county requires it).
- [ ] Odometer disclosure (the DMV form will ask for this; just know your mileage).
- [ ] VIN — the DMV may do a VIN inspection at the counter or may require one done separately. For most standard passenger vehicles transferring from another state with a clean title, this is handled at the counter. Call ahead to confirm.
- [ ] Payment for fees (see below).

**Fees (ballpark, verify current amounts)**

Oregon vehicle fees include a title fee (typically around $80–$100), registration fee (typically around $120–$175 for a standard passenger vehicle for a 2-year registration), and plate fees (around $25 for standard plates). There may also be a county-specific fee and a parks fee. Total out-the-door for titling and registering one standard vehicle is commonly in the $200–$350 range, but it varies based on vehicle type and county. Electric and hybrid vehicles may have additional fees. Check oregon.gov/odot/dmv for the current fee calculator.

**What happens**

You'll fill out a title and registration application. The DMV will process the Ohio title, issue an Oregon title (mailed to you or your lienholder), and issue Oregon plates and registration. You'll get plates and a registration card that day in most cases. Put the new plates on before you drive away.

**If the vehicle is financed**

Oregon DMV will list the lienholder on the new Oregon title. The title will be sent directly to the lienholder or held electronically. This is standard and your lienholder should expect it if you've contacted them in advance.

---

## STEP 6: DAYS 20–30 — CLOSE OUT OHIO

**Who:** M

- [ ] Cancel your Ohio vehicle registration. You can do this by mailing your Ohio plates back to the Ohio BMV or by visiting an Ohio BMV deputy registrar office (which you obviously can't do from Oregon). The standard method is to mail the plates to: Ohio BMV, P.O. Box 16520, Columbus, OH 43216-6520, with a note requesting cancellation and including your name, Ohio registration number, and new state of registration. Check the Ohio BMV site for the current process and address.
- [ ] Request a refund of any unused registration period if Ohio allows prorated refunds (they sometimes do, depending on how much time was left). Check with Ohio BMV.
- [ ] Confirm your auto insurance has been fully updated to Oregon. The old Ohio policy should be replaced, not running in parallel. You don't want to pay for both.
- [ ] Keep a copy of your Ohio registration cancellation confirmation for your records.
- [ ] Update your insurance company with the new Oregon plate numbers and registration info.

---

## QUICK REFERENCE: DOCUMENTS CHECKLIST FOR DMV VISITS

Print this and bring everything. It's better to have a document you don't need than to make a second trip.

**For driver's license (each person)**

- [ ] Current Ohio license
- [ ] U.S. passport or birth certificate
- [ ] Social Security card or W-2 (for Real ID)
- [ ] Two proofs of Oregon address (lease, utility bill, bank statement)
- [ ] Payment

**For vehicle registration (each vehicle)**

- [ ] Oregon driver's license
- [ ] Ohio title (original) or lienholder authorization
- [ ] Ohio registration card
- [ ] Oregon insurance proof
- [ ] DEQ emissions certificate (if applicable)
- [ ] Odometer reading
- [ ] Payment

---

## FEES SUMMARY (BALLPARK PER VEHICLE)

| Item | Estimated Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Oregon driver's license | $40–$60 each | Per person, 8-year license |
| DEQ emissions test | ~$25 | Only if in a required area |
| Oregon title fee | $80–$100 | Per vehicle |
| Oregon registration (2-year) | $120–$175 | Varies by vehicle type |
| Plate fee | ~$25 | Standard plates |
| County/parks fees | $10–$30 | Varies |
| **Total per vehicle** | **$275–$430** | Rough range |
| **Total for 2 licenses + 1 vehicle** | **$355–$550** | Rough range |

---

## COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID

**Don't let the 30-day window expire.** Oregon can cite you for driving with out-of-state registration beyond the residency grace period. It's not heavily enforced, but if you get pulled over or have an accident, it becomes a problem.

**Don't cancel Ohio registration before Oregon plates are on the car.** You'd be driving an unregistered vehicle, which creates insurance and legal issues.

**Don't forget the lienholder lead time.** Banks are slow. Start the conversation 2–3 weeks before the move, not after you arrive.

**Don't skip the emissions test if you're in a required area.** The DMV will not register the vehicle without it.

**Don't assume your insurance auto-transfers.** Call your insurer. Some require a new policy for a new state. If you have a gap in coverage, Oregon DMV won't register the car, and you're driving uninsured.

# Solo Piano Arrangement in A Minor (Wedding, 12 Bars)

This is in 4/4, moderate tempo (around 72–80 bpm), gentle and lyrical. The RH plays the motif and variations. The LH uses a simple broken-chord pattern throughout: bass note on beat 1, then two upper chord tones alternating on beats 2, 3, and 4 (like a slow Alberti but without rushing). Think of the LH pattern as: low note – middle – high – middle, all eighth notes, two per beat.

### Bars 1–4: Statement

**Bar 1 — Am (i)**

LH: A₂ – E₃ – C₃ – E₃ – A₂ – E₃ – C₃ – E₃ (steady broken chord, all eighths)

**Bar 2 — Am (i)**

**Bar 3 — F (VI)**

**Bar 4 — Dm (iv)**

LH: D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂ – D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂

### Bars 5–8: Development and Lift

**Bar 5 — G (VII) or C (III)**
RH: G₄ – B₄ – C₅ – E₅ (eighth notes, the phrase opens upward for a hopeful quality)
LH: G₂ – D₃ – B₂ – D₃ – G₂ – D₃ – B₂ – D₃

**Bar 6 — Am (i)**
RH: E₅ – C₅ – A₄ – C₅ (eighth notes, gently descending)
LH: A₂ – E₃ – C₃ – E₃ (same as bar 1)

**Bar 7 — Dm (iv)**
RH: D₄ – F₄ – A₄ – B₄ (eighth notes, B natural appears as a passing tone reaching toward the dominant)
LH: D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂ – D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂

**Bar 8 — E (V, harmonic minor)**

LH: E₂ – B₂ – G#₂ – B₂ (broken chord, then hold)

### Bars 9–12: Return and Close

**Bar 9 — Am (i)**
RH: C₄ – E₄ – G₄ – A₄ (the original motif returns, eighth notes)
LH: A₂ – E₃ – C₃ – E₃ (same opening pattern, like coming home)

**Bar 10 — Am (i)**
RH: G₄ – E₄ – C₄ – E₄
LH: same as bar 9

**Bar 11 — Dm (iv)**
RH: D₄ – F₄ – E₄ – D₄ (eighth notes, a gentle stepwise descent settling down)
LH: D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂ – D₂ – A₂ – F₂ – A₂

**Bar 12 — Am (i)**
RH: C₄ – A₃ (quarter note, then dotted half note — the final A rings out)
LH: A₂ – E₃ – C₃ – E₃ – A₂ (slow the pattern, let the last A₂ sustain)

### Performance Notes

The plagal feeling of Dm–Am at the end (bars 11–12) gives a gentle, hymn-like close that suits a wedding processional or a quiet moment during the ceremony. If you want a stronger ending, replace bar 11 with E major (G#₂ – B₂ – E₃ broken chord in the LH, and add G#₄ in the RH melody) for a V–i authentic cadence.

Use the sustain pedal lightly, changing on each new chord. Keep the tempo steady and unhurried. The LH broken-chord pattern should stay quieter than the RH melody throughout.

If you want to extend it, repeat bars 1–8 as a second verse with the melody up an octave (C₅ – E₅ – G₅ – A₅) for a fuller sound, then play bars 9–12 as the final ending.

Here are two four-bar arrangements. Each one states the motif in bars 1–2, then extends it to a cadence in bars 3–4. I've kept the left hand simple with half-note or quarter-note chords so the right hand can focus on the eighth-note melody.

---

## Version 1: A Minor (Melodic Minor Ascending, Natural Descending)

### Right Hand (treble clef, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** C4 – E4 – F#4 – G#4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 2:** A4 – G4 – E4 – D4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 3:** C4 – E4 – G4 – A4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 4:** G4 – E4 – D4 – A3 (last note held as a quarter, giving a half-beat rest or fermata to breathe)

The ascending F# and G# in bar 1 give the melodic minor color. Bar 2 descends naturally (G natural, no sharps). Bar 3 restates the original arpeggiated shape, and bar 4 resolves down to A.

**RH Fingering (suggested):**
Bar 1: 1 – 3 – 4 – 5. Bar 2: 5 – 4 – 3 – 2. Bar 3: 1 – 3 – 4 – 5. Bar 4: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1.

### Left Hand (bass clef, half notes or quarter notes)

**Bar 1:** Am chord (A2 – C3 – E3), held as a half note, then D major (D2 – F#2 – A2) as a half note to support the F#.
**Bar 2:** E major (E2 – G#2 – B2) half note, then Am (A2 – C3 – E3) half note.
**Bar 3:** Am (A2 – C3 – E3) whole note, held through the bar.
**Bar 4:** E major (E2 – G#2 – B2) half note, then Am (A2 – C3 – E3) half note, final chord held or with fermata.

**LH Fingering:**
For Am (A2–C3–E3): 5 – 3 – 1. For D major (D2–F#2–A2): 5 – 3 – 1. For E major (E2–G#2–B2): 5 – 3 – 1.

### Dynamics and Articulation
Start mezzo-piano. Play the eighth notes legato, connecting each note smoothly. In bar 1, let the line grow slightly (small crescendo) as it rises through F# and G#. Bar 2 relaxes dynamically as you descend. Bar 4's final A can be played a touch softer, piano, to feel like settling. The left-hand chords should stay quieter than the melody throughout.

---

## Version 2: C Minor (Harmonic Minor)

### Right Hand (treble clef, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 2:** G4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 3:** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 4:** G4 – F4 – D4 – B3 – C4 (the first four as eighth notes, final C4 as a quarter note to end)

Bar 4 introduces the B natural (harmonic minor leading tone) on the last eighth note before resolving up to C. This gives a strong sense of arrival.

**RH Fingering:**
Bar 1: 1 – 2 – 4 – 5. Bar 2: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1. Bar 3: 1 – 2 – 4 – 5. Bar 4: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1 (thumb shifts to C4 for the final note).

### Left Hand (bass clef, half notes)

**Bar 1:** Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) whole note.
**Bar 2:** Ab major (Ab2 – C3 – Eb3) half note, then Eb major (Eb2 – G2 – Bb2) half note.
**Bar 3:** Fm (F2 – Ab2 – C3) half note, then Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) half note.
**Bar 4:** G major (G2 – B2 – D3) half note, then Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) half note with fermata.

The G major chord in bar 4 contains the B natural, which doubles the leading tone in the right hand and creates the dominant-to-tonic resolution (V–i).

**LH Fingering:**
Cm (C2–Eb2–G2): 5 – 3 – 1. Ab major (Ab2–C3–Eb3): 5 – 3 – 1. Fm (F2–Ab2–C3): 5 – 3 – 1. G major (G2–B2–D3): 5 – 3 – 1.

### Dynamics and Articulation
Start mezzo-forte — C minor has a darker, fuller character, so a slightly stronger opening feels right. Keep eighth notes legato. In bar 4, make a slight ritardando (slow down) on the last two beats as the B natural resolves to C. The final Cm chord can be held with the pedal for resonance. Sustain pedal can also be used lightly at chord changes throughout, lifting and re-pressing with each new left-hand chord to keep the sound clean.

---

## General Practice Notes

Play hands separately first at a slow tempo (around 60–70 bpm, one beat per quarter note). Once each hand is comfortable, combine them. Listen for the left hand staying softer than the right so the melody sings. The A minor version has a gentler, more lyrical quality; the C minor version sounds darker and more dramatic — try both and see which suits the mood you're after.

### A Minor — Alberti Bass (Low–High–Middle–High, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** A2 – E3 – C3 – E3 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3 (eight eighth notes total)
**Bar 2:** E2 – B2 – G#2 – B2 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3

**Bar 4:** E2 – B2 – G#2 – B2 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3

LH fingering for the Alberti pattern: 5 – 1 – 3 – 1 throughout. The hand stays in one position per chord, so there is no jumping.

### C Minor — Broken Fifth (root–fifth alternating, quarter notes)

**Bar 1:** C2 – G2 – C2 – G2
**Bar 2:** Ab1 – Eb2 – Eb2 – Bb2
**Bar 3:** F2 – C3 – C2 – G2
**Bar 4:** G2 – D3 – C2 – G2

LH fingering: 5 – 1 for each pair. The hand shifts at each new chord but the interval is always a fifth, which is easy to find by feel.

### Alternative RH Fingering (Easier Spots)

In the A minor version bar 4, the original fingering 4–3–2–1 ending on low A3 can be awkward. Try instead: 5–3–2–1, which gives the pinky more room on G4 and lets the thumb land naturally on A3.

In the C minor version bar 4, the five-note bar (G4–F4–D4–B3–C4) is the trickiest moment. Instead of 4–3–2–1–1 with a thumb shift, try 4–3–2–1–2, crossing the index finger over the thumb to C4. Alternatively, simplify the bar to four notes: G4–D4–B3–C4 (fingering 4–3–2–1), which skips the F4 passing tone and still gives a clean cadence.

## Tempo, Pedal, and Performance Notes

**Metronome:** quarter note = 66–72 bpm to start. Once comfortable, 80–88 bpm feels musical without rushing. The A minor version can sit a touch slower (66–76) for its lyrical quality; the C minor version can push slightly faster (72–88) for energy.

**Pedal:** In the A minor Alberti version, use no pedal or very light pedal, changing with each chord (lift and re-press on beat 1 of each new harmony). The Alberti pattern provides its own sustain. In the C minor broken-fifth version, use pedal more freely: press on beat 1 of each bar, lift briefly on beat 3 or when the chord changes, and re-press. In bar 4, hold the pedal through the final Cm chord for resonance.

import pretty_midi

def add_single_notes(inst, notes, t0, dur, vel):

## A Minor — Classical Version

Your draft progression is solid. I'd make one small adjustment: use E7 instead of E in bar 2 for the stronger dominant pull, and end with a clear perfect cadence.

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Am | **Bar 2:** E7 | **Bar 3:** F | **Bar 4:** E7 → Am

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – E – G – A – G – E – G – A
**Bar 2:** G# – B – E – G# – B – G# – E – D
**Bar 3:** C – F – A – C – A – F – E – D
**Bar 4:** E – G# – B – E | A – C – E – A (half bar E7, half bar Am)

### Left Hand (block chords or broken, quarter notes)
**Bar 1:** A₂ – C₃ – E₃ (root position, two hits or held)
**Bar 2:** E₂ – G#₂ – B₂ – D₃ (E7, root position)
**Bar 3:** F₂ – A₂ – C₃ (root position)
**Bar 4:** E₂ – G#₂ – B₂ on beat 1, then A₂ – C₃ – E₃ on beat 3

### Voice-Leading Tips
Keep common tones between chords stationary. Am to E7: the E stays, C moves down a half step to B, A moves down to G#. E7 to F: G# resolves up to A, B moves up to C, D moves up or stays depending on voicing. This gives you smooth stepwise motion almost everywhere, which is the hallmark of classical voice leading. Avoid jumping all three voices at once.

---

## A Minor — Modern/Sparse Version

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Am (open fifth, no third) | **Bar 2:** Am/E (pedal E in bass) | **Bar 3:** F add9 (no third) | **Bar 4:** Am (open fifth)

### Right Hand (melody, same rhythm)
**Bar 1:** C – E – G – A – G – E – G – A
**Bar 2:** same motif or slight variation: C – E – G – A – B – A – G – E
**Bar 3:** C – F – G – A – G – F – E – D
**Bar 4:** C – E – G – A – G – E – D – A (land on A, hold)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** A₂ and E₃ (open fifth, held whole note)
**Bar 2:** E₂ (single bass pedal, whole note)
**Bar 3:** F₂ and C₃ (open fifth), or F₂ – G₂ – C₃ for the add9 color
**Bar 4:** A₂ and E₃ (return to open fifth, whole note)

The left hand here is deliberately still. Let the right hand do all the movement. The emptiness of open fifths leaves the major/minor quality ambiguous, which is the modern sound you're after.

---

## C Minor — Classical Version

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Cm | **Bar 2:** G7 | **Bar 3:** Ab | **Bar 4:** G7 → Cm

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – G – Ab
**Bar 2:** G – B – D – G – F – D – B – D
**Bar 3:** C – Eb – Ab – C – Ab – Eb – D – C
**Bar 4:** B – D – G – B | C – Eb – G – C (half bar G7, half bar Cm)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** C₂ – Eb₂ – G₂ (root position)
**Bar 2:** G₂ – B₂ – D₃ – F₃ (G7, root position)
**Bar 3:** Ab₂ – C₃ – Eb₃ (root position)
**Bar 4:** G₂ – B₂ – D₃ on beat 1, then C₂ – Eb₂ – G₂ on beat 3

### Voice-Leading Tips
Cm to G7: Eb moves down a half step to D, G stays, C moves down to B. G7 to Ab: B resolves up to C, D moves up to Eb, F moves up to Ab or down to Eb. The leading tone (B natural) should always resolve upward to C — this is the most important voice-leading rule in minor-key classical harmony.

---

## C Minor — Modern/Sparse Version

Your draft progression works well. I'd refine it slightly.

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Cm (open fifth) | **Bar 2:** Cm/G (G pedal) | **Bar 3:** Ab (open fifth) | **Bar 4:** Cm over Bb pedal

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – G – Ab
**Bar 2:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – D – C
**Bar 3:** Ab – C – Eb – Ab – G – Eb – D – C
**Bar 4:** C – Eb – G – C – Bb – G – Eb – C (descend to final C, hold)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** C₂ and G₂ (open fifth, whole note)
**Bar 2:** G₁ (single bass pedal, whole note — the low G gives depth)
**Bar 3:** Ab₁ and Eb₂ (open fifth, whole note)
**Bar 4:** Bb₁ (pedal, whole note — the Bb creates tension under the Cm melody that resolves when the melody lands on C)

### Voice-Leading Tips for the Modern Versions
Voice leading in sparse textures is about bass motion. Move the bass by step or by third rather than by fifth — that keeps the modern, floating quality. C pedal to G pedal (down a fourth or up a fifth) is the biggest leap here, and it works because it's a pedal tone shift rather than a chord change. The Ab to Bb bass motion at the end is stepwise, which feels natural and inevitable.

---

## General Practice Suggestion
Play through the classical versions first to internalize the harmonic gravity, then play the modern versions and notice how the same melody feels different over open voicings. That contrast will teach you a lot about how harmony shapes the character of a line.

The hardest moment is the shift from bar 2 into bar 3, where your left hand goes from a single pedal tone or open fifth to full triads on every beat. # Week 1 Lesson Plans: DNA Structure, Replication, Transcription, Translation & Modeling the Central Dogma

---

## Lesson 1: The Structure of DNA

**Daily "I Can" Objective:** I can describe the structure of DNA by identifying its components (nucleotides, base pairing, sugar-phosphate backbone, antiparallel strands) and explain how the structure allows it to store information.

**NGSS Alignment:**
- HS-LS1-1 (Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins)
- SEP: Developing and Using Models
- CCC: Structure and Function

---

### Sequence of Activities

**Engage (8 min) — "What makes a good instruction manual?"**
Display a short, corrupted instruction manual (a recipe with missing or scrambled steps) alongside a correct version. Ask students to turn and talk: "What features make one set of instructions work and the other fail?" After a brief share-out, pose the driving question for the week on the board: *How does a molecule store and transmit instructions for building a living thing?*

Tell students they will build a single model this week that answers that question, and they will revise it each day.

**Explore (18 min) — Nucleotide manipulatives build**
Provide each pair of students with a bag of color-coded card-stock cutouts (or foam pieces) representing phosphate groups, deoxyribose sugars, and the four bases (A, T, C, G — shaped so that A only fits with T and C only fits with G). Each base should be labeled with its full name on the back.

Student-facing prompt (printed on a half-sheet):
> 1. Sort the pieces into groups. What do you think each group represents?
> 2. Try to assemble a single nucleotide. Sketch what you built.
> 3. Now connect several nucleotides into a strand. What bonds hold them together?
> 4. Build a second strand that "fits" against the first. What rule seems to govern which bases pair?
> 5. Look at the two strands. Do they run in the same direction, or opposite directions? How can you tell?

Circulate and use guiding questions rather than answers. If a pair is stuck on directionality, prompt them to look at which end of the sugar the phosphate connects to.

**Explain (15 min) — Direct instruction with annotation**
Using a projected diagram of double-stranded DNA, walk through the following, pausing for students to annotate a printed scaffold diagram at their seats:
- Nucleotide = phosphate + sugar + base (the "monomer")
- Complementary base pairing (A-T with 2 hydrogen bonds, C-G with 3) and why it matters for information storage
- Sugar-phosphate backbone and 5′→3′ directionality
- Antiparallel orientation
- The double helix as a three-dimensional form of the ladder they built

Key question to pose mid-explanation: *"If I gave you one strand of DNA, could you figure out the other? Why is that important?"*

After instruction, students return to their manipulative models and check or correct their builds.

**Elaborate (10 min) — Begin the unit model (Version 1)**
Hand out a large sheet of paper (or have students open a shared digital slide). Student-facing prompt:

> **Unit Model — Version 1: DNA Structure**
> Draw or diagram the structure of DNA. Your model must show and label: at least 4 nucleotides per strand, correct base pairing, the sugar-phosphate backbone, 5′ and 3′ ends, and antiparallel orientation.
> Below your diagram, write one sentence answering: "How does the structure of DNA allow it to store information?"
> Finally, write one limitation of your model — something about real DNA that your model does not show.

Collect or photograph these; they will be revised in Lessons 2–4.

---

### Formative Check & Exit Ticket (4 min)

**Exit ticket (index card or digital form):**
> 1. A strand of DNA reads 5′-ATCGGA-3′. Write the complementary strand with correct directionality.
> 2. In one sentence, explain why the base-pairing rule is essential for DNA's function.

**Sample acceptable responses:**
1. 3′-TAGCCT-5′
2. Any response that links complementary pairing to accurate information storage or copying, e.g., "Because each base only pairs with one partner, the sequence on one strand determines the sequence on the other, so the information can be copied accurately."

---

### Materials & Prep
- Color-coded nucleotide cutouts (pre-cut card stock or foam), one bag per pair — prep time ~30 min if making from templates; reusable across periods
- Printed scaffold diagrams of DNA (one per student)
- Half-sheet explore prompt (one per pair)
- Large paper or digital slide for unit model
- Projected DNA diagram for direct instruction
- Index cards or digital exit ticket form

### Differentiation & Literacy Supports
- **Below grade level / ELL:** Provide a labeled reference card with nucleotide vocabulary (nucleotide, phosphate, deoxyribose, base, complementary) and a sentence frame for the exit ticket: "Base pairing is essential because ___."
- **Above grade level:** Ask these students to annotate their model with the chemical reason A pairs with T and C pairs with G (number of hydrogen bonds, molecular size of purines vs. pyrimidines) and to explain why the two strands must be antiparallel for the bases to align.
- **IEP/504 extended time:** These students may complete the exit ticket at the start of Lesson 2.
- **Kinesthetic / spatial:** The manipulative build is the primary access point; students who benefit from movement can stand at a lab bench to build.

### Mini-Rubric for Unit Model Version 1

| Criterion | Proficient (3) | Developing (2) | Beginning (1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Components** | All 5 required labels present and accurate | 3–4 labels present and accurate | Fewer than 3 labels or significant errors |
| **Base pairing** | All pairs correct (A-T, C-G) | One error | Multiple errors or pairing rule not evident |
| **Directionality** | 5′ and 3′ ends labeled; antiparallel shown | Labeled but not antiparallel, or vice versa | Neither shown |
| **Information sentence** | Clearly links structure to information storage | Partially links structure to function | No connection made |
| **Limitation** | Identifies a genuine limitation of the model | Identifies a limitation but it is vague | No limitation stated |

---
---

## Lesson 2: DNA Replication — Copying the Code

**Daily "I Can" Objective:** I can model the process of DNA replication, identify the roles of helicase, DNA polymerase, and primase, and explain why replication is called semiconservative.

**NGSS Alignment:**
- HS-LS1-1
- SEP: Developing and Using Models
- CCC: Cause and Effect (enzyme action causes strand separation and new strand synthesis)

---

### Sequence of Activities

**Engage (6 min) — The zipper analogy**
Hold up a closed zipper (on a jacket or a standalone zipper from a craft store). Ask: "If this zipper represents double-stranded DNA, what would you have to do to copy it? What problems might come up?" Take 3–4 student responses. Record predictions on the board under the heading *Problems to solve during replication.*

Transition: "Today you'll figure out how the cell solves each of these problems."

**Explore (20 min) — Replication simulation with manipulatives**
Students retrieve their nucleotide manipulative models from Lesson 1. Each pair also receives a small set of additional loose nucleotides (representing free nucleotides floating in the nucleus) and three labeled role cards: **Helicase** (a student who will physically separate the two strands), **Primase** (a student who places a short "primer" piece — a differently colored strip — at the start of each new strand), and **DNA Polymerase** (a student who adds complementary nucleotides to the template strand in the 5′→3′ direction only).

Student-facing prompt:
> **Replication Simulation**
> 1. Helicase: Gently separate (unzip) your DNA model at one end. What bonds are you breaking?
> 2. Primase: Place a primer on each template strand. Why might the cell need a starting point?
> 3. DNA Polymerase: Add free nucleotides to each template strand, matching bases. You may only add in the 5′→3′ direction. What problem does this create for the strand running in the opposite direction?
> 4. When you finish, how many double-stranded molecules do you have? How much of each molecule is "old" vs. "new"?
> 5. Compare your result with the pair next to you. Did you get the same sequences? Why or why not?

Circulate. When pairs reach question 3, guide them to notice that one strand can be built continuously (leading strand) while the other must be built in short pieces (lagging strand / Okazaki fragments). They do not need to master every detail, but they should feel the asymmetry.

**Explain (12 min) — Annotated animation + notes**
Show a short animation of replication (e.g., HHMI BioInteractive "DNA Replication" or a similar publicly available video, ~3 min). Pause at key moments for students to annotate a printed replication diagram:
- Origin of replication and replication fork
- Helicase unwinds; primase lays primer
- DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides 5′→3′
- Leading strand (continuous) vs. lagging strand (Okazaki fragments joined by ligase)
- Result: two identical double-stranded molecules, each with one old and one new strand → semiconservative

Pose: *"Why is it an advantage that replication is semiconservative rather than making one completely old and one completely new molecule?"*

**Elaborate (8 min) — Unit Model Version 2**
Students retrieve their Version 1 model and add a replication panel. Student-facing prompt:

> **Unit Model — Version 2: Add Replication**
> On the same sheet (or a new section of your slide), draw the replication fork. Label helicase, primase, DNA polymerase, leading strand, lagging strand, and Okazaki fragments. Use arrows to show the direction of synthesis.
> Write one sentence: "Replication ensures that ___."
> Revise your Version 1 limitation — does replication address it, or do you have a new limitation to add?

---

### Formative Check & Exit Ticket (4 min)

**Exit ticket:**
> 1. After replication, each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one new strand. What is the term for this?
> 2. DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5′→3′ direction. Explain one consequence of this constraint.

**Sample acceptable responses:**
1. Semiconservative replication.
2. Any response that references the leading/lagging strand asymmetry, e.g., "One strand has to be copied in short fragments (Okazaki fragments) that are later joined together, because polymerase can't move toward the replication fork on that strand."

---

### Materials & Prep
- Nucleotide manipulatives from Lesson 1 + extra loose nucleotide pieces (8–10 per pair)
- Primer strips (different color, pre-cut)
- Role cards: Helicase, Primase, DNA Polymerase (one set per pair/trio)
- Printed replication diagram for annotation
- Animation queued (test A/V in advance)
- Zipper prop
- Unit model sheets from Lesson 1

### Differentiation & Literacy Supports
- **Below grade level / ELL:** Provide a sequencing graphic organizer with the steps of replication listed out of order; students arrange them in the correct sequence before or after the simulation. Include a glossary strip with enzyme names and one-line definitions.
- **Above grade level:** Challenge these students to explain what would happen if DNA polymerase could add nucleotides in both directions (would there still be a leading and lagging strand?) and to research the role of telomerase.
- **IEP/504:** Allow verbal exit ticket responses recorded on a phone or spoken to the teacher.
- **Visual support:** The physical simulation and the animation provide two parallel representations of the same process, reinforcing understanding through multiple modalities.

### Mini-Rubric for Unit Model Version 2

| Criterion | Proficient (3) | Developing (2) | Beginning (1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Replication fork diagram** | Fork clearly drawn with all 6 labels accurate | 4–5 labels present and accurate | Fewer than 4 or major inaccuracies |
| **Direction of synthesis** | Arrows correctly show 5′→3′ on both strands | Correct on one strand | Arrows missing or incorrect |
| **Summary sentence** | Clearly states what replication ensures (accurate copying of genetic information) | Partially accurate | Missing or inaccurate |
| **Model revision** | Limitation revised or new limitation added with reasoning | Limitation noted but vague | No revision |

---
---

## Lesson 3: Transcription — From DNA to mRNA

**Daily "I Can" Objective:** I can model transcription by writing an mRNA sequence from a DNA template strand, identify the roles of RNA polymerase and promoter sequences, and explain why the cell makes an RNA copy rather than using DNA directly.

**NGSS Alignment:**
- HS-LS1-1
- SEP: Developing and Using Models; Constructing Explanations
- CCC: Structure and Function (RNA structure differences enable its role as a message)

---

### Sequence of Activities

**Engage (7 min) — "Why make a photocopy?"**
Display this scenario: "You have a rare, irreplaceable recipe book locked in a vault. You need to bake the cake today. What do you do?" Students quick-write (1 min), then share. Guide the analogy: DNA = the master book in the vault (nucleus). mRNA = the photocopy you carry to the kitchen (ribosome). Ask: "What are the advantages of working from a copy instead of the original?"

Record student ideas. Flag two they will confirm by the end of the lesson: the original is protected, and you can make many copies of different pages at once.

**Explore (18 min) — Transcription dry lab**
Each student receives a printed "gene card" — a double-stranded DNA sequence of 30 bases (10 codons) with the template strand (3′→5′) and coding strand (5′→3′) clearly marked, plus a highlighted promoter region upstream of the gene.

Student-facing prompt:
> **Transcription Dry Lab**
> You are RNA polymerase. Follow these steps:
> 1. Find the promoter region (highlighted). This is where you bind. Circle it.
> 2. Identify the template strand (3′→5′). Why does RNA polymerase read this strand?
> 3. Beginning at the start site (marked with an arrow), write the mRNA sequence that is complementary to the template strand. Remember: RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).
> 4. Label the 5′ and 3′ ends of your mRNA.
> 5. Compare your mRNA to the coding strand. What do you notice?
> 6. Reflection: Why does the cell transcribe only the template strand of a gene, not the entire chromosome?

Circulate with a key. Common error to watch for: students base-pairing off the coding strand instead of the template strand.

After 12 minutes, project the correct mRNA sequence. Students check their work with a colored pen and correct any errors.

**Explain (12 min) — Structured notes with RNA comparison**
Walk through a projected side-by-side comparison of DNA and RNA structure (sugar, bases, strandedness). Then trace the transcription process step by step:
- RNA polymerase binds at the promoter
- Unwinds a small section of DNA
- Reads template strand 3′→5′, synthesizes mRNA 5′→3′
- RNA processing in eukaryotes (brief mention: 5′ cap, poly-A tail, intron splicing — students do not need to memorize details, but should know the mRNA is processed before leaving the nucleus)

Key question: *"If mRNA is complementary to the template strand, what is its relationship to the coding strand?"* Confirm: same
