GENETICS UNIT: 15-DAY LESSON SEQUENCE
3 Weeks | 50-60 min periods | NGSS HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-2, HS-LS3-3

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
WEEK 1: DNA STRUCTURE, REPLICATION, AND THE CENTRAL DOGMA
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

DAY 1 — DNA Structure and Base Pairing
---------------------------------------
Learning target: I can describe the structure of DNA and explain how
complementary base pairing holds the two strands together.

NGSS: DCI LS1.A (Structure and function of DNA); SEP Developing and
Using Models; CC Structure and Function.

Warm-up (5 min): Show a photograph of Watson, Crick, and Franklin's
X-ray image. Ask: "What do you think scientists needed to figure out
before they could understand how traits are inherited?" Brief
partner share.

Main activities:
- Mini-lecture with diagram: nucleotide structure, sugar-phosphate
  backbone, A-T / G-C pairing, antiparallel strands (15 min).
- Paper or pop-bead model build: students construct a short
  double-stranded DNA segment (8-10 base pairs) and label all
  components. They photograph or sketch their model for their
  notebook (25 min).
- Whole-class debrief: "Where is the information stored — in the
  backbone or in the bases? Why?" (5 min).

Materials: Nucleotide cut-outs or pop-bead kits, colored pencils,
student handout with blank diagram to label.

Formative check / exit ticket (5 min): Given one strand
(5'-ATGCCTA-3'), write the complementary strand with correct
directionality.

Homework: Read textbook section on DNA replication (1-2 pages).
Annotate three key vocabulary terms.

Scaffolds:
- Support: Provide a base-pairing key card students keep at their
  desk. Pre-label one strand of the model so they complete only the
  complement.
- Extension: Ask students to research and write 3 sentences on how
  Chargaff's ratios provided evidence for base pairing before the
  structure was solved.

---------------------------------------
DAY 2 — DNA Replication
---------------------------------------
Learning target: I can model how DNA is copied before cell division
and explain why replication must be accurate.

NGSS: DCI LS1.A; SEP Developing and Using Models; CC Cause and Effect.

Warm-up (5 min): "If a cell is about to divide, why does it need to
copy all of its DNA first?" Think-pair-share.

Main activities:
- Animated video or simulation of replication (helicase, primase,
  DNA polymerase, leading/lagging strand) with guided notes
  handout (12 min).
- Replication modeling activity: using their Day 1 model (or a new
  paper strip), students "unzip" their DNA and build two new
  complementary strands, labeling the role of each enzyme at each
  step. They tape or glue the result into notebooks (20 min).
- Quick discussion: "What would happen if polymerase made a mistake
  and no proofreading occurred?" Introduce the word mutation
  briefly — full treatment in Week 3 (8 min).

Materials: Day 1 models or new paper strips, tape/glue, guided notes
handout, video or simulation access.

Formative check (5 min): Draw a replication fork from memory. Label
helicase, polymerase, and the direction of synthesis on the leading
strand.

Homework: Worksheet — 5 short replication questions (write
complementary strands, identify enzyme functions).

Scaffolds:
- Support: Provide a partly completed replication fork diagram;
  students fill in missing labels. Pair with a peer who finished
  the Day 1 model accurately.
- Extension: Research proofreading and mismatch repair. Write a
  short paragraph: "Why isn't the error rate zero?"

---------------------------------------
DAY 3 — Transcription
---------------------------------------
Learning target: I can explain how the information in a gene is
transcribed into mRNA and identify the key differences between DNA
and RNA.

NGSS: DCI LS1.A (role of DNA and RNA in protein synthesis); SEP
Developing and Using Models; CC Structure and Function.

Warm-up (5 min): "DNA never leaves the nucleus, but proteins are
built in the cytoplasm. How does the cell get the instructions out?"
Students write a hypothesis in notebooks.

Main activities:
- Comparison chart: DNA vs. RNA (sugar, bases, strands, location).
  Students complete a T-chart with guidance (8 min).
- Mini-lecture: RNA polymerase, promoter, template strand,
  5'→3' synthesis, mRNA processing (introns/exons) — keep
  processing brief at this level (12 min).
- Practice: Given 3 DNA template sequences, students write the
  mRNA transcript for each. Partner check and correct (10 min).
- Begin unit model: students start a poster, digital slide, or
  foldable that will trace genotype → phenotype across the unit.
  Today they add the transcription step. Explain that they will
  revise this model each week (10 min).

Materials: DNA vs. RNA comparison handout, practice sequences,
poster paper or digital template for unit model.

Formative check (5 min): "If the template strand reads
3'-TACGGAATC-5', what is the mRNA? Which end is 5'?" Collect on
index cards.

Homework: Label a diagram of transcription (provided) with the
following terms: RNA polymerase, template strand, mRNA, promoter,
5' end, 3' end.

Scaffolds:
- Support: Provide a color-coded reference strip showing DNA
  template → mRNA base conversion. Allow students to use the
  strip during practice.
- Extension: Research alternative splicing. Add a note to their
  unit model: "How can one gene produce more than one protein?"

---------------------------------------
DAY 4 — Translation
---------------------------------------
Learning target: I can use a codon table to translate an mRNA
sequence into an amino acid chain and explain how the sequence
determines protein function.

NGSS: DCI LS1.A; SEP Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking;
CC Structure and Function.

Warm-up (5 min): Display a sentence with every third letter
highlighted. Ask: "What happens to the meaning if I shift the
reading frame by one letter?" Connect to the idea of reading
mRNA in codons.

Main activities:
- Mini-lecture: ribosome, tRNA, anticodon, start codon (AUG),
  stop codons. Walk through one example translation on the board
  (12 min).
- Codon table practice: students receive 3 mRNA sequences of
  increasing difficulty. They identify codons, look up amino
  acids, and write the polypeptide. Last sequence includes a
  stop codon mid-strand (15 min).
- Unit model update: students add the translation step to their
  ongoing model (10 min).
- Brief discussion: "The amino acid chain folds into a 3D protein.
  Why would changing one amino acid matter?" Preview for mutation
  lesson (3 min).

Materials: Codon tables (one per student, laminated for reuse),
mRNA sequence handout, unit model materials.

Formative check (5 min): Translate the mRNA 5'-AUGCCCGAGUAA-3'.
Write the amino acid sequence and name the start and stop codons.

Homework: Central dogma summary — students write a paragraph tracing
information from DNA → mRNA → protein, using the terms gene,
transcription, codon, translation, amino acid.

Scaffolds:
- Support: Highlight the start codon in each practice sequence so
  students know where to begin reading. Provide a simplified codon
  table with only the 10 amino acids used in the practice sequences.
- Extension: Translate a real segment of the HBB (hemoglobin beta)
  gene. Research what protein it makes and why it matters. Add to
  unit model.

---------------------------------------
DAY 5 — ASSESSMENT 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model
---------------------------------------
Learning target: I can trace a DNA sequence through replication,
transcription, and translation, introduce a mutation, and explain
its effect on the protein and phenotype.

NGSS: HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-2; SEP Developing and Using Models,
Constructing Explanations; CC Cause and Effect.

Warm-up (5 min): Review expectations. Distribute rubric (student-
facing version). Students read criteria silently and ask clarifying
questions.

Main activities:
- Performance task (40-45 min): Students receive a DNA sequence
  (provided or the HBB segment from homework). They build or draw
  a model showing replication, transcription, and translation for
  the normal sequence, then introduce a specified mutation type
  (point, insertion, or deletion — assign or let them choose) and
  trace its effect. They write a CER paragraph and a heritability
  sentence. Students may use their codon table but not notes.
- Self-assessment (5 min): Students complete the checkbox rubric
  before submitting.

Materials: DNA sequence handout, codon tables, blank paper or
digital template, printed student rubric.

Formative check: The assessment itself. Collect models and CER
paragraphs. Quick-scan with teacher rubric checklist during next
prep period.

Homework: None (assessment day). Optional: students who want to
revise may take home a photo of their model and bring a revised
CER paragraph by Day 7 for partial credit recovery.

Scaffolds:
- Support: Provide a partially completed model template with the
  normal pathway filled in; student only needs to introduce the
  mutation and trace the mutant pathway. Offer a sentence frame
  for the CER: "The mutation at position ___ changed codon ___
  from ___ to ___, which changed the amino acid from ___ to ___,
  causing the protein to ___ because ___."
- Extension: Introduce two different mutations to the same
  sequence (one silent, one missense or frameshift). Compare
  effects in the CER and explain why not all mutations change
  the phenotype.


════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
WEEK 2: MENDELIAN GENETICS, PEDIGREES, AND PROBABILITY

DAY 6 — Mendel and Monohybrid Crosses

  ratios (8 min).
- Guided practice: 4 monohybrid crosses of increasing complexity
  (homozygous x heterozygous, heterozygous x heterozygous, test
  cross). Students work in pairs, then check with another pair

- Whole-class: discuss why predicted ratios are probabilities, not
  guarantees. Connect to coin flips (5 min).

Materials: Vocabulary four-square handout, Punnett square practice

# Student-Facing "I Can" Objectives

**Assessment 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model**
- I can model how DNA is copied and used to build a protein, step by step.
- I can introduce a mutation into a DNA sequence and trace how it changes the protein.
- I can explain whether a mutation changes the phenotype and whether it can be inherited, using evidence from my model.

**Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation**
- I can figure out the inheritance pattern of a trait from a pedigree and explain my reasoning.
- I can assign genotypes to family members and calculate the probability of a future child inheriting the trait.
- I can use a chi-square test to decide whether experimental data match a predicted ratio.
- I can explain genetic results clearly to someone without a science background.

**Assessment 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief**
- I can explain the science behind a genetic technology accurately.
- I can use evidence and data to support a clear position on how the technology should be used.
- I can discuss unintended consequences by connecting them to what I know about mutations and genetic variation.
- I can address a counterargument and explain why my position still holds.

---

# 4-Point Rubrics

## Assessment 1 Rubric: Central Dogma Mutation Model

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 4 — Mastery | My model accurately traces DNA → mRNA → protein with correct base pairing and codon reading. I clearly explain how my mutation changes (or doesn't change) the protein and phenotype, and I correctly state whether the mutation is heritable and why. |
| 3 — Proficient | My model is mostly accurate with one minor error (like a single wrong base pair). I explain the mutation's effect on the protein, but my connection to phenotype or heritability is incomplete. |
| 2 — Developing | My model shows the general idea of transcription and translation but has multiple errors. I identify that a mutation occurred but don't clearly explain how it affects the protein or phenotype. |
| 1 — Beginning | My model is missing major steps or has frequent errors. I don't connect the mutation to a change in the protein or phenotype. |

## Assessment 2 Rubric: Family Inheritance Investigation

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 4 — Mastery | I correctly identify the inheritance pattern and justify it with specific pedigree evidence. Genotypes and probability calculations are accurate. My chi-square test is computed correctly, interpreted properly, and I explain what the result means. My family letter communicates the science clearly and accurately in everyday language. |
| 3 — Proficient | I identify the correct inheritance pattern with reasonable justification. Genotypes and probability are mostly correct with one minor error. My chi-square is calculated but my interpretation is incomplete. My letter is understandable but uses some unexplained jargon. |
| 2 — Developing | I attempt an inheritance pattern but my justification doesn't fully match the pedigree. I have errors in genotypes or probability. I set up a chi-square table but make calculation or interpretation errors. My letter is vague or hard to follow. |
| 1 — Beginning | I guess at the inheritance pattern without using pedigree evidence. Genotypes or probability work is missing or mostly incorrect. Chi-square is not attempted or is fundamentally incorrect. My letter is missing or does not explain the science. |

## Assessment 3 Rubric: Gene Editing Policy Brief

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 4 — Mastery | I accurately explain the science behind the technology. My position is clear and supported by at least two pieces of evidence, including data. I connect an unintended consequence to mutation or genetic variation. I address a counterargument with a thoughtful rebuttal. |
| 3 — Proficient | My science explanation is mostly accurate with a minor gap. I state a clear position with evidence, but my use of data is weak or my connection to genetic variation is surface-level. I mention a counterargument but don't fully rebut it. |
| 2 — Developing | My science explanation has noticeable errors or is vague. I have a position but support it with opinion more than evidence. I mention an unintended consequence but don't connect it to genetics. A counterargument is missing or unclear. |
| 1 — Beginning | The science is missing or mostly inaccurate. My position is unclear or unsupported. I don't discuss unintended consequences or counterarguments. |

---

# 3-Week Daily Lesson Plan Outline

## Week 1: DNA Structure, Replication, and Protein Synthesis

**Day 1 — What is DNA made of?**
Objective: I can identify the four nucleotides and describe how they pair in a double helix.
Activity: Students build a short DNA segment using paper nucleotide cutouts or a digital simulator, enforcing base-pairing rules.
Formative check: Exit ticket — draw a 6-base-pair segment from a given single strand and label the 5' and 3' ends.

**Day 2 — How does DNA copy itself?**
Objective: I can describe the steps of semiconservative replication and explain why accuracy matters.
Activity: Students use their Day 1 models to simulate replication, physically separating strands and adding complementary nucleotides. Brief video clip (Amoeba Sisters or similar) to anchor vocabulary.
Formative check: Students annotate a replication diagram, labeling helicase, polymerase, leading/lagging strands, and explaining in one sentence why the process is called "semiconservative."

**Day 3 — From DNA to mRNA: Transcription**
Objective: I can write an mRNA sequence from a DNA template strand and explain the role of RNA polymerase.
Activity: Guided practice — students transcribe three DNA sequences of increasing length. Then a short "speed round" where partners quiz each other on template vs. coding strand.
Formative check: Whiteboard response — teacher displays a DNA template strand, students hold up the correct mRNA sequence.

**Day 4 — From mRNA to protein: Translation**
Objective: I can use a codon chart to translate an mRNA sequence into an amino acid chain and identify start and stop codons.
Activity: Students work in small groups to translate a mystery mRNA message using the codon table. Each amino acid is assigned a letter, and the correct translation spells a word or phrase.
Formative check: Students individually translate a new 15-codon sequence and identify where the protein starts and stops.

**Day 5 — Putting it all together: Central Dogma Model (Assessment 1 work day)**
Objective: I can trace a DNA sequence through replication, transcription, and translation in a single model and introduce a mutation to predict its effect.
Activity: Students begin Assessment 1. They build their model, introduce a teacher-assigned mutation type, and draft their claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph. Peer feedback using a checklist aligned to the rubric.
Formative check: Teacher circulates and stamps or initials models that have accurate base pairing before students move on to the mutation step. Students who finish early begin revising based on peer feedback.

---

## Week 2: Mendelian Genetics, Pedigrees, and Data Analysis

**Day 6 — Mendel's laws and monohybrid crosses**
Objective: I can predict the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of a monohybrid cross using a Punnett square.
Activity: Direct instruction on dominance, segregation, and Punnett squares, followed by a set of four practice crosses with increasing complexity (homozygous × heterozygous, heterozygous × heterozygous, etc.).
Formative check: Students solve a novel cross on a sticky note and post it on the board. Teacher sorts into correct/incorrect piles and addresses common errors.

**Day 7 — Dihybrid crosses and independent assortment**
Objective: I can set up a dihybrid Punnett square and calculate expected phenotypic ratios.
Activity: Students work through a guided dihybrid cross (e.g., seed shape and color in peas), then independently solve one new problem.
Formative check: Partner swap — students exchange their dihybrid problem, check each other's work, and initial if correct. Pairs that disagree work it out together before calling the teacher.

**Day 8 — Reading pedigrees**
Objective: I can determine the most likely inheritance pattern from a three-generation pedigree and assign genotypes to at least three individuals.
Activity: Students receive three different pedigrees (one autosomal dominant, one autosomal recessive, one X-linked recessive). In groups, they use a decision-tree handout to classify each one and assign genotypes. Groups rotate and critique each other's reasoning.
Formative check: Each student writes a one-sentence justification for one pedigree's inheritance pattern, citing a specific individual as evidence (e.g., "Individual II-3 is an unaffected female with an affected son, which rules out autosomal dominant because...").

**Day 9 — Probability and chi-square analysis**
Objective: I can calculate expected offspring ratios, perform a chi-square test, and interpret whether data support a genetic model.
Activity: Coin-flip or bead simulation of a monohybrid cross (each pair runs ~50 trials). Students pool class data, calculate expected values, compute χ², and compare to the critical value table.
Formative check: Students answer two questions in writing: "Do our data support the predicted 3:1 ratio?" and "What could explain any difference between expected and observed?"

**Day 10 — Inheritance Investigation (Assessment 2 work day)**
Objective: I can complete a pedigree analysis, probability calculation, chi-square test, and family letter that demonstrate my understanding of inheritance.
Activity: Students work on Assessment 2 individually. Teacher provides a structured template for the family letter (opening, explanation of the trait, probability statement, closing). Peer review of the letter section using the rubric's communication criterion.
Formative check: Teacher checks chi-square tables at each desk before the end of class and flags computation errors so students can correct before submitting.

---

## Week 3: Mutations, Gene Expression, Variation, and Ethics

**Day 11 — Types of mutations and their effects**
Objective: I can classify a mutation as a substitution, insertion, or deletion and predict whether it will change the protein.
Activity: Students receive a normal gene sequence and five mutated versions. They transcribe and translate each, then categorize the mutation type and severity (silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift).
Formative check: Table sort — students place each mutation card into a category and explain one placement to the teacher.

**Day 12 — From mutation to phenotype: Case studies**
Objective: I can construct a claim about how a specific mutation leads to a changed phenotype, citing sequence-level evidence.
Activity: Jigsaw — each group studies one real-world mutation case (sickle cell / HBB, cystic fibrosis / CFTR, lactase persistence / LCT, or Huntington's / HTT). Groups prepare a mini-poster showing the normal vs. mutated sequence, the protein change, and the phenotypic consequence, then teach another group.
Formative check: Listening groups write one "I learned..." and one "I still wonder..." statement after each presentation. Teacher collects the "still wonder" statements to address gaps the next day.

**Day 13 — Gene expression and environmental influence**
Objective: I can explain how two organisms with the same genotype can have different phenotypes because of differences in gene expression or environment.
Activity: Students examine data sets (e.g., Himalayan rabbit fur color at different temperatures, identical twin studies on height or disease risk, operon regulation in bacteria if time permits). They answer the driving question: "If the DNA is the same, why are the phenotypes different?"
Formative check: Quick-write — students explain the Himalayan rabbit example in three sentences, connecting temperature to gene expression to fur color.

**Day 14 — Genetic technologies and ethical trade-offs**
Objective: I can describe the mechanism of one genetic technology and identify at least two stakeholder perspectives on its use.
Activity: Students read a short case packet on their assigned technology (CRISPR therapy for sickle cell, embryo screening, or DTC genetic testing). Structured discussion protocol (e.g., four corners or fishbowl) where students argue from assigned stakeholder roles before stating their own position.
Formative check: Students complete a T-chart listing "strongest argument for" and "strongest argument against" with evidence from the packet.

**Day 15 — Policy Brief (Assessment 3 work day)**
Objective: I can draft a policy brief that takes a clear, evidence-supported position on a genetic technology, addresses a counterargument, and connects unintended consequences to genetics.
Activity: Students outline and draft their policy brief using a provided organizer (claim, evidence 1, evidence 2 with data, unintended consequence tied to genetics, counterargument, rebuttal). Peer review of the science explanation section using the rubric.
Formative check: Before leaving, each student submits their claim statement and one piece of supporting evidence on an index card. Teacher reviews overnight and returns cards the next morning with brief feedback so students can revise before final submission.

---

## Ongoing Across All Three Weeks: Genotype-to-Phenotype Model (Goal 5)

At the end of each week, students spend 5–10 minutes adding to or revising a running model (poster, digital slide, or notebook page) that maps the path from genotype to phenotype. After Week 1 they add DNA → protein. After Week 2 they add alleles and inheritance. After Week 3 they add mutation, gene expression, and environment. On the final day of the unit, students annotate one thing their model now shows well and one limitation it still has.

# Section 4: Program Design & Activities

**[Draft — 798 words. Bracketed items need your verification before submission.]**

---

The Eastside Early Readers Program is designed to close the specific gaps documented in the Community Need section: declining third-grade reading proficiency, insufficient free literacy services for children birth through eight, compounding barriers faced by families in poverty, and inadequate support for English-learner households. Every activity described below maps directly to one or more of those gaps, is grounded in evidence, and follows a clear participant pathway from referral through follow-up.

## Logic Model Narrative

The program operates on a straightforward theory of change: if children in the early literacy window receive consistent, evidence-based, one-on-one reading instruction while their caregivers are simultaneously equipped with strategies and materials to reinforce literacy at home, then children will build the foundational skills — phonemic awareness, phonics, and vocabulary — needed to read at grade level by third grade, and families will sustain those gains beyond the program cycle.

**Inputs** (staff, space, materials, partnerships) drive **activities** (tutoring, caregiver workshops, coaching, book deliveries) that produce **outputs** (120 children tutored, 480+ caregiver workshop seats filled, [*confirm: estimated number of book kits distributed*] kits delivered) leading to **short-term outcomes** (measurable gains in phonemic awareness and oral reading fluency) and **long-term outcomes** (increased third-grade reading proficiency in Eastside, narrowing of the 20-point gap with the county).

## Core Activities

### Activity 1: One-on-One Play-Based Literacy Tutoring
*Addresses: reading proficiency gap, waitlist/service gap*

Each child receives two 60-minute tutoring sessions per week over a 24-week cycle — a total dosage of 48 hours of individualized instruction per child. Sessions focus on phonemic awareness, systematic phonics, and vocabulary development, aligned with the Science of Reading and informed by the Success for All model [*confirm: do you hold a formal license or affiliation with Success for All, or is "informed by" the accurate framing?*]. Tutoring is play-based and developmentally appropriate for children birth through eight, using manipulatives, story play, and guided oral reading to maintain engagement across age levels.

Six tutors (0.5 FTE each) deliver sessions at [*confirm: primary site — Eastside Library, school sites, or organization facility?*], supervised by the Site Coordinator. Each tutor carries a caseload of [*confirm: approximately 10 children per cohort, assuming 2 sessions/child/week — verify scheduling feasibility*]. Volunteer aides support session preparation and provide additional reading practice under tutor supervision.

This activity directly addresses the 150-child waitlist documented in Section 2 by adding 120 annual slots of structured literacy intervention where none currently exist at this dosage.

### Activity 2: Caregiver Workshops and Family Literacy Coaching
*Addresses: poverty barriers, English-learner parent access*

Caregivers participate in monthly workshops (six per cohort cycle) covering read-aloud techniques, phonics reinforcement at home, language-rich routines, and navigating school literacy resources. Workshops are delivered in English and [*confirm: Spanish? other languages? specify*] to ensure access for English-learner families — a population identified in Section 2 as facing compounding barriers to supporting their children's literacy.

Between workshops, two family coaches (0.5 FTE each) provide biweekly one-on-one coaching sessions [*confirm: in-home, virtual, or both?*], helping caregivers apply workshop strategies and troubleshoot challenges specific to their household. Coaches also connect families to additional resources through our partnership with Eastside Community Health Clinic, which provides developmental screening and referrals for children who may need services beyond literacy support.

### Activity 3: Home Book Deliveries and Family Reading Kits
*Addresses: material access gap driven by poverty*

Each enrolled family receives [*confirm: number and frequency — e.g., one kit per month? one at enrollment and one at completion?*] curated reading kits containing age-appropriate books, activity guides, and literacy tools. Books are selected to reflect the cultural and linguistic backgrounds of Eastside families. The Eastside Library partners with us to source and curate materials and to enroll families in library programs that extend their access beyond the grant period.

This activity addresses a fundamental resource gap: in a neighborhood where 38 percent of households with children live below the poverty line, many families lack books in the home — a factor strongly associated with early reading outcomes [*confirm: cite specific study if desired, e.g., Scholastic Kids & Family Reading Report*].

## Participant Pathway

Each child's journey follows a structured sequence:

1. **Referral and screening** — Riverton School District, Eastside Community Health Clinic, and community outreach identify eligible children and refer them to the program.
2. **Baseline assessment** — Children are assessed using DIBELS [*confirm: DIBELS specifically, or another tool?*] to establish a starting point for phonemic awareness, phonics, and oral reading fluency.
3. **Enrollment** — Families are enrolled into a cohort and oriented to all three program activities.
4. **Active participation** — 24 weeks of tutoring, six caregiver workshops, biweekly coaching, and book deliveries.
5. **Post-assessment** — Children are reassessed using the same instrument to measure gains.
6. **Six-month follow-up** — Staff contact families and, where possible, collect school-reported reading data to track sustained progress.

## Scale and Timeline

The program serves 30 children per cohort across four staggered cohorts per year, reaching 120 children annually. Cohorts launch every three months beginning in month three of the grant, following a two-month start-up period for hiring and community outreach. This staggered design keeps caseloads manageable, allows staff to apply lessons from earlier cohorts, and maintains a continuous referral pipeline with the school district.

## Scope statement review

Your draft scope is solid. A few refinements to consider:

> "The Information Security Management System (ISMS) covering the development, delivery, and operation of [Company]'s SaaS platform hosted on Microsoft Azure, including supporting corporate IT systems, customer data processing activities, and third-party managed services, operated from [locations/remote]. Excluding: corporate marketing systems not connected to production data."

**Why the tweaks:**

- Auditors will probe **boundaries**. "Corporate marketing systems" needs to be defensible — if marketing tools touch customer PII or authenticate via the same SSO, they may get pulled in.
- **Third-party managed services** are in your supply chain and must be addressed (Annex A 5.19–5.22) even if partially outsourced.
- Specify **locations** (offices, remote work, Azure regions) because the certification is scoped to them.

# ISO 27001 Certification — Continued

---

## Phase 2 — Build and implement (Months 4–6)

**Month 4 — Supplier security, asset classification, and SDLC**

- Conduct supplier risk assessments for top-tier vendors (Azure, managed service providers, critical SaaS tools)
- Insert ISO 27001 clauses into vendor contracts and DPAs where missing
- Define and publish data classification scheme (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted)
- Assign asset and data owners across business units
- Formalize secure development lifecycle:
  - Security requirements in user stories
  - Threat modelling for major features
  - SAST/DAST integration in CI/CD
  - Security sign-off gate before production release
- Document secure coding standards

> 🏁 **Milestone: Supplier register assessed, classification scheme live, SDLC policy approved**

**Month 5 — BCP/DR, legal register, operational controls**

- Build or update Business Continuity Plan and IT Disaster Recovery Plan
- Define RTO and RPO per critical service
- Run a tabletop exercise and an Azure region failover test; document results
- Create register of applicable legislation, regulations, and contractual obligations
- Review and document:
  - Remote working policy (6.7)
  - Information deletion and retention schedule (8.10)
  - Data masking in non-production environments (8.11)
  - DLP controls or documented risk acceptance (8.12)
  - Threat intelligence sources and consumption process (5.7)
- Review cryptographic controls and key management documentation (8.24)
- Verify clock synchronization, log retention, and audit log integrity (8.17, 8.15, 8.34)

> 🏁 **Milestone: BCP/DR tested with evidence, legal register complete, operational control gaps closed**

**Month 6 — People controls, awareness, and measurement**

- Deliver second awareness training module with a measured assessment (quiz, phishing simulation, completion tracking)
- Review HR processes:
  - Background screening covers contractors (6.1)
  - Employment contracts include security responsibilities (6.2)
  - Disciplinary process references security violations (6.4)
  - Offboarding checklist verified with access revocation SLA (6.5)
- Define ISMS KPIs and begin measurement (9.1):
  - Percentage of risks treated on schedule
  - Mean time to revoke leaver access
  - Vulnerability patching SLA compliance
  - Awareness training completion rate
  - Incident response time vs target
- Collect first month of KPI data
- Review and finalize all remaining SoA control evidence

> 🏁 **Milestone: All 93 Annex A controls implemented or formally risk-accepted, KPI baseline established**

---

## Phase 3 — Assure and certify (Months 7–9)

**Month 7 — Internal audit**

- Execute full internal audit covering:
  - All ISMS clauses (4–10)
  - All applicable Annex A controls from the SoA
- Use independent auditors (internal staff not responsible for the area, or outsource to a consultancy — do **not** use your certification body for this to avoid conflict of interest)
- Classify findings:
  - **Major nonconformity**: requirement not met or entire process absent
  - **Minor nonconformity**: isolated lapse, evidence gap
  - **Opportunity for improvement**: working but could be stronger
- Issue internal audit report with findings and corrective action requests
- Assign corrective action owners and due dates (all must close before Stage 2)

> 🏁 **Milestone: Internal audit report issued, corrective action plan in progress**

**Month 8 — Management review and Stage 1 audit**

- Close all corrective actions from internal audit with evidence of effectiveness
- Hold formal management review meeting with minutes covering the mandatory agenda (9.3.2):
  - Status of actions from previous reviews
  - Changes in external/internal issues
  - Nonconformities and corrective actions
  - Monitoring and measurement results (KPIs)
  - Audit results
  - Risk assessment and treatment status
  - Opportunities for continual improvement
  - Resource needs
- Executive signs off on management review minutes and decisions
- **Stage 1 audit** (documentation review, typically 1–2 days on-site or remote):
  - Certification body reviews ISMS documentation, scope, SoA, risk assessment, policies
  - Outcome: readiness opinion and any areas of concern for Stage 2
  - You receive a list of issues to address before Stage 2
- Fix any Stage 1 findings immediately

> 🏁 **Milestone: Management review complete, Stage 1 passed with no blocking issues**

**Month 9 — Stage 2 audit and certification**

- Final evidence review: ensure every SoA control has accessible, current evidence
- Brief all control owners on what to expect (auditor interviews, evidence walkthroughs)
- **Stage 2 audit** (certification audit, typically 4–6 days for a 250-person org):
  - Auditors sample controls, interview staff, review evidence
  - They assess implementation effectiveness, not just documentation
  - Findings classified as major nonconformity, minor nonconformity, or OFI
- **If major nonconformities**: certification withheld until resolved (usually a follow-up audit within 90 days)
- **If only minor nonconformities**: certificate issued; you submit a corrective action plan within an agreed timeframe (typically 90 days) and evidence is reviewed at the next surveillance audit
- **If clean or OFI only**: certificate issued

> 🏁 **Milestone: ISO 27001 certificate issued 🎉**

**Post-certification (ongoing)**

- Surveillance audits at 6 or 12-month intervals (certification body decides)
- Continue internal audit cycle annually
- Hold management reviews at least annually (most orgs do quarterly)
- Recertification audit in year 3
- Continual improvement: treat the ISMS as a living system, not a project

## Role recommendations: full-time vs part-time

### Full-time for the 9-month programme (hire or assign)

**1. ISMS manager — 1.0 FTE dedicated**

This is non-negotiable. This person:
- Owns the project plan, risk register, SoA, and all ISMS documentation
- Coordinates across every department
- Is the primary contact for the certification body
- Drives corrective actions and evidence collection
- Presents at management review

If you don't have someone internally, your options are:
- **Promote or reassign** an existing senior security or GRC person and backfill their old role
- **Hire** an ISMS manager on a 12-month contract (9 months build + 3 months post-certification stabilization)
- **Engage a consultancy** for a virtual ISMS manager, though this is more expensive and you lose knowledge when they leave

> **Recommendation:** Internal hire or reassignment is best. The ISMS manager role persists post-certification for surveillance audits, continual improvement, and ongoing risk management. Making it a permanent role avoids a knowledge cliff.

**2. Security / GRC analyst — 0.5–0.75 FTE dedicated**

This person:
- Writes policies and procedures
- Runs the risk assessment workshops
- Collects and organizes evidence
- Executes the internal audit (or coordinates an outsourced one)
- Manages the awareness training programme

If you already have a GRC analyst supporting SOC 2, redirect 50–75% of their time to ISO 27001. Much of the SOC 2 evidence maintenance can run in parallel since the evidence overlaps significantly.

> **Recommendation:** Reassign your existing SOC 2 / compliance analyst. If you only have one, consider a 6-month contract analyst to handle SOC 2 BAU while your permanent analyst focuses on the ISMS.

---

### Part-time contributors (assign, do not hire)

**3. IT / engineering SMEs — 0.25–0.75 FTE pooled across 3–5 people**

You need part-time input from:
- **Platform / infrastructure lead**: Azure architecture, network controls, backup, DR, monitoring
- **Engineering / DevOps lead**: SDLC, CI/CD security gates, code review, SAST/DAST
- **IT operations / service desk lead**: ITIL processes, change management, incident management, CMDB
- **Identity / access management owner**: access reviews, PAM, joiner-mover-leaver

Each of these people contributes roughly 1–3 days per week during their peak months, then drops to a few hours per week for evidence maintenance.

> **Recommendation:** Do not hire for these roles. Assign existing leads and **protect their time** by getting executive sponsor buy-in to deprioritize non-critical project work during peak months (4–5 and 9). Put ISMS tasks in their sprint backlogs or OKRs.

**4. Executive sponsor — 0.05–0.15 FTE (a few hours per month)**

Typically the CISO, CTO, or VP Engineering. They:
- Sign off on the ISMS policy and scope
- Attend steering committee meetings (monthly, 1 hour)
- Chair or attend management review (Month 8, 2–3 hours)
- Be available for Stage 1 and Stage 2 auditor interviews (1–2 hours each)
- Unblock resources and resolve escalations

> **Recommendation:** Assign your most senior security or technology leader. They must visibly champion the programme. If you don't have a CISO, the CTO or VP Engineering is the right choice.

**5. HR / legal — 0.05–0.15 FTE (a few hours per month, spiking in months 4–6)**

HR provides:
- Background screening evidence
- Employment contract and NDA templates
- Disciplinary process documentation
- Offboarding checklist and access revocation SLA

Legal provides:
- Legal and regulatory register
- Contract clause review for supplier agreements
- Privacy and data protection input (GDPR, state laws)

> **Recommendation:** Assign one HR business partner and one in-house counsel (or external legal advisor). Brief them in Month 1 on exactly what you need and when. Give them templates to fill in rather than asking them to draft from scratch.

## Estimated auditor days for certification

ISO 27001 audit duration is calculated based on **IAF Mandatory Document 26** (MD 26), which uses the number of effective personnel in scope. For 250 employees in a mid-complexity SaaS organization:

### Stage 1 (documentation review)

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Auditor days | **2–3 days** |
| Format | On-site or remote (certification body preference) |
| Auditors | 1 lead auditor (possibly 1 technical expert for cloud/SaaS) |
| Purpose | Review ISMS documentation, scope, SoA, risk assessment; confirm readiness for Stage 2 |
| Typical output | Readiness report with observations and areas of concern |
| Gap between Stage 1 and Stage 2 | Minimum 2 weeks, recommended 4–6 weeks to address findings |

### Stage 2 (certification audit)

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Auditor days | **7–10 days** |
| Format | Primarily on-site with some remote evidence review possible |
| Auditors | 1 lead auditor + 1 auditor (possibly 1 technical expert) |
| Duration | Typically 4–5 calendar days with 2 auditors working in parallel |
| Purpose | Assess implementation effectiveness of the ISMS and all SoA controls |
| Activities | Staff interviews (8–15 people), evidence sampling, process walkthroughs, observation |
| Typical output | Audit report with findings (major NC, minor NC, OFI), recommendation for certification |

### How MD 26 calculates it

| Effective personnel in scope | Audit duration (Stage 1 + Stage 2 combined) |
|---|---|
| 126–175 | 10–12 auditor days |
| 176–275 | 11–14 auditor days |
| 276–425 | 12–15 auditor days |

For 250 people, you land in the **11–14 day range** total. The split is roughly 25% Stage 1 and 75% Stage 2, giving you approximately 3 + 9 = 12 days as a midpoint estimate. Certification bodies may adjust slightly based on:

- **Reductions** (up to 30%): mature SOC 2, low complexity, single site, single Azure region, well-documented processes
- **Increases**: multiple locations, highly regulated data (health, finance), complex supply chain, multiple development teams

> **Your org's profile** (SOC 2 in place, single product, mostly cloud, lightweight ITIL) likely qualifies for a modest reduction. Budget for **3 Stage 1 days + 8 Stage 2 days = 11 total auditor days** as a planning estimate.

### Rough cost estimate for the certification body

| Item | Range |
|---|---|
| Auditor day rate | $1,500–$2,500 USD per day depending on region and CB |
| Stage 1 (3 days) | $4,500–$7,500 |
| Stage 2 (8 days) | $12,000–$20,000 |
| **Total initial certification** | **$16,500–$27,500** |
| Annual surveillance (each) | $6,000–$12,000 (typically 3–4 auditor days) |
| Year 3 recertification | Similar to initial certification |

These are CB fees only and do not include any consultancy costs, tooling, or internal labour.

# 3 — Risk assessment methodology (5×5 qualitative)

## Methodology overview

```

│                                                                │
│  Document ref:  ISMS-RAM-001          Version: 1.0            │

## Step 1 — Likelihood scale

| Score | Label | Description | Approximate frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | Could occur only in exceptional circumstances | Less than once in 5 years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Could occur but not expected | Once in 2–5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Might occur at some point | Once per year |
| 4 | Likely | Will probably occur in most circumstances | Multiple times per year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Expected to occur frequently or already occurring | Monthly or more often |

## Step 2 — Impact scale

| Score | Label | Confidentiality | Integrity | Availability | Financial | Regulatory / legal | Reputational |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | Exposure of public data only | Error detected and corrected immediately | <15 min downtime | <$10k loss | No regulatory interest | No external awareness |
| 2 | Minor | Internal data exposed to small group | Minor data error, limited scope | 15 min–2 hr downtime | $10k–$50k | Regulatory inquiry possible | Limited customer awareness |
| 3 | Moderate | Confidential data exposed internally | Data corruption requiring restore from backup | 2–8 hr downtime | $50k–$250k | Regulatory investigation | Industry media coverage |
| 4 | Major | Customer PII exposed externally | Significant data loss, partial unrecoverable | 8–24 hr downtime | $250k–$1M | Formal regulatory action / fine | National media coverage |
| 5 | Severe | Mass customer data breach | Widespread data destruction | >24 hr downtime | >$1M | Licence / certification revoked | Lasting brand damage, customer loss |

**Rule:** When a risk affects multiple impact categories, use the **highest** single-category score.

| Tag | Meaning |

| Size | 120 employees | Small-medium ISMS scope; lean documentation is fine |

| SOC | Outsourced | Supplier management controls are critical; you need evidence the SOC meets your requirements |
| ITIL maturity | Partial (incident, change) | Good start — these map directly to key Annex A controls; gaps likely in config management, service continuity, and monitoring |
| MFA | Remote access only | Auditors will ask why not internally and for privileged accounts |
| Asset inventory | Incomplete | This is a **blocker** — almost every control domain depends on knowing what you're protecting |

# 1. Risk Assessment Workshop Template

## Instructions for the workshop facilitator

- **Pre-work**: circulate the asset register (even incomplete) and ask attendees to bring their top-5 "what keeps you up at night" scenarios.
- **Attendees**: IT manager, clinical lead, privacy officer, MSSP contact (optional), one member of senior leadership (risk owner authority).
- **Duration**: 2–3 hours for initial pass; aim for 15–25 risks in the first session.
- **Tool**: spreadsheet is fine — no need for GRC software yet.

## Template columns

Copy this header row into your spreadsheet:

```
Risk ID | Asset / Process | Threat | Vulnerability | Consequence | Likelihood (1–5) | Impact (1–5) | Risk Score (L×I) | Risk Level | Treatment Option | Planned Controls | Owner | Target Date | Residual Risk (L×I) | Status
```

### Scoring definitions

**Likelihood**

| Score | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | < once per 5 years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Once per 2–5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Once per 1–2 years |
| 4 | Likely | Several times per year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Monthly or more |

**Impact** (tailor the descriptors to healthcare)

| Score | Label | Patient safety | Data breach scope | Financial | Regulatory |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | None | < 10 records | < $10 K | Informal query |
| 2 | Minor | Discomfort, no harm | 10–100 records | $10–50 K | Letter of concern |
| 3 | Moderate | Temporary harm | 100–1 000 records | $50–250 K | Formal investigation |
| 4 | Major | Serious harm | 1 000–5 000 records | $250 K–1 M | Enforcement action / fine |
| 5 | Catastrophic | Death / permanent harm | > 5 000 records or public leak of PHI | > $1 M | OCR resolution agreement / loss of licence |

**Risk level matrix**

| | Impact 1 | Impact 2 | Impact 3 | Impact 4 | Impact 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Likelihood 5** | 5 M | 10 H | 15 H | 20 C | 25 C |
| **Likelihood 4** | 4 M | 8 M | 12 H | 16 H | 20 C |
| **Likelihood 3** | 3 L | 6 M | 9 M | 12 H | 15 H |
| **Likelihood 2** | 2 L | 4 M | 6 M | 8 M | 10 H |
| **Likelihood 1** | 1 L | 2 L | 3 L | 4 M | 5 M |

> **L** = Low (accept/monitor) · **M** = Medium (treat within 90 days) · **H** = High (treat within 30 days) · **C** = Critical (immediate action)

**Treatment options** (use these exact labels for consistency)

| Code | Option | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Mitigate** | Apply or improve controls | Default for most risks |
| **Transfer** | Insure or contractually shift | Cyber insurance, MSSP SLA |
| **Avoid** | Stop the activity | Activity not essential |
| **Accept** | Formally accept with management sign-off | Residual risk within appetite |

### Worked example row

```
R-007 | Telehealth platform | Interception of video consult | No end-to-end encryption verified | PHI disclosure, HIPAA breach | 3 | 4 | 12 | HIGH | Mitigate | Verify TLS 1.2+, enable E2EE, document in cryptography policy | IT Manager | 2026-06-30 | 2×4 = 8 M | In progress
```

### After the workshop

1. Sort by risk score descending.
2. Get the designated risk owner (must have authority) to sign off on each treatment decision.
3. Present the top-10 risks and treatment plan to leadership as your first management review input.
4. Store the register as a controlled document — version it.

---

# 2. Statement of Applicability (SoA) Skeleton

## SoA metadata header

```
Organisation : [Clinic name]
ISMS Scope : [Copy from scope statement]
ISO 27001:2022 Annex A version: 2022 (93 controls)
SoA Version : 1.0
Prepared by : [Name / role]
Approved by : [Top management name]
Date : [Date]
Risk treatment plan ref : [Document ID]
```

## Column structure

```
Annex A Ref | Control Title | Applicable? (Y/N) | Justification for Inclusion or Exclusion | Implementation Status | Implementation Evidence / Notes | Linked Risk IDs
```

### How to handle exclusions (auditors look at this closely)

Rules:

- You may **only exclude controls** that do not relate to risks identified in your risk assessment and do not affect your ability to meet ISMS requirements.
- You **cannot exclude mandatory clauses** (4–10) — only Annex A controls.
- Every exclusion needs a **documented justification**, not just "N/A."

**Good exclusion example:**

```
8.28 | Secure coding | N | Organisation does not develop software. EHR and telehealth are SaaS; vendor SDLC assurance obtained under supplier management (5.19–5.22). | — | Vendor SOC 2 report on file. | —
```

**Bad exclusion (will trigger auditor finding):**

```
8.28 | Secure coding | N | Not applicable. | — | — | —
```

## Starter rows (pre-populated for your context)

Below are examples across all four Annex A themes. Populate the remaining controls the same way.

## Policy 1 — Information Security Management System (ISMS) Policy

**ISO references**: Clauses 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 · Annex A 5.1

### 1 Purpose

This policy establishes [Organisation name]'s commitment to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information — including protected health information (PHI) — through a formal ISMS conforming to ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

### 2 Scope

The ISMS applies to:

- All information assets within the defined scope: [clinic operations, telehealth service, Azure cloud environment, on-premises infrastructure, SaaS applications including EHR, outsourced SOC].
- All employees, contractors, and third parties who access organisational information.

### 3 Objectives

- Protect patient and corporate data against unauthorised access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction.
- Comply with applicable legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations including HIPAA.
- Manage information security risks to an acceptable level defined by management.
- Continually improve the ISMS through measurement and review.

### 4 Leadership commitment

Senior management commits to:

- Providing resources for ISMS implementation and operation.
- Setting and reviewing information security objectives annually.
- Conducting management reviews at least [quarterly / annually].
- Promoting continual improvement.

### 5 Roles and responsibilities

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| [CEO / Clinic Director] | Accountable for ISMS; approves risk appetite and policies |
| [IT Manager / CISO] | Operates the ISMS; manages risk register, SoA, internal audits |
| [Privacy Officer] | HIPAA compliance, breach determination |
| Asset owners | Manage risks to their assets; approve access |
| All staff | Comply with policies; report incidents |

### 6 Risk management

Information security risks shall be identified, assessed, treated, and monitored per the Risk Assessment Procedure [ref]. Risk acceptance requires documented approval from management.

### 7 Policy framework

This overarching policy is supported by topic-specific policies: access control, data classification, incident response, supplier security, vulnerability management, backup and DR, and BYOD/MDM.

### 8 Compliance and enforcement

Violations may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination and legal proceedings.

### 9 Review

This policy is reviewed at least annually or following significant changes to the organisation, technology, or threat landscape.

**Audit evidence examples**: signed policy, management review minutes, risk appetite statement, ISMS scope document.

**HIPAA alignment**: satisfies the administrative safeguard requirement for a security management process (§164.308(a)(1)) and assigned security responsibility (§164.308(a)(2)).

## Policy 2 — Access Control

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.15, 5.16, 5.17, 5.18, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

### 1 Purpose

Ensure that access to information and systems is authorised, appropriate, and reviewable.

### 2 Principles

- **Least privilege**: users receive the minimum access required for their role.
- **Need-to-know**: access to PHI only when required for job function.
- **Segregation of duties**: no single person controls all stages of a critical process.

### 3 User access lifecycle

| Stage | Requirement | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Request** | Formal access request approved by asset owner | Ticket / form in ITSM |
| **Provisioning** | Based on role-based access profiles in Entra ID / EHR | Entra ID group membership logs |
| **Review** | Quarterly review of all access rights by asset owners | Signed review spreadsheet or tool export |
| **Revocation** | Same-day disable on termination; next business day on role change | HR notification → IT ticket → Entra ID audit log |

### 4 Privileged access

- Privileged accounts managed via Entra ID PIM (just-in-time activation, approval required, time-limited).
- Separate admin accounts — no daily work on privileged credentials.
- All privileged sessions logged and reviewed monthly.

### 5 Authentication

- MFA enforced for all users on all cloud services and VPN.
- Password policy: minimum 14 characters, complexity, 90-day rotation or passwordless alternative.
- Service accounts: managed identities or vaulted secrets; no shared passwords.

### 6 Remote and telehealth access

- VPN or Azure conditional access policy required.
- Device compliance check (managed device, patched, encrypted) before access granted.

### 7 Review and audit

Access reviews conducted quarterly. Results documented and exceptions remediated within 14 days.

**Audit evidence examples**: Entra ID conditional access policy exports, PIM activation logs, quarterly access review records, joiner/mover/leaver tickets.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.312(a)(1) access control, §164.312(d) authentication, §164.312(a)(2)(i) unique user ID, §164.312(a)(2)(iii) automatic logoff.

## Policy 3 — Data Classification and Handling

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, 5.33, 5.34, 8.10, 8.11, 8.12

### 1 Classification levels

| Level | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Restricted** | Severe harm if disclosed; legal/regulatory obligation | PHI, ePHI, psychotherapy notes, financial account data |
| **Confidential** | Business harm if disclosed | Employee HR records, contracts, internal audit reports |
| **Internal** | Not sensitive but not for public release | Staff newsletters, internal procedures, meeting notes |
| **Public** | Approved for unrestricted distribution | Marketing materials, published policies |

### 2 Labelling

- Documents: classification label in header/footer.
- Emails containing Restricted data: sensitivity label applied via Microsoft Purview / equivalent.
- Cloud storage: Azure Information Protection labels or container-level tagging.

### 3 Handling rules

| Activity | Restricted (PHI) | Confidential | Internal | Public |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Storage | Encrypted at rest (AES-256); access-controlled | Encrypted or access-controlled | Access-controlled | No restriction |
| Transmission | TLS 1.2+ or VPN; encrypted email | TLS 1.2+ | Standard email OK | No restriction |
| Printing | Collect immediately; secure shred when done | Secure shred | Recycle bin OK | No restriction |
| Sharing external | Only via approved, encrypted channel; BAA required | NDA required | Management approval | Freely |
| Disposal | Crypto-erase / NIST 800-88 media sanitisation | Secure delete | Standard delete | Standard delete |
| Retention | Per HIPAA (6 years for policies; state law for medical records) | Per retention schedule | Per retention schedule | No minimum |

### 4 PHI-specific requirements

- PHI inventory maintained and linked to asset register.
- Minimum necessary standard applied to every access and disclosure.
- De-identification follows HIPAA Safe Harbor or Expert Determination method when sharing for secondary purposes.

### 5 Responsibilities

Data owners classify their data at creation. All staff handle data according to its classification. IT manager enforces technical controls.

**Audit evidence examples**: classification policy, labelling screenshots, Purview/AIP config exports, sample classified documents, PHI inventory, media destruction certificates.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption and decryption, §164.530(j) retention, §164.514 de-identification, §164.502(b) minimum necessary.

## Policy 4 — Incident Response and Breach Notification

**ISO references**: Annex A 5.24, 5.25, 5.26, 5.27, 5.28, 6.8

### 1 Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Security event** | Observable occurrence that may affect information security |
| **Security incident** | Event that has actually compromised CIA of information |
| **Breach (HIPAA)** | Unauthorised acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of unsecured PHI |

### 2 Severity classification

| Severity | Criteria | Response SLA | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P1 — Critical** | Active data exfil, ransomware, PHI breach confirmed | Immediate; all-hands | Ransomware on EHR server, mass PHI leak |
| **P2 — High** | Likely compromise, service outage affecting patient care | ≤ 1 hour | Compromised admin account, EHR down |
| **P3 — Medium** | Contained incident, no PHI exposure confirmed | ≤ 4 hours | Phishing with credential entry, malware on single endpoint |
| **P4 — Low** | Near-miss, policy violation | ≤ 24 hours | Misdirected internal email, failed brute-force |

### 3 Response process

```
Detect → Triage → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Lessons learned
```

| Phase | Actions | Responsible |
|---|---|---|
| **Detect** | MSSP SOC alert, staff report, automated tool alert | MSSP / All staff |
| **Triage** | Classify severity, assign incident lead, open ITSM ticket | IT Manager |
| **Contain** | Isolate affected systems, disable compromised accounts, preserve evidence | IT Manager + MSSP |
| **Eradicate** | Remove threat actor/malware, patch vulnerability, reset credentials | IT team + MSSP |
| **Recover** | Restore from backup, confirm integrity, monitor closely | IT team |
| **Lessons learned** | Post-incident review within 5 business days, update risk register and controls | IT Manager |

### 4 HIPAA breach notification procedure

```
Step 1 → Determine if unsecured PHI was involved
Step 2 → Conduct 4-factor breach risk assessment:
           (a) Nature and extent of PHI involved
           (b) Unauthorised person who accessed or received PHI
           (c) Whether PHI was actually acquired or viewed
           (d) Extent of risk mitigation
Step 3 → If breach is not excluded by risk assessment:
           • Individual notice: ≤ 60 calendar days from discovery
           • HHS/OCR notice: ≤ 60 days (if ≥ 500 individuals: also notify media)
           • If < 500 individuals: log and report annually to HHS
Step 4 → Document determination and rationale regardless of outcome
Step 5 → Notify [Privacy Officer] immediately upon suspicion of PHI involvement
```

### 5 Evidence preservation

- Do not reboot or reimage affected systems until forensic image taken or MSSP confirms evidence captured.
- Screenshot alerts, timestamps, affected accounts.
- Maintain chain-of-custody log for any physical media.

### 6 Communication

| Audience | Channel | Authorised by |
|---|---|---|
| Internal staff | Email / meeting | IT Manager |
| Patients / individuals | Written notice per HIPAA | Privacy Officer + Legal |
| HHS/OCR | HHS breach portal | Privacy Officer |
| Media (if ≥ 500) | Press statement | [CEO / Legal] |
| Cyber insurer | Per policy terms | [CFO / IT Manager] |

### 7 Testing

Tabletop exercise at least twice per year; one scenario must involve PHI breach. Document results and corrective actions.

**Audit evidence examples**: incident log / ITSM tickets, MSSP alert reports, post-incident reviews, breach risk assessment forms, breach notification letters (redacted), tabletop exercise records.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(6) security incident procedures, §164.404–408 breach notification rule.

**Audit evidence examples**: supplier register, executed BAAs, SOC 2 / ISO certs on file, supplier review meeting minutes, contract clauses, shared-responsibility documentation.

# Policy 6 (continued) — Vulnerability Management

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.8, 8.7, 8.32

### 1 Scope

All assets in the ISMS scope: Azure resources, on-prem servers, endpoints, network devices, SaaS configurations.

### 2 Vulnerability identification

| Source | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Automated infrastructure scanning (Defender for Cloud / Qualys) | Weekly minimum; daily for internet-facing assets |
| Application scanning (DAST / SaaS config review) | Monthly |
| Annual penetration test (third-party) | Annually + after major architecture change |
| Vendor advisories and CVE feeds | Continuous (automated alerting) |
| MSSP threat intelligence | Continuous |

### 3 Severity rating and remediation SLAs

Use CVSS v3+ base score, then adjust for environmental context (PHI exposure, internet-facing, exploitability).

| Rating | CVSS range | Remediation SLA | Approval to defer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | 9.0–10.0 | ≤ 48 hours | [CISO / IT Manager] only, documented risk acceptance |
| **High** | 7.0–8.9 | ≤ 7 calendar days | IT Manager approval |
| **Medium** | 4.0–6.9 | ≤ 30 calendar days | Standard change process |
| **Low** | 0.1–3.9 | ≤ 90 calendar days or next patch cycle | Batch with scheduled maintenance |

### 4 Remediation process

```
Scan → Triage → Prioritise → Remediate/Mitigate → Verify → Close
```

- All remediation tracked as ITSM tickets linked to the vulnerability scan finding.
- Patches follow the change management process (RFC with security impact field).
- Where patching is not possible, document compensating control and risk acceptance in the risk register.
- Re-scan to verify remediation within 5 business days of fix.

### 5 Emergency patching

For actively exploited zero-days affecting PHI systems, the IT Manager may authorise emergency change outside normal CAB, with retrospective documentation within 24 hours.

### 6 Reporting

| Report | Audience | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| Scan results and open findings | IT team | Weekly |
| KPI dashboard (mean-time-to-remediate, overdue count, trend) | Management review | Monthly |
| Pen test report and remediation tracker | Senior management | Annually |

### 7 Exceptions

Any vulnerability exceeding its SLA must have a documented exception with: justification, compensating controls, risk owner approval, and expiry date (maximum 90 days, then re-evaluate).

**Audit evidence examples**: scan reports, remediation tickets with timestamps, pen test report and remediation tracker, exception approvals, KPI dashboard, emergency change records.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) risk management implementation, §164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B) protection from malicious software.

> 1. Last three monthly scan reports with finding counts and closure rates
> 2. Sample of five remediation tickets showing scan-to-close lifecycle
> 3. Most recent pen test report plus remediation status tracker
> 4. Any active exception forms with risk owner sign-off
> 5. KPI trend chart (mean-time-to-remediate by severity, last 6 months)

# Policy 7 — Backup and Disaster Recovery

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30

### 1 Purpose

Ensure information and systems can be restored within defined timeframes to maintain patient care continuity and protect PHI integrity.

### 2 Scope

All systems within the ISMS scope: Azure-hosted services, on-prem servers, EHR (SaaS — vendor-managed backup confirmed separately), endpoint configurations, identity directory (Entra ID).

### 3 Backup requirements by asset criticality

| Asset class | RPO | RTO | Backup method | Retention |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EHR database** (SaaS) | Per vendor SLA (verify ≤ 1 hr) | Per vendor SLA (verify ≤ 4 hrs) | Vendor-managed; confirm in BAA and supplier review | Per vendor + local export monthly |
| **Azure workloads** (VMs, PaaS databases) | ≤ 4 hours | ≤ 8 hours | Azure Backup vault, geo-redundant (GRS) | 30 daily, 12 monthly, 7 yearly |
| **On-prem servers** | ≤ 24 hours | ≤ 24 hours | Azure Backup agent or equivalent to offsite vault | 30 daily, 12 monthly |
| **Entra ID / M365 config** | ≤ 24 hours | ≤ 8 hours | Third-party SaaS backup tool (e.g., Veeam for M365) | 12 months |
| **Network device configs** | At every change | ≤ 4 hours | Automated config backup to secured repo | Last 10 versions |
| **Endpoint (SOE image)** | N/A — rebuild | ≤ 4 hours | Standard image + Intune policy re-push | Current image always available |

### 4 Backup security

- All backup data encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+).
- Backup storage access restricted to named backup administrators only.
- Backup credentials stored in a secrets vault, rotated every 90 days.
- At least one backup copy stored in a separate Azure region or offsite location (3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite).
- Immutable / WORM backup enabled for ransomware resilience where supported.

### 5 Restore testing

| Test type | Scope | Cadence | Documented output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Individual file restore** | Random sample from each asset class | Monthly | Restore log with timestamp, integrity hash comparison |
| **Full system restore** | One critical system (rotate quarterly) | Quarterly | Restore report: time taken vs RTO, data integrity verified |
| **Tabletop DR exercise** | End-to-end scenario (e.g., ransomware, Azure region outage) | Twice per year | Exercise report, action items, lessons learned |
| **Full DR failover** (if DR environment exists) | All critical systems | Annually | Failover and failback report |

### 6 Disaster recovery plan summary

| Phase | Actions | Responsible |
|---|---|---|
| **Activation** | Incident declared P1; DR lead notified; communication tree activated | IT Manager / CISO |
| **Assessment** | Determine scope of outage, estimate recovery time, notify leadership | IT Manager |
| **Recovery** | Execute restore / failover per runbooks; prioritise by RTO | IT team |
| **Validation** | Confirm data integrity, application functionality, PHI availability | IT team + clinical lead |
| **Return to normal** | Failback to primary, full backup, post-incident review | IT team |
| **Lessons learned** | Document within 5 business days; update risk register and runbooks | IT Manager |

### 7 Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| IT Manager | DR plan owner, authorises activation, reports to leadership |
| Backup administrator | Configures and monitors backups, executes restores |
| MSSP | Monitors backup job alerts (if in scope), supports forensic recovery |
| Clinical lead | Validates clinical system functionality post-restore |
| EHR vendor | Executes SaaS-side restores per BAA obligations |

### 8 Review

DR plan and runbooks reviewed annually and after every DR activation or significant infrastructure change. Restore test results feed into management review.

**Audit evidence examples**: backup configuration screenshots, backup job success/failure logs, restore test reports with integrity verification, DR tabletop exercise report, DR plan document with version history, vendor SLA confirmation for EHR backups.

**HIPAA alignment**: §164.308(a)(7) contingency plan (data backup plan, disaster recovery plan, emergency mode operation plan, testing and revision procedures).

> **Quick evidence checklist for auditors (hand this over):**
> 1. Last three months of backup job success/failure reports (all asset classes)
> 2. Most recent quarterly full-system restore test report with RTO comparison
> 3. Latest tabletop DR exercise report and action tracker
> 4. EHR vendor SLA / BAA section confirming vendor backup and RPO/RTO
> 5. Backup encryption and access control configuration evidence

**ISO references**: Annex A 8.1, 6.7, 8.10, 8.11, 8.12

### 1 Purpose

Enable staff to use personal and mobile devices for work while protecting organisational information and PHI from loss, theft, or unauthorised access.

All personally owned devices (smartphones, tablets, laptops) and organisation-issued mobile devices used to access organisational email, applications, or data, including telehealth platforms.

|---|---|

| Teams messaging and calls | Sharing device credentials with family members or third parties |
| VPN access from compliant device | Connecting to organisational resources from public Wi-Fi without VPN |

### 6 Data segregation

- Corporate data containerised within managed apps (Intune App Protection).
- Organisation cannot view personal photos, messages, or apps.
- On unenrolment or wipe, only the corporate container is removed; personal data untouched (selective wipe).

### 7 Lost, stolen, or compromised device

| Step | Action | SLA |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | User reports loss/theft to IT service desk immediately | ≤ 1 hour from discovery |
| 2 | IT initiates remote selective wipe of corporate container | ≤ 2 hours from report |
| 3 | Entra ID sign-in sessions revoked, device marked non-compliant | Immediate |
| 4 | If PHI exposure suspected, escalate to incident response procedure (Policy 4) | Per incident severity SLA |
| 5 | Log event in ITSM and incident register | Same day |

### 8 Staff responsibilities

- Keep device OS and apps updated within [14 days] of patch release.
- Do not disable MDM/MAM profiles.
- Report loss, theft, or suspected compromise immediately.
- Consent to corporate container management as a condition of BYOD access (documented at enrolment).

### 9 Monitoring and compliance

- Intune compliance dashboard reviewed weekly by IT.
- Non-compliant devices automatically blocked from corporate resources via conditional access.
- Quarterly report on BYOD fleet: enrolment count, compliance rate, wipe events, OS version distribution.

### 10 Exit process

On employment termination:

- Selective wipe triggered on termination day (linked to HR leaver process and access revocation in Policy 2).
- Device unenrolled from Intune.
- User confirms removal of any residual corporate data.
