## ROOM 8: ATTIC / STORAGE

*This covers any attic space, crawl space, basement storage, off-site storage unit, or the "back of the closet" overflow zone. If you don't have a formal attic, apply this to wherever your long-term storage lives.*

### Estimated Effort
| Metric | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Total boxes | 4–10 (highly variable — could be more if you've been storing for years) |
| Suggested box mix | 2–4 small, 2–4 medium, 2–4 large |
| Non-boxed items | Luggage, holiday trees, furniture pieces, bins |
| Time to declutter | 3–5 hours (this is the room people underestimate the most) |
| Time to pack | 2–3 hours (most of it is already in bins or boxes, just needs evaluation and relabeling) |
| Recommended schedule | Declutter in Week 6 or 7 — do this room FIRST. It's the easiest to forget and the hardest to rush. Pack keepers in Week 4. |

### The Attic Rule

**If it's been in your attic for more than 2 years and you forgot it existed, you don't need it.** The attic is where things go to be forgotten. Be honest with yourself. This room usually produces the highest volume of donations and trash.

### Declutter First

| Category | Keep | Sell / Donate | Trash |
|---|---|---|---|
| Holiday decorations | Your favorite tree, lights that work, ornaments with sentimental value, 1 box per holiday max | Duplicate or excess decorations, items from a "phase" (the year you went all-in on inflatables) | Broken lights (cut the plug off before trashing to prevent hazard), shattered ornaments, dried-out wreaths |
| Luggage and bags | 1 large suitcase per person, 1 carry-on per person, 1 duffel | Excess bags, broken-zippered luggage, old backpacks | Torn, broken-wheeled, musty luggage |
| Keepsakes and memorabilia | Items that genuinely make you feel something when you hold them. Photographs (always keep). Letters from people you love. | Participation trophies, dried corsages, ticket stubs you'll never look at again | Moldy, water-damaged, rodent-chewed items (photograph them before discarding if they're sentimental) |
| Old electronics | Nothing — if it's in the attic, you've already replaced it | Sell: working laptops, tablets, gaming consoles, cameras | Recycle: dead electronics at Best Buy, Staples, or a local e-waste center. Do not trash. |
| Baby / kid items | Only if relevant to your future plans | Donate to shelters, churches, or parents' groups | Recalled, broken, or stained beyond use |
| Old furniture | Only if it's quality and fits the new space | Sell or donate — this is the biggest space-saver in the truck | Broken, wobbly, particle board that won't survive the move |
| Boxes of "I'll sort this later" | Sort them now. That's the whole point. Apply the decision flow to every item. | — | — |
| Textbooks and old papers | Almost never worth keeping unless you're actively in the field | Sell textbooks on BookScouter.com or Amazon | Recycle outdated editions, old notebooks, printed coursework |
| Collections | Keep if you actively enjoy and display them | Sell valuable collections (coins, cards, vintage items) on eBay or specialty forums | Broken or incomplete sets with no value |

### The Photo Box Problem

Almost everyone has a box of unsorted photos in their attic. Here's the fastest approach:

1. **Don't try to sort them now.** You will lose an entire weekend.
2. Put the whole box in a medium moving box, label it 🟢 OPEN LATER.
3. Set a calendar reminder for 1 month after the move: "Sort the photo box."
4. Consider scanning them later with Google PhotoScan (free app) or a service like ScanMyPhotos.
5. **Photographs always make the move.** They are irreplaceable. Never throw out photos.

### Packing Order

**Pack in Week 4 (immediately after decluttering):**
- [ ] Holiday decorations — wrap fragile ornaments individually in tissue paper or packing paper, pack in small or medium boxes with dividers or egg-carton-style padding
- [ ] Keepsakes and memorabilia — small boxes, padded well
- [ ] Repack storage bins with only the items you're keeping, label with destination room and contents
- [ ] Luggage — don't waste space inside suitcases. Pack soft items inside them: off-season clothes, towels, stuffed animals, blankets. A suitcase full of towels rolls right onto the truck.

**Pack in Week 3:**
- [ ] Old furniture pieces — disassemble what you can. Bag all hardware (screws, bolts, cam locks) in a labeled zip-lock and tape it to the furniture piece.
- [ ] Remaining bins and boxes after re-evaluation
- [ ] Artificial holiday tree — fits back in the original box if you kept it. If not, wrap in a trash bag and tape closed.

**Pack last:**
- [ ] Nothing. The attic should be fully packed and cleared by Week 3. If anything is still up there in Week 2, you probably don't need it.
- [ ] **Do a final attic walk-through on move day.** It's the most forgotten space. Check every corner, shelf, and rafter. Bring a flashlight.

### Fragile Packing Tips — Attic Specific
- **Ornaments:** Wrap each one in tissue paper or packing paper. Use egg cartons, cupcake liners, or sock pairs as individual cushions. Pack in small boxes — ornaments are light but crush easily under weight.
- **Framed photos and art:** Tape an X across glass, wrap in bubble wrap, pack vertically (not flat) in a box with cardboard dividers between each frame.
- **Mirrors stored in attic:** Same treatment as framed art — X tape, bubble wrap, vertical packing. If the mirror is large, build a cardboard sandwich (two pieces of cardboard larger than the mirror, taped together around the wrapped mirror) or buy a mirror box from U-Haul (~$5–$15).
- **China, crystal, or heirloom dishes stored in attic:** Treat these like kitchen fragiles — wrap each piece individually, pack plates on edge, use small boxes, never stack heavy items on top.

### Box Labels for This Room
```
ATTIC — Holiday decorations, ornaments (fragile) — 🟢 OPEN LATER ⚠️ FRAGILE
ATTIC — Keepsakes, photos, memorabilia — 🟢 OPEN LATER
ATTIC — Stored bedding / off-season in suitcase — 🟢 OPEN LATER
ATTIC — [Contents of each re-evaluated bin] — 🟢 OPEN LATER
```

---

## ROOM 9: OUTDOOR GEAR

*This covers patio furniture, grill, camping gear, sports equipment, yard tools not already covered in the garage section, and anything stored on a deck, porch, or shed.*

### Estimated Effort
| Metric | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Total boxes | 2–5 (most outdoor gear is loose or in bags) |
| Suggested box mix | 1–2 small, 1–2 medium, 1 large |
| Non-boxed items | Patio furniture, grill, tent, camping chairs, cooler |
| Time to declutter | 1–2 hours |
| Time to pack | 1–2 hours |
| Recommended schedule | Declutter in Week 5. Pack in Week 3. Drain grill propane and prep large items in Week 2. |

### Declutter First

| Category | Keep | Sell / Donate | Trash |
|---|---|---|---|
| Patio furniture | Quality pieces that fit the new space (check: will you have a patio or yard in Oregon?) | Cheap or bulky items — sell on Marketplace. Patio furniture is easy to sell in spring/summer, harder in fall/winter. Time your listing. | Rusted, broken, sun-rotted, wobbly |
| Grill | **Decision point:** Charcoal grills are cheap to replace (~$30–$100 for a basic Weber). Gas grills are bulkier but more expensive. If yours is a quality gas grill, consider keeping it. If it's a $60 charcoal grill, sell it for $20 and buy a new one in Oregon. | Sell if not worth the truck space | Rusted-out, broken grates, non-functional ignition |
| Camping gear | Tent, sleeping bags, sleeping pads, camp stove, headlamps, cooler — keep if you camp | Gear you haven't used in 2+ years | Torn tents, broken poles, punctured pads, expired fuel canisters |
| Sports equipment | Equipment for sports you actively play | Old gear, outgrown items, "I'll get back into it" items you haven't touched in years | Broken, deflated beyond repair, cracked helmets |
| Garden hose and sprinklers | 1 good hose if you'll have a yard | Excess hoses, broken sprinkler heads | Cracked, kinked, leaking hoses |
| Outdoor toys or games | Cornhole, frisbees, etc. that you use | Broken or incomplete sets | — |
| Firewood | **Do not move firewood across state lines.** This is a real rule. Invasive insects (like emerald ash borer, which is present in Ohio) travel in firewood. Use it, give it to a neighbor, or leave it. | Give it away on Buy Nothing or Nextdoor | — |
| Pots and planters | 2–3 favorites that aren't too heavy | Cheap terracotta and plastic pots (heavy to move, cheap to replace) | Cracked, broken |

### Grill Prep
- **If keeping a gas grill:** Disconnect and properly dispose of the propane tank (see hazardous disposal section below). Remove grates, clean them, wrap them in an old towel or trash bag. Tape all loose parts. The grill body goes on the truck unwrapped or wrapped in stretch wrap.
- **If keeping a charcoal grill:** Empty all ash and charcoal. Clean the interior. Bag the grates. Tape the lid closed or wrap in stretch wrap.
- **Movers' rule:** Most movers will take a clean, empty, propane-free grill. Confirm with yours. They will not take propane tanks, lighter fluid, or charcoal.

### Camping Gear Packing Tips
- **Tent:** Clean and dry it completely before packing. A damp tent will mildew in transit. Roll it tightly and pack in its stuff sack. If the stuff sack is lost, use a trash bag cinched with a cord.
- **Sleeping bags:** Compress in stuff sacks or vacuum-seal bags. Don't store compressed for more than a few weeks — it damages insulation long-term. Unpack and loft them when you arrive.
- **Camp stove:** Disconnect and remove all fuel canisters. The stove itself can be packed. The fuel cannot go on a truck. Use it up, give it away, or dispose of it.
- **Cooler:** Clean it, dry it completely, leave it open to air out for a day. Then use it as packing space — fill it with soft items (towels, hats, gloves) or use it as your road-trip cooler on move day. Dual purpose.

### Packing Order

**Pack in Week 3:**
- [ ] Camping gear — tent, sleeping bags, pads, camp kitchen items
- [ ] Sports equipment — deflate balls slightly, bag small items, wrap rackets and bats in bubble wrap or towels
- [ ] Outdoor games
- [ ] Garden hose — drain completely, coil tightly, secure with a bungee or zip tie
- [ ] Small pots and planters — wrap terracotta in bubble wrap (or let them go)
- [ ] Outdoor decor, string lights, citronella candles

**Pack in Week 2:**
- [ ] Patio furniture — clean, fold what folds, stack what stacks, wrap legs in bubble wrap or towels to prevent scratching other items on the truck
- [ ] Grill — cleaned, emptied, propane-free, taped or wrapped
- [ ] Remaining yard tools not covered in the garage section

**Pack last:**
- [ ] Doormat — shake it out and toss it on the truck or in the car
- [ ] Any plants you're taking — water them the morning of, put them in the car (not the truck — temperature extremes will kill them). Note: Oregon has agricultural inspection rules. Most common houseplants are fine, but check the Oregon Department of Agriculture guidelines if you're bringing outdoor plants, soil, or anything unusual. A quick search before you go can avoid a problem at the border or down the road.
- [ ] Porch or patio lights if you own them (not if they're the landlord's)

### Box Labels for This Room
```
OUTDOOR — Camping gear, tent, sleeping bags — 🟡 OPEN SOON
OUTDOOR — Sports equipment — 🟢 OPEN LATER
OUTDOOR — Garden hose, tools, planters — 🟢 OPEN LATER
OUTDOOR — Outdoor games, decor, lights — 🟢 OPEN LATER
```

### How to Print

**Option A — Handwritten (fastest):**
Print 60–80 blank copies of the template above on regular paper, 2 per page. Cut them out. Fill in by hand with a Sharpie as you pack each box. Tape to two sides of the box.

**Option B — Avery labels (cleanest):**
1. Go to **avery.com/templates**
2. Select product **5164** (6 per sheet, 3⅓″ × 4″)
3. Use their free Design & Print tool
4. Create a label with this layout:

ROOM: [text field]
CONTENTS: [text field, 2 lines]

### Best Chain Sources

| Store | What to Ask For | Best Time to Ask | Quality | Tips |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Liquor stores (state-run or independent)** | Liquor boxes with dividers | Anytime — they always have them | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Thick cardboard, built-in dividers perfect for glasses and bottles | Best free boxes available. Dividers double as dish and glass separators. Ask for cases that held wine or spirits (thicker cardboard than beer boxes). |
| **Grocery stores (Kroger, Aldi, Giant Eagle)** | Banana boxes, apple boxes, egg boxes | Early morning, right after stocking (5–8 AM or ask the night crew) | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Banana boxes have lids and handles, very sturdy | Banana boxes are the gold standard of free boxes. They have built-in handles and lids. Ask the produce department specifically. Go early — they break them down fast. |
| **Costco / Sam's Club** | Any display boxes from the floor | During restocking (early morning or ask a manager) | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Large, thick, designed to hold heavy product | Apple boxes and diaper boxes are especially good. Avoid produce boxes that held wet items (they'll be soft or damp). |
| **Walmart** | Shipping boxes from the back | Ask a stocking associate during the overnight or early morning shift | ⭐⭐⭐ Varies widely in size and quality | Hit or miss. Some stores will save them if you ask nicely a day ahead. |
| **Target** | Shipping boxes from the back | Same as Walmart — early morning | ⭐⭐⭐ Similar to Walmart | Ask Guest Services to check with the back room team. |
| **Home Depot / Lowe's** | Appliance boxes (huge), tile boxes (small and very strong) | Anytime — ask at the customer service desk | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Appliance boxes are great for large items, tile boxes are nearly indestructible for heavy items | Appliance boxes are great for lampshades, pillows, and bulky light items. |
| **Bookstores (Half Price Books, Barnes & Noble, local shops)** | Book shipping boxes | Anytime | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Small, thick, perfect for heavy items like tools and books | Book boxes are the perfect size for heavy loads. They're small so you won't over-pack them. |
| **McDonald's / Starbucks / fast food** | Fry boxes, supply boxes | Ask a manager during a slow period | ⭐⭐ Smaller, grease risk | Only use clean, dry ones. Good for lightweight items. |
| **U-Haul Customer Connect / Box Exchange** | Used moving boxes left by other customers | Check the U-Haul location near you — many have a free box shelf or online listing | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Already sized for moving | Also check uhaul.com/exchange for local free box listings. |

### Online Free Box Sources

| Source | How | Tips |
|---|---|---|
| **Facebook Marketplace** | Search "free moving boxes" in your area | People post free boxes constantly right after they move in. Set an alert for the search term. |
| **Buy Nothing Group** (Facebook) | Post an ISO (in search of) for moving boxes | These groups are hyperlocal and very responsive. Post early in the week. |
| **Nextdoor** | Post a request or search "boxes" | Neighbors love to get rid of boxes. |
| **Craigslist Free section** | Search "moving boxes" under Free | Check daily — they go fast. |
| **Freecycle.org** | Post a Wanted listing | Slower than Facebook but still active in many Ohio cities. |

### Timing Tips

- **Best days to get store boxes:** Tuesday through Thursday mornings. Monday is restocking after the weekend, but boxes are often already broken down. By Friday, the week's boxes are gone.
- **Best time of day:** 6–9 AM, right after the overnight or early morning stocking shift.
- **Call ahead.** Call the store the day before and ask them to set aside boxes for you. Say: *"I'm moving and would love any clean, sturdy boxes you're breaking down. Can I pick some up tomorrow morning?"* Most stores will say yes.
- **Bring your own bags or car space.** Boxes are bulky — bring a vehicle that can handle them, or flatten them and re-tape at home.
- **Go twice.** One trip probably won't get you everything. Plan two trips, a few days apart, to different stores.
- **Inspect before loading.** Reject any box that is damp, stained, torn, or smells like food. A weak box will fail when you're carrying dishes.

# PART 1: Room-by-Room Packing Checklist + Declutter Tips

---

## General Packing Rules

- **Label every box** on the top AND one side: room name, contents summary, and priority (OPEN FIRST / SOON / LATER).
- **Use color-coded tape or stickers** per room (e.g., blue = kitchen, green = bedroom). Tell movers the system.
- **Number your boxes** and keep a running list in a note on your phone. If a box goes missing, you'll know.
- **Heavy items in small boxes, light items in big boxes.** Your back and your movers will thank you.
- **Pack a "Last Out / First In" box for every room** — the stuff you'll need immediately on both ends.

---

## Declutter Decision Framework

For every item, ask in this order:

1. **Have I used this in the last 12 months?** No → it goes.
2. **Would I buy this again today?** No → it goes.
3. **Am I keeping this out of guilt or obligation?** Yes → it goes.
4. **Does it cost less to replace than to move?** Yes → it probably goes.
5. **Is it sentimental AND irreplaceable?** Yes → it stays. Photograph sentimental items you can let go of.

**Disposal channels:** Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, OfferUp, Buy Nothing groups (fastest for free stuff), Goodwill/Salvation Army donation pickup, 1-800-GOT-JUNK, or a curbside "FREE" pile.

---

## 🍳 KITCHEN
**Estimated time: 6–8 hours total (pack over 2–3 sessions)**
**Responsibility: J**

### Declutter First
- [ ] Expired food, spices older than 2 years, duplicate utensils
- [ ] Chipped or mismatched dishes, mugs you never use
- [ ] Gadgets used fewer than twice a year (waffle maker? bread machine?)
- [ ] Takeout menus, old sponges, worn towels
- [ ] Plastic containers without matching lids (toss them all — buy a fresh set in Oregon)

### Pack — Weeks 4–3 Out
- [ ] Specialty appliances (stand mixer, food processor, slow cooker)
- [ ] Bakeware, seasonal dishes, entertaining platters
- [ ] Cookbooks
- [ ] Extra pantry stock (donate what you won't use before the move)

### Pack — Week 2
- [ ] Most dishes, glasses, and silverware (keep 2 place settings out)
- [ ] Pots and pans except one skillet and one pot
- [ ] Small appliances except coffee maker and toaster
- [ ] Wrap glasses individually in packing paper; stand them upright in boxes, never flat

### Pack — Moving Day Morning
- [ ] Coffee maker, toaster, last 2 place settings, dish soap, paper towels
- [ ] Remaining food → cooler for the road or trash
- [ ] Clean and photograph the fridge, oven, and countertops

### Last Out / First In Box — Kitchen
- [ ] Paper plates, plastic utensils, 2 mugs
- [ ] Coffee maker + filters + coffee
- [ ] Dish soap, one towel, trash bags, paper towels
- [ ] Snacks for the first night
- [ ] Corkscrew / bottle opener (you'll want it)
- [ ] Pet bowls and one meal's worth of dog food

## 🛋️ LIVING ROOM / FAMILY ROOM

**Responsibility: J**

- [ ] Worn throw pillows, blankets with holes
- [ ] Cables, chargers, remotes for devices you no longer own

- [ ] Board games, media, decorative objects

- [ ] Power strip

## 🧺 LAUNDRY / UTILITY ROOM

**Responsibility: P**

### Declutter First

### Pack — Week 1
- [ ] Cleaning supplies (tape lids, bag upright, don't mix chemicals)
- [ ] Iron, ironing board, drying rack

## 🏗️ GARAGE / STORAGE / ATTIC
**Estimated time: 4–8 hours (the black hole — start early)**
**Responsibility: J**

### Declutter First — Hardest Room, Do It First

### Pack — Weeks 4–3

### Hazmat Reminder
Movers cannot transport and you should not put in a moving truck:
- Gasoline, propane tanks, lighter fluid
- Paint, solvents, aerosols with flammable propellants
- Pesticides, pool chemicals
- Ammunition and fireworks
- Perishable food

Dispose of these properly or use them up before the move.

# Packing Supplies Shopping List — 2BR Apartment/House

---

## How to Estimate Your Box Count

A 2BR household typically needs **40–70 boxes** depending on how much you decluttered and how densely you pack. The list below assumes a moderate amount of stuff — a couple that cooks, reads, and has a normal amount of clothing and decor but already did a solid declutter pass.

If you're a minimalist, buy toward the low end. If you have a packed garage or a lot of books, buy toward the high end. Most suppliers let you return unused boxes, so overestimate slightly.

**Ways to cut this in half:**
- Get free boxes from liquor stores, grocery stores, Costco, Nextdoor, or Buy Nothing groups. Liquor store boxes are great — they're sturdy and have dividers perfect for glasses.
- Use your own towels, t-shirts, and linens as wrapping instead of buying packing paper.
- Skip packing peanuts entirely — crumpled paper works fine.
- Borrow a dolly and moving straps instead of buying.
- Return unused boxes and supplies (keep receipts).
- If using full-service movers who pack for you, you need almost none of this — confirm what they provide.

## 🛒 WHERE TO BUY

| Store | Best For | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Home Depot** | Boxes, tape, moving kits, wardrobe boxes, mattress bags | Sells bundled moving kits (small/medium/large household). Decent prices. Can order online for store pickup. *(J — do one big trip)* |
| **Lowe's** | Same as Home Depot | Compare prices — they often match. *(J)* |
| **U-Haul** | Specialty boxes (TV, dish barrel, wardrobe), tape, furniture pads | Sells individual boxes at good prices. Also rents dollies, furniture pads, and hand trucks. Buy-back program for unused boxes. *(M — combine with truck reservation visit)* |
| **Amazon** | Bulk tape, bubble wrap, stretch wrap, labeling supplies, foam pouches | Best for items you can wait 1–2 days for. Subscribe & Save can save 5–15%. *(P — order early)* |
| **Walmart** | Tape, markers, zip-lock bags, trash bags, cleaning supplies | Cheapest for basics. *(P — combine with a regular shopping trip)* |
| **U-Pack / PODS** | Moving kits | If you use their container service, ask about bundled supply kits. Sometimes discounted. *(J)* |
| **Facebook Marketplace / Buy Nothing / Nextdoor** | Free used boxes | Post "ISO moving boxes" in your local group. People who just moved are desperate to get rid of theirs. Best free source. *(J — check daily starting 6 weeks out)* |
| **Liquor stores and grocery stores** | Free sturdy boxes | Ask the manager when shipments come in (usually Tue–Thu). Go the next morning. Liquor boxes have built-in dividers. *(P — make 2–3 trips over 2 weeks)* |
| **Costco / Sam's Club** | Free boxes at checkout | Grab them while shopping. Sturdy but irregular sizes. *(J)* |
| **Staples / Office Depot** | File boxes, shredder, label stickers | Good for office-specific supplies. *(M)* |

## 1) Unique Volunteers (B3)

```
=SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF(
  IF(Clean!K2:K421<>"", Clean!K2:K421, "name:"&Clean!L2:L421),
  IF(Clean!K2:K421<>"", Clean!K2:K421, "name:"&Clean!L2:L421)
))
```

Enter with **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** (you'll see `{curly braces}` appear around it in the formula bar — that confirms it registered as an array formula).

**How it works:** It builds an in-memory array where each row becomes the email if present, otherwise `name:` + the lowercase name. COUNTIF counts how many times each key appears, 1/count gives the fractional contribution, and SUMPRODUCT sums the fractions to get unique count.

**Edge case:** If any row has both email and name completely blank, the formula will error (division by zero from an empty key matching other empty keys). Guard against that by wrapping the inner IF:

```
=SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF(
  IF(Clean!K2:K421<>"", Clean!K2:K421,
    IF(Clean!L2:L421<>"", "name:"&Clean!L2:L421, "unknown:"&ROW(Clean!L2:L421))),
  IF(Clean!K2:K421<>"", Clean!K2:K421,
    IF(Clean!L2:L421<>"", "name:"&Clean!L2:L421, "unknown:"&ROW(Clean!L2:L421)))
))
```

This gives each fully-blank row a unique key based on its row number, so it counts as 1 and doesn't break the formula.

   - **Sort** the Rows section by COUNTA descending
4. Rename the pivot sheet `ParkReview`
5. Your top 5 are simply the first 5 rows

Each time you add a variant to `ParkMap`, come back and refresh the pivot (**Data → Refresh** or just re-open it). The list shrinks as you map more variants.

---

## 3) Total Unmapped Park Rows (one-liner)

Paste this wherever you want it on the Dashboard (say B36):

```
=COUNTIF(Clean!J2:J421,"REVIEW")
```

Label in A36: `Unmapped Park Rows`

That's it — it counts every row whose canonical park is still REVIEW. As you add entries to `ParkMap`, this number drops in real time. When it hits 0, every park value is mapped.

## Helper Columns on Clean Sheet

You need two columns. I'll use **Q** and **R**.

### Column Q — Lowered/trimmed raw park (only for unmapped rows)

In Q2, fill down to 421:

```
=IF(J2="REVIEW", LOWER(TRIM(F2)), "")
```

This gives you a consistent key only for rows that are still unmapped. Mapped rows stay blank and don't interfere.

### Column R — Count of that variant across all unmapped rows

In R2, fill down to 421:

```
=IF(Q2<>"", COUNTIF($Q$2:$Q$421, Q2), 0)
```

---

## Dashboard Formulas (A31:B35)

### A31 — #1 variant name

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$R$2:$R$421,1), Clean!$R$2:$R$421, 0)), "")
```

### B31 — #1 count

```
=IFERROR(LARGE(Clean!$R$2:$R$421, 1), "")
```

### A32 / B32 — #2 variant

The trick is you need to skip rows that match the #1 variant. Use an array formula (**Ctrl+Shift+Enter**) for A32:

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(0, (Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421="")+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A31), 0)), "")
```

B32:

```
=IF(A32<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A32), "")
```

### A33 / B33 — #3 variant

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(0, (Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421="")+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A31)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A32), 0)), "")
```

B33: `=IF(A33<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A33), "")`

### A34 / B34 — #4 variant

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(0, (Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421="")+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A31)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A32)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A33), 0)), "")
```

B34: `=IF(A34<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A34), "")`

### A35 / B35 — #5 variant

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(0, (Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421="")+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A31)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A32)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A33)+(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A34), 0)), "")
```

B35: `=IF(A35<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A35), "")`

**Remember:** Every A-column formula in rows 32–35 needs **Ctrl+Shift+Enter**.

---

## How it works

- Q gives you a clean key for every unmapped row
- R gives each row its variant count (so LARGE can find the highest)
- A31 grabs the first variant with the highest count
- A32 onward each exclude previously found variants by adding another `+(Q=Aprevious)` condition, so MATCH finds the next new variant
- As you add entries to ParkMap, column J stops saying REVIEW, column Q goes blank, and the top-5 list reshuffles automatically

---

## Pivot Table — Does It Auto-Refresh?

**No.** Pivot tables in Google Sheets update automatically when the **source data values** change — but only the values in cells it already covers. So:

- If column J changes from REVIEW to "West Side" because you updated ParkMap → **yes, the pivot updates on its own**
- If you add new rows beyond row 421 → **no, you need to manually update the range** (right-click pivot → Edit range)

So for your use case (mapping variants and watching the REVIEW count drop), the pivot would actually auto-update just fine. But the helper-column approach above keeps everything on the Dashboard sheet, which is tidier.

## Non-CSE Dashboard Formulas

The trick is to sort by count descending in column R, then pick off distinct values using COUNTIF on the growing range above. No arrays needed.

### B31 — #1 count

```
=IFERROR(LARGE(Clean!$R$2:$R$421, 1), "")
```

### A31 — #1 variant

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(B31, Clean!$R$2:$R$421, 0)), "")

Finds the first row whose count equals the largest count. Simple MATCH, no array.

### B32 — #2 count

```
=IFERROR(LARGE(IF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421<>A31, Clean!$R$2:$R$421), 1), "")
```

**Wait — that's still an array.** Here's the non-array approach instead:

---

### Better approach: helper column S

Add **one more column** on Clean. In S2, fill down to 421:

```
=IF(Q2<>"", Q2&"|"&TEXT(R2,"0000"), "")
```

This creates a sortable key like `westside|0014` — the variant name with its zero-padded count. Now everything below is plain MATCH/INDEX against S.

---

### Dashboard formulas (all regular, no CSE)

**A31:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$R$2:$R$421,1), Clean!$R$2:$R$421, 0)), "")
```

**B31:**

```
=IF(A31<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A31), "")
```

**A32:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(1, COUNTIF(A$31:A31, Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421)+1, 0)), "")
```

Hmm — that's array again. Let me give you the cleanest truly non-array path.

---

## Cleanest approach: RANK in column S, skip arrays entirely

Replace column S with a **unique rank per variant**. In S2, fill down:

```
=IF(Q2="", "",
  R2*100000 - COUNTIF($Q$1:Q1, Q2))
```

This gives each row a score: count × 100000 minus how many times that same variant appeared above. So the **first occurrence** of the highest-count variant gets the highest score, the second occurrence of the same variant gets a lower score, and lower-count variants rank below. Ties between different variants are broken by row order, which is fine.

Now on Dashboard:

**A31:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**B31:**

```
=IF(A31<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A31), "")
```

**A32:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421,
  MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, SUMPRODUCT((Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421=A31)*1)+1),
        Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

No — SUMPRODUCT is basically an array too. Let me just be honest with you.

---

## The honest answer

There is no clean way to get "top N distinct values" from an unsorted list using **only** plain MATCH/INDEX and zero implicit arrays. Every approach either uses CSE, SUMPRODUCT, or UNIQUE — all of which are array operations under the hood.

**Your two realistic options:**

### Option A — Use UNIQUE (your Sheets supports it since B3 works with SUMPRODUCT)

Put this single formula in **A31** and it spills into A31:B35:

```
=IFERROR(
  SORTN(
    UNIQUE(FILTER(
      HSTACK(Clean!Q2:Q421, Clean!R2:R421),
      Clean!Q2:Q421<>"")),
    5, 0, 2, FALSE),
  "")
```

If HSTACK doesn't work, try the two-column approach:

**A31 (single formula, spills down):**

```
=SORTN(UNIQUE(FILTER(Clean!Q2:Q421, Clean!Q2:Q421<>"")), 5)
```

Then B31 (fill down to B35):

```
=IF(A31<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A31), "")
```

SORTN with UNIQUE doesn't need LET/BYROW and works in older Sheets.

### Option B — Pivot table (zero formulas)

Right-click your existing pivot → edit, or create one:

1. Source range: **Clean!F:J** (whole columns — answers your range question)
2. Rows: column Q or column F
3. Values: COUNTA of F
4. Filter: column J = REVIEW
5. Sort descending by count
6. Read the top 5 visually

---

## Pivot range question

Use **whole-column references** (`Clean!F:J` or `Clean!A:R`) so new rows are automatically included. The only downside is a tiny speed cost on a 420-row sheet, which is negligible.

---

**My recommendation:** Try the `SORTN`+`UNIQUE`+`FILTER` formula in A31 first. It's one formula, no CSE, no helpers beyond Q and R, and it works in any Sheets version from the last few years. If it errors, fall back to the pivot with whole-column range.

That means R is correctly counting each variant, but your expected dashboard output shows `west side | 15`, which sums 12+3 — combining `west side` and `west-side` as if they're the same.

**They're not the same in column Q.** Your Q formula lowercases and trims but keeps punctuation. So `west-side` ≠ `west side`.

You have two choices:

### Choice 1 — Keep them separate on the dashboard
The dashboard would show `west side | 12` and `west-side | 3` as separate rows. This is actually useful because it tells you exactly which raw variants to add to ParkMap.

### Choice 2 — Strip punctuation in Q so they merge
Change Q2 (fill down) to:

```

```

Now `west-side` and `west side` both become `west side`, and R will count them together as 15. But you lose visibility into the exact raw variants.

**I'd recommend Choice 1** — keep them separate so you know exactly what to type into ParkMap. That's the whole point of this list.

---

## Dashboard Formulas (no HSTACK, no LET, no CSE)

Given that SORTN and UNIQUE work for you (just not HSTACK), put these in as **two separate spilling formulas**:

**A31:**

```
=IFERROR(SORTN(UNIQUE(FILTER(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421<>"")), 5, 0, COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, UNIQUE(FILTER(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421<>""))), FALSE), "")
```

**That's too nested.** Here's the simple two-step version:

### A31 (spills to A35) — top 5 variant names sorted by frequency:

```
=SORTN(UNIQUE(FILTER(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421<>"")), 5, 0, COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, UNIQUE(FILTER(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421<>""))), 0)
```

The last argument `0` means descending. SORTN's syntax is:

```
SORTN(range, n, tie_mode, sort_column, is_ascending)
```

Here the `sort_column` is an array of counts generated inline by COUNTIF, and `0` = descending (FALSE also works, try both if one errors).

### B31 (fill down to B35) — count for each:

```
=IF(A31<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A31), "")
```

---

If the SORTN formula errors (some older Sheets don't allow an array as the sort_column argument), use this **completely manual fallback** that uses only MATCH, INDEX, LARGE, and COUNTIF:

### Fallback: add column S on Clean

S2 (fill down to 421):

```
=IF(Q2="", 0, R2 + (1-COUNTIF(Q$2:Q2,Q2)/1000000))
```

This gives every row a score equal to its count, with a tiny tiebreaker that ensures the **first occurrence** of each variant scores highest among its duplicates. Second occurrence of `west side` scores 12.000000 vs 11.999999.

### Dashboard with column S

**A31:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421,1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**B31:**

```
=IF(A31<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A31), "")
```

**A32:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, B31+1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**B32:**

```
=IF(A32<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A32), "")
```

**A33:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, B31+B32+1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**B33:** same pattern, `=IF(A33<>"", COUNTIF(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, A33), "")`

**A34:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, B31+B32+B33+1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**A35:**

```
=IFERROR(INDEX(Clean!$Q$2:$Q$421, MATCH(LARGE(Clean!$S$2:$S$421, B31+B32+B33+B34+1), Clean!$S$2:$S$421, 0)), "")
```

**B34, B35:** same `IF(Ax<>"", COUNTIF(...), "")` pattern.

### Why this works

S gives each row a score based on its count. LARGE(S, 1) finds the highest-scoring row — that's the first occurrence of the most frequent variant. All duplicates of that variant occupy ranks 1 through B31. So LARGE(S, B31+1) skips past all of them and lands on the first occurrence of the **second** most frequent variant. And so on.

No arrays. No CSE. No LET. Just LARGE, MATCH, INDEX, COUNTIF.

---

## Pivot range: whole-column is fine

At ~420 rows, using `Clean!F:J` or even `Clean!A:S` has **zero noticeable performance impact**. Whole-column references scan for the last row with data and stop. You'd need tens of thousands of rows with heavy formulas before it matters. Use whole columns and never worry about updating the range.

Here you go. Each version is four bars of 4/4 at roughly **♩ = 84**.

---

## Version 1: A Melodic Minor (Ascending)

**Key center:** A minor
**Accidentals to remember:** F# (raised 6th), G# (raised 7th) on the way up; natural minor (F, G) on the way down.

```
Bar 1                          Bar 2
Chord: Am                      Chord: D
Beat: 1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +  1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +
Note: C  E  F# G# A  -  -  -  A  G  E  D  C  B  A  -
RH:   1  2  3  4  5           5  4  3  2  1  2  1
LH:   A2-C3-E3 (hold bar)     D2-F#2-A2 (hold bar)

Bar 3                          Bar 4
Chord: Am                      Chord: E → Am
Beat: 1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +  1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +
Note: C  E  F# G# A  G  E  D  C  B  G# A  -  -  -  -
RH:   1  2  3  4  5  4  2  1  1  2  3  4
LH:   A2-C3-E3 (hold bar)     E2-G#2-B2 (beats 1-2)
                               A2-C3-E3  (beats 3-4)
```

**Notes:**
- Dashes (–) are eighth-note rests or you can sustain the previous note as a longer value.
- Bar 2 descends in natural minor (G and F natural), which is the melodic minor rule going down.
- Bar 4 ends with E major (V) resolving to Am (i). Hold the final A as a half note.

---

## Version 2: C Harmonic Minor

**Key center:** C minor
**Key signature flats:** Eb, Ab, Bb
**Accidental to remember:** B natural (raised 7th)

```
Bar 1                          Bar 2
Chord: Cm                      Chord: Ab
Beat: 1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +  1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +
Note: C  Eb G  Ab G  Eb D  C  Eb G  Ab G  Eb D  C  Bb
RH:   1  2  4  5  4  2  1  1  2  4  5  4  2  1  1  2
LH:   C2-Eb2-G2 (hold bar)    Ab2-C3-Eb3 (hold bar)

Bar 3                          Bar 4
Chord: Fm                      Chord: G → Cm
Beat: 1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +  1  +  2  +  3  +  4  +
Note: C  Eb G  Ab G  Eb D  C  B  C  D  Eb D  B  C  -
RH:   1  2  4  5  4  2  1  1  1  2  3  4  3  1  2
LH:   F2-Ab2-C3 (hold bar)    G2-B2-D3  (beats 1-2)
                               C2-Eb2-G2 (beats 3-4)
```

**Notes:**
- Bar 2 repeats the motif shape but starts on Eb, landing on Bb at the end to show the natural minor 7th before the B natural appears in Bar 4.
- Bar 4 is the payoff: B natural over G major (V) pulls hard into the final C. Hold the last C as a half note.
- The LH G major chord (G–B–D) is what makes harmonic minor sound dramatic. That B natural against the Eb and Ab elsewhere is the signature tension.

## Quick Fingering Tips
- In the A melodic minor version, the F#–G#–A run (fingers 3–4–5) is the trickiest spot. Practice that three-note group slowly.
- In the C harmonic minor version, the skip from C to Eb (fingers 1–2) repeats often. Keep the hand relaxed and let the thumb pivot.

# C Melodic Minor — Two-Hand Voicings and Fingerings

## Right Hand — Ascending (A♮ and B♮ raised)

```
Notes:  C – Eb – G – A♮ – B♮ – C
Finger: 1   2    4   5    4    5
```

Alternative ascending fingering:

```
Notes:  C – Eb – G – A♮ – B♮ – C
Finger: 1   2    3   4    5    5
```

The A♮ is the raised 6th degree, replacing Ab. The B♮ is the raised 7th degree, replacing Bb. Together they smooth out the augmented 2nd from harmonic minor and create a stepwise ascending line.

## Right Hand — Descending (Natural Minor Returns: Bb, Ab)

```
Notes:  C – Bb – Ab – G – F – Eb – D – C
Finger: 5   4    3    2   1   3    2   1
```

The descent drops both accidentals. A returns to Ab, B returns to Bb. This is the melodic minor rule: raise ascending, flatten descending.

## Full Phrase — Motif with Ascent and Descent Combined

```
Ascend (motif shape):
Notes:  C – Eb – G – A♮ – G – Eb – G – A♮ – B♮ – C
Finger: 1   2    4   5    4   2    4   1    2    3

Descend:
Notes:  C – Bb – Ab – G – F – Eb – D – C
Finger: 5   4    3    2   1   3    2   1
```

All as eighth notes except the final C, which should be held as a half note or longer.

## Cadence — ii – V – i (Melodic Minor Flavor)

**Dm7b5 – G – Cm**

```

The ii – V – i is the strongest minor cadence. The half-diminished chord creates tension, the G major with B♮ pulls to C, and Cm is home.

| Version | Accidentals | Where They Appear |
|---|---|---|
| C harmonic minor | B♮ | raised 7th, always |
| C melodic minor ascending | A♮ and B♮ | raised 6th and 7th |
| C melodic minor descending | none beyond key signature | returns to Bb and Ab (natural minor) |

## Practice Order

1. Play the harmonic minor melody alone until B♮ resolving to C feels natural under the fingers.
2. Add single-note bass to anchor the harmony.
3. Move to broken triads to hear the chord changes, especially G major with B♮.
4. Try the Alberti pattern for flowing texture.
5. For melodic minor, play the ascent and descent separately first, then combine.
6. Listen for the moment where A♮ becomes Ab and B♮ becomes Bb on the descent. That is the melodic minor rule in action.
7. Always end with the cadence. Train your ear to hear C as home.

# Assessment Rubrics, Formative Checks, and Student Checklists

---

## Analytic Rubrics (3-Point Scale)

For all rubrics: **3 = Proficient**, **2 = Developing**, **1 = Beginning**

---

### Assessment 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model

| Criterion | 3 — Proficient | 2 — Developing | 1 — Beginning | Aligned Goal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Base pairing & replication accuracy** | All complementary base pairs are correct across the replicated strand; student labels 5′→3′ directionality and identifies the template strand | 1–2 base-pairing errors or directionality is missing but overall logic is sound | Multiple errors or replication step is absent/fundamentally incorrect | Goal 1 (HS-LS1-1) |
| **Transcription** | mRNA is correctly transcribed from the template strand; student labels the process and identifies RNA polymerase's role | mRNA is present but contains 1–2 errors, or the explanation of the process is vague | mRNA is missing, copied from the wrong strand without recognition, or transcription is not explained | Goal 1 (HS-LS1-1) |
| **Translation & codon reading** | Every codon is correctly read using the codon table; amino acid chain is accurate, and start/stop codons are identified | 1–2 codon-reading errors or start/stop codons are not identified, but the overall chain is reasonable | Multiple codon errors, codon table is not used, or translation step is absent | Goal 1 (HS-LS1-1) |
| **Mutation analysis** | The specified mutation is correctly introduced; student accurately traces the change through mRNA to amino acids and clearly states whether the protein's function is likely altered and why | Mutation is introduced correctly but the downstream effect is only partially traced or the reasoning is incomplete | Mutation is incorrectly introduced, or no connection is made between the sequence change and protein/phenotype | Goal 4 (HS-LS3-2) |
| **Claim-Evidence-Reasoning paragraph** | Claim directly answers the prompt; evidence cites specific sequence positions and amino acid changes; reasoning explicitly links protein structure/function to phenotype | Claim is present but evidence is vague (e.g., "the protein changed") or reasoning does not connect to phenotype | Claim is missing or unsupported; no evidence from the model is cited | Goal 4 (HS-LS3-2) |
| **Heritability statement** | Correctly identifies whether the mutation is in a somatic or germ-line cell (or states the condition under which it would be heritable) with accurate reasoning | Identifies heritability but does not distinguish somatic vs. germ-line, or reasoning is incomplete | Statement is missing or scientifically inaccurate | Goal 4 (HS-LS3-2) |

**Proficient overall = 15–18 pts | Developing = 10–14 pts | Beginning = 6–9 pts**

---

### Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation

| Criterion | 3 — Proficient | 2 — Developing | 1 — Beginning | Aligned Goal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Inheritance pattern identification** | Correctly identifies the pattern (e.g., autosomal recessive) and provides at least two pieces of pedigree evidence (e.g., "Two unaffected parents have an affected child, so the trait cannot be dominant") | Correct pattern but only one piece of evidence, or evidence is stated but not clearly connected to the pattern | Incorrect pattern, or pattern is stated with no supporting evidence | Goal 2 (HS-LS3-3) |
| **Genotype assignments** | All assigned genotypes are consistent with the identified pattern and pedigree data; uncertainties (e.g., carrier vs. homozygous dominant) are explicitly noted | Most genotypes are correct but one is inconsistent or uncertainty is not acknowledged | Multiple genotype errors or assignments contradict the stated inheritance pattern | Goal 2 (HS-LS3-1) |
| **Probability calculation** | Punnett square is set up correctly with the right parental genotypes; probability is accurately calculated and expressed as a fraction, percentage, or ratio | Punnett square has a minor setup error (e.g., wrong parental genotype carried forward) but method is sound | Punnett square is missing, fundamentally incorrect, or probability does not follow from the cross | Goal 2 (HS-LS3-3) |
| **Chi-square analysis** | Expected values are correctly calculated from the predicted ratio; χ² is computed accurately; the value is compared to the correct critical value (df and p stated); conclusion about the model is logically stated | One computational error or the conclusion is vague (e.g., "it fits" without referencing the critical value) | Expected values or χ² computation are missing/fundamentally wrong, or no conclusion is drawn | Goal 3 (HS-LS3-3) |
| **Family letter communication** | Results are restated in plain, accurate language a nonscientist could understand; no jargon is left undefined; tone is respectful and appropriate | Letter is mostly clear but includes undefined jargon or oversimplifies to the point of inaccuracy | Letter is missing, scientifically inaccurate, or written in technical language with no audience awareness | Goal 2, SEP: Communicating |

**Proficient overall = 13–15 pts | Developing = 9–12 pts | Beginning = 5–8 pts**

---

### Assessment 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief

| Criterion | 3 — Proficient | 2 — Developing | 1 — Beginning | Aligned Goal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scientific accuracy of mechanism** | The genetic technology's mechanism is explained correctly and connected to relevant concepts (e.g., how CRISPR creates a double-strand break and how repair can introduce or correct a mutation) | Mechanism is partially correct but missing a key step, or connection to unit concepts is vague | Mechanism is absent or contains significant scientific errors | Goal 4 (HS-LS3-2) |
| **Use of evidence** | At least two provided sources are cited; at least one piece of quantitative data (e.g., efficacy rate, off-target frequency) is interpreted correctly and integrated into the argument | Two sources cited but data are mentioned without interpretation, or only one source is used effectively | Fewer than two sources, or evidence is absent/misrepresented | Goal 6, SEP: Evaluating Information |
| **Unintended consequences** | At least one unintended consequence is identified and explicitly connected to a genetics concept (e.g., off-target edits creating new mutations, reduced genetic diversity, mosaicism) | An unintended consequence is named but not connected to a genetics concept, or the connection is superficial | No unintended consequence is discussed | Goal 4 (HS-LS3-2), Goal 6 |
| **Stakeholder perspectives** | At least two stakeholder viewpoints are accurately described; the student explains how the science looks different from each perspective | Two stakeholders named but perspectives are superficial or not connected to the evidence | Fewer than two stakeholders, or perspectives are missing | Goal 6 |
| **Counterargument & rebuttal** | A plausible counterargument is stated fairly; the rebuttal addresses it with specific evidence or reasoning rather than dismissing it | Counterargument is present but the rebuttal is weak or opinion-based | Counterargument is missing or is a straw man with no real rebuttal | Goal 6, SEP: Argumentation |
| **Claim clarity & structure** | The brief opens with a clear, specific policy claim (e.g., "CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease should be approved for clinical use with mandatory long-term monitoring"); the document is logically organized with an introduction, evidence sections, and a conclusion | Claim is present but vague (e.g., "gene editing is good"); organization is loosely logical | No discernible claim, or the brief reads as a disconnected list of facts | Goal 6, SEP: Communicating |

**Proficient overall = 15–18 pts | Developing = 10–14 pts | Beginning = 6–9 pts**

---

## Six Quick Formative Checks (One Per Lesson Block)

Use as a warm-up, exit ticket, or mid-lesson pause. Each should take ≤5 minutes.

### Week 1: DNA Structure, Replication, and Protein Synthesis

**Day 2 — Exit Ticket: Replication Sketch**
> Draw a replication fork from memory. Label the template strand, the new strand, the direction of synthesis, and the enzyme responsible. In one sentence, explain why replication is called "semi-conservative."

*What you're checking:* Whether students can recall the basic model before you layer on transcription. Quick scan for directionality misconceptions.

**Day 4 — Warm-Up: Codon Challenge**
> Here is a short mRNA sequence: 5′-AUG UCU GAA UGA-3′. Use your codon table to write the amino acid chain. Then answer: If the second U in UCU is changed to an A, what happens to the amino acid? What type of mutation is this?

*What you're checking:* Codon table fluency and whether students can already connect a single-base change to a protein consequence before the full mutation lesson.

---

### Week 2: Mendelian Genetics, Pedigrees, and Data Analysis

**Day 7 — Exit Ticket: Quick Cross**
> In pea plants, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled seeds (r). Cross two heterozygous plants. (a) What is the expected phenotypic ratio? (b) If you grew 200 offspring and got 142 round and 58 wrinkled, does that seem close to the expected ratio? Explain without calculating χ² — just reason about it.

*What you're checking:* Punnett square mechanics and intuitive proportional reasoning, which sets up the chi-square lesson.

**Day 9 — Warm-Up: Pedigree Snapshot**
> Show a simple 2-generation pedigree with two unaffected parents and one affected child. Ask: (a) Can this trait be dominant? Why or why not? (b) Write the most likely genotypes for all three individuals using "A" and "a."

*What you're checking:* Whether students can use pedigree evidence to rule out an inheritance pattern — the core reasoning skill for Assessment 2.

---

### Week 3: Mutations, Gene Expression, and Ethics

**Day 12 — Exit Ticket: Mutation Sort**
> Give students three short scenarios (a silent mutation, a missense mutation that changes protein function, and a frameshift that creates a premature stop codon). Ask them to rank the three from least to most likely to affect phenotype and write one sentence of justification for their ranking.

*What you're checking:* Whether students can distinguish mutation types by severity of effect, which is the core reasoning in Assessment 1's CER paragraph and feeds into Assessment 3.

**Day 14 — Warm-Up: Stakeholder Stand**
> You're preparing for the policy brief. Read this one-paragraph summary of a CRISPR sickle-cell trial. In 2–3 sentences, state one benefit and one risk from the perspective of (a) the patient and (b) a health insurance company. Are the benefit and risk the same for both? Why not?

*What you're checking:* Whether students can shift perspective and connect science to societal impact before they write the full brief.

---

## Student Self-Assessment Checklist (Universal — Adapt Header for Each Assessment)

Print at the top of each assignment or post on your LMS. Students check each box before submitting.

---

### ✅ Before I Turn This In…

| ✓ | Question to Ask Myself |
|---|---|
| ☐ | **Did I answer the actual prompt?** Re-read the task. Does every required deliverable (model, paragraph, calculation, letter, brief) appear in my submission? |
| ☐ | **Is my science accurate?** Have I double-checked base pairing, codon reading, genotype assignments, or mechanism descriptions against my notes or the codon table? |
| ☐ | **Did I use specific evidence, not just general statements?** Look for vague phrases like "the protein changes" or "it's bad for society." Replace each one with a specific detail (which base, which amino acid, which data point, which stakeholder). |
| ☐ | **Did I explain *why*, not just *what*?** For every claim I make, can I point to a sentence that gives the reasoning? (If I only stated a fact, I need to add the "because…" sentence.) |
| ☐ | **Would someone outside our class understand this?** Read my work as if I'm the family in the letter, the policymaker reading the brief, or a classmate who missed the lesson. Is anything confusing, undefined, or out of order? |

---

*Tip for implementation:* Have students initial each box. If they can't check one honestly, that's their revision target — which makes the checklist a metacognitive tool, not just a compliance step.

# Part 1: Formative Check Answer Keys & Teacher Notes

---

## Week 1

### Day 2 Exit Ticket: Replication Sketch

**Solution:** The fork should show the original double helix unwinding, with each original strand (template) paired with a newly synthesized complementary strand running antiparallel. DNA helicase unwinds; DNA polymerase synthesizes. Semi-conservative means each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and one new strand.

**Look for:** Correct antiparallel orientation and the student labeling both a template and a new strand rather than drawing two entirely new strands from scratch.

**Common misconception:** Students often draw both new strands running in the same direction, or they think "semi-conservative" means only half the DNA is copied.

---

### Day 4 Warm-Up: Codon Challenge

**Solution:** AUG → Met, UCU → Ser, GAA → Glu, UGA → Stop. The chain is Met-Ser-Glu (three amino acids, then translation stops). Changing the second U in UCU to A gives UAU → Tyr, so the chain becomes Met-Tyr-Glu — a missense (substitution) mutation that swaps one amino acid.

**Look for:** Correct use of the codon table (reading across the right row and column) and the student identifying this as a missense mutation specifically, not just "a substitution."

**Common misconception:** Students frequently read the codon table using the DNA sequence instead of converting to mRNA first, or they confuse the terms "substitution" (the DNA-level event) and "missense" (the protein-level consequence).

---

## Week 2

### Day 7 Exit Ticket: Quick Cross

**Solution:** Rr × Rr → 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. Phenotypic ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled. Expected with 200 offspring: 150 round, 50 wrinkled. Observed (142:58) is reasonably close; small deviations are expected from chance alone in biological data, so this likely still supports a 3:1 model.

**Look for:** A correctly set-up 2×2 Punnett square and the student reasoning that 142:58 is "close enough" by comparing it proportionally to 150:50 rather than demanding an exact match.

**Common misconception:** Students often say the data "disprove" the 3:1 ratio because the numbers aren't exactly 150 and 50. This is the perfect moment to preview why we need a statistical test like chi-square rather than relying on intuition.

---

### Day 9 Warm-Up: Pedigree Snapshot

**Solution:** The trait cannot be dominant because two unaffected parents (who would both have to be aa if dominant were needed to show the trait — wait, let's be precise) — if the trait were dominant, at least one parent would need to carry a dominant allele and would therefore show the trait. Since neither parent is affected, the trait must be recessive. Parents are both Aa (carriers); the affected child is aa.

**Look for:** The student explicitly ruling out dominant inheritance with a logical sentence ("If it were dominant, at least one parent would be affected") rather than just guessing recessive.

**Common misconception:** Students confuse "carrier" with "affected" and may write both parents as AA, then struggle to explain where the affected child's aa genotype came from. Push them to reconcile genotypes with phenotypes.

---

## Week 3

### Day 12 Exit Ticket: Mutation Sort

**Solution:** Ranking from least to most effect on phenotype: (1) silent mutation — codon still codes for the same amino acid, protein is unchanged; (2) missense mutation — one amino acid is swapped, protein may or may not lose function depending on location and chemistry; (3) frameshift with premature stop — every downstream codon is shifted and the protein is truncated, almost certainly nonfunctional.

**Look for:** A clear rationale for ranking that references what happens at the protein level, not just at the DNA level. The strongest answers will mention that a missense mutation's severity depends on where in the protein it occurs and whether the new amino acid has similar properties.

**Common misconception:** Students often assume all mutations are harmful. Watch for students ranking the silent mutation as damaging, or treating missense and frameshift as equally severe because "they both change the DNA."

---

### Day 14 Warm-Up: Stakeholder Stand

**Solution:** Patient perspective — benefit: potential cure for a painful, life-shortening disease; risk: unknown long-term side effects or off-target edits. Insurance perspective — benefit: one-time treatment could replace a lifetime of costly care; risk: extremely high upfront cost and uncertainty about whether it works long-term, making it hard to price coverage. The benefit and risk are not the same because each stakeholder weighs health outcomes and financial outcomes differently.

**Look for:** The student distinguishing between a scientific/health lens and an economic/access lens, and explicitly stating that the same technology looks different depending on who is evaluating it.

**Common misconception:** Students often write the same generic "pro and con" for both stakeholders (e.g., "it could help people" / "it could be dangerous") without differentiating perspectives. Push for specificity: *how* does the risk differ for a patient versus an insurer?

---

# Part 2: Simplified Formative Checks (EL / IEP Accommodations)

Each check is reduced to one clear sentence prompt, a sentence starter or frame, a single correct-answer line for quick grading, and key vocabulary provided (bolded). These can be printed on half-sheets or displayed as slides.

---

### Check 1 (Day 2): Replication

**Prompt:** DNA makes a copy of itself. This is called **replication**. Draw the two new DNA molecules that come from one original molecule. Label which strand is **old** and which is **new**.

**Sentence frame:** Replication is called semi-conservative because each new DNA molecule has \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

**Correct answer line:** …one old (original) strand and one new strand.

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** replication, semi-conservative, template strand, complementary

---

### Check 2 (Day 4): Codon Reading

**Prompt:** Use the **codon table** to find the amino acids for this mRNA: **AUG UCU GAA UGA**. Write each amino acid below its codon. Then change the U in the middle of UCU to an A (making UAU). What amino acid does **UAU** code for?

**Sentence frame:** When one base changes and the amino acid changes, this is called a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ mutation.

**Correct answer line:** AUG = Met, UCU = Ser, GAA = Glu, UGA = Stop. UAU = Tyr. This is a **missense** mutation.

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** codon, amino acid, missense, substitution

---

### Check 3 (Day 7): Punnett Square

**Prompt:** Round seeds (**R**) are **dominant**. Wrinkled seeds (**r**) are **recessive**. Both parents are **Rr**. Fill in the Punnett square below.

*(Provide a pre-drawn empty 2×2 grid with Rr on each axis.)*

**Sentence frame:** I expect \_\_\_\_ out of 4 offspring to have round seeds and \_\_\_\_ out of 4 to have wrinkled seeds.

**Correct answer line:** 3 out of 4 round, 1 out of 4 wrinkled (3:1 ratio).

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, ratio

---

### Check 4 (Day 9): Pedigree Reading

**Prompt:** Look at this pedigree. Neither parent is affected (shaded). One child IS affected.

*(Provide the simple pedigree image — two unshaded parents, one shaded child, one unshaded child.)*

**Question:** Can this trait be **dominant**? Circle: YES / NO. Explain using the sentence frame.

**Sentence frame:** This trait is **recessive** because both parents are \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ but their child is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

**Correct answer line:** NO. Both parents are **unaffected (carriers, Aa)** but their child is **affected (aa)**. A dominant trait would show in at least one parent.

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** dominant, recessive, carrier, affected, unaffected, pedigree

---

### Check 5 (Day 12): Mutation Ranking

**Prompt:** Read these three mutations. Rank them **1 (least effect)** to **3 (most effect)** on the protein.

| Mutation | What happens | Rank |
|---|---|---|
| **Silent** | The codon changes but the amino acid stays the same | \_\_\_\_ |
| **Missense** | One amino acid changes to a different amino acid | \_\_\_\_ |
| **Frameshift** | Every amino acid after the mutation changes; protein is cut short | \_\_\_\_ |

**Sentence frame:** The \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ mutation has the biggest effect because \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

**Correct answer line:** Silent = 1, Missense = 2, Frameshift = 3. The **frameshift** mutation has the biggest effect because **all amino acids after the change are wrong and the protein is too short to work.**

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** silent, missense, frameshift, amino acid, protein, phenotype

---

### Check 6 (Day 14): Stakeholder Perspectives

**Prompt:** Scientists used **CRISPR** (a gene-editing tool) to treat a patient with **sickle cell disease**. Read the summary paragraph. Then fill in the table.

| | One benefit | One risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient** | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| **Insurance company** | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |

**Sentence frame:** The patient and the insurance company see this differently because the patient cares most about \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ and the insurance company cares most about \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

**Correct answer line:** Patient — benefit: could cure the disease; risk: treatment might have side effects. Insurance — benefit: one treatment could replace years of hospital costs; risk: the treatment is very expensive right now. The patient cares most about **health/quality of life** and the insurance company cares most about **cost**.

**Key vocabulary provided on the page:** CRISPR, gene editing, sickle cell disease, stakeholder, benefit, risk

## Feedback on Your Draft Rubric for Assessment 1

Your draft is strong. A few targeted suggestions before the full version:

- **Accuracy (12 pts) is weighted correctly** — it's the core skill. But break it into replication, transcription, and translation separately so you can pinpoint where a student's understanding breaks down.
- **Mutation identification (4 pts) is underweighted relative to CER (10 pts).** That's actually fine — the reasoning matters more than the label — but make sure the CER row explicitly requires students to connect all three levels (DNA → protein → phenotype), not just two.
- **Model clarity (6 pts) could conflate neatness with scientific accuracy.** Split it: labels/annotations vs. correct use of the codon table.
- **Revision/reflection (4 pts) is a great inclusion.** Tie it to the modeling practice by requiring students to name a specific limitation and a specific change they made, not just general reflection.
- **Add a row or modifier for scientific language** — students at this level should be using terms like "complementary base pairing," "codon," "amino acid," and "polypeptide" correctly.

## WEEK 1: DNA Structure, Replication, & Protein Synthesis (Goals 1 & 5)

### Day 1 — Unit Hook & DNA Structure
| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | Describe the structure of DNA and explain how complementary base pairing enables information storage. |
| **Warm-up (5 min)** | "What makes you, *you*? List 3 traits you think are genetic and 1 you're unsure about." |
| **Activity (30 min)** | Build a paper or candy nucleotide model in pairs → assemble into a double helix → answer guided questions: What holds the strands together? Why does A pair with T? |
| **Quick check (10 min)** | Exit ticket: "Draw a 6-nucleotide DNA strand; write the complementary strand. Explain why C never pairs with A." |
| **Materials** | Paper nucleotide cutouts or candy model kits, tape, guided question sheet |
| **Differentiation** | **S:** Pre-labeled cutouts with color-coded bases and a base-pairing key card. **E:** Add a question — "If the ratio of A to T in an organism is not 1:1, what might that mean? Is that possible?" **ML:** Vocabulary card with diagram: nucleotide, complementary, hydrogen bond. |

### Day 2 — DNA Replication

# Proficiency-Scale Rubrics (0–4) & Exemplar Responses

---

## Assessment 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model

| Criterion | 4 Exemplary | 3 Proficient | 2 Developing | 1 Beginning | 0 Missing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Replication accuracy** | Complementary strand fully correct; base-pairing rules and directionality explained | Strand correct; explanation present but incomplete (e.g., directionality missing) | 1–2 base-pairing errors or explanation vague | Multiple errors; no explanation | Not attempted |
| **Transcription accuracy** | mRNA fully correct; template vs. coding strand identified; 5'→3' labeled | mRNA correct; strand ID or directionality missing | 1–2 mRNA errors or significant conceptual gap | mRNA largely incorrect or absent | Not attempted |
| **Translation accuracy** | Amino acid sequence fully correct; codon table used properly; start/stop codons identified | Sequence correct; start or stop codon not noted | 1–2 amino acid errors or codon table misread | Sequence largely incorrect or absent | Not attempted |
| **Mutation ID & classification** | Type (sub/ins/del) and effect category (silent/missense/nonsense/frameshift) both correct | Type correct; effect category partially correct | Type or effect category incorrect | Neither correctly identified | Not attempted |
| **CER: mutation → protein → phenotype** | Specific claim; evidence cites exact sequence and amino acid change; reasoning links all three levels (DNA → protein → phenotype) | Claim and evidence correct; reasoning links only two of three levels | Claim present but vague; evidence or reasoning missing | No clear claim or logic incorrect | Not attempted |
| **Model clarity & annotations** | All molecules labeled; annotations explain each step; codon table referenced correctly | Most labels present; annotations incomplete | Several labels missing; annotations minimal | Model unclear or unlabeled | Not attempted |
| **Heritability explanation** | Correctly distinguishes germline vs. somatic; explains whether and why the mutation can be inherited | Identifies germline vs. somatic; explanation incomplete | Attempts distinction but contains misconception | No distinction made | Not attempted |
| **Revision & reflection** | Names a specific limitation AND a specific revision, with reasoning tied to new understanding | Names both but reasoning vague | Names only a limitation or only a revision | Reflection is generic or off-topic | Not attempted |

### Assessment 1 Exemplar Responses
*Prompt: Explain how your mutation affects the phenotype (CER paragraph).*

**4 — Exemplary:**
"The deletion of the second nucleotide in codon 3 causes a frameshift that changes every downstream codon, replacing the original amino acid sequence Leu-Arg-Gly with Phe-Thr-Stop. Because the protein is truncated and missing its active site, the enzyme cannot catalyze the pigment reaction, so the organism lacks pigmentation. This mutation would be heritable only if it occurs in a germline cell, because somatic mutations are not passed to offspring."

**3 — Proficient:**
"The deletion causes a frameshift that changes the amino acids after codon 3, so the protein doesn't fold correctly. This means the enzyme won't work and the organism's phenotype changes. The mutation could be passed on if it's in a reproductive cell."

**2 — Developing:**
"The deletion changes the protein because the codons are different now. The organism would look different because the protein is wrong."

**1 — Beginning:**
"There is a deletion in the DNA. This is a mutation that changes things."

---

## Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation

| Criterion | 4 Exemplary | 3 Proficient | 2 Developing | 1 Beginning | 0 Missing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Inheritance pattern ID** | Correct pattern identified; justification cites ≥2 specific pedigree clues with generation references | Correct pattern; justification cites only 1 clue | Correct pattern but no justification, or incorrect pattern with partial reasoning | Incorrect pattern with no reasoning | Not attempted |
| **Genotype assignments** | All specified individuals correct; carriers and uncertain genotypes noted with explanation | Most correct; carriers noted but not fully explained | Some correct; carriers not addressed | Most incorrect or missing | Not attempted |
| **Punnett square & probability** | Cross set up correctly; probability accurate and expressed as fraction/percent/ratio; interpretation stated in context | Cross and calculation correct; interpretation missing or generic | Setup error leading to incorrect probability | Cross missing or fundamentally incorrect | Not attempted |
| **Chi-square analysis** | Expected values, χ² computation, df, and comparison to critical value all correct; conclusion (fail to reject/reject) stated and interpreted | Computation correct; interpretation present but imprecise (e.g., df or alpha not stated) | Setup or computation error; conclusion still attempted | Chi-square missing or fundamentally incorrect | Not attempted |
| **Data → model connection** | Explicitly states whether χ² supports the model AND explains sources of deviation (sample size, chance, wrong model) | States whether result supports model; deviation explanation vague | States result without connecting to model | No connection made | Not attempted |
| **Family letter communication** | Accurate, jargon-free, empathetic; probability contextualized for a non-scientist | Accurate and mostly jargon-free; tone appropriate | Contains inaccuracies or excessive jargon | Inaccurate or missing | Not attempted |
| **Scientific notation & conventions** | Pedigree symbols, allele notation, and probability notation correct and consistent throughout | Minor inconsistencies | Frequent errors causing confusion | Notation incorrect or absent | Not attempted |

### Assessment 2 Exemplar Responses
*Prompt: Identify the inheritance pattern and justify with pedigree evidence.*

**4 — Exemplary:**
"The trait is autosomal recessive. In Generation II, two unaffected parents (II-3 and II-4) have an affected child (III-2), which means both parents must be carriers — this rules out dominant inheritance. Additionally, both males and females are affected in roughly equal numbers across three generations, which rules out X-linked inheritance because affected females would require two copies of the allele, which is unlikely if the trait is rare."

**3 — Proficient:**
"The trait is autosomal recessive because two unaffected parents in Generation II have an affected child, so the trait must be able to hide in carriers. Both sexes are affected, so it's probably not X-linked."

**2 — Developing:**
"I think the trait is recessive because it skips a generation. Some people have it and some don't."

**1 — Beginning:**
"The trait comes from the parents. It shows up in Generation III."

---

*Prompt: Interpret your chi-square result.*

**4 — Exemplary:**
"My χ² value is 1.87 with 1 degree of freedom. The critical value at α = 0.05 is 3.84. Because 1.87 < 3.84, I fail to reject the null hypothesis, meaning my observed data (32 purple, 12 white) are consistent with the predicted 3:1 ratio and the deviation is likely due to chance and small sample size."

**3 — Proficient:**
"My χ² is 1.87, which is less than 3.84, so I fail to reject the null hypothesis. My data support the 3:1 ratio."

**2 — Developing:**
"I got 1.87 for chi-square. That's lower than the critical value so my results are probably right."

**1 — Beginning:**
"I calculated chi-square and got a number. I think the data is close to what I expected."

---

## Assessment 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief

| Criterion | 4 Exemplary | 3 Proficient | 2 Developing | 1 Beginning | 0 Missing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scientific accuracy of mechanism** | Technology's mechanism explained correctly and connected to genetics concepts (mutation, gene expression, base pairing) | Mostly correct; connection to genetics concepts implicit | Significant error or oversimplified | Mechanism missing or incorrect | Not attempted |
| **Use of evidence** | ≥2 sources cited; ≥1 quantitative data point interpreted and integrated into argument (not just dropped in) | 2 sources cited; data present but not fully interpreted | Only 1 source or no quantitative data | No credible evidence cited | Not attempted |
| **Claim & reasoning** | Claim is specific and arguable; reasoning explicitly links science to policy position | Claim clear; link between science and policy underdeveloped | Claim vague or reasoning weak | No clear claim | Not attempted |
| **Unintended consequences** | ≥1 consequence identified and connected to a genetics concept (e.g., off-target edits, reduced diversity) | Consequence identified; genetics connection vague | Consequence mentioned but not connected to science | Not addressed | Not attempted |
| **Stakeholder perspectives** | ≥2 perspectives accurately represented; student engages with an opposing perspective | 2 perspectives present; engagement with opposition superficial | Only 1 perspective or perspectives stereotyped | No stakeholder analysis | Not attempted |
| **Counterargument & rebuttal** | Substantive counterargument stated fairly and rebutted with evidence or reasoning | Counterargument stated; rebuttal present but weak | Counterargument stated but not rebutted | No counterargument | Not attempted |
| **Writing quality & structure** | 1–2 pages; organized with clear sections; formal, precise language | Organized and mostly clear; minor structural gaps | Disorganized or significantly under/over length | Difficult to follow; major structural problems | Not attempted |

### Assessment 3 Exemplar Responses
*Prompt: Explain how the technology works and connect it to a genetics concept.*

**4 — Exemplary:**
"CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA sequence complementary to the target DNA to direct the Cas9 enzyme to a specific location in the genome, where it creates a double-strand break. The cell's DNA repair mechanisms then either disable the gene (non-homologous end joining, which introduces insertions or deletions) or correct it using a provided template (homology-directed repair). In the case of sickle cell disease, the target is the mutated HBB gene where a single A→T substitution causes valine to replace glutamic acid in the beta-globin protein, and the goal is to restore the normal sequence so that hemoglobin no longer polymerizes."

**3 — Proficient:**
"CRISPR uses a guide RNA to find a specific DNA sequence and the Cas9 protein cuts the DNA at that spot. The cell then repairs the break, which can fix a mutation. For sickle cell disease, it targets the HBB gene where one nucleotide change causes the wrong amino acid."

**2 — Developing:**
"CRISPR is a tool that edits DNA by cutting it at a specific place. Scientists can use it to change genes that cause diseases like sickle cell."

**1 — Beginning:**
"CRISPR changes DNA. It can be used to fix genetic diseases."

---

*Prompt: Identify an unintended consequence and connect it to genetics.*

**4 — Exemplary:**
"One unintended consequence is off-target editing, where the guide RNA binds to a similar but non-identical sequence elsewhere in the genome, creating an insertion or deletion at an unintended locus. This is essentially an induced mutation — if it occurs in a tumor suppressor gene, for example, it could disrupt gene expression and increase cancer risk, meaning the therapy could introduce a new genetic disease while curing the original one."

**3 — Proficient:**
"CRISPR might accidentally cut DNA in the wrong place, creating a new mutation. If this off-target edit disrupts an important gene, it could cause new health problems for the patient."

**2 — Developing:**
"CRISPR could make mistakes and cut the wrong part of the DNA. This could cause problems."

**1 — Beginning:**
"There could be side effects from using CRISPR."

---

## Gradebook Quick-Reference

For a streamlined gradebook, score each criterion 0–4 and use this conversion:

| Scale Score | Label | General Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Exemplary | Exceeds the standard; complete, accurate, and insightful |
| 3 | Proficient | Meets the standard; minor gaps that don't undermine understanding |
| 2 | Developing | Approaching the standard; partial understanding with significant gaps |
| 1 | Beginning | Below the standard; minimal or inaccurate response |
| 0 | Missing | No evidence submitted or entirely off-task |

**Overall assessment score** = mean of all criterion scores for that assessment, rounded to the nearest 0.5.

| Mean | Suggested Grade Equivalent (if needed) |
|---|---|
| 3.5–4.0 | A |
| 3.0–3.4 | B |
| 2.0–2.9 | C |
| 1.0–1.9 | D |
| 0–0.9 | F / Incomplete — reassess |

**Reassessment recommendation:** Any student scoring 1 or 0 on two or more criteria should receive targeted reteaching and an opportunity to reassess on those specific criteria within one week.

Copy and paste these directly. Each targets a common error pattern across the three assessments.

**1. Miscoded amino acid (Assessment 1)**

---

**2. Wrong inheritance pattern or weak justification (Assessment 2)**

> Your inheritance pattern identification needs stronger pedigree evidence. Go back to Generation [X] and look at the parents of the affected individual — are they both unaffected? **4. Weak or missing evidence interpretation (Assessment 3)**
