# Room-by-Room Packing Plan + Declutter Guide

**Built around your move day: Thursday, July 16, 2026.** Time estimates assume a 1–2 bedroom home with two people working together. **Rule of thumb: everything takes 1.5× longer than you think**, so the schedule has buffer built in.

**Total estimated time: ~45–75 hours** across 5 weeks (≈ 10–15 hrs/week).

---

## 🗓️ THE ORDER (and Why)

Pack from **least-used to most-used.** Kitchen, bathrooms, and bedrooms go last.

| # | Area | Target Dates | Est. Time | Who |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Storage unit** (if any) | Jun 13–14 | 4–8 hrs | J |
| 2 | **Garage / shed / attic** | Jun 20–28 | 6–12 hrs | J |
| 3 | **Spare room + hall/storage closets** | Jun 25–28 | 3–5 hrs | P |
| 4 | **Books, decor, art, off-season clothes** | Jun 27–Jul 2 | 3–6 hrs | M |
| 5 | **Living room** | Jul 3–8 (use July 4 weekend) | 4–6 hrs | J |
| 6 | **Dining room** | Jul 3–8 | 2–3 hrs | P |
| 7 | **Home office** | Jul 6–10 (work gear last) | 3–5 hrs | Owner of the gear |
| 8 | **Kitchen** (80% packed) | Jul 8–13 | 8–12 hrs | J |
| 9 | **Bathrooms** | Jul 12–14 | 1–2 hrs each | M |
| 10 | **Bedrooms + closets** | Jul 12–15 | 6–10 hrs | J |
| 11 | **Dog gear + Open First box + car kit** | Jul 15 | 1–2 hrs | M |

---

## ✂️ DECLUTTER PHASE: Jun 11–24 (Do This *Before* Packing)

Do one fast sorting pass through every room with four bins or piles: **KEEP · SELL · DONATE · TRASH.**

**The Cross-Country Decision Rule**
Long-distance moves are priced largely by **weight**, often roughly $0.50–$1+ per pound with full-service movers. Get rid of an item if **2 or more** of these are true:
- [ ] You haven't used it in 12 months
- [ ] Replacing it in Oregon would cost less than moving it
- [ ] It's particle-board or flat-pack furniture (it often doesn't survive a move)
- [ ] It won't fit or suit the new place (measure first!)
- [ ] You're keeping it "just in case"

**Where Things Go**

| Item Type | Best Outlet | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Furniture, appliances, electronics | Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, OfferUp, Nextdoor | **List by Jun 14**; final sale cutoff **Jul 10** |
| Furniture/building materials (donate) | Habitat ReStore (free pickup), Salvation Army | **Book pickup 2–3 wks ahead** |
| Clothes, housewares, books | Goodwill, local thrift, library book sales | Drop off weekly |
| Anything (fast and free) | Buy Nothing groups, curbside "free" post | Anytime |
| Old towels, blankets, sheets | **Animal shelters** (they love these) | Anytime |
| Unopened pantry food | Food pantries | Week 2 |
| Paint, chemicals, batteries, e-waste | **County household hazardous waste drop-off** | Check hours early |
| Documents you don't need | Shred event or office store shredding | Week 3 |

**Declutter Tips**
- **Price to sell, not to profit.** Price 30–50% below market. Unsold items cost you money to move or haul away.
- **Sell big items first.** Pick up any replacements in Oregon.
- **Set a hard "last donation run" date (Jul 11).** Anything left goes to the curb or junk removal.
- **Measure the new place** (rooms, doorways, stairs) before deciding on large furniture.
- **Don't pack trash.** Toss expired food, meds, makeup, broken items, and orphan cables as you go.

---

## 🏷️ LABELING SYSTEM

**1. Color-code each room with colored tape or stickers**

| Room | Color |
|---|---|
| Kitchen | 🔴 Red |
| Living / Dining | 🟠 Orange |
| Primary Bedroom | 🔵 Blue |
| Spare / Office | 🟢 Green |
| Bathroom | 🟣 Purple |
| Garage / Tools | ⚫ Black |
| Dog | 🟡 Yellow |

**2. Write this format on the top and 2 sides of every box**

```
KIT-14  |  P1  |  Coffee maker, mugs, filters  |  FRAGILE ↑
```
- **Room code + number** (KIT, LIV, BED, OFF, BATH, GAR, DOG)
- **Priority:** **P1** = open first day · **P2** = first week · **P3** = whenever
- **Short contents** plus **FRAGILE** and **↑ THIS SIDE UP** where needed

**3. Keep a shared box inventory** in a Google Sheet or Notes app with columns for **Box # · Room · Contents · Priority · Fragile?** Snap a photo of each open box before sealing.
→ At delivery, **check off box numbers** to confirm nothing's missing. This matters if you need to file a claim.

**4. At the new house:** tape a matching color square on each room's door so movers (or you) know where boxes go.

---

## 🧰 SUPPLIES (Buy by Jun 20)

| Item | Qty (1–2 BR) |
|---|---|
| Small boxes (books, heavy items) | 20–25 |
| Medium boxes (most stuff) | 25–30 |
| Large boxes (light, bulky items only) | 10–15 |
| Wardrobe boxes | 3–5 |
| Dish-pack boxes (double-wall) with cell dividers | 2–4 |
| TV box kit (if no original box) | 1 per TV |
| Mirror/picture boxes + corner protectors | As needed |
| Packing tape | 6–10 rolls |
| Packing paper (plain newsprint) | 20–25 lbs |
| Bubble wrap | 1–2 large rolls |
| Stretch wrap (furniture/drawers) | 1–2 rolls |
| Mattress bags | 1 per mattress |
| Markers, colored tape, zip bags (hardware) | 1 pack each |

---

## 🥚 FRAGILE PACKING RULES

**General**
- [ ] **Max ~50 lbs per box.** Heavy items go in **small** boxes, light items in large ones.
- [ ] Crumpled paper on the **bottom and top**. **No empty space.** If the box rattles, add more fill.
- [ ] Use **plain packing paper, not newspaper** (ink transfers onto dishes).
- [ ] Tape the bottom with an **"H" pattern**.

**Dishes and Glassware**
- [ ] **Plates:** wrap individually, stand them **on edge like records**, never flat.
- [ ] **Glasses and stemware:** wrap, stuff the inside with paper, use cell dividers, and put them **rim-down**.
- [ ] **Bowls:** nest 2–3 with paper between them, wrapped together.
- [ ] Heaviest items on the bottom, lightest on top.

**Electronics**
- [ ] **Photograph the cable setup** before unplugging. Bag and label cords together.
- [ ] Use original boxes if you have them. Otherwise, wrap in an anti-static or bubble layer.
- [ ] **TVs travel upright**, never flat.
- [ ] **Laptops, hard drives, and cameras go in the car, not the truck.**

**Art, Mirrors, Glass**
- [ ] Tape a large **"X" across glass** to hold shards if it cracks.
- [ ] Add corner protectors and bubble wrap, then use a mirror/picture box.
- [ ] Mark **"FRAGILE: DO NOT LAY FLAT"** and transport upright.

**Lamps and Odd Shapes**
- [ ] Remove bulbs and shades. Pack shades separately, nested if possible, with no heavy items on top.
- [ ] Wrap the base in bubble wrap.

**Furniture**
- [ ] Remove legs and hardware. Put screws in a **labeled zip bag taped to the furniture**.
- [ ] Stretch-wrap drawers shut (don't tape directly on wood finishes).
- [ ] Photograph furniture condition for insurance.

---

## 🏠 ROOM-BY-ROOM CHECKLISTS

### 1. 🏬 STORAGE UNIT (Jun 13–14 · 4–8 hrs · J)
*Goal: empty it early and stop paying rent on it.*
- [ ] Check your contract's move-out notice (often 10–30 days). **Give notice now.**
- [ ] Sort on-site: KEEP / SELL / DONATE / TRASH. Bring bins and trash bags.
- [ ] Book a truck or van, or ask a friend with a pickup.
- [ ] Consolidate keepers into the garage or a spare room.
- [ ] Check for items affected by heat or moisture (electronics, documents, mildew).
- [ ] Sweep out, remove your lock, and **get written move-out confirmation**.
- [ ] Cancel autopay and confirm the deposit refund.

### 2. 🔧 GARAGE / SHED / ATTIC (Jun 20–28 · 6–12 hrs · J)
*Usually the most time-consuming area to sort, so don't leave it late.*

**⚠️ Movers will NOT transport these.** Plan to use up, give away, or properly dispose of them:
- [ ] Gasoline, propane tanks, lighter fluid, kerosene
- [ ] Paint, stains, solvents, aerosols
- [ ] Pool or cleaning chemicals, fertilizer, pesticides
- [ ] Ammunition, fireworks
- [ ] Car batteries; loose lithium batteries (tape the terminals and keep them with you)
- [ ] **Firewood: don't move it.** It can spread invasive pests like the emerald ash borer.

**Checklist**
- [ ] **Drain gas and oil** from mowers, trimmers, and other gas tools (required by most movers).
- [ ] Donate duplicate tools and cleaning supplies, or leave them for the next occupant if allowed.
- [ ] Sell bulky items you won't need (snowblower? Depends where in Oregon you're going).
- [ ] Clean and dry outdoor gear, bikes, and coolers.
- [ ] Bundle long-handled tools with tape or stretch wrap.
- [ ] Pack small tools in small, heavy-duty boxes. Bag hardware by type.
- [ ] Set aside a **"Moving Toolkit"** for the car: drill, screwdrivers, Allen keys, tape measure, utility knife, hammer.
- [ ] Attic: check for forgotten boxes, holiday decor, and anything stored in eaves.
- [ ] **Plants:** Oregon has agricultural quarantine rules, and Ohio is in the Japanese beetle range. **Check Oregon Department of Agriculture guidance** before moving potted plants or soil. Gifting them is often easiest.

### 3. 🛏️ SPARE ROOM + STORAGE CLOSETS (Jun 25–28 · 3–5 hrs · P)
- [ ] Pack guest bedding, keeping one set out for the trip if needed.
- [ ] Hobby and craft supplies, luggage you won't use, and keepsakes.
- [ ] Holiday decorations (P3).
- [ ] Hall closet: extra linens, coats you won't need in July.
- [ ] **Donate:** duplicate linens, unused gifts, old electronics.

### 4. 📚 BOOKS, DECOR, ART, OFF-SEASON (Jun 27–Jul 2 · 3–6 hrs · M)
- [ ] Books in **small boxes only** (they get heavy fast). Pack them flat or spine-down.
- [ ] Take down art and mirrors. Pack using the fragile rules above.
- [ ] Bag wall hardware. Patch holes now if your lease requires it.
- [ ] Off-season clothes: winter coats, boots, sweaters. Vacuum bags save space.
- [ ] **Declutter:** books you won't reread (library donation), decor that won't fit the new space.

### 5. 🛋️ LIVING ROOM (Jul 3–8 · 4–6 hrs · J)

- [ ] Throw pillows and blankets: use them as padding in other boxes.
- [ ] Remove furniture legs and bag the hardware.
- [ ] Games, media, and remotes (batteries out).
- [ ] Rugs: vacuum, roll, and wrap.
- [ ] **Keep out:** the dog's bed and a couple of seating options until the last 2 days.
- [ ] **Sell:** furniture that won't fit, extra side tables, worn-out pieces.

### 6. 🍽️ DINING ROOM (Jul 3–8 · 2–3 hrs · P)
- [ ] China, serving pieces, and special-occasion glassware go in dish packs.
- [ ] Table leaves wrapped in blankets. Remove the table legs.
- [ ] Linens and placemats.
- [ ] **Declutter:** rarely used serving pieces and duplicate platters.

### 7. 💻 HOME OFFICE (Jul 6–10 · 3–5 hrs · whoever owns the gear)
- [ ] Shred old documents, scan important ones, and back up computers to the cloud **and** an external drive.
- [ ] Pack supplies and reference materials (P3).
- [ ] **Important documents go in the car folder, not a box.**
- [ ] Pack work equipment **last**. Laptops, monitors if possible, and chargers ride with you.
- [ ] Return any employer-owned equipment you won't need, or confirm shipping instructions.
- [ ] **Declutter:** old cables, dead electronics (e-waste), expired paperwork.

### 8. 🍳 KITCHEN (Jul 8–13 · 8–12 hrs · J)
*The most time-intensive room. Split it across several days.*

**Days 1–2 (Jul 8–9): Rarely used items**
- [ ] Specialty appliances (stand mixer, slow cooker, waffle maker).
- [ ] Bakeware, extra pots and pans, serving dishes.
- [ ] Extra glassware and mugs, keeping 2 each out.

**Days 3–4 (Jul 10–11): Most of the rest**

**Day 5 (Jul 12–13): Survival kit only**

- [ ] Survival kit gets packed into the **Open First box** on Jul 15.

**Declutter:** expired spices, duplicate gadgets, mismatched containers, chipped dishes.

## 📅 Using .ics Instead of CSV

**Why .ics:** It's the universal calendar format, and it can carry **built-in alerts**, which CSV can't.

**How to import:**
- **iPhone/Mac (Apple Calendar):** On a Mac, double-click the `.ics` file, or use **File → Import** and choose a "Move" calendar. On iPhone, open the file from Mail, Messages, or Files and tap **Add All**. **Alerts are kept.**
- **Google Calendar:** Use the same steps as CSV (**Settings → Import & export → Import**). **Google ignores the alerts in the file on import**, so set default notifications on the Move calendar instead.
- **Sharing:** Import once into a shared calendar (Google or iCloud) so you don't both have to import.

**Format:** Each event looks like this. Save the file as `move.ics` (UTF-8):

```
BEGIN:VCALENDAR
VERSION:2.0
PRODID:-//Move Plan//EN
BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:mover-confirm-20260709@moveplan
DTSTAMP:20260507T060000Z
DTSTART;TZID=America/New_York:20260709T090000
DTEND;TZID=America/New_York:20260709T093000
SUMMARY:⭐ Mover confirmation
DESCRIPTION:Arrival window, crew size, payment, final estimate, parking/elevator access (J)
BEGIN:VALARM
TRIGGER:-PT30M
ACTION:DISPLAY
DESCRIPTION:Reminder
END:VALARM
END:VEVENT
END:VCALENDAR
```

To add more events, repeat everything from `BEGIN:VEVENT` to `END:VEVENT` with a **unique UID** for each. The `TRIGGER:-PT30M` line sets a 30-minute-before alert. Change it to `-PT1H` (1 hour) or `-P1D` (1 day) as you like.

I can generate the **complete `.ics` file with all 38 events and alerts** if you'd prefer that over CSV.

### Declutter rules (J)
1. **Weight costs money.** Movers charge by weight, roughly $0.70–$1.20/lb cross-country. A 100-lb bookshelf can cost $70–120 to move. If an item is cheap to replace, sell it.
2. **Oregon has no sales tax.** Buying replacements there is cheaper than in Ohio.
3. **The 12-month rule.** If you haven't used it in a year and it isn't sentimental, let it go.

# Part 2: Room-by-Room Packing Checklist + Declutter Tips

## Packing Timeline (target load date: Thu, July 16, 2026)

| Weeks out | Focus |
|---|---|
| **10–7** (now → mid-June) | Declutter, sell big furniture, eat down the freezer and pantry |
| **6–4** | Pack off-season items, books, decor, guest room, storage, archives |
| **3–2** | Pack most closets, office, garage, and the bulk of the kitchen |
| **Week 1** | Everything except daily essentials. Kitchen goes down to a survival kit |
| **Last 48 hrs** | Defrost fridge, pack essentials bags, load the car, label "OPEN FIRST" boxes |

**Labeling system:** room name + box number + 2–3 word contents (e.g., `KITCHEN 07 – pots, pans`). Use one tape color per room. Mark 1–2 boxes per room **OPEN FIRST**. Keep a simple box-count list on your phone.

## Room-by-Room

**Kitchen** *(most time-consuming: 6–10 hrs)*
- [ ] Declutter duplicate gadgets, mismatched containers, and expired food
- [ ] Wrap dishes vertically (like records). Pad glasses with towels or dish packs
- [ ] Pack small appliances in original boxes if you have them
- [ ] Use pantry items up from week 4. Donate unopened food (movers won't take perishables)
- [ ] **Essentials kit:** 2 plates, 2 cups, utensils, 1 pan, knife, coffee setup, dish soap, sponge
- [ ] Defrost the fridge and freezer 24–48 hrs out. Prop the doors open

**Living Room** *(3–5 hrs)*
- [ ] Photograph TV and electronics cable setups before unplugging
- [ ] Bag and label cords and remotes per device
- [ ] Remove and bag furniture hardware. Tape the bag to the furniture
- [ ] Wrap framed art in blankets. Use mirror boxes for anything large

**Bedrooms** *(2–4 hrs each)*
- [ ] Use wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes
- [ ] Leave lightweight clothes in dresser drawers if the mover allows
- [ ] Pack jewelry and valuables yourself; they travel in the car
- [ ] Last items: bedding (goes in the first-night box)

**Bathrooms** *(1 hr each)*
- [ ] Toss near-empty bottles. Tape caps or bag liquids
- [ ] Medications travel with you, not on the truck
- [ ] Keep a travel toiletry kit out

**Home Office** *(2–4 hrs)*
- [ ] Back up computers to the cloud and an external drive
- [ ] Shred old paperwork. Digitize what you can
- [ ] Important files go in the documents folder, not the truck

**Closets / Storage** *(2–6 hrs)*
- [ ] Decide on every "maybe" box: is it worth paying to move?
- [ ] Pack off-season clothes and holiday decor early

**Garage / Outdoor** *(3–8 hrs)*
- [ ] **Movers can't take:** propane, gasoline, paint, aerosols, cleaning chemicals, ammunition, batteries in bulk. Use them up, give them away, or take them to hazardous waste disposal
- [ ] Drain fuel from the mower and other gas tools
- [ ] Clean outdoor furniture and tools. Mud and pests are an issue across state lines
- [ ] **Plants:** Oregon restricts plants from Japanese beetle–infested states, including Ohio. Check the Oregon Department of Agriculture rules before moving potted plants. Many people give plants away instead

**Dog Gear** *(30 min)*
- [ ] Pack toys, extra beds, and grooming supplies (except the travel bag items)
- [ ] Keep the crate, leash, food, and bowls out until departure

## Declutter Tips

- **Weight costs money.** Interstate movers price by weight and distance. If something is heavy and cheap to replace (particleboard furniture, old books, small appliances), sell it or donate it.
- **Measure the new place first.** Get room dimensions from the Oregon listing before deciding on furniture.
- **Sell big items early.** Facebook Marketplace and similar sites take time. Start in weeks 10–8.
- **One-year rule.** If you haven't used it in a year and it isn't sentimental, let it go.
- **Book donation pickups early.** Charities book up near month-end, especially in summer.
- **Use the 3-bin method in every room:** Keep / Sell-Donate / Trash. Decide fast.
- **Don't pack junk to sort later.** It costs money to move and time to unpack.

# Part 5: Vehicle Shipping vs. Driving

## Ballpark Costs (Ohio → Oregon, ~2,400–2,500 miles, summer)

| Option | Cost per car | Time | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Drive it yourselves** | **~$1,000–$1,700 total trip** (fuel $300–450 / dog-friendly lodging 3–4 nights $450–900 incl. pet fees / food $200–400) | 4–5 days | You want the dog with you in a familiar space (usually the easiest option for a dog) |
| **Open carrier** | ~$1,000–$1,600 | 7–10 days transit + 1–5 day pickup window | You're flying, or you have 2 cars and only 1 driver per car is impractical |
| **Enclosed carrier** | ~$1,500–$2,500 | Same as open, sometimes longer | Classic, luxury, or low-clearance cars |
| **Tow behind a DIY truck** | Auto transport trailer ~$300–700 / tow dolly ~$200–500 (added to truck rental) | Same as truck | One of you drives the truck. Lower fuel economy and harder to drive in mountains |

**Hidden costs to include:**
- **Driving:** wear and tear (~2,500 miles), PTO days, possibly an oil change on arrival, and Oregon gas, which often runs $0.50–$1+/gal above Ohio.
- **Shipping:** a rental car or rideshares if your car arrives after you do, plus airfare and in-cabin or cargo pet fees if you fly with the dog. Flying a dog adds cost and stress, which is another point in favor of driving.

**Quick verdict:** For two people, one dog, and one car, **driving is usually cheaper and easier on the dog.** With two cars, it's often worth comparing "drive both" against "drive one and ship one," especially if one of you is driving a rental truck.

## Booking and Timing Notes

**If shipping:**
- **Book 3–4 weeks ahead** in summer. Your calendar reminder is Jun 18. Booking any later raises prices and widens pickup windows.
- Most quotes come from **brokers**, who hand the job off to a carrier. Check the broker's MC number on FMCSA SAFER. Ask who the actual carrier is and whether the quote is guaranteed or an estimate. Low-ball quotes often go unclaimed or get raised later.
- **Don't pay in full upfront.** A small deposit is normal, with the balance paid at delivery (often in cash or certified funds).
- **Pickup windows are typically 1–5 days, not an exact date.** Have the car ready by around Jul 13 so it doesn't collide with load day, or plan to arrange a stand-in contact.
- **At pickup:** wash the car, photograph all sides with timestamps, keep about 1/4 tank of gas, remove E-ZPass and personal items, and note existing damage on the inspection report. At delivery, inspect before signing.

**If driving:**
- **Book lodging 2–4 weeks ahead** (Jun 18 reminder). Confirm pet fees, weight limits, and number of dogs. Chains like La Quinta, Red Roof, and Motel 6 are often dog-friendly, but policies vary by location.
- **Route:** I-80 → I-84 is the common path. Plan for about 600 miles a day over 4 days with dog breaks every 2–3 hours.
- **Summer risks:** heat in Nebraska, Wyoming, and Idaho (never leave the dog in the car), and **wildfire smoke and road closures** in Oregon and Idaho during July and August. Check ODOT TripCheck and AirNow the night before each leg.
- **Mountain passes:** check brakes and coolant during your Jul 10 service. Grades in Wyoming and the Blue Mountains in eastern Oregon are steep.

A row is superseded if another row with the same email has a newer timestamp, or the same timestamp and sits lower on the sheet.

# Left-Hand Voicings (Middle-C Area)

**Notation:** Middle C = **C4**. C3 is the C one octave below. Fingerings are listed bottom to top (5 = pinky, 1 = thumb).

**General fingering rule for 3-note LH triads:**
- Root position: **5-3-1**
- First inversion: **5-3-1** (5-2-1 also works if it feels better)
- Second inversion: **5-2-1**

## 1. A Natural Minor
| Chord | Position | Notes | Fingering |
|---|---|---|---|
| Am (i) | Root | A2 – C3 – E3 | 5-3-1 |
| Am/C | 1st inv | C3 – E3 – A3 | 5-3-1 |
| C (III) | Root | C3 – E3 – G3 | 5-3-1 |
| C/E | 1st inv | E3 – G3 – C4 | 5-3-1 |

## 2. A Harmonic Minor
| Chord | Position | Notes | Fingering |
|---|---|---|---|
| Am (i) | Root | A2 – C3 – E3 | 5-3-1 |
| Am/C | 1st inv | C3 – E3 – A3 | 5-3-1 |
| E (V) | Root | E3 – **G#3** – B3 | 5-3-1 |
| E/G# | 1st inv | **G#2** – B2 – E3 | 5-3-1 |

**Tip:** E/G# → Am root position is very smooth. G# moves up to A, B moves up to C, and E stays put.

## 3. A Melodic Minor
| Chord | Position | Notes | Fingering |
|---|---|---|---|
| Am (i) | Root | A2 – C3 – E3 | 5-3-1 |
| D (IV, raised 6th) | Root | D3 – **F#3** – A3 | 5-3-1 |
| D/F# | 1st inv | **F#3** – A3 – D4 | 5-3-1 |
| E (V) | Root | E3 – **G#3** – B3 | 5-3-1 |
| E/G# | 1st inv | **G#2** – B2 – E3 | 5-3-1 |

**Descending:** use Am, or C (natural-minor chords). Avoid F# and G# on the way down.

## 4. C Natural Minor
| Chord | Position | Notes | Fingering |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cm (i) | Root | C3 – Eb3 – G3 | 5-3-1 |
| Cm/Eb | 1st inv | Eb3 – G3 – C4 | 5-3-1 |
| Ab (VI) | Root | Ab2 – C3 – Eb3 | 5-3-1 |
| Ab/C | 1st inv | C3 – Eb3 – Ab3 | 5-3-1 |

## 5a. C Harmonic Minor
| Chord | Position | Notes | Fingering |
|---|---|---|---|

# 4-Bar Cadences: i – iv – V7 – i

These are in 4/4 time. The right hand plays eighth notes, and the left hand holds one chord per bar (whole notes). The LH voicings are chosen so each finger moves a step or less between chords.

**V7 tip:** A full four-note V7 is a stretch for many hands, so this version uses three notes (root, 3rd, 7th, with the 5th omitted). It still sounds like a complete V7.

## A Minor: Am – Dm – E7 – Am

| Bar | Chord | LH (fingering) | RH (8 eighth notes) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Am | A2 – C3 – E3 (5-3-1) | C4 E4 G4 A4 G4 E4 C4 E4 |
| 2 | Dm/A | A2 – D3 – F3 (5-2-1) | D4 F4 A4 G4 F4 E4 D4 F4 |
| 3 | E7 | **G#2** – D3 – E3 (5-2-1) | E4 **G#4** B4 **G#4** E4 D4 E4 **G#4** |
| 4 | Am | A2 – C3 – E3 (5-3-1) | A4 E4 C4 E4 A4 (half note) |

**Listen for:** G# → A in both hands at the bar 3 → bar 4 change (RH G#4 → A4, LH G#2 → A2). That is the harmonic-minor leading tone resolving.

## C Minor: Cm – Fm – G7 – Cm

| Bar | Chord | LH (fingering) | RH (8 eighth notes) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cm | C3 – Eb3 – G3 (5-3-1) | C4 Eb4 G4 Ab4 G4 Eb4 C4 Eb4 |
| 2 | Fm/C | C3 – F3 – Ab3 (5-2-1) | F4 Ab4 C5 Bb4 Ab4 G4 F4 Ab4 |
| 3 | G7 | **B2** – F3 – G3 (5-2-1) | G4 **B4** D5 **B4** G4 F4 G4 **B4** |
| 4 | Cm | C3 – Eb3 – G3 (5-3-1) | C5 G4 Eb4 G4 C5 (half note) |

**Listen for:** B → C at the bar 3 → bar 4 change (RH B4 → C5, LH B2 → C3).

**Notes:**
- Bar 1 of each cadence is your original motif.
- In both bar 2s, the iv chord is in second inversion (fingered 5-2-1). This keeps the left hand nearly still.
- The Bb in bar 2 of the C minor version is fine because the melody is descending. Only the V7 bar needs the raised 7th (B natural).

## Practice Steps
1. Play the LH chords alone, holding each for four slow beats. Feel how little your hand moves.
2. Play the RH alone, slowly and evenly.
3. Put the hands together at a slow tempo (around ♩ = 60).
4. Once that feels comfortable, try playing the LH as two half notes per bar (repeating the chord on beat 3) for a bit more motion.

user: Nice — can you give a very compact one-paragraph summary of natural vs harmonic vs melodic minor (what gets raised where and why it sounds different), plus two quick ear-training exercises I can do at the piano to tell them apart (what to play, what to listen for, and how to check answers)? reply:
# Natural vs. Harmonic vs. Melodic Minor

**Natural minor** uses only the key signature (A: A B C D E F G). The 7th is a whole step below the tonic, so cadences sound soft or modal. **Harmonic minor** raises the 7th (G#), creating a half-step leading tone that pulls strongly to the tonic and makes the V chord major (E). It also creates an augmented 2nd between 6 and 7 (F–G#), which gives the scale its "exotic" sound. **Melodic minor** raises both 6 and 7 going up (F#, G#), keeping the leading tone but smoothing out the augmented 2nd, so the top half sounds like major. Coming down, it reverts to natural minor because the leading tone isn't needed when you're moving away from the tonic.

---

# Ear-Training Exercises

## 1. Top-Four-Notes Test (scale degrees 5–8)
- **Play** one of these at random, slowly, after first playing an Am chord:
  - E F G A (natural)
  - E F G# A (harmonic)
  - E F# G# A (melodic)
- **Listen for:**
  - **Natural:** the last step G–A is a whole step, so the ending feels relaxed.
  - **Harmonic:** a "gap" between F and G#, then a tight half step into A.
  - **Melodic:** an even, bright climb that sounds like the end of A major.
- **Check:** Write N, H, and M on three cards, shuffle them, and draw one face-down. Play it without looking, guess, then flip the card. Aim for 10 in a row correct, then switch to C minor (G Ab Bb C, G Ab B C, G A B C).

## 2. Stop-Before-Home Test (the cadence pull)
- **Play** bars 6–7 from any version of your practice sheet, then **stop** without playing bar 8.
- **Listen for:**
  - **Strong urge to resolve** (B or G# over E7 or G7) means harmonic or melodic, because there is a leading tone.
  - **Mild urge** (Em7 or Gm7, no leading tone) means natural.
- **Check:** Sing the note you expect next. It should be the tonic (A or C). Then play bar 8 to confirm. For a harder version, have someone else pick and play the version while you listen with your eyes closed.

# Revised Genetics Unit: Meiosis Added, Assessments Realigned

## Revised Goal 4 (only goal changed)

Goals 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 stay as written. Goal 4 is expanded to cover all three sources of variation named in HS-LS3-2.

**4. Sources of heritable variation and their effects on phenotype (HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1)**
Students will make and defend a claim, based on evidence, that heritable genetic variation results from (a) new allele combinations produced during meiosis through independent assortment and crossing over, (b) viable errors during DNA replication, and (c) mutations caused by environmental factors. Students will also explain how a specific mutation (substitution, insertion, deletion, or frameshift) changes a protein and, in turn, the organism's phenotype.

*"I can" checks:*
- **Meiosis:** Given a cell with two pairs of homologous chromosomes carrying alleles *A/a* and *B/b*, I can draw all four possible gamete combinations produced by independent assortment. I can show how crossing over between two genes on the same chromosome produces a recombinant gamete. I can also explain in 2–3 sentences why both processes increase variation among offspring.
- **Mutation:** I can compare a normal and a mutated sequence, predict the effect on the protein, and classify the mutation as likely harmful, neutral, or beneficial, with reasoning.
- **Sources:** I can sort examples of variation (such as a UV-induced skin cell mutation, a replication error in a sperm cell, or a sibling's unique allele combination) by source and state whether each can be passed to offspring.

*Boundary note:* The HS-LS3-2 assessment boundary excludes naming the phases of meiosis. Assess the outcomes (gamete combinations, recombination, variation), not stage identification. You can still teach the phases for context.

---

## Revised Performance Assessments

### Assessment 1 (Week 1): Protein Pathway Model (HS-LS1-1; SEP: Developing and Using Models)
This version requires no prior instruction on mutations.

**Task:** Students receive a short template DNA sequence (about 15–18 bases) from a real gene segment, such as HBB. They build a physical or digital model and use it to:
1. Show replication by writing the complementary strand and explaining why each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one new strand.
2. Transcribe the template into mRNA.
3. Translate the mRNA into an amino acid sequence using a codon table.
4. Explain how the order of bases ultimately determines the protein's shape and function.

**Extension item (no mutation knowledge required):** Students receive two different DNA sequences that code for the same amino acid sequence and explain how both can produce the same protein. This introduces codon redundancy and sets up silent mutations in Week 3.

**Deliverables:**
- An annotated model showing the strands, mRNA, codons, and amino acids
- A claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) paragraph answering: *How does the structure of DNA determine the structure of a protein?*
- A model-limitations statement: one thing the model shows well and one thing it leaves out or oversimplifies

**Scoring focus:** Accurate base pairing and codon reading, a logical sequence-to-protein explanation, and a meaningful limitations statement.

**Carry-forward:** Students keep this model. They revise it in Week 3, which supports Goal 5.

---

### Assessment 2 (Week 2): Family Inheritance Investigation (HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-2, HS-LS3-3)
This assessment is unchanged except for one new meiosis component in Part 1.

**Tasks:**
1. **Meiosis link (new):** For a parent who is heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes, draw the possible gametes and explain how independent assortment produces them. Then use these gametes to set up a dihybrid cross.
2. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern from a three-generation pedigree and justify it with evidence.
3. Assign genotypes to specified individuals and explain any uncertainty.
4. Use a Punnett square to calculate the probability that a future child will express the trait.
5. Run a chi-square test on class simulation data and state whether the data support the predicted ratio.

**Deliverables:** A gamete diagram, a pedigree analysis, a probability calculation, a chi-square table, and a plain-language letter to the family.

### Assessment 3 (Week 3): Variation and Gene Editing (HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1, ETS1.B)
This assessment now has two parts. The mutation work moved here from Assessment 1.

**Part A: Mutation Model Revision (1 class period)**
- Students return to their Week 1 Protein Pathway Model and apply three assigned mutations: one silent, one missense, and one frameshift.
- They trace each mutation through to the protein and predict the effect on phenotype.
- They write a CER on the claim: *Which mutation is most likely to affect phenotype, and why?*
- They state whether each mutation would be heritable if it occurred (a) in a skin cell or (b) in a cell that produces gametes.
- **Variation sort:** Students classify 4–5 scenarios by source of variation (meiosis, replication error, or environmental mutation) and by heritability.

**Part B: Gene Editing Policy Brief (2–3 class periods)**
This part is the same as the original brief. Students must now connect at least one argument to a source of heritable variation. For example, they might explain how off-target CRISPR edits act as new mutations, or how editing embryos differs from editing body cells.

**Scoring focus:** Accurate mutation tracing and heritability reasoning in Part A. Evidence quality, stakeholder trade-offs, and science-to-policy reasoning in Part B.

| **2** | 1 | **Meiosis: independent assortment and crossing over** (lesson below) | 4, 2 | Exit ticket |

**Why meiosis goes on Week 2, Day 1:** Independent assortment is the physical explanation for Mendel's laws. Teaching it before Punnett squares means dihybrid ratios (9:3:3:1) come from something students have already modeled, rather than from a rule to memorize.

---

## Week 2, Day 1 Lesson: Meiosis and Heritable Variation

**Lesson objective (HS-LS3-2):**
Students will model how independent assortment and crossing over during meiosis produce gametes with new allele combinations. By the end of class, they will correctly draw all four gamete types from an *AaBb* cell and explain in writing why siblings with the same parents are genetically different.

**Materials:**
- Per pair: 4 paper or pipe-cleaner chromosomes (2 homologous pairs, one color per parent), each labeled with alleles: Chromosome 1 = *A* / *a*, Chromosome 2 = *B* / *b*
- Per pair: one extra chromosome pair with two genes on it (*C–D* and *c–d*), plus scissors and tape
- A coin per pair
- A class tally chart on the board

### Warm-Up (8 minutes)
1. **Prompt (3 min):** "You and a full sibling have the exact same two parents. Give two reasons you are not genetically identical." Students write individually.
2. **Quick math (3 min):** Humans have 23 chromosome pairs, and each pair can line up in 2 orientations. How many different chromosome combinations can one person's gametes have? Guide students to 2²³, which is about 8.4 million, *before* crossing over.
3. **Share (2 min):** Collect 2–3 answers and note "random sorting" ideas on the board to revisit later.

### Core Activity (28 minutes)

**Part 1: Independent assortment (13 min)**
1. Partners line up both homologous pairs at the cell's "equator." They flip a coin for each pair to decide which version, maternal or paternal, faces up.
2. They "divide" the cell and record the alleles that end up in the gamete, such as *AB* or *Ab*.
3. They repeat 8 times and tally their results.
4. Pairs add their tallies to the class chart. Students should see four gamete types (*AB*, *Ab*, *aB*, *ab*) in roughly equal numbers.
5. **Discussion question:** "Why do we get four types and not just two?" The key idea: the orientation of one pair does not affect the orientation of the other pair.

**Part 2: Crossing over (10 min)**
1. Partners take the *C–D* / *c–d* chromosome pair. Without crossing over, they record the gametes: only *CD* and *cd*.
2. They cut both chromosomes between the two genes, swap the segments, and tape them back together. Now they record the new gametes: *Cd* and *cD*.
3. **Discussion question:** "Independent assortment can't separate *C* and *D*. Why not, and how does crossing over solve that?" The key idea: genes on the same chromosome travel together unless crossing over separates them.

**Part 3: Exit ticket (5 min)**
1. Draw all possible gametes from a cell that is *AaBb* (genes on different chromosomes).
2. Explain how crossing over creates new combinations that independent assortment cannot.
3. Revisit your warm-up answer: give one reason siblings differ that you can now explain with evidence from today's model.

**Success criteria for the exit ticket:** All four gametes are correct, crossing over is described as an exchange between homologous chromosomes, and the warm-up revision references either assortment or recombination.

**Teacher note:** Keep the tally chart on the board. On Day 3, show that combining the four gamete types from two *AaBb* parents produces the 9:3:3:1 ratio.

# 2) Lesson Plan: Point Mutations and Frameshifts (45 min)

**Learning objective:** I can identify substitution and frameshift mutations in an mRNA sequence and predict how each changes the protein.

**Materials:** Codon chart, mini whiteboards, practice sheet (sequences below)

### Warm-up (5 min): Sentence analogy
Display: **THE CAT ATE THE RAT**
Ask students to make these changes and read each result:
- Change one letter: THE **B**AT ATE THE RAT (the meaning changes slightly)
- Delete the first "C": THE ATA TET HER AT (the sentence becomes nonsense)

Ask: *Which change did more damage, and why?*

### Mini-lesson (10 min)
- **Point mutation (substitution):** One base is swapped. There are three possible outcomes:
  - **Silent:** The new codon codes for the same amino acid.
  - **Missense:** The new codon codes for a different amino acid.
  - **Nonsense:** The new codon is an early stop codon.
- **Frameshift (insertion or deletion):** Adding or removing bases (not in multiples of 3) shifts the reading frame. Every codon after the change is altered.
- **Real example:** In sickle cell disease, the HBB gene has a single substitution (mRNA GAG → GUG). This changes glutamic acid to valine, which changes the shape of hemoglobin.
- **Heritability:** A mutation in a sex cell (germline) can be passed to offspring. A mutation in a body cell (somatic) cannot.

### Guided practice (15 min, pairs)
**Original mRNA:** AUG GCU UGG AAA UAG, which codes for Met–Ala–Trp–Lys–Stop

Students translate each mutated sequence and classify it:

| Mutated mRNA | Protein | Type |
|---|---|---|
| AUG GC**C** UGG AAA UAG | Met–Ala–Trp–Lys–Stop | Silent |
| AUG GCU UGG **G**AA UAG | Met–Ala–Trp–**Glu**–Stop | Missense |
| AUG GCU UG**A** | Met–Ala–Stop | Nonsense |
| AUG CUU GGA AAU AG… (first G deleted) | Met–Leu–Gly–Asn… | Frameshift (deletion) |
| AUG **A**GC UUG GAA AUA G… (A inserted) | Met–Ser–Leu–Glu–Ile… | Frameshift (insertion) |

### Formative check (8 min, whiteboards)
Read each scenario aloud. Students hold up their answer: **S / M / N / F**
1. One base changes, and the amino acid stays the same. (S)
2. Two bases are deleted. (F)
3. A codon becomes UAA. (N)
4. A base swap changes Gly to Ala. (M)

Reteach any item that fewer than 80% of students get right.

### Exit ticket (7 min)
Original mRNA: **AUG UUU GGC UAA** (Met–Phe–Gly–Stop)
1. UUU changes to UUC. What type of mutation is this, and what is the effect? *(Silent. UUC still codes for Phe.)*
2. The first U of UUU is deleted. Write the new codons and amino acids. *(AUG UUG GCU AA… which codes for Met–Leu–Ala…)*
3. In one sentence, explain why frameshifts are usually more harmful than substitutions. *(A frameshift changes every codon after the mutation, while a substitution affects at most one codon.)*

These cells block blood vessels, causing pain and anemia. This mutation can be inherited because it is in the germline; a mutation in a somatic cell, like a skin cell, would not be passed on.

**Level 2:**

## Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation (Pedigree + Probability + χ²)

**Level 4:**
> The trait is autosomal recessive because two unaffected parents (II-3 and II-4) have an affected child (III-2), so both parents must be carriers (Aa). It is not X-linked recessive because affected daughter III-2 has an unaffected father. A cross of Aa × Aa gives a 1/4 (25%) chance that their next child is affected. Our χ² was 1.2, which is less than the critical value of 3.84 (df = 1), so the difference from 3:1 is likely due to chance and the data support the model.

**Level 2:**
> The trait is recessive because it skips a generation. The parents are probably Aa, so the child has a 50% chance of having it. Our χ² was 1.2, so the data do not support the model.

### Feedback Phrases
1. "Check your mRNA: RNA uses U, not T."
2. "A single base swap is a substitution. Frameshifts come from insertions or deletions not in multiples of 3."

4. "Connect the dots: how does this amino acid change affect the protein's shape and function?"
5. "Would this mutation be passed on if it happened in a skin cell? Explain germline vs. somatic."
6. "Strong, specific reasoning from sequence to phenotype. Well done."

# Revised Genetics Unit (~3 Weeks)

## What Changed

- **Meiosis and recombination** are now a dedicated goal and occupy two days at the start of Week 2. Meiosis comes before Mendelian crosses because segregation and independent assortment explain why Punnett squares work.
- **Assessment 1 is split.** Part A, the central dogma model, happens at the end of Week 1. Part B, the mutation analysis, happens in Week 3 after mutations are taught. Students revise their Part A model in Part B, which also builds in the modeling goal.
- **Assessment 2 moves to Day 11.** Week 2 now holds meiosis, crosses, chi-square, and pedigrees, so the assessment fits better at the start of Week 3.
- **Anchor phenomenon: sickle cell disease.** It runs through every week: the HBB sequence (Week 1), autosomal recessive inheritance (Week 2), a point mutation (Week 3), and CRISPR therapy (the policy brief).
- **Alignment corrections to my earlier draft:**
  - DNA replication fits **HS-LS3-2** (errors during replication), not HS-LS1-1. HS-LS1-1 covers how DNA structure determines protein structure.
  - HS-LS1-1's assessment boundary excludes the biochemistry of protein synthesis. Codon-table tracing is a useful teaching scaffold, but it goes beyond what the performance expectation requires.
  - Chi-square goes beyond HS-LS3-3, so treat it as an extension. It is a good fit for honors or AP-prep classes.
  - I replaced widow's peak as a pedigree example. It is not actually a simple single-gene trait, so the new pedigrees use cystic fibrosis and red-green color blindness.

---

## Revised Learning Goals

| # | Goal | Standards | "I can" check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Explain, using a model, how DNA's nucleotide sequence determines the amino acid sequence, structure, and function of a protein, and how DNA is copied before cell division. | HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-1 | I can trace a DNA sequence to mRNA to amino acids and explain why the sequence matters for protein function. |
| 2 | Use a model of meiosis to explain how segregation, independent assortment, and crossing over produce genetically unique gametes and offspring. | HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-2 | I can model meiosis and explain why siblings with the same parents are genetically different. |
| 3 | Predict genotypic and phenotypic ratios for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, and determine inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked) from pedigrees, connecting each prediction to allele behavior in meiosis. | HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3 | I can calculate cross probabilities and justify a pedigree's inheritance pattern with evidence. |
| 4 | Apply probability and statistics, including chi-square as an extension, to compare observed and expected offspring data and explain variation in trait distribution. | HS-LS3-3 | I can calculate χ² and explain whether the deviation from expected values is likely due to chance. |
| 5 | Make and defend a claim that inheritable variation results from (a) recombination in meiosis, (b) viable replication errors, and/or (c) environmentally caused mutations. Explain how a specific mutation alters a protein and phenotype, and how the environment affects trait expression. | HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1 | I can compare normal and mutated sequences, predict the effect on the protein and phenotype, and identify the source of the variation. |
| 6 | Develop, use, and revise a genotype-to-phenotype model, identifying its strengths and limitations. | SEP 2 (Models); HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-1 | I can revise my model when new evidence appears and explain what it can't show. |
| 7 | Evaluate the evidence and societal trade-offs of a genetic technology and communicate a defensible position. | ETS1.B; SEP 8 (Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information); HS-LS3-2 | I can explain the science behind a technology, weigh stakeholder perspectives, and support a position with evidence. |

---

## Revised Performance Assessments

### Assessment 1: Central Dogma and Mutation Model (two parts)

**Part A (Day 5): Normal sequence**
Students receive a short coding-strand segment from the start of the HBB gene. They build an annotated model, either physical or digital, that shows:
- the complementary strand
- the replicated DNA, labeled to show semi-conservative replication
- the mRNA
- the codons and amino acids
- a 2–3 sentence explanation of why the amino acid sequence matters for hemoglobin's shape and function

**Part B (Day 13): Mutation analysis**
Students apply the sickle cell substitution to their own model. In the coding strand, codon 6 changes from GAG to GTG, so the amino acid changes from Glu to Val. Students also analyze one assigned frameshift for comparison. They submit:
- a revised model with the changes marked
- a CER paragraph on how the mutation changes the protein and phenotype
- a heritability explanation (germline vs. somatic; replication error vs. environmental mutagen)
- one stated limitation of their model

### Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation (Day 11)

**Part 1. Pedigree A (cystic fibrosis)**
- Identify the inheritance pattern and justify it with evidence.
- Assign genotypes to specified individuals and explain any uncertainty.
- Calculate the probability that a specified future child is affected.

**Part 2. Pedigree B (red-green color blindness)**
- Identify the X-linked pattern and explain why males are affected more often.

**Part 3. Meiosis connection**
- Draw or describe how a heterozygous parent's chromosomes separate in meiosis. Explain how this produces the ratio predicted in Part 1.
- Explain why two siblings can differ even though they have the same parents.

**Part 4. Data analysis**
- Analyze class dihybrid simulation data from Day 9 using a chi-square test.

**Part 5. Family letter**
- Write a short plain-language letter to the Pedigree A family explaining the results.

### Assessment 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief (launched Day 14, due ~2 days after the unit ends)

Students choose one case study:
- CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease (Casgevy, FDA-approved Dec. 2023)
- Polygenic embryo screening
- Direct-to-consumer genetic testing

The brief is 1–2 pages and must include:
- a clear claim
- evidence from at least 2 sources, including at least 1 piece of quantitative data
- at least 1 unintended consequence tied to mutation or variation (e.g., off-target edits)
- a counterargument and rebuttal

## Exemplar Student Responses: Assessment 1 (Mutation Model)

**Context for teachers:** Students analyzed the sickle cell mutation in the *HBB* gene. At codon 6, the DNA coding strand changes from **GAG to GTG**, so the mRNA codon changes from **GAG to GUG**, and the amino acid changes from **glutamic acid to valine**.

### Exemplary (4)
> "The mutation changes the mRNA codon from GAG to GUG, so the sixth amino acid in hemoglobin becomes valine instead of glutamic acid. Valine is nonpolar, so the hemoglobin proteins stick together and bend red blood cells into a sickle shape that can block blood vessels. This mutation can be passed to offspring because it is inherited through egg or sperm cells, not just in one person's body cells."

**Why this score:** Cites the exact codon and amino acid change, explains *why* the protein's behavior changes, connects protein to phenotype, and correctly explains germ-line inheritance.

### Proficient (3)
> "The mutation changes the codon from GAG to GUG, which changes the amino acid from glutamic acid to valine. This changes the hemoglobin protein, which makes red blood cells sickle-shaped. The mutation can be passed to children because it is in the DNA."

**Why this score:** Accurate sequence evidence and a clear chain to phenotype, but does not explain *why* the protein changes, and the heritability reasoning lacks the germ-line distinction.

### Developing (2)
> "The mutation changes one letter in the DNA, so the protein is different. This makes the blood cells shaped like a sickle. It can be passed on because DNA is inherited."

**Why this score:** The general idea is correct, but there is no specific codon or amino acid evidence, and the reasoning jumps from DNA to phenotype without explaining the protein's role.

### Beginning (1)
> "The DNA changed so the person gets sickle cell. Mutations are always bad. It can't be passed on because it's a mutation."

**Why this score:** No sequence evidence, skips the protein completely, and includes two misconceptions: that all mutations are harmful, and that mutations cannot be inherited.

---

**Teacher calibration tip:** Before scoring, have teachers score these four exemplars independently on the Reasoning & Evidence and Heritability rows, then compare. This quickly surfaces differences in how teachers interpret "Proficient" versus "Exemplary."

- **Developing (3 pts):** Several errors, or one major error (for example, using T in mRNA or misreading codons) that changes the protein.

- **Proficient (3 pts):** Model is labeled and shows all steps. The mutation is shown but comparison is less clear.
- **Developing (2 pts):** Model is missing a step or key labels. The mutation is hard to locate.

- **Developing (2 pts):** Says the mutation can or cannot be passed on, with weak or partly incorrect reasoning.

# General Scoring Tips (All Three Assessments)

- **Score one criterion at a time across a stack of papers** rather than one paper at a time. This keeps your judgment consistent.
- **Between two levels?** Give the higher score only if the work meets *most* of the higher descriptor. Otherwise, give the lower score and write a note about what was missing.
- **Score what is on the page.** Do not give credit for what you think the student meant.
- **Use 0 only when there is no evidence** of the criterion at all. An attempt with errors earns at least the Beginning score.
- **Overall bands:** Exemplary 22–24 · Proficient 17–21 · Developing 12–16 · Beginning 11 or below

# ASSESSMENT 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model

## Teacher Scoring Guide

**Before you score:** Tell students (and fellow scorers) whether the given DNA is the **template strand** or the **coding strand**. Mixing these up is the most common source of "wrong" answers that are actually reasonable.

**Quick-sample tip:** Read the CER paragraph first. If it cites a specific codon and amino acid change, the model is usually accurate too. If it doesn't, check the model closely for transcription errors.

**Science Accuracy (6 pts)**
- Check that mRNA uses **U, not T**.
- Check that complementary pairs are correct (A–T, G–C in DNA; A–U in RNA).
- Check that codons are read in groups of three from the start codon (AUG), and that translation stops at a stop codon.
- Red flag: amino acids listed for every single base instead of every codon.

**Use of Models (4 pts)**
- Look for all three processes: replication, transcription, and translation.
- Look for the original and mutated versions shown **side by side** with the change circled or highlighted.
- Red flag: the mutation is mentioned in writing but cannot be found in the model.

**Reasoning & Evidence (6 pts)**
- Exemplary work names the **specific codon and amino acid change** (for example, GAG → GUG, glutamic acid → valine).
- Exemplary work explains **why** the protein changes (shape, charge, polarity, or a shortened protein).
- Red flag: reasoning jumps straight from "the DNA changed" to the phenotype, skipping the protein.

**Communication & Organization (4 pts)**
- Look for correct use of: codon, amino acid, protein, and the mutation type (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift).
- Check that the mutation type matches what actually happened. A frameshift requires an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three.

**Heritability (4 pts)**
- Exemplary work states the mutation is inherited **only if it is in germ-line cells** (egg or sperm).
- Red flags: "All mutations are bad," "Mutations can't be inherited," or "It's inherited because it's in DNA" with no germ-line distinction (Proficient at best).

---

## Student Checklist: Mutation Model

*Use this while you work. Check each box before you turn in your project.*

**My Model**
☐ I wrote the complementary DNA strand correctly (A–T, G–C).
☐ My mRNA uses **U** instead of T.
☐ I split the mRNA into codons (groups of 3) and used the codon table to find each amino acid.
☐ I showed the original and mutated sequences **side by side** and highlighted the change.
☐ Everything in my model is labeled.

**My Explanation (CER)**
☐ My claim says whether the mutation changes the phenotype.
☐ My evidence names the exact codon change and amino acid change.
☐ My reasoning explains how the protein changes and why that affects the organism.
☐ I named the type of mutation (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift).
☐ I explained whether this mutation can be passed to offspring and mentioned egg or sperm cells.

---

## Next Steps by Overall Band

**Exemplary (22–24)**
- Have students compare their mutation with a silent mutation and a frameshift in the same gene, and rank them by likely impact with reasoning.
- Extend to evolution: Why does the sickle cell allele remain common in some populations? (Introduce heterozygote advantage and malaria resistance.)
- Invite students to serve as peer reviewers using the checklist during revision time.

**Proficient (17–21)**
- Give an amino acid property chart (polar, nonpolar, charged) and have students revise their reasoning to explain *why* the protein's shape or behavior changes.
- Run a quick card sort: "germ-line cell or body cell?" with scenarios (skin cell sunburn mutation, mutation in sperm, mutation in a lung cell). Students then revise their heritability sentence.

**Developing (12–16)**
- Reteach transcription and translation with a color-coded template (one color per codon) and a shorter sequence of 9–12 bases.
- Provide a CER sentence frame: *"The mutation changes codon ___ to ___, which changes the amino acid from ___ to ___. This affects the protein by ___, which causes ___."*
- Allow a revision of the CER paragraph after the reteach.

**Beginning (11 or below)**
- Pull a small group for hands-on reteaching with paper or bead manipulatives, building DNA → mRNA → protein one codon at a time.
- Use a three-box flowchart (DNA → mRNA → Protein → Trait) that students fill in for their mutation before writing anything.
- Address misconceptions directly with examples: a harmless mutation (silent), a helpful one (lactase persistence), and an inherited one (sickle cell). Reassess with a single-codon mutation task.

# ASSESSMENT 2: Family Inheritance Investigation

## Teacher Scoring Guide

**Quick-sample tip:** Check the pedigree pattern first. If the pattern is wrong, the genotypes and Punnett square will usually be wrong too. Score each criterion separately, though. A student can set up a Punnett square correctly from incorrect genotypes and still earn credit for the setup.

**Science Accuracy (6 pts)**
- Pattern clues to look for in student reasoning:
  - **Autosomal recessive:** Unaffected parents can have an affected child. Males and females are affected about equally.
  - **Autosomal dominant:** Every affected child has at least one affected parent. The trait appears in every generation.
  - **X-linked recessive:** Mostly males are affected. No father-to-son transmission. Affected males often have carrier mothers.
- Uncertain genotypes should be shown with a blank (for example, *A_*) or listed as two possibilities.

**Reasoning & Evidence (6 pts)**
- Exemplary work points to **specific individuals** by label (for example, "II-3 and II-4 are unaffected but III-2 is affected").
- Exemplary work **rules out** at least one other pattern.
- Red flag: "It's recessive because it skips a generation" with no individuals named (Developing).

**Use of Data: Chi-Square (4 pts)**
- Formula: χ² = Σ (Observed − Expected)² ÷ Expected
- Expected values = total offspring × predicted ratio. They must be **counts, not percentages**.
- Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1. Critical values at p = 0.05: **3.84** (df = 1), **5.99** (df = 2), **7.81** (df = 3).
- Common errors: dividing by observed instead of expected, using percentages, or forgetting to square.
- Interpretation: If χ² is **less than** the critical value, the differences are likely due to chance and the data support the model. Red flag: "This proves the model is correct."

**Communication & Organization: Letter (4 pts)**
- The probability must be stated clearly and explained.
- Watch for the misconception "1 in 4 means one of their four kids will have it." Exemplary letters explain that **each child has the same chance**.
- Tone should be clear and caring, not clinical.

**Probability & Punnett Square (4 pts)**
- Parent genotypes must come from the pedigree, not be invented.
- Probability can be a fraction or a percent, and the student should say what it means.
- Correct answer with no Punnett square or work shown = Developing.

---

## Student Checklist: Inheritance Investigation

*Use this while you work. Check each box before you turn in your project.*

**Pedigree**
☐ I named the inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked).
☐ I pointed to **specific people** in the pedigree as evidence (for example, "II-3 and II-4").
☐ I explained why at least one other pattern does not fit.
☐ I wrote genotypes for the people asked and used *A_* when I wasn't sure.

**Punnett Square and Probability**
☐ I used the parents' genotypes from the pedigree.
☐ I wrote the probability as a fraction or percent and explained what it means.

**Chi-Square**
☐ I calculated expected values using **counts**, not percentages.
☐ I used the formula (O − E)² ÷ E for each category and added them up.
☐ I compared my χ² value to the critical value and explained whether the difference is due to chance.

**Letter to the Family**
☐ I explained the results in plain language with no unexplained science terms.
☐ I explained that each child has the same chance of inheriting the trait.

---

## Next Steps by Overall Band

**Exemplary (22–24)**
- Give a challenge pedigree with an X-linked trait or incomplete dominance, and have students defend their pattern to a partner.
- Introduce conditional probability: What is the chance that an unaffected sibling of an affected person is a carrier? (Answer: 2/3.)
- Have students design a set of class data that would cause the chi-square test to reject the model, then explain what that would mean.

**Proficient (17–21)**
- Practice "rule it out" with three short pedigrees. Students write one sentence per pedigree explaining why a pattern does **not** fit.
- Give sample chi-square conclusions (some correct, some using "prove") and have students fix the wording.
- Do a jargon swap: students circle every science term in their letter and replace or explain it.

**Developing (12–16)**
- Provide a pedigree clue card listing the key signs of each inheritance pattern for students to use while revising.
- Walk through a worked chi-square example, then give a partially completed table for students to finish.
- Practice Punnett squares with parent genotypes provided before asking students to pull them from a pedigree.

**Beginning (11 or below)**
- Reteach core vocabulary in a small group: dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, carrier.
- Use coin flips to build the idea of probability (one coin = one allele from each parent), then connect to a Punnett square.
- Start with a simple two-generation pedigree and build up to three generations. Reassess with a shorter version of the task.

---
---

# ASSESSMENT 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief

## Teacher Scoring Guide

**Quick-sample tip:** Read the claim and the counterargument section first. Strong briefs have a specific claim and a counterargument that is fair to the other side. Then check the science explanation for accuracy.

**Science Accuracy (6 pts)**
- **CRISPR basics:** A guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence, where it cuts the DNA. The cell's repair process then changes the sequence.
- **Accuracy check for sickle cell therapy:** The FDA-approved CRISPR treatment (Casgevy, approved in December 2023) does **not** directly fix the sickle cell mutation. It edits a gene region (BCL11A) to turn fetal hemoglobin back on, which compensates for the faulty adult hemoglobin. Students who say it "fixes the sickle cell gene" are oversimplifying. Accept this at Proficient if the rest is accurate, and treat it as a teachable moment.
- **Connect to Assessment 1:** These therapies edit a patient's own blood stem cells (body cells), so the edits are **not passed to children**. Strong briefs make this germ-line vs. body-cell distinction.
- Look for unintended consequences linked to genetics: off-target edits (new mutations in the wrong place), false positives in testing, or limited accuracy of predictions.

**Reasoning & Evidence (6 pts)**
- The claim should be specific (for example, "approve with income-based coverage") rather than vague ("gene editing is good").
- Evidence should be **explained**, not just quoted. Look for phrases like "This shows…" or "This matters because…"
- Red flag: quotes or statistics dropped in with no explanation.

**Use of Data (4 pts)**
- Look for at least one number used accurately (cost, success rate, number of patients, accuracy rate).
- Exemplary work names a **limit** of the data, such as small trial size, short follow-up time, or data from one group only.

**Communication & Organization (4 pts)**
- Check for all sections: claim, background, evidence, counterargument, recommendation.
- Writing should be concise and aimed at a policymaker, not a classmate.

**Stakeholders, Trade-offs & Counterargument (4 pts)**
- Stakeholders should be represented fairly. Red flag: a "straw man" version of the other side.
- Look for trade-offs such as access, cost, consent, accuracy, and long-term risk.
- The rebuttal should use evidence, not just opinion.

---

## Student Checklist: Policy Brief

*Use this while you work. Check each box before you turn in your project.*

**Science**
☐ I explained how the technology works in my own words.
☐ I described at least one unintended consequence and connected it to mutations or genetic variation.
☐ I stated whether the changes could be passed to future children and why.

**Claim and Evidence**
☐

# Meiosis Mini-Unit: 3-Day Lesson Sequence
*Bridges Week 1 (DNA and the central dogma) to Week 2 (Mendelian crosses and pedigrees)*

## Overview

**Placement:** Week 2, Days 1–3, before Punnett squares

**NGSS alignment:**
- **HS-LS3-1:** Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring.
- **HS-LS3-2:** Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from new genetic combinations through meiosis, viable errors during replication, and/or mutations.
- **SEP:** Developing and Using Models; Engaging in Argument from Evidence
- **CCC:** Cause and Effect; Patterns

**Big idea:** Meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles alleles. That shuffling is why Punnett squares work and why siblings differ.

**Pacing note:** Adding three days makes Week 2 tight. To save time, use the class coin-flip data from Day 2 as the dataset for the chi-square lesson later in the week.

---

## Teacher Prep: Paper Chromosome Kits (Make Once, Use All 3 Days)

Each pair of students gets one envelope containing:
- **4 long strips** (about 2 cm × 15 cm): 2 red, 2 blue
- **4 short strips** (about 2 cm × 8 cm): 2 red, 2 blue
- **4 paper clips** (these act as centromeres)
- **Masking tape and scissors** (for Day 2)

**Label the strips before class, or have students label them on Day 1:**
- Long red strips: **A** near the top, **D** near the bottom
- Long blue strips: **a** near the top, **d** near the bottom
- Short red strips: **B** in the middle
- Short blue strips: **b** in the middle

**Color key:** Red = chromosomes from Mom. Blue = chromosomes from Dad.
**Model organism:** 2n = 4 (two homologous pairs)

*Alternative:* Pop beads or pipe cleaners work for Days 1 and 3, but paper strips are easiest for the cutting and swapping in Day 2.

**Cells:** Use 4 paper plates per pair, or have students draw circles on a whiteboard or butcher paper.

---
---

# DAY 1: Why Meiosis? Making Haploid Gametes

**Time:** 50 minutes (flex options for 60)

## Learning Objective
Students will **use a model** to explain how meiosis produces four haploid gametes from one diploid cell, and why halving the chromosome number is necessary for sexual reproduction. *(HS-LS3-1; SEP: Developing and Using Models)*

**Student "I can":** I can use a model to show how one cell with 4 chromosomes becomes four cells with 2 chromosomes each, and explain why this matters.

## Materials
- Paper chromosome kits (1 per pair)
- 4 paper plates per pair (or whiteboards)
- Day 1 tracking sheet (below, 1 per student)
- Projected human karyotype image
- Exit tickets

## Warm-Up (6 min)
Project this prompt:

> *A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. Suppose an egg and a sperm each had 46 chromosomes.*
> *1. How many chromosomes would the baby have?*
> *2. How many would that baby's child have?*
> *3. What problem do you notice?*

**Teacher directions:**
1. Give students 3 minutes to answer individually.
2. Take 2–3 responses. Steer students toward this idea: chromosome number would double every generation (46 → 92 → 184), so gametes must carry **half**.
3. Write the driving question on the board: **"How do cells cut the chromosome number in half, and why?"**

## Main Activities

### Activity 1: Key Vocabulary Mini-Lesson (10 min)
1. Project a human karyotype. Point out that chromosomes come in **23 pairs**: one from Mom and one from Dad.
2. Introduce each term with a quick example. Students record them on their tracking sheet.
   - **Homologous chromosomes:** a matching pair (same genes, same size, possibly different alleles)
   - **Diploid (2n):** two sets of chromosomes (human body cells: 46)
   - **Haploid (n):** one set (human eggs and sperm: 23)
   - **Gamete:** an egg or sperm cell
   - **Sister chromatids:** two identical copies of one chromosome, joined at the centromere after DNA replication
3. **Connect to Week 1:** "Last week you learned how DNA replicates. That replication happens right before meiosis, which is why each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids."

### Activity 2: Model Meiosis (25 min)
Pass out kits. Students work in pairs. Lead them through each step, pausing so they can fill in the tracking sheet.

**Step 1: Starting cell (2 min)**
- Place one long red, one long blue, one short red, and one short blue strip on a plate.
- *Ask:* "How many chromosomes? How many homologous pairs? Is this cell diploid or haploid?" (4 chromosomes, 2 pairs, diploid)

**Step 2: DNA replication (3 min)**
- Add the matching copy of each strip. Clip identical strips together at the middle with a paper clip.
- *Ask:* "How many chromosomes now?" Clarify: still **4 chromosomes**, but each now has **2 sister chromatids**.

**Step 3: Meiosis I, pairing (3 min)**
- Students place each homologous pair side by side: long red next to long blue, short red next to short blue.
- *Say:* "This pairing up only happens in meiosis, not mitosis. It's the key step."

**Step 4: Meiosis I, lining up (2 min)**
- Line up the pairs across the middle of the cell, side by side.
- For now, have every pair put **red on the left**. (Day 2 explores other arrangements.)

**Step 5: Meiosis I, separating (3 min)**
- Pull each homologous pair apart: one chromosome to each side. Move each side to a new plate.
- *Ask:* "How many chromosomes in each new cell? Are they still paired?" (2 each, no pairs, so each cell is now haploid)
- **Check:** Paper clips should still be on. Sister chromatids stay together in meiosis I.

**Step 6: Meiosis II (5 min)**
- In each of the two cells, line up the chromosomes single file down the middle.
- Remove the paper clips and pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite sides.
- Split each cell into two plates. Students should now have **4 plates**.

**Step 7: Check results (5 min)**
- *Ask:* "How many cells? How many chromosomes in each? Does every cell have one long and one short chromosome?"
- Students complete the last row of the tracking sheet.
- **Key point:** Every gamete gets **one chromosome from each homologous pair**.

**Teacher tip:** Circulate and look for the two most common errors: separating sister chromatids in meiosis I, and putting two long chromosomes in the same gamete.

**Keep kits:** Students return strips to envelopes, keeping all labels intact for Day 2.

### Activity 3: Meiosis vs. Mitosis Quick Compare (5 min)
Have students fill in this comparison as a class:

- **Purpose:** Mitosis makes body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes gametes.
- **Number of divisions:** Mitosis has 1. Meiosis has 2.
- **Number of cells made:** Mitosis makes 2. Meiosis makes 4.
- **Chromosome number:** Mitosis keeps the diploid number. Meiosis produces haploid cells.
- **Genetically identical?** Mitosis cells are identical. Meiosis cells are not (we'll find out why tomorrow).

*Skip this if your students haven't studied mitosis yet. Use the time for extra modeling practice instead.*

## Program Plan: Activities & Timeline

### Theory of Change

When low-income adults with limited literacy receive structured, individualized instruction delivered by trained tutors — combined with practical skills application and consistent follow-up support — they gain the foundational competencies needed to pursue employment, access services, and sustain learning independently.

---

### Program Logic

LiteracyBridge's program is designed around a simple but evidence-grounded logic: literacy gains that happen in isolation rarely transfer to real-world function. Our model therefore pairs individualized skill-building with applied practice contexts — the job application, the benefits form, the online job board — so that participants build confidence and competency simultaneously. Three mutually reinforcing activity streams deliver this model: one-on-one tutoring, small-group skills workshops, and digital literacy sessions. Each stream addresses a distinct dimension of the literacy barrier identified in our needs assessment, and each feeds into the same participant pathway from intake to exit and follow-up. Together they constitute a coherent intervention rather than a menu of services. [Reference: Logic Model, Attachment A.]

This approach is consistent with best practices identified in adult literacy research. The National Institute for Literacy's framework for effective adult education programs emphasizes individualized assessment, evidence-based instruction, and integration of workforce-relevant content — all three of which are structural features of LiteracyBridge's model ([source, e.g., National Institute for Literacy, year]). Programs using similar designs have demonstrated reading-level gains of [X] grade levels over [timeframe] in comparable populations ([source, year]).

---

### Participant Pathway

Every participant moves through the same structured sequence, with pacing adjusted to individual progress.

**Intake and Assessment.** Prospective participants complete a TABE (Test of Adult Basic Education) assessment and a barriers screener administered by the Program Coordinator. The TABE establishes a baseline reading level and identifies specific skill gaps; the barriers screener captures practical obstacles — transportation, childcare, work schedule, prior negative educational experiences — that could affect attendance and retention. Together these tools inform the individualized learning plan developed for each participant before their first tutoring session.

**Individualized Learning Plan.** Within one week of intake, the Program Coordinator and assigned volunteer tutor jointly develop an Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) with the participant. The ILP specifies short-term skill targets, the mix of activities the participant will engage in, accommodations for identified barriers, and a projected timeline for reaching exit-level benchmarks. Participants review and sign the ILP, reinforcing their active role in the process.

**Core Services.** Participants engage in three concurrent activity streams over the program period, described in detail in the Activities section below. The standard service dosage is two 50-minute one-on-one tutoring sessions per week, one 90-minute small-group skills workshop per week, and one 2-hour digital lab session per month. At full dosage, participants receive approximately [X] hours of direct instruction over 12 months — consistent with the threshold associated with measurable literacy gains in the research literature ([source, year]).

**Progress Checks.** Every eight weeks, participants complete a mini-TABE administered by the Program Coordinator. Results are reviewed against ILP targets and used to adjust instruction. Participants who are progressing ahead of schedule may be advanced; those who have fallen behind receive additional tutor support or a modified schedule. Progress check results are recorded in [data management system] and reported to the Program Director quarterly.

**Exit and Placement Support.** At program completion — defined as reaching the participant's ILP goal or completing 12 months of enrollment — participants take a full exit TABE. The Program Coordinator meets with each exiting participant to review results, document next steps, and connect them to placement resources: job application assistance, referrals to GED programs, workforce development partners, or benefits navigation support, depending on individual goals.

**Six-Month Follow-Up.** Six months after exit, the Program Coordinator contacts each participant by phone or in person to document employment status, educational enrollment, and self-reported use of literacy skills. Follow-up data are recorded in [system] and reported to the funder. This contact also serves as a re-engagement touchpoint: participants who have not yet reached their goals are invited to re-enroll or connect with partner services.

---

### Activities

#### Activity 1: One-on-One Tutoring

**What it is.** Individualized reading and writing instruction delivered by a trained volunteer tutor, guided by each participant's ILP and focused on skills directly relevant to that participant's goals — workforce entry, service access, daily function, or further education.

**Who delivers it.** Volunteer tutors recruited, trained, and supervised by the Volunteer Coordinator (0.5 FTE). All tutors complete a [X]-hour initial training curriculum covering adult learning principles, the TABE framework, trauma-informed practice, and LiteracyBridge's instructional protocols before placement. Tutors receive monthly group supervision and are observed at least once per quarter by the Volunteer Coordinator.

**Dosage.** Two sessions per week, 50 minutes per session, for up to 12 months. Each participant is matched with one primary tutor; backup tutors are available to maintain continuity if a primary tutor is unavailable.

**Location.** Sessions are held at [location 1] and [location 2], selected for proximity to participant neighborhoods and access by public transit. Evening and weekend slots are available to accommodate participants with daytime work or caregiving obligations.

**Evidence base.** One-on-one tutoring is the most consistently supported instructional format in adult literacy research, associated with stronger gains than group instruction alone, particularly for learners at the lowest skill levels ([source, e.g., Kruidenier, 2002; ProLiteracy, year]).

---

#### Activity 2: Small-Group Skills Workshops

**What it is.** Weekly 90-minute workshops organized around applied literacy tasks drawn directly from workforce and daily-life contexts: reading a pay stub, completing a rental application, interpreting a benefits letter, writing a professional email. Groups are capped at eight participants to allow interactive practice and peer support.

**Who delivers it.** The Program Coordinator (1.0 FTE), who holds [relevant credential or experience], designs and facilitates the workshop curriculum. A rotating volunteer co-facilitator supports small-group breakout activities. The workshop curriculum is reviewed and updated annually based on participant feedback and labor market data from [local workforce board or source].

**Dosage.** One session per week, 90 minutes, available to all enrolled participants. Attendance is tracked; participants who miss two consecutive sessions are contacted by the Program Coordinator to identify and address barriers.

**Location.** [Community center / library / partner site], accessible by [transit line]. Childcare is available on-site during workshop hours through a partnership with [partner organization].

**Evidence base.** Group instruction in contextualized literacy — where reading and writing tasks are drawn from real-life applications — produces stronger transfer to daily function than decontextualized drill ([source, e.g., Equipped for the Future framework; Beder et al., year]). The peer cohort structure also supports retention, which is the primary challenge in adult literacy programming ([source, year]).

---

#### Activity 3: Digital Literacy Sessions

**What it is.** Monthly two-hour lab sessions in which participants build foundational digital skills: using email, navigating job search platforms, completing online forms, accessing online benefits portals, and using word processing for basic documents. Sessions are structured around the same applied tasks as the skills workshops, so digital instruction reinforces rather than duplicates classroom learning.

**Who delivers it.** A part-time Digital Literacy Instructor ([X] hours per week) with demonstrated experience in adult digital education. The instructor works in coordination with the Program Coordinator to align lab content with participants' current ILP goals.

**Dosage.** One session per month, two hours per session. Participants who identify digital access as a specific employment barrier are offered an additional monthly session in [month range] when demand is highest.

**Location.** [Partner computer lab location — library, community college, workforce center]. LiteracyBridge has a formal agreement with [partner] to use [X] workstations on [scheduled days] at no cost. [Reference: MOU, Attachment E.]

**Evidence base.** Digital literacy has become inseparable from workforce entry in Eastside County's current labor market, where [X]% of job applications are submitted online ([source, year]). Programs that integrate digital skills with foundational literacy instruction show stronger employment outcomes than those that treat the two as sequential ([source, year]).

---

### Referrals and Partnership Flow

Participants reach LiteracyBridge through four primary referral channels: [Partner 1, e.g., county workforce development center], [Partner 2, e.g., community health clinic], [Partner 3, e.g., public library system], and self-referral through community outreach. Each partner organization has a designated point of contact who routes referrals to the Program Coordinator using a shared intake form. LiteracyBridge responds to all referrals within [X] business days with a scheduled intake appointment.
