## Evaluation Plan

LiteracyBridge's evaluation plan is designed to answer three questions: Are participants gaining measurable literacy skills? Are they achieving employment and education outcomes after exit? And is the program being delivered as designed? The plan uses validated assessment tools, structured data collection points built into the participant pathway, and a quarterly review process that connects findings directly to program adjustments. Data collection and analysis responsibilities are distributed across existing staff positions, with no additional evaluation personnel required.

---

### SMART Objectives

The following three objectives define success for this grant period. Each is specific, measurable, achievable based on prior program performance, relevant to the stated need, and time-bound to the 12-month grant period.

**Objective 1 — Literacy Gains.** By [end date, month 12], 75% of participants who complete the full program (defined as attending at least [X] sessions and completing an exit TABE) will advance at least one full grade level on the TABE Reading subtest, compared with a baseline of [X]% in LiteracyBridge's most recent program year [or "to be established at program launch using Q1 intake data"].

**Objective 2 — Program Completion.** By [end date, month 12], at least 70% of enrolled participants (84 of 120) will complete the full program as defined above, compared with a baseline completion rate of [X]% in [prior year] and consistent with the adult literacy field benchmark of [X]% ([source, year]).

**Objective 3 — Post-Exit Outcomes.** Of participants who complete the program and are reached at six-month follow-up, at least 60% will report at least one of the following: new or improved employment, enrollment in further education or training, or increased independent use of literacy skills for a defined daily-life task, compared with a baseline of [X]% documented in LiteracyBridge's [year] follow-up data [or "to be established with Q1–Q2 exiters"].

---

### Outcomes Table

| Objective | Baseline | Target | Measure | Data Source | Collection Point |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Literacy gains | [X]% advancing 1+ grade level | 75% of completers | TABE Reading pre/post score change | TABE assessment records | Intake + exit (+ mini-TABE every 8 weeks) |
| 2. Program completion | [X]% completion rate | 70% of enrollees (84/120) | Sessions attended vs. required threshold | Attendance logs, ILP records | Ongoing; calculated at exit |
| 3. Post-exit outcomes | [X]% reporting employment/education gain | 60% of reached exiters | Self-report: employment, education, skill use | 6-month follow-up survey | 6 months post-exit |

---

### Measurement Tools and Data Sources

**TABE (Test of Adult Basic Education).** The TABE is the primary instrument for measuring literacy gains. It is a norm-referenced, nationally validated assessment widely used in adult education programs and accepted by [funder name] and comparable funders as a reliable measure of reading-level change. LiteracyBridge administers the full TABE at intake and exit, and an abbreviated mini-TABE at eight-week intervals to track interim progress and flag participants who need instructional adjustment. All TABE administrations are conducted by the Program Coordinator, who holds [TABE certification or equivalent training, placeholder]. Score records are stored in [data system placeholder] immediately following each administration.

**Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) Progress Records.** Each participant's ILP documents short-term skill targets and is updated at every eight-week progress check. ILP records provide a qualitative complement to TABE scores, capturing skill-specific progress that a single composite score may not reflect. The Program Coordinator maintains all ILP records; the Program Director reviews a random sample of [X]% quarterly as part of the fidelity check process described below.

**Attendance Logs.** Session attendance is recorded by volunteer tutors (for one-on-one sessions) and the Program Coordinator (for workshops and digital lab sessions) in [data system] at the conclusion of each session. Attendance data are used to calculate dosage, identify participants at risk of non-completion, and determine eligibility for the completer analysis under Objective 1.

**Placement Tracking Records.** At exit, the Program Coordinator documents each participant's immediate next step — employment application in progress, job placement, GED program referral, workforce training enrollment, or no placement activity — using a structured exit form. These records establish the baseline against which six-month follow-up data are compared.

**Six-Month Follow-Up Survey.** At six months post-exit, the Program Coordinator contacts each participant using a brief structured survey ([X] questions, estimated [X] minutes) administered by phone or in person. The survey captures current employment status, educational enrollment, and self-reported frequency of independent literacy skill use. A written version is available for participants who prefer it. LiteracyBridge targets a follow-up response rate of at least [X]%; participants who cannot be reached after [X] attempts are recorded as lost to follow-up and excluded from the Objective 3 denominator.

---

### Data Collection Schedule

| Data Point | Timing | Collected By |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline TABE + barriers screener | Intake (prior to first tutoring session) | Program Coordinator |
| ILP development and documentation | Within 1 week of intake | Program Coordinator + tutor |
| Attendance logs | Each session | Tutor (1:1) / Program Coordinator (workshop, lab) |
| Mini-TABE progress check | Every 8 weeks from intake | Program Coordinator |
| ILP review and update | Every 8 weeks, concurrent with mini-TABE | Program Coordinator |
| Exit TABE + placement documentation | At program completion or 12-month mark | Program Coordinator |
| Six-month follow-up survey | 6 months post-exit | Program Coordinator |
| Quarterly data summary | End of each quarter | Program Director |

---

### Analysis Methods

LiteracyBridge's primary analytic approach is a pre/post comparison using TABE scale scores. For each participant who completes both an intake and an exit TABE, we will calculate the change in Reading subtest scale score and determine whether the change represents advancement of at least one full grade-level equivalent, consistent with standard TABE scoring conventions. Results will be reported as the percentage of completers meeting the Objective 1 threshold, with the full distribution of score changes provided in the final report.

For Objective 2, completion rates will be calculated as the number of participants reaching the defined dosage threshold divided by total enrollment, reported monthly and summarized quarterly. Participants who exit early will be categorized by reason (voluntary withdrawal, life circumstances, program-initiated exit, lost to contact) to allow the program to identify patterns and adjust retention strategies.

For Objective 3, follow-up outcomes will be reported as the percentage of reached exiters meeting at least one of the defined outcome criteria, disaggregated by outcome type (employment, education, skill use) where sample size permits.

Where appropriate, LiteracyBridge will benchmark its results against comparable adult literacy programs using published data from [source, e.g., National Reporting System for Adult Education, ProLiteracy annual report, state adult education data]. We do not propose a formal control or comparison group, as the program population and service context do not support random assignment; instead, benchmarking against field norms provides an external reference for interpreting our outcomes.

---

### Data Management and Privacy

All participant data — TABE records, ILPs, attendance logs, placement records, and follow-up surveys — are stored in [data management system, e.g., Salesforce, Apricot, internal database]. Access is restricted to program staff by role-based permissions; volunteer tutors access only their own participants' session logs and do not have access to assessment records or personal contact information. The Program Director holds administrator access and conducts a quarterly permissions audit.

Participants provide written informed consent at intake covering data collection, storage, use for program evaluation, and reporting to [funder name] in aggregate form. Consent forms are retained in [system/file location] for [X] years per [applicable records retention policy]. No individually identifiable data are shared with external parties, including the funder; all reported outcomes are aggregated.

---

### Continuous Improvement and Stakeholder Reporting

Evaluation findings are not held until the final report. The Program Director convenes a quarterly data review meeting with the Program Coordinator and Volunteer Coordinator to examine completion rates, TABE progress trends, attendance patterns, and any early signals of participant disengagement. If fewer than [X]% of participants are on track to meet the Objective 1 threshold at the midpoint review, the team will convene a corrective action process to identify whether the gap reflects instructional quality, dosage, population match, or assessment administration — and will document and implement a specific adjustment within [X] weeks.

Findings are reported to LiteracyBridge's board of directors [quarterly / semiannually] in summary form and to [funder name] through required progress and final reports. Partner organizations receive an annual program summary. Where results demonstrate significant gains, LiteracyBridge will seek opportunities to share findings through [local adult education network, state literacy coalition, or comparable venue] to contribute to the broader field.

---

### Fidelity and Quality Checks

**Tutor Observation.** The Volunteer Coordinator conducts a structured observation of each active volunteer tutor at least once per quarter using a standardized observation rubric covering session structure, ILP alignment, instructional technique, and participant engagement. Observation notes are shared with the tutor as a coaching tool, not a punitive record. Tutors whose observations identify consistent gaps receive additional coaching or, if issues persist, are reassigned or separated from the program.

**ILP Review.** The Program Director reviews a random sample of [X]% of active ILPs at the end of each quarter to verify that plans are current, goals are appropriately challenging, and progress check findings are reflected in updated targets. Any ILPs that have not been updated within the required window are flagged for immediate follow-up with the Program Coordinator.

---

### Evaluation Capacity, Staffing, and Budget

LiteracyBridge's evaluation activities are carried out by existing program staff — the Program Coordinator (data collection and participant-level tracking) and the Program Director (analysis, fidelity checks, and reporting) — with no separate evaluation budget line required. The Program Coordinator's 1.0 FTE allocation includes approximately [X]% of time dedicated to evaluation tasks; the Program Director's 0.25 FTE allocation includes approximately [X]% for data review and reporting. Combined, this represents approximately [X] hours per year of staff evaluation capacity, sufficient for the scope and participant volume of this program. Data system costs of $[X] are included in the budget under [line item]. This approach reflects LiteracyBridge's commitment to building evaluation into standard program operations rather than treating it as a separate, grant-funded add-on.

## Statement of Need

Eastside County faces a literacy crisis that is measurable, persistent, and consequential for residents across generations. According to the State Department of Education (2023), 18% of Eastside County adults are functionally illiterate — a rate 50% higher than the state average of 12%. That gap represents thousands of residents who struggle to read a prescription label, complete a job application, or help a child with homework. Without targeted intervention, the data suggest this gap will not close on its own.

The impact begins early. The Eastside County School District (2022) found that 40% of local third graders are reading below grade level — a benchmark researchers consistently identify as a turning point, because students who are not reading proficiently by third grade are four times less likely to graduate high school on time. In Eastside County, that means roughly four in ten children enter their middle school years already behind. The connection between childhood and adult literacy is well established: children whose parents read proficiently at home develop literacy skills faster and are more likely to meet grade-level benchmarks themselves. Low adult literacy does not stay with adults alone — it moves forward through families.

The economic consequences are equally clear. A 2023 workforce survey conducted across Eastside County employers ranked "basic reading and digital literacy" as the single greatest barrier to entry-level employment, cited more frequently than transportation, childcare, or prior criminal history. Residents face this barrier daily. At intake, BrightPath learners regularly describe situations that reflect what the data show: being passed over for promotions because they could not complete required paperwork, avoiding the doctor because medical forms felt impossible to navigate, or feeling unable to advocate for their children at school. These are not isolated experiences — they are patterns rooted in a systemic gap between community need and available service.

That gap is not filled by existing providers. Eastside County currently has no public adult education program operating at the scale the population requires. The public library offers limited drop-in literacy support two days per week, with no structured curriculum and no case management. The nearest community college's adult basic education program serves fewer than 100 learners per year and maintains its own waitlist. BrightPath is the only community-based organization in the county providing structured, one-on-one adult literacy tutoring with wraparound coordination — and demand has outpaced our capacity.

BrightPath currently serves 350 adult learners annually. As of this application, 120 additional residents are on our waitlist, with an average wait time of six months. For someone who needs literacy skills to pursue a job, support a child's education, or manage a health condition, six months is not a minor inconvenience — it is a semester of school their child finishes without them, a job opportunity that will not wait, a prescription that goes misread. The waitlist is not a number; it is a measure of unmet need in real time.

Eastside County's literacy gap is wider than the state's, growing faster than local services can address it, and carrying consequences that compound across generations. The residents who come to BrightPath are not asking for something extraordinary — they are asking for the foundational skills that most people take for granted. The question this grant asks the funder to answer is straightforward: how many more residents should wait before they get that chance?

## Program Design & Activities

**Theory of Change**

BrightPath operates from a straightforward theory of change: when adults with low literacy receive structured, individualized instruction delivered at sufficient dosage over a sustained period, paired with goal-aligned support services, they gain measurable literacy skills that translate into improved employment outcomes, greater capacity to support their children's education, and stronger long-term self-sufficiency. The logic model attached as Figure 1 maps inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes in full. The narrative below describes how that logic works in practice.

**Core Activities**

BrightPath's program model is built on three mutually reinforcing core activities: individualized literacy instruction, digital literacy and workforce readiness training, and family engagement support. Together they address the layered barriers Eastside County residents face — not just reading skill, but the applied contexts in which that skill must function.

*Activity 1: Individualized Literacy Instruction*

The foundation of BrightPath's model is one-on-one tutoring delivered by trained volunteer tutors and supervised by a certified literacy specialist. Each participant is matched with a tutor within two weeks of completing intake and begins a personalized learning plan based on their TABE assessment results and stated goals. Sessions meet twice weekly for 90 minutes each, yielding a weekly dosage of three hours of direct instruction — consistent with the dosage threshold identified in research on adult literacy program effectiveness (Kruidenier, MacArthur & Woo, 2010). Participants remain in active tutoring for a minimum of six months, with an option to continue for a second six-month term based on progress and goals.

Each cohort enrolls 35 participants and launches on a rolling quarterly basis, yielding four cohorts per year and a total active enrollment of up to 140 participants at any given time. Across the full year, with cohort cycling and re-enrollment, BrightPath serves 350 unduplicated adult learners. Instruction takes place at BrightPath's Eastside County Learning Center and at two satellite locations — a branch library and a community health clinic — chosen specifically to reduce transportation barriers for participants in the county's lower-income eastern and southern neighborhoods.

This activity directly addresses the literacy gap documented in the Statement of Need and links to Outcome 1: participants demonstrating measurable gains on post-program TABE assessment.

*Activity 2: Digital Literacy and Workforce Readiness Training*

Recognizing that the 2023 Eastside County workforce survey identified "basic reading and digital literacy" as the top barrier to employment, BrightPath integrates a six-week digital literacy module into every participant's second month of enrollment. Delivered in small groups of eight to ten participants by BrightPath's Workforce Readiness Coordinator, sessions cover email and internet basics, navigating online job applications, and using digital tools for household and health management. The module draws on the Northstar Digital Literacy framework, which has demonstrated effectiveness across diverse adult learner populations in community-based settings (Digital Literacy Alliance, 2021).

One participant, now employed full-time after completing the program, described the shift this way: she had always avoided applying for certain jobs because the online application felt like a wall she couldn't get past. Learning to navigate that process was, she said, the moment things started to open up. Her experience reflects what the data consistently show — that literacy gains translate into employment outcomes only when participants also have practice applying those skills in real-world digital contexts.

This activity links to Outcome 2: participants reporting increased confidence in digital navigation and demonstrating improved workforce readiness competencies.

*Activity 3: Family Engagement Support*

Because 40% of Eastside County third graders read below grade level, and because parental literacy is one of the strongest predictors of children's reading development, BrightPath offers monthly family literacy workshops for participants who have children in grades K–5. Workshops, capped at 20 families, are facilitated by the Family Engagement Coordinator and focus on shared reading strategies, library use, and how to support homework without formal tutoring. Research consistently links structured family literacy programming to improvements in both adult learner persistence and children's reading outcomes (Wasik & Hendrickson, 2004). A father enrolled in the program last year put it plainly: he came for himself, but staying was about his daughter — once he could read with her at night, she stopped dreading school.

This activity links to Outcome 3: participants reporting increased engagement in their children's literacy development, and to the intergenerational dimension of the community impact criteria.

**Participant Pathway**

Participants move through four clearly defined phases. During intake, prospective learners contact BrightPath by phone, referral, or walk-in; complete an eligibility screening; and are scheduled for a TABE assessment within five business days. During matching and orientation, assessed participants are matched with a tutor, receive a one-hour program orientation, and co-develop their learning plan with staff. Active services then begin, running for a minimum of six months as described above, with monthly check-ins between the participant, tutor, and literacy specialist to review progress and adjust the plan. At exit, participants complete a post-program TABE assessment, receive a transition plan outlining next steps — workforce programs, community college, continued independent learning — and are scheduled for a 90-day follow-up contact to track employment and continued progress outcomes.

## Section 7: Evaluation Plan

BrightPath's evaluation plan is designed to answer three questions continuously across the grant period: Are we reaching the right people? Are participants making meaningful gains? And are we using what we learn to get better? The plan uses a pre/post design with benchmark comparisons, mixed data collection methods, and a structured continuous improvement cycle.

**Evaluation Design**

BrightPath will use a pre/post design with a quasi-experimental benchmark comparison as its primary evaluation approach. Each participant serves as their own control, with TABE scores, Northstar competency assessments, employment status, and survey responses collected at intake (baseline), at the program midpoint (three months), at exit (six months), and at 90-day follow-up. Outcome rates will be benchmarked against published national averages for community-based adult literacy programs — specifically the most recent ProLiteracy national program data and the National Reporting System for Adult Education — to contextualize BrightPath's results within the broader field. While a randomized control design is not feasible in a community-based setting serving a waitlisted population, the pre/post structure with external benchmarking provides a credible and transparent basis for outcome claims.

**Data Collection Tools and Frequency**

TABE assessments are administered at intake and exit by the Certified Literacy Specialist, who holds the required certification for standardized administration. Northstar Digital Literacy competency checks are administered by the Workforce Readiness Coordinator at the start and end of the six-week module. Attendance is recorded by volunteer tutors at every session and entered into BrightPath's participant database by the Administrative Assistant within 48 hours. Employment status is documented at intake through participant self-report and verified at 90-day follow-up through a structured phone or in-person contact conducted by the Program Director or a designated staff member. Family engagement outcomes are measured through a brief pre/post survey, developed internally and reviewed annually, administered by the Family Engagement Coordinator at the first and last workshop of each cohort cycle.

**Data Management, Analysis, and Privacy**

All participant data are stored in BrightPath's secure case management database, accessible only to authorized staff and protected by password authentication and role-based permissions. No participant data are shared externally in identifiable form. Aggregate, de-identified data are used for all reporting, presentations, and publications. The Program Director conducts a quarterly data review, pulling outcome rates by cohort, attendance trends, and assessment completion rates, and presents findings to the Executive Director and Board Program Committee at each quarterly meeting.

**Continuous Improvement**

Findings from quarterly reviews feed directly into program adjustments through a structured continuous improvement protocol. If cohort-level TABE gain rates fall below 70% at the midpoint review, the Certified Literacy Specialist conducts individual plan reviews with the relevant tutors and participants within 30 days. If Northstar completion rates fall below target, the Workforce Readiness Coordinator reviews module pacing and delivery format. Staff reflect collectively on outcome trends at a annual program retreat each January, producing a written improvement plan that is shared with the Board and incorporated into the following year's work plan. Findings are also shared with key community partners — the County School District, workforce development partners, and the county health department — annually, both to strengthen referral relationships and to contribute to the broader evidence base for literacy programming in Eastside County.

**Reporting**

BrightPath will provide the funder with a midyear progress report at month six of each grant year, including output data, preliminary outcome rates, and a brief narrative on any program adjustments made. A full annual report will be submitted within 60 days of each grant year's close, including final outcome data against all four SMART objectives, a budget variance explanation, and a forward-looking narrative describing plans for year two (or sustainability, in the final year report).

Instruction follows the Evidence-Based Adult Education framework, contextualized to real-life tasks — reading utility bills, filling out job applications, interpreting school communications — to maximize engagement and relevance for low-income parents. Each participant receives an individualized learning plan developed at intake by a credentialed adult education instructor, with progress reviewed every eight weeks. GED preparation is introduced at the intermediate level and accelerated for participants who reach benchmark literacy scores, ensuring the most ready learners move toward credentialing within the grant period.

*Component 2: Parent-Child Shared Reading.* Twice monthly, participants attend a 90-minute Family Reading Night, offered in coordination with the Eastside County Public Library. Each session is facilitated by a literacy coach and pairs adult learners with their K–3 children for structured read-aloud activities, followed by brief parent coaching on at-home reading strategies. This component directly addresses the district's finding that 1,200 K–3 students are reading below grade level, recognizing that classroom instruction alone is insufficient without reinforcement at home. Participants receive a take-home book bag at enrollment and replenish their libraries at each Family Reading Night, removing cost as a barrier to daily reading practice.

*Component 3: Employment Readiness Coaching.* In months 10–18, participants who have reached intermediate literacy benchmarks transition into a six-session employment readiness workshop series, covering résumé writing, interview skills, workplace communication, and financial literacy basics. Sessions are delivered in partnership with the Eastside County Workforce Board, which has pledged $20,000 toward this component and will provide direct connections to job placement services for participants who complete GED preparation. This sequencing is intentional: employment content is introduced after participants have built sufficient literacy skills to engage with written materials and self-advocacy tasks, increasing the likelihood that coaching translates into actual job attainment.

**Participant Pathway**

All participants enter through a standardized intake process that includes a literacy assessment (TABE 11/12), goal-setting interview, and eligibility verification. ReadForward's current waitlist of 78 adults will be prioritized for Cohort 1 enrollment, ensuring immediate impact from grant launch. Participants who miss three consecutive sessions are contacted by the program coordinator for a retention check-in; those facing acute barriers (childcare, transportation, work schedule conflicts) are connected to wraparound supports through partner referrals. At program exit, each participant receives a transition plan outlining next steps — GED testing, job placement services, or enrollment in postsecondary education — with a 90-day follow-up contact to track outcomes.

## B. Program Design & Activities
*(2 pages — target: 1,075 words)*

**Theory of Change**

Family Literacy Pathways is built on a well-established premise: when parents gain literacy and educational credentials, the benefits extend directly to their children. Adults who complete GED programs demonstrate higher rates of employment and economic stability, and research consistently shows that parental literacy is one of the strongest predictors of early childhood reading success (Mol & Bus, 2011; National Institute for Literacy, 2020). ReadForward Community Literacy has operationalized this two-generation logic into three integrated program components delivered over 18 months: adult literacy and GED preparation, parent-child shared reading, and employment readiness coaching. **Program Components**

## Section 4: Program Design & Activities (Final Draft)

**Rubric criteria addressed:** Program Design & Activities (30%) — logic, evidence base, activity descriptions, staffing, timeline

---

**Theory of Change**

Community Literacy Collaborative operates from a clear and evidence-grounded theory of change: when adults with low literacy receive intensive, individualized instruction paired with family-centered supports, they develop the foundational skills needed to participate more fully in employment, healthcare, and civic life — and in doing so, they become more effective literacy partners for their own children, interrupting the intergenerational cycle documented in Section 2. Inputs include trained volunteer and professional tutors, structured curriculum, bilingual family workshop facilitators, and community referral partnerships. These inputs drive three core activities — high-dosage one-on-one tutoring, family literacy workshops, and coordinated wraparound navigation — which together produce the participant-level changes measured in our outcomes framework. The full logic model, including inputs, activities, short-term outputs, intermediate outcomes, and long-term impact, is provided as **Attachment A: Logic Model.**

**[PULL-QUOTE candidate: "When adults gain literacy skills, they don't just find better jobs — they become their children's first teachers. Our model is designed around that chain of impact."]**

---

**Core Activity 1: High-Dosage One-on-One Tutoring**

The centerpiece of our program model is high-dosage, structured one-on-one tutoring delivered to 240 adult participants per year across three 12-week cohort cycles. Each participant receives a minimum of three tutoring sessions per week, each 60 minutes in duration, for a total of at least 36 hours of direct instruction per cohort cycle. This dosage level is intentional: research consistently shows that adults reading below a 6th-grade level require sustained, intensive contact hours — not episodic support — to achieve durable skill gains ([cite: National Institute for Literacy / ProLiteracy research, year]).

Sessions are delivered in person at [location: e.g., Westbrook Community Center / branch library / program site], with a hybrid remote option available for participants facing transportation or scheduling barriers. Tutoring is delivered by a combination of trained volunteers and 4 part-time paid tutor positions, all supervised by the Adult Education Specialist (see Section 5: Staffing). All tutors use the Everybody Wins Literacy Framework, an evidence-informed adult literacy curriculum selected for its structured progression and demonstrated effectiveness with low-literacy adult populations ([cite: program evaluation or clearinghouse source, year]).

At launch, 40% of tutoring capacity will be delivered in Spanish, reflecting the linguistic profile of Westbrook's low-literacy population and our commitment to reducing language as a barrier to access. Spanish-language capacity is distributed across both volunteer and paid tutor roles and will be maintained or expanded in subsequent grant years as bilingual tutor recruitment deepens.

Participants are assessed at intake, week 6 (midpoint), and week 12 (exit) using the Test of Adult Basic Education (TABE), a nationally normed instrument that measures reading, language, and math skills and allows for standardized grade-level comparison across cohorts. Assessment results are used to adjust instruction in real time and to populate the outcome tracking system described in Section 6. This activity directly addresses the service gap identified in Section 2: unlike Westbrook Literacy Center's current waitlisted model, our program maintains rolling cohort enrollment, reducing wait times from six months to no more than two weeks.

**[PULL-QUOTE candidate: "Our tutoring model is built on a simple premise: dosage matters. Three sessions a week, every week, for twelve weeks — that's what the research says it takes."]**

---

**Core Activity 2: Family Literacy Workshops**

The second core activity addresses the intergenerational dimension of low literacy documented in Section 2. Adult participants who are parents or caregivers of children ages 4–8 are enrolled in a concurrent series of six biweekly family literacy workshops, held on-site and offered in both English and Spanish. Each workshop runs 90 minutes and is facilitated by our Family Literacy Coordinator, a bilingual staff role (see Section 5). Workshops cover shared reading strategies, home literacy environment building, and age-appropriate phonemic awareness activities participants can use with their children between sessions.

The family literacy workshop model is grounded in evidence from the Even Start Family Literacy Program and subsequent research showing that parent-focused literacy interventions produce measurable gains in children's kindergarten readiness, particularly when paired with adult instruction ([cite: St. Pierre et al., year; Harvard Family Research Project, year]). This directly addresses the finding from Westbrook Unified (2023) that 32% of children enter Westbrook kindergartens without foundational literacy skills — a figure disproportionately concentrated in households with low-literacy caregivers.

Workshops reach 160 children indirectly per year through caregiver skill-building. Child-specific outcomes are tracked via caregiver-reported home literacy activity logs and, where available, school readiness data shared by Westbrook Unified through our data-sharing agreement (see **Attachment B: MOU with Westbrook Unified School District**).

---

**Core Activity 3: Wraparound Navigation & Referral Support**

Low literacy rarely exists in isolation. Participants frequently face intersecting barriers — unstable housing, transportation gaps, benefit enrollment complexity, and limited healthcare access — that undermine engagement in any literacy program. To address this, Community Literacy Collaborative embeds a part-time Community Navigator (0.5 FTE) within the program who conducts a structured needs assessment with each participant at intake and connects them to partner services as needed. Navigation touchpoints occur at intake, week 4, and exit.

This activity is not incidental to the literacy program — it is integral to retention. Research on adult education programs consistently identifies life instability as the primary driver of participant dropout ([cite: Comings et al., year]). By addressing barriers proactively, navigation supports the dosage integrity of Activity 1: participants who remain enrolled accumulate the contact hours necessary for skill gains. The Navigator maintains active referral relationships with four formal partner organizations: Westbrook Literacy Center (participant referrals and waitlist coordination), Westbrook Workforce Board (job-placement and workforce training pathways), Westbrook Community Health Clinic (health navigation and social determinants screening), and Westbrook Unified School District (family liaison coordination and kindergarten readiness data sharing). Formal referral agreements with each partner are included as **Attachment C: Partner Letters of Support and MOUs.**

---

**Participant Pathway: Intake → Services → Exit → Follow-Up**

The participant pathway is designed to minimize friction at every transition point. The full workflow is illustrated in **Attachment D: Participant Pathway Diagram.**

Outreach and referral channels include Westbrook Literacy Center's existing waitlist (by formal referral agreement), partner social service agencies, Westbrook Unified family liaisons, and targeted community canvassing in the Northside, Harborview, and Elmwood neighborhoods, which together account for the highest concentrations of low-literacy adults in Westbrook ([source, year] — insert neighborhood-level data if available). Outreach materials are available in English and Spanish, and canvassing staff include bilingual community members.

At intake, participants complete a TABE assessment, a structured needs assessment with the Community Navigator, and an enrollment agreement. Tutor matching occurs within two weeks. Participants enter the first 12-week cohort cycle, with a midpoint TABE check-in at week 6 to assess progress, adjust instruction, and address any emerging barriers. Eligible caregivers are simultaneously enrolled in the family literacy workshop track.

At exit (week 12), participants complete a post-assessment TABE, a program satisfaction survey, and a goal-attainment review with their tutor and the Adult Education Specialist. Participants who have not yet reached a 6th-grade reading level are offered re-enrollment in a second cohort cycle. Participants who have met their literacy goals are connected to next-step pathways — GED preparation, workforce training, or community college enrollment — through Westbrook Workforce Board and other partner referrals.

Follow-up contact occurs at 90 days post-exit via phone or email to assess employment, education, and home literacy outcomes. Data collected at follow-up feed directly into the evaluation framework described in Section 6.

**[PULL-QUOTE candidate: "No participant leaves without a next step. Whether that means a second cohort cycle or a referral to GED prep, our exit process is a beginning, not an ending."]**

# ISO 27001:2022 Gap Analysis Checklist
### Healthcare Provider | 250 staff | Hybrid cloud | PHI in scope

---

## How to read this

**Gap severity** = H (likely missing/critical), M (partial), L (probably exists, needs documenting).
**Evidence** = what an auditor will actually ask to see, not just "a policy exists."

---

## Phase 1: Foundation (Months 1–2) — Quick Wins + Mandatory Clause Work

These are either fast to complete or mandatory before anything else can be assessed. Auditors look here first.

---

### Clause 4–6: Context, Leadership, Risk (Mandatory clauses — not Annex A)

These are **not optional**. No certificate without them.

| # | Requirement | Gap | Actions | Auditor evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scope statement (4.3) | H | Define ISMS boundary: include cloud EHR, on-prem, staff devices, third-party connections. Be specific about PHI systems. | Signed, dated scope document referencing systems and locations |
| 2 | Context and interested parties (4.1–4.2) | H | Document internal/external issues (HIPAA, state regs, payer requirements, cyber insurers). List stakeholders and their requirements. | Context register or equivalent document |
| 3 | Information security policy (5.2) | M | You likely have fragments. Consolidate into a top-level IS policy signed by CEO/COO. One page is fine. | Signed policy, evidence of communication to all staff |

| 5 | Statement of Applicability (6.1.3) | H | List all 93 Annex A controls, justify inclusions/exclusions. This is the central audit artifact. | Completed SoA with justification column and control owner for each included control |
| 6 | Risk treatment plan (6.1.3) | H | Assign owners, timelines, and treatment decisions (accept/mitigate/transfer) to each identified risk. | Risk register with treatment decisions, risk owner signatures |

| Gap | Action | Evidence |

| Gap | Action | Evidence |

### Cryptography — A.8.24

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |

| Control | Gap | Actions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.8 Technical vulnerability management | H | Implement a formal patching process: scan, assess, prioritize (CVSS + asset criticality), patch, verify. For PHI systems, target critical patches within 30 days. | Vulnerability management procedure, scan reports (Tenable/Qualys/Nessus or equivalent), patch records with timestamps, remediation SLAs |

Recommended approach given your ITIL base: create a vulnerability management practice that feeds into your existing change enablement process. Critical patches become emergency changes; routine patches become standard changes with a defined cadence (e.g., monthly patch Tuesday equivalent).

You have ITIL incident management, which is a significant head start, but security incident management requires specific additions.

Include PHI breach assessment steps (is this a HIPAA reportable breach?). | Incident classification matrix, response playbooks for top scenarios (ransomware, PHI exposure, credential compromise) |

Schedule with your chosen certification body approximately 1–2 months before your target certification date. They review documentation only. Common failures at Stage 1: incomplete SoA, missing risk treatment plan, no internal audit evidence, scope too vague.

### Stage 2 Audit (Certifier on-site/remote assessment)

Auditors will interview staff, test controls, and sample evidence. Prepare staff in these roles: ISMS owner, IT manager, HR (joiner/leaver process), a clinician (awareness training), cloud/infrastructure lead.

## Healthcare-specific notes

A few things that matter more in your context than in a typical organization:

**HIPAA overlap is significant.** Many Annex A controls map directly to HIPAA Technical and Administrative Safeguards. Your SoA justification can note HIPAA alignment, and your existing HIPAA documentation (risk analysis, policies, training records) can serve dual purpose as ISO 27001 evidence. Don't rebuild from scratch — map what you have first.

**PHI data flows need explicit documentation.** Auditors will want to see that you know exactly where PHI is created, stored, transmitted, and disposed of. A data flow diagram covering the EHR, any integrations (labs, payers, referral systems), and staff devices will make this much easier.

**Cloud EHR shared responsibility.** Your EHR vendor's SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certificate covers their controls, not yours. The auditor will ask what you are responsible for — access provisioning, audit log review, configuration of security features — and expect evidence that you are actively managing those responsibilities.

**Downtime procedures** are worth documenting now even if basic. They satisfy both ISO 27001 continuity requirements and HIPAA contingency plan requirements.

# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Statement of Applicability (SoA)
### Organization: [Your Organization Name] | Version: 1.0 | Date: [Date] | ISMS Owner: [Name/Role]

---

## How to use this document

The SoA is the central artifact of your ISMS. Every auditor begins here. It must demonstrate that a responsible person made a deliberate, justified decision about every control — not that you implemented everything, but that you thought carefully about what applies and why. Gaps are acceptable at Stage 1; unjustified gaps are not.

**Before your Stage 1 audit, ensure:**
- Every row has a completed justification (not just "N/A")
- Every included control has a named owner
- The document is version-controlled and signed by senior leadership
- It cross-references your risk treatment plan (risks should map to controls)

---

## Document control

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Document title | Statement of Applicability |
| Standard | ISO/IEC 27001:2022 |
| Annex A reference | ISO/IEC 27002:2022 (93 controls, 4 themes) |
| Version | 1.0 DRAFT |
| Classification | Confidential — Internal |
| Approved by | [CEO / COO / CISO] |
| Next review date | [12 months from approval] |
| ISMS scope | Provision of healthcare services including management of PHI via cloud-hosted EHR, hybrid on-premises and cloud infrastructure, and all staff and contractors with access to PHI systems |

## Column definitions

| Column | Guidance |
|---|---|
| **Control ID** | ISO 27002:2022 reference (e.g., 5.15) |
| **Control name** | Official ISO 27002:2022 title |

Great! You now have the full SoA framework in place. Here's a quick summary of where you stand and what to do next to stay on track for Stage 1 in roughly two months.

**What you have completed:**
The full 93-control SoA CSV mapped to your healthcare environment, the top 10 filled examples with specific auditor evidence requirements, and the exec checklist for CEO sign-off. These are your three core Stage 1 artifacts.

**Your critical path for the next eight weeks:**

Weeks 1 and 2 are about foundation. Get the asset register built, the IS policy consolidated and signed, roles and responsibilities documented, and the scope statement finalized. Everything else depends on these being done. The SoA itself needs to be signed by leadership this week if possible — auditors date-check it.

Weeks 3 and 4 focus on access and suppliers. Run the first access rights review on the EHR, confirm MFA is enforced for all admin and EHR accounts, and get BAAs confirmed or executed for every PHI-processing supplier. These are the two highest-probability findings at Stage 1 for a healthcare provider.

Weeks 5 and 6 are for the technical gap closures. Get the patch management procedure written and the first vulnerability scan run, finalize the IR playbooks, and complete the backup restore test. Document everything as you go — the evidence matters as much as the control.

Weeks 7 and 8 are your pre-audit dry run. Do an internal walkthrough against the SoA, check every High-rated control has at least some evidence, and confirm the management review meeting has been held and minuted.

**Three things that most commonly cause Stage 1 failures** in organizations at your starting point: an SoA with vague or missing justifications for excluded controls, no evidence that the risk assessment methodology was approved before the risk assessment was run, and access reviews that exist as a policy but have no completed records. You are now well-positioned to avoid all three.

## How to read the priority ratings

**P1 — Critical** (audit failure risk / regulatory exposure in fintech)
**P2 — High** (significant gaps, evidence typically requested early)
**P3 — Medium** (important but buildable on P1/P2 foundations)

---

## Clause-by-clause gap analysis

| Interested parties not documented | Likely implicit only | P2 | List regulators (FCA/PCI-DSS/etc.), customers, insurers, cloud providers. Document their requirements. |
| No context of the organization document | Absent | P2 | Produce internal/external issues register (can be a simple SWOT-style document) |

| No defined ISMS roles and responsibilities | Informal | P1 | Assign ISMS Owner (typically CISO or equiv.), document roles formally |
| Security not visibly on leadership agenda | Unknown | P2 | Establish a security steering group or add InfoSec to board/exec reporting cycle |

### Clause 6 — Planning (Risk)

| No formal risk assessment | Absent | P1 | This is the heart of ISO 27001. Choose a methodology (FAIR, simple likelihood/impact matrix, etc.), assess risks against your asset inventory |

| No Statement of Applicability (SoA) | Absent | P1 | The SoA is a required document listing all 93 Annex A controls, whether each is applicable, and justification. Auditors will ask for this on day one. |

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policies not consolidated | Scattered | P1 | Build a document management system (even SharePoint is fine) with version control, review dates, and ownership |

| Competence records absent | Unknown | P2 | Document security-relevant roles and evidence of competence (certs, training records) |

This is where your Azure/SaaS/hybrid profile creates the most specific gaps.

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|

Prioritize: Azure resources (use Azure Resource Graph/Defender for Cloud), SaaS apps (use Entra ID app registrations as a proxy), endpoints (Intune). Doesn't need to be perfect, needs to be defensible. |
| **Partial vendor inventory** | Incomplete | P1 | In fintech, supplier security (5.19–5.22) is heavily scrutinized. Build a register of critical suppliers: cloud providers, SaaS vendors, payment processors, data processors under GDPR. Document contractual security requirements. |
| **No formal change management** | Jira exists but informal | P2 | Formalize change records to show approval, testing, and rollback. Annex A 8.32. Your Jira workflow is a good foundation — add approval gates and security review for significant changes. |

| **No formal incident management** | Jira exists | P2 | Add a security incident classification to your Jira incident process. Document roles, escalation, and post-incident review. Annex A 5.24–5.28. |

| 5.23 Cloud services security | No cloud security policy documented | P1 |
| 8.5 Secure authentication | MFA not universal | P1 |
| 8.8 Technical vulnerability management | Patching exists but SLAs and reporting not formalized | P2 |
| 8.15/8.16 Logging and monitoring | Azure Monitor/Defender for Cloud likely partially configured — needs policy and review process | P2 |
| 6.3 Awareness and training | No formal program | P2 |
| 5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity | Likely undocumented for Azure/SaaS dependencies | P2 |

---

## Priority audit evidence to prepare first

These are the documents and records a certification auditor will ask for in Stage 1 (documentation review) and Stage 2 (evidence audit). Build these before anything else.

**Tier 1 — Must exist before Stage 1 audit**

The Statement of Applicability, ISMS scope document, Information Security Policy (exec-signed), risk assessment methodology and completed risk register, risk treatment plan with owners and timelines, and asset inventory (even if imperfect, it must exist and be actively maintained).

**Tier 2 — Must exist before Stage 2 audit**

Internal audit report (at least one cycle completed), management review minutes, MFA rollout evidence (Entra ID conditional access policies and coverage report), supplier register with security classification and contractual evidence, joiner/mover/leaver process documentation and recent access review records, patch compliance reports (at least 2–3 months of data), security awareness training completion records, incident log with at least a few closed security incidents showing the process working end-to-end, change records in Jira showing approval and security review steps, and logging/monitoring configuration evidence (Azure Defender for Cloud, SIEM if applicable).

**Tier 3 — Strongly recommended before certification**

Data classification policy with handling examples, cryptography/encryption standard, cloud security policy (covering Azure and each significant SaaS provider), business continuity and DR plan for critical systems, corrective action register showing at least one completed improvement cycle, and network architecture diagram (even a high-level one).

---

## Suggested sequencing (approximate 6–9 month roadmap)

Months 1–2 should focus on foundations: ISMS scope, Information Security Policy, asset inventory sprint, MFA rollout to all users, and appointing an ISMS owner. Months 2–4 should tackle the risk work: complete the risk assessment, produce the risk treatment plan, and draft the SoA. Simultaneously, formalize your Jira change and incident processes and build the supplier register. Months 4–6 should address the remaining P2 controls: awareness training, patching SLAs, logging review, JML process, and data classification. Months 6–8 should run the internal audit, hold management review, resolve findings, and engage a certification body for a readiness check. Months 8–9 is Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit.

---

A few fintech-specific notes worth flagging: if you're subject to FCA regulations, PCI-DSS (if card data in scope), or UK GDPR, there's significant overlap with ISO 27001 controls but also additional requirements. It's worth mapping those obligations into your risk register from the start rather than treating them separately. ## 1. Prioritized Gap Analysis Checklist

The logic here: **Must-have** items are either mandatory clauses (4–10) or Annex A controls that your regulator, auditor, or risk profile will scrutinize first in a finance/customer-data context. **Nice-to-have** items strengthen your posture but won't block certification in year one.

### Mandatory Clauses (4–10) — all required, no exceptions

## 2. Highest-Priority Controls Mapped to Your Tools — with Audit Evidence Examples

These are the controls auditors hit hardest in finance environments, matched to what you already have.

### 5.9 — Asset Inventory
**Your tools:** CMDB, Azure portal, Intune, Salesforce admin console, O365 admin center

What you need to do: extend your CMDB to cover cloud VMs, SaaS accounts, and data assets, not just on-prem major assets. Create an owner field and a data classification field.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- An exported asset register (Excel or CMDB report) covering on-prem, Azure VMs, and licensed SaaS accounts with owner and classification columns
- A documented process for how new assets get added (e.g., triggered by Azure subscription tag policy or Intune enrollment)
- A periodic review record showing the register was reviewed in the last 12 months

---

### 8.2 / 8.3 / 8.5 — Privileged Access, Access Restriction, Secure Authentication
**Your tools:** Azure AD / Entra ID, Intune, potentially PIM (Privileged Identity Management)

What you need to do: document your RBAC role matrix, enable and evidence MFA across all users (especially privileged), run and retain quarterly access reviews, and enable just-in-time access for admin roles via Azure PIM if not already done.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Azure AD access review reports (run from Entra Identity Governance — these are exportable)
- MFA registration status report showing % coverage, exported from Entra
- A role matrix document mapping job titles to Azure AD groups and permissions
- PIM activation logs showing privileged access is time-bound
- A leavers/movers process document with example tickets showing access was removed within your SLA

---

### 8.8 — Technical Vulnerability Management
**Your tools:** SCCM/Intune for patching, Splunk for logs, outsourced SOC/MDR

What you need to do: formalize a vulnerability management policy with patch SLAs by severity (e.g., critical: 48h, high: 7 days, medium: 30 days). Extend scanning to Azure workloads (Microsoft Defender for Cloud gives you this). Document what happens when a patch can't be applied (risk acceptance).

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Intune/SCCM compliance reports showing patch status by device, exportable on a schedule
- Microsoft Defender for Cloud secure score and recommendation exports for Azure assets
- A vulnerability management policy with SLAs signed by the CISO/IT director
- A risk acceptance log for patches that couldn't be deployed in SLA (even one or two examples show the process works)
- SOC/MDR monthly reports showing vulnerability findings and remediation tracking

---

### 5.19–5.22 / 5.23 — Supplier Security and Cloud Services
**Your tools:** existing vendor contracts, Azure, O365, Salesforce

What you need to do: build a supplier register, tier your suppliers by risk (Azure and Salesforce handle customer data — they're tier 1), document what security assurances you've obtained (SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certs, Microsoft shared responsibility model), and add security review clauses to new contracts.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- A supplier register with risk tier, data processed, contractual security clauses column, and last-review date
- Downloaded SOC 2 Type II reports for Salesforce and Microsoft (available via their trust portals)
- Microsoft's shared responsibility matrix for your Azure workloads, annotated to show your side
- Meeting minutes or email trail showing annual supplier security reviews
- A supplier onboarding checklist for new vendors

---

### 5.24–5.28 — Information Security Incident Management
**Your tools:** ITIL incident process, outsourced SOC/MDR, Splunk

What you need to do: overlay an IS-specific classification scheme (security event → security incident → major incident) on your existing ITIL process. Define what triggers regulatory notification (in finance this is often mandatory within 24–72h depending on jurisdiction). Document the SOC escalation path.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- An IS incident classification procedure document (can be an annex to your existing incident policy)
- SOC/MDR escalation runbook or SLA document
- A sample incident log (even from a tabletop exercise) showing classification, response, and closure
- A post-incident review record for any real or simulated security incident
- Evidence of a tabletop exercise (agenda, attendees, outcomes) — auditors love this

---

### 8.15–8.16 — Logging and Monitoring
**Your tools:** Splunk, outsourced SOC/MDR

What you need to do: document log sources, retention periods (typically 12 months online, 7 years for finance), and the alert/response SLA with your SOC. Ensure logs are protected from tampering.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- A log management policy covering sources, retention, and review frequency
- Splunk dashboard screenshot or export showing active log ingestion from key sources (Azure, on-prem, O365)
- SOC/MDR contract or SLA document referencing alert response times
- A sample SOC report or alert closure ticket showing end-to-end handling
- Evidence of log integrity protection (Splunk index checksums, or Azure Monitor immutable storage)

---

### 8.32 — Change Management
**Your tools:** ITIL change process

What you need to do: add an information security review step to your change advisory board (CAB) process. This doesn't need to be heavyweight — a checkbox and a named reviewer on the change record is enough for most audits.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Change records (from your ITSM tool) showing an IS review field populated
- CAB meeting minutes referencing security sign-off on significant changes
- A change management procedure document referencing the IS review step

---

## 3. Statement of Applicability — Template Outline

The SoA is a mandatory document (Clause 6.1.3d). It lists all 93 Annex A controls, states whether each is applicable, provides a justification, and references the implementation evidence. Here is a working structure.

---

**[Organisation Name] — Statement of Applicability**

The main body of the SoA is a table with one row per control. Use this column structure:

| Control ref | e.g., 5.9 |

Include a simple count: total controls applicable, total excluded, total fully implemented, partially implemented, and planned. This shows the auditor you have a handle on your programme.

---

**Section 4 — Review and Approval**

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISMS Owner | | | |
| IT Director / CISO | | | |
| Management Representative | | | |

Review frequency: annually, or following significant changes to scope, risk profile, or the standard.

Owners are abbreviated: **IL** = IT Lead, **SEC** = Security/CISO, **HR** = HR Manager, **LGL** = Legal/Compliance, **MGT** = Senior Management. Effort estimates are realistic for a 250-person firm running this alongside business-as-usual. Where a task says "ongoing" it means it needs a recurring calendar entry, not constant active work.

*Goal: ISMS exists on paper, risk assessment complete, SoA drafted, executive buy-in secured.*

## Completing the Vulnerability Management Policy

---

**Remediation SLAs (completed)**

| Severity | Definition | Remediation SLA | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) | Actively exploited or unauthenticated remote code execution | 48 hours | Log4Shell, MOVEit-style zero-day |
| High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) | Significant exposure, likely exploitable, no active exploitation confirmed | 7 calendar days | Unpatched RDP, privilege escalation on domain controller |
| Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) | Exploitable under specific conditions, limited blast radius | 30 calendar days | Outdated TLS version, missing security headers |
| Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) | Minimal risk, requires local access or chained exploitation | 90 calendar days | Informational misconfigurations, deprecated cipher suites |
| Informational | No direct risk, best-practice recommendation | Next scheduled maintenance window | Banner disclosure, verbose error messages |

Where a patch is unavailable from the vendor, a compensating control (network isolation, WAF rule, enhanced monitoring) must be documented and approved by the CISO within the same SLA window. The absence of a vendor patch does not pause the SLA clock.

**Escalation.** If a Critical or High vulnerability cannot be remediated within its SLA, the IT Lead must notify the CISO within 24 hours of the SLA breach. The CISO must notify the relevant business owner and, where customer data is at material risk, the Legal/Compliance team within a further 24 hours. All escalations must be logged in the risk register as a risk acceptance or treatment item.

**Exceptions.** Any exception to this policy (including SLA extensions) requires written approval from the CISO, must document the business justification and compensating controls in place, and must be reviewed every 30 days until resolved. Exceptions exceeding 90 days require sign-off from senior management. The exception log is reviewed at each management review meeting.

**Measurement.** The IT Lead produces a monthly vulnerability dashboard covering: total open findings by severity, SLA compliance rate, mean time to remediate by severity, and number of active exceptions. This report is provided to the CISO and tabled at the quarterly security review.

**Review.** This policy is reviewed annually or following a significant vulnerability incident, material change to the IT estate, or relevant regulatory guidance update.

| Regulation / body | Trigger | Notification deadline |
|---|---|---|

On the SoA, fill in every row even if the status is "Not started" — a blank cell looks worse to an auditor than an honest "planned with justification." On the incident rubric, share it with your outsourced SOC so their escalation thresholds match yours — a mismatch there is a common Stage 2 audit finding. ## Access Control Policy

---

**Document title:** Access Control Policy
**Document reference:** POL-003
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Draft
**Owner:** IT Lead / CISO
**Approved by:** *(signature block at end)*
**Date issued:** [date]
**Next review date:** [date + 1 year]
**Classification:** Internal

---

**1. Purpose**

This policy defines how [Organisation Name] controls access to its information assets, systems, and data to ensure that access is granted on a need-to-know, least-privilege basis, is actively managed throughout the access lifecycle, and is reviewed regularly. It supports compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls 5.15, 5.16, 5.17, 5.18, 8.2, 8.3, and 8.5, and with applicable regulatory requirements including [UK FCA/PRA rules / GDPR — confirm with Legal].

---

**2. Scope**

This policy applies to all employees, contractors, third-party suppliers, and any other individuals accessing [Organisation Name] systems, applications, or data, whether on-premises, via Microsoft Azure, or via SaaS platforms including Microsoft 365 and Salesforce. It covers all access methods including corporate devices, remote access, and service accounts.

---

**3. Roles and Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| CISO / Security Lead | Policy ownership, annual review, exception approval, privileged access oversight |
| IT Lead | Technical implementation, access provisioning and deprovisioning, access review execution, MFA enforcement |
| People / HR Manager | Triggering joiners/movers/leavers notifications, confirming role changes, maintaining employment records |
| Line Managers | Requesting access for their staff, approving access requests, confirming access is still required at review |
| All Users | Complying with this policy, not sharing credentials, reporting suspected unauthorised access immediately |
| Legal / Compliance | Advising on regulatory access obligations, reviewing access logs where required for investigations |

---

**4. Access Provisioning — Principles**

All access must be formally requested and approved before it is granted. Requests must specify the system, the level of access required, and the business justification. The IT Lead provisions access only on receipt of an approved request; verbal requests are not sufficient.

**Least privilege.** Users are granted the minimum level of access required to perform their role. Access to customer data, financial records, and systems classified Confidential or Restricted requires explicit business justification approved by the relevant line manager and, for Restricted data, the CISO.

**Need to know.** Access to sensitive data is restricted to individuals who require it to fulfil a specific, defined business function. Broad or department-wide access to sensitive data stores is not permitted without documented justification.

**Segregation of duties.** No single individual should have end-to-end control over a sensitive process. Where technically feasible, the person who requests a change should not be the same person who approves and implements it.

---

**5. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**

Access to all systems must be managed through defined roles rather than individual permissions wherever technically possible. Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) groups and roles are the primary mechanism for RBAC enforcement across cloud and hybrid systems.

A role matrix must be maintained by the IT Lead, mapping job titles and functions to system roles and permission levels. The role matrix is reviewed as part of each access review cycle and updated within 5 business days of any role change. The current role matrix is maintained at [document location / SharePoint link].

Default access for new starters is defined per role in the role matrix. Any access beyond the default requires a separate approved access request.

---

**6. Privileged Access and Just-in-Time (JIT) Access**

Privileged access — including domain administrator, global administrator, subscription owner, and any role with the ability to modify security controls, access bulk customer data, or alter audit logs — is subject to the following controls in addition to standard access rules.

Privileged roles must not be used for routine day-to-day tasks. Individuals requiring privileged access must hold a separate privileged account distinct from their standard user account. Privileged accounts must not have mailboxes or be used for browsing or email.

Just-in-time access via Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is mandatory for all Azure and Microsoft 365 privileged roles. Activation requires business justification, is time-limited (maximum 8-hour sessions unless CISO-approved exception), and generates an audit log. Standing privileged access is not permitted for cloud roles except where technically unavoidable, in which case a documented exception approved by the CISO is required.

The number of privileged accounts must be kept to the minimum necessary. The IT Lead reviews the full list of privileged accounts monthly and reports exceptions to the CISO.

---

**7. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)**

MFA is mandatory for all user accounts without exception. The following minimum standards apply.

| Access type | MFA requirement |
|---|---|
| All corporate users (standard) | MFA required for all authentication, enforced via Entra ID Conditional Access |
| Privileged / admin accounts | Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 key or certificate-based) required |
| Remote access / VPN | MFA required as a condition of connection |
| SaaS platforms (O365, Salesforce) | MFA enforced at identity provider (Entra ID SSO) |
| Service accounts | MFA not applicable — mitigated by IP restriction, certificate auth, and no interactive login |
| Third-party / contractor access | MFA required; provisioned via guest account or approved remote access method only |

Exceptions to MFA requirements are not permitted without written CISO approval and a documented compensating control. MFA registration status is reviewed monthly by the IT Lead using the Entra ID MFA registration report.

---

**8. Joiners, Movers, and Leavers (JML)**

HR must notify the IT Lead of all starters, role changes, and leavers within the timelines below. The IT Lead is responsible for acting within the specified window.

| Event | HR notification | IT action required | SLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| New starter (joiner) | Before or on first day | Provision access per role matrix, enrol MFA, issue device | Same day as start |
| Role change (mover) | Before effective date | Adjust access to new role, remove access no longer required | Within 2 business days |
| Resignation / termination (leaver) | Immediately on confirmation | Disable account, revoke all sessions, remove from all groups | Within 2 hours for involuntary; end of last working day for voluntary |
| Contractor end of engagement | Before end date | As per leaver process | End of last day |
| Prolonged absence (>30 days) | When confirmed | Disable account for duration | Within 2 business days of confirmation |

Leavers' accounts must be disabled, not deleted, for a minimum of 30 days following departure to allow for investigation if required, then deleted in accordance with the Data Classification and Retention Policy.

---

**9. Access Reviews**

Formal access reviews must be conducted at the following cadence. All review outputs must be retained as evidence for a minimum of 3 years.

| Review type | Frequency | Owner | Method | Evidence retained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All-user access review | Quarterly | IT Lead | Entra ID access review (Identity Governance) | Exported review report, remediation log |
| Privileged account review | Monthly | IT Lead + CISO | Manual review of PIM role assignments | Review log, any removals documented |
| Service account review | Quarterly | IT Lead | Manual review of service principals and managed identities | Review log |
| SaaS platform review (Salesforce, O365) | Quarterly | IT Lead | Admin console user export, manager confirmation | Exported user list, manager sign-off emails |
| Supplier / third-party access review | Annually (or on contract change) | IT Lead + Legal | Review of active guest accounts and VPN credentials | Review log |

Where a review identifies access that is no longer required or appropriate, it must be removed within 5 business days of identification. Where removal is not immediately possible, it must be logged as an exception and approved by the CISO.

---

**10. Exceptions**

Any exception to this policy requires written approval from the CISO, must document the business justification and any compensating controls, and must be reviewed every 30 days. Exceptions are logged in the Policy Exception Register maintained by the CISO. Exceptions exceeding 90 days require sign-off from senior management.

---

**11. Non-Compliance**

Breach of this policy may result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal, in accordance with [Organisation Name]'s disciplinary procedure. Where a breach constitutes a criminal offence or regulatory violation, the matter will be referred to the appropriate authority.

---

**12. Related Documents**

Information Security Policy (POL-001) | Acceptable Use Policy (POL-002) | Data Classification Policy (POL-004) | Vulnerability Management Policy (POL-005) | Incident Management Policy (POL-006) | Supplier Security Policy (POL-007)

---

**13. Review and Sign-Off**

This policy is reviewed annually by the CISO or following any material change to the access control environment, a significant access-related incident, or relevant regulatory guidance update.

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policy Owner (CISO / IT Lead) | | | |
| Senior Management Sponsor | | | |
| Legal / Compliance Review | | | |

---
