## Data Classification Policy

---

**Document title:** Data Classification Policy
**Document reference:** POL-004
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Draft
**Owner:** CISO / Legal & Compliance
**Approved by:** *(signature block at end)*
**Date issued:** [date]
**Next review date:** [date + 1 year]
**Classification:** Internal

---

**1. Purpose**

This policy defines how [Organisation Name] classifies, handles, labels, retains, and disposes of information assets to ensure that data is protected proportionately to its sensitivity, regulatory weight, and business value. It supports compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls 5.9, 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, and 8.10, and with applicable regulatory obligations including UK GDPR, FCA data management rules, and PCI DSS where card data is in scope. All employees, contractors, and third parties handling [Organisation Name] data must comply with this policy.

---

**2. Scope**

This policy applies to all information assets owned or processed by [Organisation Name] in any format — digital or physical — including documents, emails, database records, system logs, configuration files, and verbal communications where they relate to classified information. It covers all environments within the ISMS scope: on-premises systems, Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and any other SaaS platform processing organisational data.

---

**3. Classification Tiers**

[Organisation Name] uses four classification tiers. Every information asset must be assigned a classification at creation or first receipt. When in doubt, classify at the higher tier.

---

**Tier 1 — Public**

Information that has been approved for unrestricted external release and would cause no harm if disclosed to any audience.

*Examples:* Published marketing materials, press releases, job advertisements, publicly available product information, the organisation's website content.

*Default assumption:* Nothing is Public unless explicitly approved for external release by an authorised owner.

---

**Tier 2 — Internal**

Information intended for use within [Organisation Name] that is not sensitive but is not approved for external distribution. Disclosure would cause minor embarrassment or operational inconvenience but no material harm.

*Examples:* Internal process documentation, meeting agendas with no sensitive content, general staff communications, internal project plans not containing financial or personal data, IT asset lists with no security-sensitive detail.

---

**Tier 3 — Confidential**

Information that is sensitive, commercially valuable, or subject to contractual or regulatory protection. Unauthorised disclosure could cause financial loss, reputational damage, regulatory sanction, or harm to individuals.

*Examples:* Customer personal data (names, contact details, account references), employee records, financial reports not yet published, contracts and commercial agreements, audit findings, security policies and procedures, system architecture diagrams.

*This tier covers the majority of data processed in the normal course of business in a finance firm.*

---

**Tier 4 — Restricted**

The highest classification. Information whose unauthorised disclosure would cause severe harm to the organisation, its customers, or individuals — including regulatory breach, significant financial loss, criminal liability, or risk to personal safety.

*Examples:* Customer financial account credentials or payment card data, bulk personal data exports, cryptographic keys and certificates, privileged access credentials, active incident investigation records, merger and acquisition information, regulatory investigation correspondence, data subject access request responses containing third-party data.

---

**4. Handling Rules by Tier**

| Control | Public | Internal | Confidential | Restricted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access | Anyone | All staff | Need-to-know, role-based | Named individuals only, CISO approval for new access |
| Storage (digital) | Any approved system | Any corporate system | Encrypted storage only; no personal devices or unapproved cloud | Encrypted storage with access logging; Azure storage with private endpoint and no public blob access |
| Storage (physical) | No restriction | Locked away when unattended | Locked cabinet; clear desk enforced | Secure cabinet with restricted key access; logged in and out |
| Transmission (email) | Unrestricted | Internal email acceptable | Encrypted email or secure file transfer; no unencrypted external email | Encrypted channel only; explicit recipient approval required; no bulk export without CISO sign-off |
| Transmission (file share) | Public-facing systems permitted | Internal SharePoint / Teams | SharePoint with appropriate permissions; no personal cloud storage (Dropbox etc.) | Dedicated SharePoint site with restricted membership and audit logging enabled |
| Printing | Unrestricted | Permitted | Collect immediately from printer; do not leave unattended | Avoid printing; if essential, supervised printing only and secure disposal immediately after use |
| Disposal (digital) | Standard deletion | Standard deletion | Secure deletion per disposal procedure; confirm in asset register | Cryptographic erasure or verified secure wipe; documented and signed off by IT Lead |
| Disposal (physical) | Recycling | Cross-cut shredding | Cross-cut shredding or confidential waste contractor | Witnessed destruction; certificate of destruction retained |
| Sharing with third parties | Permitted | Permitted with manager approval | Permitted only under NDA or DPA; log the disclosure | CISO approval required; legal review recommended; log in supplier register |
| Incident notification if lost | Not required | Log internally | Notify IT Lead and CISO within 1 hour | Treat as security incident immediately; invoke incident procedure |

---

**5. Labelling**

All documents and files must carry a visible classification label. Use the standard labels below. In Microsoft 365, sensitivity labels must be applied using Microsoft Purview Information Protection (configured by IT Lead). Physical documents must be marked in the header and footer.

| Classification | Label text | Microsoft Purview label name | Physical document marking |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public | PUBLIC | Public | Header and footer: PUBLIC |
| Internal | INTERNAL | Internal | Header and footer: INTERNAL |
| Confidential | CONFIDENTIAL | Confidential | Header and footer: CONFIDENTIAL |
| Restricted | RESTRICTED — [reason, e.g., CUSTOMER DATA] | Restricted | Header and footer: RESTRICTED — [reason]; cover page required for multi-page documents |

Automated labelling policies in Microsoft Purview should be configured to detect and suggest labels for content containing personal data, financial account numbers, or payment card data. The IT Lead is responsible for maintaining the Purview label configuration.

---

**6. Labelling and Handling Examples by Platform**

**Salesforce records**

Customer account records in Salesforce containing name, contact details, and financial account references are classified **Confidential** by default. Records containing payment card numbers, authentication credentials, or bulk data exports are **Restricted**. Access must be provisioned via role-based profiles in Salesforce, aligned to the role matrix in the Access Control Policy. Salesforce reports or exports containing customer PII must not be saved to personal devices or unapproved storage. Any bulk export of customer records requires CISO approval and must be logged in the asset register as a data extract with a defined retention period and deletion date. Salesforce fields containing card data must be masked at display level and access-logged.

**SharePoint documents**

All SharePoint sites must have a designated owner responsible for access and classification. Documents must carry a Microsoft Purview sensitivity label matching their classification tier. SharePoint sites containing Confidential or Restricted content must have external sharing disabled, guest access blocked, and audit logging enabled. Documents auto-classified by Purview as containing personal data or financial information must be reviewed by the site owner within 10 business days and confirmed or reclassified. HR records, legal correspondence, and security documentation must be stored in dedicated SharePoint sites with restricted membership, not in general department sites. No Restricted documents should be stored in SharePoint without IT Lead confirmation that the site has the correct access controls and audit logging in place.

**Azure storage blobs**

All Azure storage accounts must be configured with public blob access disabled by default; this must be enforced via Azure Policy at the subscription level. Storage accounts containing Confidential or Restricted data must enable encryption at rest using Microsoft-managed keys as a minimum, with customer-managed keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault required for Restricted data stores. Blob containers must be tagged with the data classification, data owner, and retention date using the organisation's standard Azure tagging policy. Access to storage accounts must be via private endpoints only for Confidential and Restricted tiers; no public endpoint exposure is permitted. Shared Access Signature (SAS) tokens for Confidential or Restricted storage must be time-limited (maximum 24 hours), scoped to the minimum required permissions, and their generation logged. Storage accounts must not use account-level access keys for application access; managed identities or service principals with RBAC are required.

---

**7. Retention and Deletion**

Information must be retained for the minimum period required by law, regulation, or business need, and deleted securely when that period expires. The table below gives standard retention periods for common data types in a finance firm. Legal must confirm these against your specific regulatory obligations before this policy is finalised.

| Data type | Classification | Minimum retention | Maximum retention | Deletion method |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Customer financial records | Confidential / Restricted | 6 years (FCA COBS / SYSC) | 7 years | Secure deletion; confirmed in asset register |
| Customer personal data (non-financial) | Confidential | Duration of relationship + 6 years | As above unless shorter purpose limitation applies | Secure deletion; subject access / erasure requests handled per GDPR procedure |
| Employee records | Confidential | Duration of employment + 6 years | 7 years post-employment | Secure deletion by HR, confirmed by IT Lead |
| Payment card data (if in scope) | Restricted | As short as possible; PCI DSS prohibits retention of sensitive authentication data post-authorisation | Do not retain beyond authorisation | Cryptographic erasure or verified secure wipe; certificate retained |
| Security logs and audit trails | Internal / Confidential | 12 months online (Splunk) | 7 years archived (regulatory requirement for finance) | Standard deletion from archive after retention period; IT Lead confirms |
| Contracts and legal agreements | Confidential | Duration + 7 years | 10 years for significant contracts | Secure deletion; legal sign-off before deletion |
| Incident records | Confidential | 3 years | 7 years if regulatory investigation involved | Secure deletion; CISO sign-off before deletion |
| Backup data | Varies (inherits source classification) | Per backup policy | Must not exceed retention period of source data | Cryptographic erasure on decommission; backup job deletion logs retained |
| System and application logs | Internal | 90 days online | 12 months; 7 years if subject to investigation hold | Standard deletion; IT Lead confirms |

**Deletion process.** When a retention period expires, the data owner is responsible for initiating deletion. The IT Lead confirms technical deletion and updates the asset register. For Restricted data, deletion must be witnessed or verified by a second person and recorded with date, method, and confirmation in the asset register. Deletion must not be deferred without a documented legal hold or CISO-approved exception.

**Legal holds.** Where data is subject to litigation, regulatory investigation, or a subject access request, normal retention and deletion schedules are suspended for the relevant data until Legal confirms the hold is lifted. Legal is responsible for notifying the IT Lead of holds and their removal.

---

**8. Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| CISO | Policy ownership, annual review, exception approval, oversight of classification programme |
| IT Lead | Technical implementation of labelling tools, storage controls, deletion procedures, and Azure tagging policy |
| Legal / Compliance | Confirming regulatory retention requirements, managing legal holds, reviewing third-party data sharing |
| Data Owners (business leads) | Assigning classification to assets they own, reviewing and confirming labels annually, approving access requests |
| All Staff | Applying correct labels at creation, handling data per tier rules, reporting suspected misclassification or data loss immediately |
| HR | Applying policy to employee records, triggering deletion on leaver process completion |

---

**9. Exceptions**

Any exception to handling or retention rules requires written approval from the CISO, must document the justification and risk, and is reviewed every 30 days. Exceptions are logged in the Policy Exception Register. Exceptions involving Restricted data or regulatory retention requirements must also be reviewed by Legal.

---

**10. Related Documents**

Information Security Policy (POL-001) | Acceptable Use Policy (POL-002) | Access Control Policy (POL-003) | Supplier Security Policy (POL-007) | Incident Management Policy (POL-006) | Asset Register | Microsoft Purview Label Configuration Guide (IT-DOC-012)

---

**11. Review and Sign-Off**

This policy is reviewed annually by the CISO and Legal, or following a data classification-related incident, a material change to the data environment, or relevant regulatory or legislative update.

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policy Owner (CISO) | | | |
| Legal / Compliance Review | | | |
| Senior Management Sponsor | | | |

# ISO 27001 Certification Readiness: Healthcare Hybrid Org (~350 employees)

---

## 1. Prioritized Gap-Analysis Checklist

Your existing stack gives you a strong foundation. The gaps below reflect what healthcare hybrid orgs typically find missing at Stage 1 audit. Work through these before engaging a certification body.

**Risk rating logic:** High = likely audit nonconformity or PHI exposure risk. Medium = required but often partially in place. Low = typically evidenced by existing tooling with minor documentation work.

---

### Clause 4–10 (Management System Requirements)

| Gap | Risk | Quick win? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Formal ISMS scope document (Clause 4.3) | High | Yes | One-page document defining boundaries, locations, exclusions. Do this first. |
| Interested parties register (Clause 4.2) | High | Yes | List regulators (HHS/OCR), patients, insurers, cloud providers. Document their requirements. |
| Information security policy signed by top management (Clause 5.2) | High | Yes | Must be explicit, dated, and communicated. Often exists but isn't formally approved. |
| Formal risk assessment methodology (Clause 6.1.2) | High | No | Needs documented criteria for likelihood, impact, and risk acceptance. PHI context adds weight. |
| Risk treatment plan and Statement of Applicability (Clause 6.1.3) | High | No | The SoA is the central audit document. Every Annex A control must be included with justification for inclusion or exclusion. |
| Information security objectives with metrics (Clause 6.2) | Medium | Yes | Link to existing KPIs if you have them (patch SLA, incident MTTR, etc.). |
| Internal audit programme (Clause 9.2) | High | No | Needs independence. Can use internal resource if not auditing own work. |
| Management review meeting (Clause 9.3) | Medium | Yes | Schedule one and minute it. Agenda items are prescribed by the standard. |
| Continual improvement register (Clause 10.2) | Medium | Yes | A simple log of identified improvements. Can be a spreadsheet initially. |

---

### Annex A Control Gaps (2022 version, 93 controls)

**Organisational controls (5.x) — High priority gaps**

| Control | Risk | Quick win? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.9 Inventory of information assets | High | No | CMDB covers IT assets well. PHI data flows, data stores, and classifications likely undocumented. Add data asset layer. |
| 5.10 Acceptable use of information assets | Medium | Yes | Policy likely exists. Confirm it covers BYOD, Azure, and PHI handling explicitly. |
| 5.12 Classification of information | High | No | Healthcare orgs frequently lack a formal classification scheme (PHI, confidential, public). Required for Annex A and HIPAA alignment. |
| 5.13 Labelling of information | Medium | No | Follows from 5.12. Azure Information Protection (AIP/Purview) can help but needs policy first. |
| 5.15 Access control policy | High | No | AD covers authentication. Need documented policy covering need-to-know, role-based access, privileged access, and review cycles. |
| 5.19–5.22 Supplier security | Medium | No | Basic vendor management exists. Needs formal supplier information security policy, risk assessments for critical suppliers (Azure, EHR vendor), and contract clauses. |
| 5.23 Information security for cloud services | High | No | Specific to 2022 update. Azure shared responsibility model must be documented. Azure Policy and Defender for Cloud help evidence this. |
| 5.24–5.28 Incident management | Low | Yes | Strong ITIL foundation here. Gaps likely in classification of security events vs. service incidents, and PHI breach notification timelines. |
| 5.29 Information security during disruption | Medium | No | Business continuity planning for IS. Likely partial. Document recovery objectives for PHI systems explicitly. |
| 5.34 Privacy and protection of PII | High | No | Direct PHI relevance. Needs a privacy notice, data subject rights process, and retention schedule. |
| 5.36 Compliance with policies | Medium | Yes | Define how compliance is checked. SCCM/Intune compliance reporting can evidence this. |

**People controls (6.x)**

| Control | Risk | Quick win? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 Screening | Medium | No | Pre-employment background checks. Document process and retain evidence. |
| 6.3 Information security awareness | High | No | Healthcare is a top phishing target. Need documented annual training with completion records. E-learning platforms work well here. |
| 6.4 Disciplinary process | Low | Yes | HR policy likely exists. Confirm it references IS violations explicitly. |
| 6.5 Responsibilities after termination | Medium | Yes | AD offboarding process likely exists. Document it formally and include Intune device wipe. |

**Physical controls (7.x)**

| Control | Risk | Quick win? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1–7.4 Physical security perimeter, entry controls | Medium | No | On-prem estate needs documented physical security controls, visitor logs, and clear desk policy. Often overlooked. |
| 7.9 Security of assets off-premises | Medium | Yes | Laptops and mobile devices. Intune/BitLocker gives you technical controls. Document the policy. |

**Technological controls (8.x) — Your strongest area**

| Control | Risk | Quick win? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.2 Privileged access management | High | No | AD likely has privileged accounts. Need PAM policy, just-in-time access consideration, and review schedule. Azure PIM can help for cloud. |
| 8.4 Access to source code | Low | Yes | If applicable. Document controls around any development systems. |
| 8.7 Protection against malware | Low | Yes | Defender for Endpoint via Intune. Document the control and evidence coverage reporting. |
| 8.8 Technical vulnerability management | Medium | Yes | SCCM/Intune patching is strong. Document SLAs (e.g. critical patches within 72 hours), exceptions process, and evidence patch compliance reports. |
| 8.9 Configuration management | Medium | Yes | CMDB plus SCCM baselines. Document configuration standards (CIS benchmarks are a good reference). |
| 8.15 Logging | Low | Yes | Azure Sentinel is excellent evidence. Document retention periods (minimum 12 months for ISO, longer for HIPAA). |
| 8.16 Monitoring activities | Medium | Yes | Sentinel alert rules exist presumably. Document what is monitored, alert thresholds, and response SLAs. |
| 8.23 Web filtering | Medium | No | Document if in place. If not, proxy or DNS filtering (e.g. Defender for Endpoint web protection) is a quick add. |

| 8.32 Change management | Low | Yes | ITIL change process is strong evidence. Confirm security impact assessment is a formal step in CAB. |

---

## 3. Proposed 9–12 Month Roadmap to Certification

The roadmap assumes you'll pursue Stage 1 audit (documentation review) around month 8–9 and Stage 2 audit (evidence and operations review) around month 11–12. Most certification bodies require at least 3 months of ISMS operation before Stage 2.

---

### Phase 1: Foundations (Months 1–3)

The goal here is to establish the management system skeleton. Everything else hangs off this.

**Month 1 — Scope and context**
Appoint an ISMS lead (internal or consultant). Define and document the ISMS scope, context, and interested parties. Begin the asset inventory extension to cover PHI data stores and flows. This is your highest-value early activity because risk assessment depends on it.

**Month 2 — Risk and policy**
Develop the risk assessment methodology and run your first formal risk assessment. Prioritise PHI assets and hybrid infrastructure. Draft the information security policy, access control policy, and classification scheme. Get top management sign-off on policy — this is a frequent Stage 1 failure point.

**Month 3 — Statement of Applicability**
Produce the SoA. For each of the 93 Annex A controls, document whether it is included or excluded and why. This document is the centrepiece of your audit. For excluded controls, the justification must be documented and risk-based.

---

### Phase 2: Control Implementation (Months 4–7)

Focus on closing the high and medium gaps identified above.

**Month 4 — Access and privilege**
Document the access control policy and implement a formal access review cycle (quarterly recommended for healthcare). Configure Azure PIM for privileged cloud roles if not already done. Document AD privileged account inventory and review process.

**Month 5 — Supplier and cloud security**
Formalise the supplier management process: risk-tier your vendors, issue security questionnaires to critical suppliers (EHR vendor, Azure, any PHI processors), and confirm BAAs are in place. Document the Azure shared responsibility model and pull Defender for Cloud compliance reports as evidence for 5.23.

**Month 6 — Awareness training and physical security**
Roll out security awareness training (KnowBe4, Proofpoint, or Microsoft Security Training all work well). Healthcare phishing simulation is worth doing here. Conduct a physical security walkthrough of on-prem sites and document findings. Implement or document clean desk, visitor log, and secure print controls.

**Month 7 — Remaining technical controls**
Document cryptography policy covering BitLocker key management, TLS standards, and Azure encryption. Formalise patch management SLAs and document exceptions process. Add security impact assessment to the CAB RFC template. Document web filtering and malware protection configurations with evidence of coverage.

---

### Phase 3: Operate and Evidence (Months 7–9)

This phase is critical. Auditors don't just review documents — they look for evidence that the ISMS has been operating.

**Months 7–8 — Run the ISMS**
Hold the first management review meeting and minute it formally. Run the internal audit programme (at least one full cycle before Stage 2). Document nonconformities and corrective actions. Ensure Sentinel alert handling, patch cycles, change records, and incident tickets are accumulating as evidence. The minimum operating period most certification bodies look for is 3 months, so this window matters.

**Month 9 — Stage 1 audit (documentation review)**
Engage your chosen accredited certification body. Stage 1 is a desk review of your ISMS documentation. Common findings at this stage include an incomplete SoA, missing risk treatment plan linkage, and undocumented management review. Treat any findings as corrective actions immediately.

---

### Phase 4: Certification (Months 10–12)

**Months 10–11 — Close Stage 1 findings**
Address any nonconformities from Stage 1. Continue accumulating operational evidence. Consider a pre-audit readiness review with your certification body or an external consultant.

**Month 12 — Stage 2 audit (certification audit)**
Auditors will interview staff, review evidence, test controls, and verify that the ISMS is operational and effective. For healthcare, expect particular scrutiny on PHI asset classification, access control, incident response (including breach notification), and supplier security for PHI processors. Successful Stage 2 results in ISO 27001 certification valid for 3 years, subject to annual surveillance audits.

---

### A note on HIPAA alignment

Your PHI context means ISO 27001 and HIPAA Security Rule controls overlap significantly. The risk assessment methodology, access controls, audit logging, incident response, and workforce training requirements map closely. Running them in parallel adds modest overhead but avoids duplication of effort. It's worth mapping your SoA to the HIPAA Security Rule safeguards as a secondary column — auditors and OCR both respond well to this.

# Deliverable 2: Risk Assessment Scoring Matrix

## How to use this matrix

This matrix implements the ISO 27001:2022 Clause 6.1.2 risk assessment methodology calibrated for your environment. Every identified risk gets a Likelihood score, an Impact score, and a resulting Risk Rating. The Risk Owner column maps to your ISMS RACI. Treat any risk scoring 15 or above as requiring immediate treatment before Stage 2 audit.

For Excel implementation, Likelihood and Impact should be dropdown fields (1–5). The Risk Rating cell should be a formula: `=Likelihood*Impact`. The Treatment column should be a dropdown: Treat / Tolerate / Transfer / Terminate.

---

## Scoring scales

**Likelihood (1–5)**

| Score | Label | Definition in your context |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | No known occurrence in similar healthcare orgs in past 3 years. Requires sophisticated, targeted attack. |
| 2 | Unlikely | Occurs occasionally in the sector. Requires deliberate effort to exploit. |
| 3 | Possible | Known attack vector in healthcare. Could occur without significant attacker skill. |
| 4 | Likely | Commonly exploited in healthcare. Existing controls are partial or unverified. |
| 5 | Almost certain | Actively exploited in the wild against Epic, PACS, or hybrid Azure environments. Minimal current control. |

**Impact (1–5)**

| Score | Label | Definition in your context |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | No PHI exposure. No operational disruption. No regulatory consequence. |
| 2 | Minor | Limited PHI exposure (<10 records). Brief disruption to non-critical system. Low regulatory risk. |
| 3 | Moderate | PHI exposure requiring OCR notification assessment. Disruption to non-Epic clinical support systems. Reputational risk. |
| 4 | Significant | Confirmed PHI breach requiring OCR notification. Epic or PACS unavailability >4 hours. Potential OCR investigation. |
| 5 | Severe | Large-scale PHI breach (>500 records, triggering OCR wall-of-shame). Epic ransomware with patient safety impact. Regulatory action, litigation, or financial penalty. |

**Risk rating**

| Score range | Rating | Action required |
|---|---|---|
| 20–25 | Critical | Immediate treatment. Escalate to exec sponsor. Must be remediated before Stage 2 audit. |
| 15–19 | High | Treatment plan required within 30 days. Document in risk treatment plan. |
| 10–14 | Medium | Treatment plan required within 90 days. Accept with documented rationale if deferred. |
| 5–9 | Low | Monitor. Accept with documented rationale or treat in next planning cycle. |
| 1–4 | Negligible | Accept. Document rationale. Review annually. |

---

# Packing Timeline & Room-by-Room Checklist

---

## THE LABELING SYSTEM

Simple and consistent beats elaborate. Use this across every box.

**Box Label Formula:**
```
DESTINATION ROOM — Contents (brief)
Priority: FIRST IN / NORMAL / LAST LOAD
Fragile: YES / NO
Owner: M / P / J
Box #: ___ of ___ (fill in total when the room is done)
```

**Color Code (use colored tape or markers):**
- 🔴 Red = Kitchen
- 🔵 Blue = Bedroom(s)
- 🟢 Green = Bathroom
- 🟡 Yellow = Living Room
- ⬜ White / Black = Office / Documents
- 🟠 Orange = Garage / Tools
- 🟣 Purple = Dog / Pet supplies
- ✳️ Star sticker = FIRST IN (unpack immediately)

---

## PRINTABLE BOX LABEL

Print or write on an index card and tape to the TOP and one SIDE of every box.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROOM: _________________________________│
│  CONTENTS: _____________________________│
│  _______________________________________│
│  PRIORITY:  □ FIRST IN  □ NORMAL        │
│             □ LAST LOAD □ DO NOT LOAD * │
│  FRAGILE:   □ YES   □ NO               │
│  OWNER:     □ M   □ P   □ J            │
│  BOX #: _______ of _______ (this room) │
│  TOTAL WEIGHT (approx): _______________│
└─────────────────────────────────────────│
  * DO NOT LOAD = stays in the car
```

Tape one label to the **top** and one to a **side** so you can read it in a stack. Mark FRAGILE boxes on all four sides and the top.

---

## THE "LAST OUT / FIRST IN" BOX PLAN

Each room gets one dedicated box that is **packed last and loaded last** so it comes off the truck first. Mark it with a star sticker and "FIRST IN" on every side. These boxes ride together near the back of the truck door, not buried inside.

**What goes in a First In box — by room:**

**Kitchen First In Box** *(red star)*
One pot, one pan, one baking sheet, 2 sets of plates and cutlery, 2 mugs, dish soap, sponge, paper towels, coffee maker and coffee, can opener, and 2–3 days of non-perishable food.

**Bedroom First In Box** *(blue star)*
Bedding set for each bed (sheets, pillowcases, one blanket), pajamas, alarm clock or phone charger, eye masks if used, and any white noise machine.

**Bathroom First In Box** *(green star)*
Toilet paper (bring at least 4 rolls), hand soap, 2 towels per person, shower curtain and rings if yours, basic cleaning spray, and a small mirror.

**Office / Documents First In Box** *(white star)*
Power strip, laptop charger, router and cables, pens and notepad, any work items needed on day one.

**Living Room First In Box** *(yellow star)*
TV remote, any streaming device, one throw blanket, phone charger, and a lamp if overhead lighting is poor.

**Dog First In Box** *(purple star — stays in the car, not the truck)*
Food and bowls, water, leash, bed, familiar toy, poop bags, and a small treat bag.

**"Survival Kit" Bag — Rides in the Car**
This is not a box. It's a duffel or tote that never goes in the truck: 3–4 days of clothes per person, all medications, toiletry kits, phone chargers, documents folder, dog bag, cash, and snacks.

---

## PACKING SCHEDULE OVERVIEW

Your move is 10 weeks out. The goal is to have everything except daily essentials packed by **the end of Week 2 before move day** (8 weeks of packing across the schedule below).

| Week | Focus | Owner | Est. Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10–9 | Declutter whole house; order supplies | J | 4–8 hrs total |
| 8 | Storage, garage, off-season items | J | 4–6 hrs |
| 7 | Books, decor, guest room, spare closets | J | 3–5 hrs |
| 6 | Living room non-essentials, art, media | J | 2–4 hrs |
| 5 | Bedrooms (off-season clothes, extras) | J | 3–5 hrs |
| 4 | Kitchen (keep 1 week of essentials out) | J | 4–6 hrs |
| 3 | Bathrooms, office, remaining bedrooms | J | 3–4 hrs |
| 2 | Final sweep, First In boxes, essentials only remain | J | 2–3 hrs |
| 1 | Pack survival kit and dog bag. Done. | J | 1–2 hrs |

---

## DECLUTTER PRINCIPLES (do this before you pack anything)

The goal is simple: **don't pay to move things you don't want.** Moving costs scale with weight and volume, so every bag you donate is money saved.

Work through each room with three bins or areas: **Keep, Donate/Sell, and Trash.** A good rule of thumb is the 12-month rule — if you haven't used it in a year and it has no sentimental or practical value at the destination, let it go.

For selling: list on Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, or OfferUp. Give yourself a deadline of 3 weeks before move day for pickups — after that, donate the rest. Don't let the perfect sale delay a donation run. Schedule a Goodwill or Salvation Army pickup online so it happens whether or not you get around to dropping things off.

For furniture: measure the new space before you move a single piece. If a couch doesn't fit the new living room, it's better to sell it in Ohio than to move it 2,400 miles and sell it in Oregon.

For sentimental items: keep them, but be intentional. One box of meaningful keepsakes is fine. Five boxes of "I might feel bad throwing this away" is a moving tax.

---

## ROOM-BY-ROOM PACKING CHECKLIST

---

### STORAGE UNIT / ATTIC / BASEMENT
**Owner: J | Estimated time: 4–6 hours | Timeline: Weeks 10–8**

This is your easiest win and your first priority. These spaces hold things you're already not using.

- [ ] **J** Sort everything into Keep, Donate, Trash before touching a single box *(2 hrs)*
- [ ] **J** Donate or sell holiday decorations you haven't used in 2+ years
- [ ] **J** Recycle or shred old documents you no longer need (keep 3–5 years of tax records)
- [ ] **J** Disassemble any furniture stored here and label hardware bags to the piece
- [ ] **J** Pack holiday decor and seasonal items you are keeping *(1–2 hrs)*
- [ ] **J** Pack sporting equipment, camping gear, and hobby items *(1 hr)*
- [ ] Label all boxes: STORAGE, contents, priority NORMAL unless you use them seasonally

**Declutter tip:** If you have duplicate tools, holiday decorations for a house size you're leaving, or exercise equipment with cobwebs on it, this is the moment. Shipping a treadmill cross-country costs more than buying a used one in Oregon.

---

### GARAGE
**Owner: J (M leads) | Estimated time: 4–6 hours | Timeline: Weeks 9–8**

- [ ] **M** Sort tools: keep what you use, donate or sell duplicates *(1 hr)*
- [ ] **M** Properly dispose of hazardous materials — paint, motor oil, pesticides, propane tanks. Movers will not transport these and you legally cannot pack them in a rental truck. Check your city's hazardous waste drop-off schedule. *(1 hr to sort and schedule)*
- [ ] **M** Drain and clean the lawn mower and any gas-powered equipment before packing
- [ ] **J** Decide what large equipment is worth moving vs. selling (lawn mower, snowblower, patio furniture). Oregon has different needs than Ohio.
- [ ] **M** Pack hand tools in toolboxes; wrap power tools in moving blankets or bubble wrap *(1–2 hrs)*
- [ ] **M** Pack garage shelving contents into clearly labeled boxes *(1 hr)*
- [ ] **J** Disassemble shelving units and label hardware
- [ ] **J** Measure large items (patio furniture, bikes) against the new space before packing

**Declutter tip:** Snowblowers, heavy-duty ice scrapers, and Ohio-specific winter gear may not be worth the cost to ship to Portland or Bend. Patio furniture is bulky and cheap to replace. Bikes are worth moving. Tools are worth moving unless duplicated.

**Hazardous items to dispose of, NOT pack:**
Paint and stain, motor oil, gasoline, propane tanks (even "empty"), pesticides and herbicides, pool chemicals, batteries (car batteries), and aerosol cans. Search "[your city] hazardous waste disposal" for drop-off locations.

---

### GUEST ROOM / SPARE ROOM
**Owner: J | Estimated time: 2–3 hours | Timeline: Week 8–7**

- [ ] **J** Strip and donate any bedding you're replacing
- [ ] **J** Declutter the closet — this is often where things go to be forgotten
- [ ] **J** Pack extra linens and bedding into vacuum compression bags (saves 60–70% of space)
- [ ] **J** Pack decor, lamps, and wall art
- [ ] **J** Disassemble bed frame; bag and label hardware, tape the bag to the headboard
- [ ] **J** Pack dresser contents in drawers or into boxes; tape drawers shut for the move if the dresser is staying assembled
- [ ] **J** Pack closet contents into wardrobe boxes or garbage bags (clothes on hangers can go directly into a wardrobe box in 5 minutes)

---

### LIVING ROOM
**Owner: J | Estimated time: 3–4 hours | Timeline: Weeks 7–6**

- [ ] **J** Declutter books — donate what you won't reread. Books are extremely heavy and expensive to move. *(30 min)*
- [ ] **J** Pack books into small boxes only (a large box of books will break or be unmovable)
- [ ] **J** Wrap and pack decorative items, picture frames, and sculptures *(1 hr)*
- [ ] **J** Remove and roll area rugs; wrap in plastic stretch wrap or old sheets
- [ ] **J** Pack media: DVDs, vinyl, games *(30 min)*
- [ ] **J** Wrap TV in moving blankets or original box if kept; label the TV box FRAGILE on all sides
- [ ] **J** Disassemble entertainment center and label all hardware
- [ ] **J** Take down and wrap all wall art and mirrors (mirrors get a dedicated mirror box or cardboard sandwich — don't wrap them in a standard box)
- [ ] **J** Pack throw pillows and blankets into vacuum compression bags
- [ ] **J** Leave out: one lamp, one throw, remote, phone charger until moving week

**Declutter tip:** Oversized furniture that won't fit the new space should be sold now, not moved and then sold. Measure your new living room and compare it to what you have before packing a single piece.

---

### HOME OFFICE
**Owner: M | Estimated time: 2–3 hours | Timeline: Week 6–5**

- [ ] **M** Shred and recycle old documents (keep tax records, legal docs, medical records)
- [ ] **M** Back up computer files to an external drive and cloud storage before packing
- [ ] **M** Photograph cable setups before unplugging everything
- [ ] **M** Label every cable with masking tape and a marker before coiling and packing
- [ ] **M** Pack monitors with original boxes if kept, or use mirror/picture boxes with padding
- [ ] **M** Pack desk accessories, office supplies, and books into small and medium boxes
- [ ] **M** Disassemble desk; label hardware
- [ ] **M** Keep in car: laptop, chargers, external drive, documents folder, any work-critical items

---

### BEDROOMS (PRIMARY AND SECONDARY)
**Owner: J | Estimated time: 3–5 hours total | Timeline: Weeks 6–4**

**Week 6–5 (non-essentials):**
- [ ] **J** Donate or sell clothing you haven't worn in a year — do this before packing anything
- [ ] **J** Pack off-season clothing into vacuum compression bags or medium boxes *(1 hr)*
- [ ] **J** Pack extra shoes (keep one or two pairs out per person)
- [ ] **J** Pack books, decor, extra bedding

**Week 4–3 (the rest):**
- [ ] **J** Pack remaining clothing into wardrobe boxes or suitcases (use your suitcases as boxes — they're going anyway)
- [ ] **J** Pack nightstand contents; leave out what you use nightly
- [ ] **J** Disassemble bed frame; bag and label hardware
- [ ] **J** Wrap and pack lamps (shades in separate boxes, lightly stuffed with tissue)
- [ ] **J** Pack dresser contents; tape drawers or remove and pack contents separately
- [ ] **J** Pack jewelry and valuables in a bag that rides in the car, not the truck
- [ ] **J** Leave out: one set of bedding, one pillow per person, phone charger, alarm, 3–4 days of clothes

**Declutter tip:** Suitcases, duffel bags, and laundry baskets all make excellent boxes. Fill them with soft items like clothing, linens, and stuffed animals. It costs nothing and reduces the number of boxes you need.

---

### KITCHEN
**Owner: J | Estimated time: 4–6 hours | Timeline: Week 5–4**

The kitchen is the most time-consuming room and the one most people underestimate. Start earlier than you think you need to.

**Week 5 — Declutter and start:**
- [ ] **J** Go through every cabinet. Donate duplicate gadgets, appliances you never use, chipped dishes, and expired pantry items. *(1–2 hrs)*
- [ ] **J** Decide which pantry staples you'll use up vs. donate vs. move. Plan meals around what's left.
- [ ] **J** Decide on large appliances: stand mixer, air fryer, instant pot. Each is heavy. Only keep what you genuinely use monthly.

**Week 4 — Pack almost everything:**
- [ ] **J** Pack small appliances (wrap cords around the appliance and tape them, or bag them separately) *(1 hr)*
- [ ] **J** Pack dishes: wrap each plate individually in packing paper, stack vertically (not flat — they break flat), into dish pack boxes *(1–2 hrs)*
- [ ] **J** Pack glasses and mugs: each one in paper, stuffed with paper inside, into dish boxes
- [ ] **J** Pack pots and pans: nest them with paper between each layer
- [ ] **J** Pack pantry items in small boxes (canned goods are very heavy — keep boxes under 30 lbs)
- [ ] **J** Pack spices in a zip-lock bag inside a box; they spill everywhere
- [ ] **J** Pack sharp knives wrapped in paper and taped, or in a knife block, labeled SHARP
- [ ] **J** Label all kitchen boxes FRAGILE on the sides and top

**Leave out until moving week:**
One pot, one pan, one baking sheet, 2 plates and sets of cutlery, 2 mugs, coffee maker, dish soap, sponge, and can opener. These become your First In box.

**Declutter tip:** A cross-country move is a natural kitchen reset. Duplicate pans, gadgets used twice a year, mismatched plastic containers without lids, water bottles you have 11 of — now is the time. The dollar-per-pound cost to ship cast iron or a full set of dishes is real. Keep what you love

# 2) FINAL 14-DAY PACKING CHECKLIST
### Day 0 = Move Day. Count back from your date.

**Key:** Each day has a primary owner, a focus area, and an estimated active working time. "Active time" means hands-on packing, not the whole day.

---

**DAY 14 | Owner: J | Est. time: 2–3 hrs**
Whole-house sweep and supply check. Walk every room and make a written list of what still needs packing. Confirm you have enough boxes, tape, bubble wrap, and markers. Order or buy anything missing today — don't wait. Identify any large items (furniture, rugs, mirrors) that need special materials and get those too. This is a planning day, not a packing day.

---

**DAY 13 | Owner: M | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Office and electronics. Back up the computer to cloud and an external drive before unplugging anything. Photograph all cable setups. Label every cable before coiling. Pack monitors, printers, and desk accessories. Disassemble the desk and bag hardware. Leave out: laptop, one charger, external drive. These ride in the car.

---

**DAY 12 | Owner: P | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Guest room and spare closets. Strip the guest bed, pack linens into compression bags, disassemble the frame and bag hardware. Clear and pack the spare closet completely — this is usually the last holdout of random unsorted items, so leave extra time for decision-making. Donate anything that surfaces here rather than packing it.

---

**DAY 11 | Owner: J | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Living room. Pack all remaining books (small boxes only — heavy), wall art, mirrors, and decor. Roll and wrap area rugs. Pack media. Wrap and box the TV if not already done. Leave out: one lamp, one throw blanket, remote, phone charger.

---

**DAY 10 | Owner: J | Est. time: 4–5 hrs**
Kitchen — the big one. Pack all small appliances, pantry items (small boxes for canned goods), spices (sealed in zip-lock bags), and serveware. Wrap and box all dishes and glasses individually. Pack pots and pans with paper between each. Label every box FRAGILE. Leave out: one pot, one pan, 2 plates and sets of cutlery, 2 mugs, coffee maker, dish soap, sponge, can opener.

---

**DAY 9 | Owner: J | Est. time: 2–3 hrs**
Kitchen overflow and fridge prep. Finish any remaining kitchen packing. Use up, donate, or discard remaining perishables. Begin running down the fridge. Do a full declutter pass on the pantry — moving canned goods 2,400 miles rarely makes sense. If you have a chest freezer, start running it down now.

---

**DAY 8 | Owner: J | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Primary bedroom non-essentials. Pack off-season and extra clothing into compression bags or suitcases. Pack shoes (keep 2 pairs per person out). Pack jewelry and valuables into a bag that will ride in the car. Pack extra bedding. Leave out: 3–4 days of clothes per person, one pillow each, phone chargers.

---

**DAY 7 | Owner: J | Est. time: 2–3 hrs**
Midpoint check and buffer day. Do a room-by-room walk with your box list. Number all packed boxes and log them (a simple spreadsheet or notes app works). Confirm the mover's arrival time and parking plan. If anything is behind, use today to catch up. If you're on track, start building the First In boxes so they're ready to go.

---

**DAY 6 | Owner: J | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Bathrooms and linen closet. Pack everything except a 3-day toiletry kit per person. Pack towels (great box fillers around fragile items), extra toilet paper, and cleaning supplies. Leave out: toilet paper (at least 4 rolls), hand soap, 2 towels per person, toothbrushes and toothpaste, any daily medications. Medications never go in the truck.

---

**DAY 5 | Owner: M | Est. time: 2–3 hrs**
Dog bag and pet supplies. Pack everything for the dog that isn't needed daily: extra food, backup leash, carrier or crate (if it fits in the car), grooming supplies. Build the dog's First In box: food and bowls, water, leash, bed, familiar toy, poop bags, records. Set this aside and label it DO NOT LOAD — it goes in the car.

---

**DAY 4 | Owner: J | Est. time: 3–4 hrs**
Final bedroom sweep and garage stragglers. Pack the last remaining bedroom items — nightstand contents, lamps, remaining decor. Finish anything left in the garage. Confirm all hazardous materials have been disposed of. Disassemble any remaining furniture and bag all hardware. Take photos of assembled furniture before disassembly if it helps with reassembly.

---

**DAY 3 | Owner: J | Est. time: 2–3 hrs**
Build all First In boxes. One per room: kitchen, bedroom(s), bathroom, office, living room. Seal and star-label them. Stack them together near the door so they load last and come off the truck first. Fridge should be fully emptied and defrosting by end of day. Do a full walk-through of every room, cabinet, closet, shelf, and drawer. If it's not in a box or labeled as staying out, it should be.

---

**DAY 2 | Owner: J | Est. time: 1–2 hrs**
Survival kit and final loose ends. Pack the car survival bag: 3–4 days of clothes per person, all medications, toiletry kits, phone chargers, documents folder, dog bag, snacks, water, cash. Confirm it all fits in the car with the dog and the dog's crate. Charge all devices and battery packs overnight. Confirm the mover's arrival window one more time by phone.

---

**DAY 1 (Eve of Move Day) | Owner: J | Est. time: 1 hr**
Nothing should need packing today. Wipe down the fridge interior once fully defrosted and dry. Take a final photo walk-through of the whole home while it still has your stuff in it. Lay out the moving day essentials checklist (the one-pager) on the kitchen counter. Set an early alarm. Sleep.

---

**DAY 0 — MOVE DAY | Owner: J**
Use the printed moving day essentials checklist. Everything else is done.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist with Declutter Tips

A note on timing: start packing the lowest-use rooms first (storage, guest room, garage) around weeks 6–7, then work toward daily-use rooms in the final week. The kitchen and bathrooms go last.

---

## Label System

Every box gets three pieces of information written on at least two sides and the top.

**Room** — write the destination room in Oregon, not the Ohio room. This tells movers exactly where to put it and saves you re-sorting later. Use a color-coded dot sticker per room if you want a visual system: blue for bedroom, red for kitchen, green for living room, yellow for bathroom, orange for office, purple for garage/storage.

**Priority** — a number from 1 to 3. Priority 1 means open within the first 24 hours (sheets, coffee maker, dog stuff, toiletries). Priority 2 means open within the first week. Priority 3 means open whenever — seasonal items, books, decor.

**Fragility** — write FRAGILE in red marker on all sides if it contains breakables. Write HEAVY if it's books or tools. Write THIS SIDE UP with an arrow if orientation matters.

A finished label looks like: *Kitchen / P1 / FRAGILE — glasses and French press*

---

## Room-by-Room Checklist

### Kitchen
**Estimated boxes: 8–15 depending on your cookware, pantry size, and how many appliances you own.**

Pack in this order: rarely used appliances first (bread maker, stand mixer, fondue set), then pantry dry goods, then cookware, then plates and glasses, then daily-use items last.

**Declutter prompts:** Do you have duplicate gadgets? Expired spices (check every single one)? A "junk drawer" that hasn't been touched in a year? Small appliances you've used fewer than 3 times? Mismatched containers without lids?

- [ ] Small appliances (wrap each in bubble wrap or towels, fill cavities with packing paper)
- [ ] Pots and pans (nest them with paper between each; skillets can share a box if separated)
- [ ] Plates and bowls (pack vertically like records, not stacked flat — they survive better that way)
- [ ] Glasses and mugs (wrap each individually; use dish-pack boxes with cell dividers if possible)
- [ ] Baking dishes and sheet pans (wrap in paper; they can go in a wardrobe box standing up)
- [ ] Pantry dry goods (pack heavy items like canned goods in small boxes — these get very heavy fast)
- [ ] Spices (transport in a small bin you keep in the car so they don't overheat or spill)
- [ ] Knives (wrap in a dish towel, secure with rubber bands; label SHARP)
- [ ] Dish towels and pot holders (great filler material for fragile boxes)
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink (many are hazmat and can't go on a moving truck — verify with your mover)
- [ ] Trash: use moving week to run down perishables. Donate canned goods to a food bank rather than moving them.

**Keep out until moving day:** coffee maker, one pot, one pan, two mugs, dish soap, sponge, paper towels, a few plates and utensils. Pack these in the "last out" box.

---

### Primary Bedroom
**Estimated boxes: 6–10 (more if you have extensive clothing or a large closet)**

- [ ] Off-season clothing (pack first, in large wardrobe boxes or vacuum bags to compress)
- [ ] Current-season clothing (wardrobe boxes make hanging clothes easy and protect them)
- [ ] Shoes (each pair in a bag or wrapped; original boxes are ideal if you kept them)
- [ ] Bedding and pillows (use your duvet as padding in a large box; compression bags save space)
- [ ] Mattress (movers handle this or buy a mattress bag — don't skip this, Oregon rain is real)
- [ ] Nightstand contents (keep medication, glasses, phone charger, and ear plugs out until moving day)
- [ ] Dresser contents (you can often leave clothes in drawers for a local move; ask your mover about interstate moves — drawers should usually be emptied to reduce weight and prevent damage)
- [ ] Jewelry and valuables (transport these yourself in the car, never on the truck)
- [ ] Wall art and mirrors (use mirror boxes; tape a large X of masking tape across glass to hold shards if it cracks)

**Declutter prompts:** The rule of thumb is if you haven't worn it in a year, it goes. Try the bin method: put "maybe" items in a box and seal it. If you don't open it for 3 weeks, donate it without looking inside.

---

### Guest Bedroom / Spare Room
**Estimated boxes: 4–8**

This room is your first packing target since it's lowest priority. Start here as early as week 7 or 8.

- [ ] Spare bedding and pillows
- [ ] Books and media (small boxes only for books — they become brutally heavy in large boxes)
- [ ] Hobby and craft supplies
- [ ] Extra furniture (decide now what goes and what gets sold or donated)
- [ ] Seasonal decor and holiday items

**Declutter prompts:** This is where things go to be forgotten. Be ruthless. Books you won't reread, decor you don't love, duplicate items that migrated here from other rooms.

---

### Living Room
**Estimated boxes: 6–12**

- [ ] Books (small boxes, labelled HEAVY)
- [ ] Media: DVDs, vinyl, gaming equipment (wrap electronics in anti-static bubble wrap if possible)
- [ ] Decorative items, candles, picture frames (wrap each in paper; frames go in mirror/picture boxes or between two pieces of foam)
- [ ] Throw blankets and pillows (use as filler in furniture gaps on the truck)
- [ ] Electronics: TV (original box if you have it; otherwise a TV box from a moving supply store), gaming consoles, speakers, routers (take photos of all cable setups before unplugging)
- [ ] Cables and remotes (label each cable with masking tape; bag remotes per device)
- [ ] Furniture (sofa, coffee table, bookshelves — photograph assembly instructions if you're disassembling)
- [ ] Rugs (roll tightly and secure with rope or plastic wrap; they go on the truck last/first off)

**Declutter prompts:** Furniture is the highest cost item to move by weight and cubic feet. If a piece is worn, cheap to replace, or doesn't suit your Oregon vision, sell it now. Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist move furniture fast.

---

### Bathrooms (all)
**Estimated boxes: 2–4 total**

Pack these last — you need them every day until moving day.

- [ ] Medications (carry these in the car — temperature extremes in a truck can degrade them)
- [ ] Toiletries (seal everything in zip-lock bags; pumps and liquid lids leak under pressure changes and jostling)
- [ ] Hair tools and accessories
- [ ] Towels (great box filler and padding around fragile items)
- [ ] Cleaning supplies (check what your mover permits; most flammable or corrosive products can't go on the truck)
- [ ] First aid kit (keep this in the car)
- [ ] Extra toilet paper (keep a roll out until literally the last moment)

**Declutter prompts:** Expired medications (dispose of properly at a pharmacy drop-box, not the trash or toilet), half-empty products you won't finish, duplicate tools.

---

### Home Office
**Estimated boxes: 4–8**

- [ ] Computer equipment (use original boxes if you have them; otherwise double-box electronics with foam or clothing padding)
- [ ] Monitors (buy monitor boxes from a moving store — worth it)
- [ ] External drives, USB hubs, peripherals
- [ ] Important documents (transport in the car — see the documents list from phase one)
- [ ] Books and binders
- [ ] Desk supplies (consolidate aggressively; most office supplies are cheap to replace)
- [ ] Printer (ink cartridges can leak — remove them and bag them separately)
- [ ] Cables (photograph setups before unplugging; label every cable)
- [ ] Artwork and diplomas (wrap and use picture boxes)

**Declutter prompts:** Old paperwork is the enemy. Shred anything financial that's more than 7 years old. Scan and digitize documents you want to keep but rarely touch. Recycle old cables, tech accessories, and anything that's been "I'll deal with that later" for over a year.

---

### Garage / Storage / Basement
**Estimated boxes: varies wildly — budget 10–20+ for a typical garage**

This is usually the most time-consuming and most declutter-able space. Start here.

- [ ] Tools (wrap blades and sharp edges; group by type)
- [ ] Hardware (sort and label — a tackle box or small bin works well for screws, bolts, anchors)
- [ ] Sporting and outdoor equipment (bikes, kayaks, camping gear — photograph for insurance before loading)
- [ ] Seasonal items (lawn equipment, holiday decorations, fans/space heaters)
- [ ] Cleaning equipment (mops, brooms, vacuums)
- [ ] Moving hazmat checklist: paint, propane tanks, gasoline, batteries, pesticides, and pool chemicals typically cannot go on a moving truck. Use them up, dispose of them properly at a hazmat drop-off, or donate them to neighbors.
- [ ] Garden hoses, tools, pots (consider whether the Oregon outdoor space warrants them)

**Declutter prompts:** Be honest about what you actually used in Ohio. Cross-country moves are priced partly by weight and volume. A lawn mower, a bag of potting soil, and a leaky garden hose are expensive to move and cheap to replace.

---

### Dog's Stuff
**Keep accessible throughout — do not pack in the truck**

- [ ] Food and treats (a 1–2 week supply in a sealed container that travels in the car)
- [ ] Water and bowls
- [ ] Leash, collar, harness, and tags
- [ ] Crate or bed (the dog may need this during packing chaos — keep it out until the last moment)
- [ ] Favorite toy and blanket (familiar smells reduce anxiety)
- [ ] Poop bags, paper towels, cleaning spray
- [ ] Medications and calming aids (keep these at room temperature in the car)
- [ ] Vet records pouch (keep with your documents, in the car)
- [ ] A printed card with the dog's name, your phone number, and your Oregon destination address (tape inside the crate and keep one in your wallet)

---

## A Note on Box Quantities

The estimates above assume a 2-bedroom household with a moderate amount of stuff. The real variable is books, clothing, and kitchen gear. If you're heavy on any of those, add 20–30% to that room's count. Total for a 2BR household typically runs 60–100 boxes. If you're over 80, that's a good reason to declutter harder.

---

---

# Services and Subscriptions: Cancellation and Transfer Timeline

The rule of thumb is to give providers more notice than you think you need, because holds, billing cycles, and contracts create friction. When in doubt, call rather than relying on an app.

---

## 8 Weeks Out — Research and Notify

- **Internet/cable:** Contact your Ohio provider. Ask about contract termination fees and the exact cancellation process. Research Oregon providers at the new address *now* — fiber availability varies and installation wait times can be 2–3 weeks. Book the Oregon install as soon as you have a confirmed move date. *(Joint)*
- **Renter's insurance:** Call your insurer. Ask whether the policy can be transferred to Oregon or needs to be cancelled and restarted. Get a quote for the Oregon address. *(Joint)*
- **Health insurance:** If employer-provided, confirm coverage continues during and after the move. If individual (ACA marketplace), research Oregon plans. A move is a qualifying life event, so you have a special enrollment window. *(Joint)*
- **Gym membership:** Check your contract. Many national gyms (Planet Fitness, LA Fitness) allow transfer to a local club. Local gyms usually require cancellation. Give the required notice. *(M or P)*
- **Vehicle insurance:** Notify your insurer of the move date. Ask what changes when you register in Oregon and whether you need to switch to an Oregon-based policy. Update as soon as registration changes. *(M)*

---

## 6 Weeks Out — Start Cancellations with Long Lead Times

- **Storage unit (Ohio):** Give notice per your contract. Clear it before the move. *(Joint)*
- **Newspaper or local subscriptions:** Cancel or update address. *(M or P)*
- **Professional memberships:** Update your address with any state bar, licensing board, or professional organization. Some licenses need to transfer to Oregon. *(M or P)*
- **HSA/FSA:** Notify your administrator of the address change. *(Joint)*
- **Bank accounts:** Update your address online or in-branch. If you use a local Ohio-only bank, consider whether to open a national account or Oregon credit union now so it's ready when you arrive. *(Joint)*
- **Investment accounts and retirement:** Update address. These will also need to be updated for tax documents. *(Joint)*
- **Life insurance:** Update beneficiary address info and notify of the move. *(Joint)*
- **Pet insurance:** Transfer or update address. *(M)*

---

## 4 Weeks Out — Address Change Wave

File your USPS change of address (usps.com) about 2 weeks before the move date, so it activates on time. Then notify the following directly (USPS forwarding is a backup, not a plan):

- [ ] Social Security Administration (ssa.gov)
- [ ] IRS (file Form 8822; can also update with next year's return but proactive is better)
- [ ] All banks and credit unions
- [ ] All credit card companies
- [ ] Mortgage servicer or student loan servicer
- [ ] Investment accounts (Fidelity, Vanguard, Schwab, etc.)
- [ ] Ohio BMV (address update on license before you leave; Oregon will replace it)
- [ ] Voter registration (Ohio cancellation is handled automatically when you register in Oregon)
- [ ] Employer payroll and HR
- [ ] Your accountant or tax preparer
- [ ] Alumni associations, professional organizations
- [ ] Magazine and subscription box services
- [ ] Amazon, eBay, and any e-commerce accounts you buy from regularly
- [ ] PayPal, Venmo, Cash App (less critical but billing address matters for some)
- [ ] Pharmacy — transfer all prescriptions to a national chain (CVS, Walgreens) or confirm your Oregon pharmacy can receive records

---

## 2 Weeks Out — Schedule Utility Shutoffs and Starts

- **Ohio electric:** Schedule shutoff for the day after move-out. *(M)*
- **Ohio gas:** Same. *(M)*
- **Ohio water:** Notify the city. *(M)*
- **Ohio internet/cable:** Schedule cancellation for the day after move-out. Return equipment before you leave. *(Joint)*
- **Ohio trash:** Cancel pickup. *(M)*
- **Oregon electric:** Confirm start date. *(M)*
- **Oregon gas:** Confirm start date. *(M)*
- **Oregon internet:** Confirm installation appointment and that it falls before your first full day there. *(Joint)*
- **Ohio alarm or security system:** Cancel or transfer. Contract buyout may apply. *(Joint)*
- **Ohio HOA:** If applicable, notify and confirm dues are current. *(Joint)*

---

## Moving Week — Final Cuts

- [ ] Cancel any meal kit deliveries (HelloFresh, etc.) or pause until Oregon address is set up
- [ ] Cancel or redirect any recurring deliveries (pet food subscriptions, Amazon Subscribe & Save)
- [ ] Update streaming services (Netflix, Hulu, etc.) with new billing address
- [ ] Update your phone carrier's billing address
- [ ] Confirm your Ohio utilities are scheduled for shutoff
- [ ] Confirm your Ohio internet equipment is returned and the account is closed

---

## First 2 Weeks in Oregon — Finish the List

- [ ] Confirm all Ohio services are terminated and final bills are paid
- [ ] Get Oregon renter's or homeowner's insurance active
- [ ] Register vehicles (Oregon DMV)
- [ ] Update driver's license
- [ ] Find a local pharmacy and transfer prescriptions
- [ ] Update voter registration (auto-registered via DMV in Oregon — confirm)
- [ ] Update

**How to use this:** Your move day is Day 0. All dates below are relative to that. To use in Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, or Outlook, replace "Day 0" with your actual move date and count backward. Each entry includes a suggested reminder time and who's responsible. For recurring items, set them to repeat as noted.

For Google Calendar: create a new calendar called "Move 2025" so you can toggle it on and off without cluttering your main view. Set each event to "all day" with a notification at 8am.

Book Oregon internet installation today.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist + Timeline

---

## DECLUTTER PRINCIPLES (read once, apply everywhere)

Before packing any room, run everything through this quick filter. It takes about 10 minutes per room before you start and saves hours of moving things you'll just throw out later.

**Keep** if you've used it in the last 12 months, it has clear sentimental value, or it's expensive to replace.

**Donate** if it's in good condition but hasn't been used, doesn't fit, or duplicates something else you own.

**Sell** if it has real resale value. Use Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist for furniture and large items; eBay for electronics and collectibles. Don't spend more than 30 minutes listing something — if it doesn't sell in a week, donate it.

**Trash/Recycle** if it's broken, stained, missing parts, or not worth anyone's time.

**Oregon Rule:** Moving cross-country costs roughly $0.50–$1.50 per pound with a truck or mover. If an item costs less than that to replace and you don't love it, leave it behind.

---

## WEEK-BY-WEEK PACKING TIMELINE

You have 10 weeks. Packing starts in earnest around Week 6 and intensifies from Week 4 onward. Weeks 1–5 are for decisions and supplies, not boxes.

**Week 10–8 (now — Deciding and Acquiring)**
Focus on decluttering decisions, not packing. Walk every room once with a trash bag and a donate box. Order or collect supplies. **J, ~3–4 hrs total.**

**Week 7–6 (Supplies ready, start non-essentials)**
Pack storage areas: garage, basement, attic, storage unit, holiday decorations, sports equipment, tools you won't need before the move. These spaces tend to be the most cluttered and benefit most from a hard declutter pass. **J, ~4–6 hrs per large space.**

**Week 5–4 (Secondary rooms)**
Pack the guest room completely. Pack books, art, décor, and anything decorative throughout the house. Pack off-season clothes. Pack the office (except daily-use items). Pack the living room except the couch, TV, and one lamp. **J, ~2–3 hrs per room.**

**Week 3 (Kitchen and dining)**
Pack 80% of the kitchen: duplicates, rarely used appliances, baking equipment, most pantry items. Leave out enough to cook simple meals for 2–3 weeks. Use up pantry food aggressively. **J, ~3–4 hrs.**

**Week 2 (Bedrooms, bathrooms, final push)**
Pack bedrooms down to sleeping essentials (one set of sheets, towels, toiletries). Pack bathrooms except daily-use items. Pack remaining living room items. Mark all boxes clearly. **J, ~2–3 hrs per room.**

**Week 1 (Essentials only)**
Everything remaining fits in your overnight bags, the moving-day essentials box, and the dog bag. Fridge gets emptied and defrosted 24 hrs before movers or truck pickup. **J, ~2–3 hrs.**

---

## ROOM-BY-ROOM PACKING CHECKLIST

Each room has three sections: **Declutter first**, **Pack early** (weeks 6–4), and **Pack last** (weeks 2–1). The "Last Out" box for each room stays unpacked until moving day and goes in the car or is loaded last on the truck, clearly labeled.

---

### KITCHEN — J, ~3–4 hrs to pack fully

**Declutter first:**
Toss expired pantry items. Donate duplicate gadgets (how many spatulas do you need in Oregon?). Discard mismatched containers missing lids. If you haven't used an appliance in a year, seriously consider leaving it. Small appliances are heavy and cheap to replace.

**Pack early (weeks 5–3):**
- Baking sheets, muffin tins, cake pans
- Rarely used appliances: stand mixer, waffle iron, bread maker, juicer
- Extra sets of dishes or glasses (pack one full set last)
- Cookbooks
- Pantry: canned goods, dry goods, spices (use up what you can; donate the rest to a food bank)
- Vases, serving platters, decorative items
- Bar tools, holiday entertaining items

**Pack last (week 2–1):**
- One pot, one pan, one baking dish
- Enough dishes and glasses for two (wrap carefully)
- Knives and cutting board
- Coffee maker or kettle
- Daily-use utensils
- Dish soap, sponge, hand towel

**Last Out box label: KITCHEN — OPEN FIRST**
Include: paper plates and cups, coffee supplies, one pot, two mugs, utensils, dish soap, sponge, one roll of paper towel.

---

### LIVING ROOM — J, ~2–3 hrs

**Declutter first:**
Donate books you won't reread (be honest). Recycle old magazines. Part with decorative items you don't love. Assess furniture: some pieces cost more to move than to replace.

**Pack early (weeks 6–4):**
- All books
- Art and wall décor (wrap frames in clothing or bubble wrap)
- Throw pillows, extra blankets
- Board games, puzzles, DVDs, gaming accessories
- Candles, vases, decorative objects
- Shelving contents

**Pack last (week 2–1):**
- TV and cables (label every cable with tape and a marker before unplugging)
- One lamp (if the new place won't have overhead lighting immediately)
- Remote controls

**Last Out box:** TV remotes and cables, one power strip, your laptop charger.

---

### PRIMARY BEDROOM — J, ~2–3 hrs

**Declutter first:**
One pass through every drawer and shelf. Donate clothes you haven't worn in 12 months. Be especially ruthless with duplicates (10 t-shirts becomes 6). Same rule for shoes. Discard or donate any bedding you won't use.

**Pack early (weeks 5–4):**
- Off-season clothing (pack by person, label clearly)
- Extra bedding (keep one set per person out)
- Books on nightstands
- Jewelry and accessories except daily-use items
- Décor, frames, art

**Pack last (week 2–1):**
- Current-season clothing (leave out a week's worth per person)
- One set of sheets and pillows per person
- Toiletry organizers (transfer to toiletry bag week 1)
- Alarm clock or charger

**Last Out box:** One set of sheets, two pillows, phone chargers, one change of clothes per person.

---

### GUEST ROOM / SPARE ROOM — P or J, ~1–2 hrs

This room gets packed first (week 6–7) since nothing in it is daily-use.

**Declutter first:**
If the guest room has become a storage room, treat it as such — this is where the most ruthless decluttering happens.

**Pack everything:**
- All bedding and linens
- Stored clothing
- Holiday items and seasonal décor
- Hobby supplies, craft materials, instruments
- Luggage (pack smaller bags inside larger ones; use the inside of luggage to pack soft items)
- Books, games, whatever else has ended up in here

---

### BATHROOMS (Primary and Guest) — M or J, ~1–2 hrs total

**Declutter first:**
Toss expired medications (use an Ohio DEA take-back program or a pharmacy — don't flush). Toss expired makeup, skincare, and hair products. Donate duplicates. Be realistic about what you actually use.

**Pack early (weeks 5–4):**
- Extra towels and washcloths (keep 2 sets out)
- Hair tools you don't use daily
- First aid kit (pack it, but note which box it's in)
- Cleaning supplies (most can be replaced cheaply — check whether movers will transport them; many won't take flammables or bleach)

**Pack last (week 1):**
- Daily-use toiletries
- Medication (carry prescriptions with you in the car, not on the truck)
- Two towels per person
- Toilet paper (leave a half-roll out until literally the last moment)
- Shower curtain and liner

**Last Out box / Overnight bag:** Toiletries, prescriptions, 2 towels, one roll of toilet paper. These go in the car.

---

### HOME OFFICE — M or P (whoever uses it), ~2–3 hrs

**Declutter first:**
Shred documents you don't need (shred anything with personal data). Recycle old cables that go to nothing. Donate books, binders, and equipment you no longer use. Assess furniture — office desks and chairs are heavy and inexpensive on Facebook Marketplace.

**Pack early (weeks 6–5):**
- Books and binders
- File boxes and archives
- Printer and extra toner
- Monitors (wrap well; use original box if you have it)
- Extra peripherals and cables (label before packing)
- Art and décor

**Pack last (week 2):**
- Daily-use laptop, charger, mouse, keyboard
- Current files and notebooks
- Any external hard drives or USB drives (carry in the car)

**Critical:** All hard drives, flash drives, important physical documents, and backup drives go in the car. Not the truck.

---

### GARAGE / BASEMENT / STORAGE — J, ~4–6 hrs per large space (start week 7)

This is your biggest declutter opportunity. The rule here is simple: if you couldn't tell someone what it is or when you last used it, donate or trash it.

**Declutter hard:**
Power tools you haven't used in 2 years. Duplicate gardening tools. Sporting equipment for sports you don't play. Random hardware (keep one good toolkit, donate the rest). Old paint (most movers won't take it; check Oregon's hazardous waste program for disposal at the new end, and Ohio's for disposal now).

**Pack:**
- Neatly boxed tools with labels
- Sports equipment you'll actually use
- Holiday decor (clearly labeled by holiday)
- Camping and outdoor gear
- Bike (may need partial disassembly for the truck)
- Garden hoses and hand tools worth keeping

**Don't move:**
Propane tanks, gas cans, paint cans, aerosol cans, fertilizer, pesticides, pool chemicals, fire extinguishers. Dispose of properly before the move. Check FMCSA rules — these are prohibited on moving trucks by regulation.

---

### DOG'S STUFF — M, ~1 hr

**Keep accessible (goes in the car, not the truck):**
- Food and treats (at least 3–4 days' worth)
- Water and collapsible travel bowl
- Leash, harness, collar with current ID tag
- Crate or travel bed (familiar scent helps with anxiety)
- Favorite toy or blanket
- Poop bags
- Medications and vet records
- Paper towels and cleaner (car accidents happen)
- Dog first aid kit basics

**Pack early:** Extra crates, beds, or pet furniture. Extra bags of food if you're stocked.

---

### GENERAL PACKING TIPS

Label every box with its destination room, a brief contents description, and a priority: **Open First**, **Normal**, or **Storage**. Mark fragile boxes on all four sides, not just the top. Pack heavy items in small boxes (books, canned goods). Pack light items in large boxes (linens, pillows). Don't leave empty space in boxes — fill gaps with clothing, towels, or packing paper so boxes don't collapse. Take a photo of the inside of each box before closing if you're anxious about contents.

---

---

Great — you now have the full master checklist, room-by-room packing guide, packing timeline, complete ICS calendar file, and both print layouts all in one place. That's a serious amount of planning knocked out in one session.

A few things worth bookmarking for the coming weeks:

The two tasks that catch people off guard most often on a cross-country move are the internet installation lead time in Oregon (book it this week if you haven't) and the Oregon DMV window after you arrive — it goes faster than you'd expect and the emissions test requirement in the Portland metro area can add a few days if you don't plan for it.

For the dog, the test car ride is worth doing soon. If motion sickness or anxiety shows up, you'll want a few weeks to work with your vet on options before the actual drive.

When you're ready, the natural next steps would be working through the finances and budget in more detail, drafting the landlord notice letter, or building out a service cancellation tracker. Just say the word.

## Improved Park Mapping Approach

The honest answer is that Google Sheets formulas get awkward fast for fuzzy matching at this scale. The cleanest solution here is a two-layer approach: an **exact key lookup** (fast, reliable) plus a **pattern/prefix fallback** (catches abbreviations), with a confidence flag on each.

## Formula (3 columns)

**Column J — Canonical name:**
```
=IF(TRIM(F2)="", "",
  IFERROR(
    VLOOKUP(LOWER(REGEXREPLACE(F2,"[^a-zA-Z]","")),
            ParkMap!$A:$B, 2, FALSE),
    "Unmapped"))
```

**Column K — Confidence flag:**
```
=IF(TRIM(F2)="", "REVIEW",
  IFERROR(
    VLOOKUP(LOWER(REGEXREPLACE(F2,"[^a-zA-Z]","")),
            ParkMap!$A:$C, 3, FALSE),
    "Unmapped"))
```

**Column P — Review flag (updated to include confidence):**
```
=IF(OR(G2="REVIEW", H2="REVIEW", I2="REVIEW",
       J2="Unmapped", K2="Low", K2="REVIEW",
       M2<>"", N2<>""),
    "REVIEW", "OK")
```

---

## Auto-accept vs. Manual Review Rules

**Auto-accept (High confidence) when all of these are true:**
- The stripped key matches exactly one canonical park with no ambiguity
- The raw entry has more than 2 characters (single letters are too risky)
- The match isn't one of your known ambiguous short forms (np, central, west, thenorth)

**Send to manual review when any of these are true:**
- Confidence is Low — short or ambiguous abbreviation
- Confidence is Unmapped — not in your table at all
- The raw entry is 1–2 characters
- The key could plausibly match more than one canonical park (you don't have this problem now, but if you ever add "Northwest Park" then `npark` and `np` become ambiguous)

**The practical threshold I'd use:** if stripping non-letters and lowercasing produces a key of 6+ characters that matches exactly, treat it as High. Under 6 characters, treat as Low unless it's a well-known full abbreviation like `semeadow`. This isn't a hard rule — it's a heuristic. The real standard is whether *you* would feel comfortable auto-accepting it without looking at it.

---

## One gap to flag

"The North" is tricky. It's Low confidence and maps to North Park here, but that's really an inference — it could mean something colloquial that doesn't map to any park at all. I'd treat every instance of `thenorth` as Unmapped rather than Low, unless you already know from context that volunteers always use it to mean North Park. **Bar 7** | E major (full bar, harmonic minor V chord) | *mf, hold and let ring — peak of the phrase*

```
RH: C4(3) – E4(1) – G#4(2) – A4(1) – G#4(2) – E4(3) – D4(4) – B3(5)
    fingers: 3  –  1  –  2   –  1  –  2    –  3  –  4  –  5
    [motif shape returns with G#4; descends to B3 pulling toward resolution]

LH: E2(5)–B2(2)–E3(1) [block chord, beats 1–2, hold]
    E2(5)–G#2(3)–B2(2) [tighten voicing, beats 3–4, let ring into bar 8]
```

*Small breath/pause at the end of bar 7 before resolving.*

---

**Bar 8** | Am (final) | *mp, then p on the final chord — calm and certain*

```
RH: A4(1) – rest – E4(3) – rest – C4(3)–E4(2)–A4(1) [block chord, held]
    fingers:  1          3           3   2   1
    [quarter note A4, quarter rest, quarter note E4, then final block Am chord held]

LH: A1(5) [beat 1, low open bass, let ring]
    A2(3)–E3(2)–A3(1) [beat 3, full Am chord]
    [hold both through the bar — the low A1 gives the final cadence its weight]
```

---

## Fingering and Dynamic Summary

A few things worth knowing before you sit down:

The thumb (finger 1) will frequently land on A4 as the tonic in the right hand — treat it as your anchor and let the other fingers fan out from it. In bars 3 and 7, the shift from G4 to G#4 is small but needs a deliberate finger change (use 2 on G# rather than trying to slide). In the left hand, finger 5 always takes the bass note and finger 1 always takes the top of the chord — keep that consistent and the broken pattern becomes automatic quickly.

For dynamics, the shape of the piece is mp through bars 1–4, a gentle lift to mf at bars 5–6, the peak at bar 7 (mf, let it ring), and then a pullback to mp then p for the final bar. That arc gives it a ceremonial feeling without being dramatic.

## Stretch Notes and Simplifications

**Bar 2 (Dm):** A2+D3 is a fourth, comfortable for most hands. No issue here.

**Bar 3 and 4 (E chord):** B2+E3 is also a fourth, fine. The only potential stretch is if you try to keep finger 5 on E2 while reaching up — just lift and re-place rather than holding the bass through the chord.

**Bar 6 (G):** B2+D3 is a minor third, the easiest interval in the piece. No stretch at all.

**Bar 7 (E):** Same as bars 3–4. If E2 feels low and awkward, you can move the whole chord up an octave to E3+B3+E4 and play it as a block chord on beats 2 and 4 instead of alternating. It will sound thinner but is much easier to manage while reading the right hand melody at the same time.

**General tip:** Keep finger 5 loose on the bass notes rather than pressing hard. The two-note chord on beats 2 and 4 carries the harmony — the bass just marks the beat.
