Bracketed items need your input. Please resolve them before submitting.

---

## Outcomes & Evaluation

Our evaluation asks whether more Riverbend adults gain measurable reading skills than before, and whether those gains hold. We will track four SMART objectives against a documented 2024 baseline. (See Attachment [#]: Logic Model and Attachment [#]: Evaluation Plan.)

| Outcome | Baseline | Target | Measure | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Reading gain:** learners advancing at least one level | 40% (124 of 310, 2024) | **55%** by month 12, maintained each year after | TABE Reading, pre/post | Pre at intake; post at exit or after [X] instructional hours |
| **2. Reach:** adults enrolled per year | 310 (2024) | **420 per year**, including at least [X] waitlisted adults | Enrollment records | Quarterly |
| **3. Post-test completion:** enrollees with valid pre/post pairs | [X]% (2024) | **At least [80]%** of enrollees | Data system | Quarterly |
| **4. Sustained progress:** exiters reached and showing retained level or a next step (HSE, ESL, training, employment) | Not previously collected; set in Year 1 | **At least [X]%** of exiters reached; [X]% retaining level or in a next step | Phone/text follow-up | 3 and 6 months after exit |

**Baseline and design.** Our baseline is the 2024 result: 124 of 310 learners (40%) gained at least one level on TABE Reading. We will calculate the gain rate the same way each year, as learners with valid pre- and post-tests who advanced at least one level divided by all learners with valid test pairs. We will also report gain as a share of all enrollees, so reviewers can see the effect of attrition. We will use a pre/post design with the same instrument and alternate forms, with post-testing timed to publisher guidelines for minimum instructional hours. This design shows change in participants but cannot prove that instruction caused it. To strengthen the evidence, we will, if consent and capacity allow, pre-test adults on partner waitlists and retest them at comparable intervals as a matched comparison. Otherwise, we will compare results with our 2024 cohort and report the comparison as descriptive.

**Data, privacy, and improvement.** The Program Manager will collect intake, attendance, and post-test data in [data system] and run monthly completeness checks. A contracted evaluator, [name or "an external M&E consultant"], will analyze gain, attendance, and completion quarterly by class, site, and learner subgroup. Learners consent to data use at intake. Records are stored in a password-protected, access-restricted system, and only de-identified aggregate results are reported externally [add applicable requirements, e.g., FERPA or state rules]. Findings drive action. Staff, instructors, and partners will review quarterly results, and any class falling below [X]% gain or [X]% attendance triggers a response within 30 days, such as schedule changes, added tutoring, or intensified persistence outreach. We will share annual results with the funder and partners and use them to refine the next year's design.

1. **Baseline denominator.** Earlier you said 310 adults were *served*. Now 124 of 310 were *post-tested*. # ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Gap-Analysis Checklist: Mid-Sized Fintech (AWS, Entra ID, Terraform, JSM)

**Caveats:** I'm inferring likely gaps from your description, so validate each against what you actually have. "Azure AD" is now **Microsoft Entra ID**, which auditors will expect in your documentation. Because you process payments, **PCI DSS** probably applies and overlaps heavily with this list. Your financial regulator's requirements (which depend on jurisdiction) belong in the legal register under 5.31.

**Effort key:** **QW** = quick win (days to ~4 weeks). **PRJ** = project (2+ months, needs planning and owners).

---

## Priority 0: ISMS Clauses 4-10 (mandatory, not Annex A)

Certification bodies fail organizations on these more often than on technical controls, and "no formal ISMS" means this is likely your biggest gap.

| Requirement | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope, context, interested parties (Cl. 4) | Scope undefined | Scope statement (e.g., "payments API platform, supporting AWS accounts, and staff"), interested-parties register | **QW** |
| Leadership, roles, policy (Cl. 5) | No ISMS owner or top-management commitment | Signed information security policy, ISMS roles, steering committee minutes | **QW** |
| Risk methodology, register, treatment plan (Cl. 6.1) | Ad hoc risk handling | Documented methodology, risk register with owners, treatment plan, risk acceptance sign-offs | **PRJ** |
| Statement of Applicability (6.1.3) | Doesn't exist | SoA listing all 93 controls with include/exclude, justification, status | **PRJ** (after risk assessment) |
| Objectives, competence, documented information (Cl. 6.2, 7) | Informal | Measurable objectives, training records, document control in Confluence or SharePoint | **QW** |
| Internal audit, management review, corrective action (Cl. 9-10) | None | Audit program and report, management review minutes, nonconformity log in Jira | **PRJ** |

---

## Priority 1: Foundations and gating controls

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.37 | Policies, roles, procedures | Policies exist but aren't approved, versioned, or communicated | Approved policy set with owners and review dates, acknowledgment records | **QW** |
| 5.31, 5.36 | Legal and regulatory requirements | No consolidated register | Register of regulatory, contractual, and PCI obligations, with owner and control mapping | **QW** |
| 5.9, 5.11 | Asset inventory | Partial CMDB | AWS Config/Resource Explorer export, tagging standard (owner, environment, data class), SaaS inventory | **PRJ** (QW: tag policy plus SaaS list) |
| 5.12, 5.13 | Classification and labeling | Likely none | 3-4 level scheme, data-flow diagram showing where cardholder or customer data lives | **QW** |
| 5.19-5.22 | Supplier security (MSPs, SaaS) | Weak or missing due diligence, SLAs, and monitoring | Supplier register with criticality tiers, security clauses in MSP contracts, SOC 2/ISO reports reviewed, annual review records | **PRJ** (QW: register and tiering) |
| 5.23 | Cloud services security | Shared-responsibility not documented | AWS account structure (Organizations, SCPs), cloud security standard, shared-responsibility matrix | **PRJ** |
| 8.2, 8.5, 5.15-5.18 | Access control, authentication, privileged access | Inconsistent MFA, standing admin rights, no access reviews | Conditional Access policies enforcing MFA, PIM/JIT for admins, IAM Identity Center federation, no long-lived IAM keys, root MFA, quarterly access review sign-offs, joiner/mover/leaver tickets in JSM | **PRJ** (QW: MFA everywhere, remove stale accounts) |

## Priority 2: Core technical and operational controls (auditors will sample these)

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.8 | Vulnerability management | Periodic scanning but no SLAs or tracking | Severity-based remediation SLAs, findings tracked in Jira, scan and pen test reports with closure evidence | **QW** (formalize process) |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | Terraform in place, but baselines and drift unmanaged | Hardened baselines (CIS), drift detection, policy-as-code (Checkov, AWS Config rules), state file access controls | **PRJ** |
| 8.32, 8.19 | Change management | Process may not be consistently followed | JSM change records linked to Git PRs, branch protection, required approvals, emergency change procedure | **QW** |
| 5.24-5.28, 6.8 | Incident management | Plan may be informal, with no exercises | IR plan, severity matrix, runbooks, tabletop exercise report, post-incident reviews, staff reporting channel | **PRJ** (QW: IR plan and tabletop) |
| 8.15-8.17 | Logging, monitoring, clock sync | Datadog in place, but retention, coverage, and alert ownership unclear | CloudTrail/VPC flow logs centralized, retention policy, alert rules mapped to use cases, on-call records, protected log storage | **QW** |
| 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30 | Backup, redundancy, continuity | Backups exist but restores are untested | Backup configs, restore test results, defined RTO/RPO, BC/DR plan, DR exercise report | **PRJ** |

| 8.20-8.22 | Network security | MSP-managed, so you may lack visibility or evidence | VPC/security group reviews, segmentation diagrams, MSP-supplied firewall rule reviews, WAF configs for APIs | **PRJ** |

| 6.7, 7.7 | Remote working, clear desk and screen | Policy gaps | Remote working policy, screen lock enforced via MDM | **QW** |
| 7.1-7.14 | Physical security | Cloud-first, so mostly office-focused | Office access logs, visitor log, media disposal records. Datacenter controls can be justified in the SoA by relying on AWS attestations | **QW** |
| 5.5-5.7 | Authorities, special interest groups, threat intel | Typically absent | Regulator contact list, threat feed subscriptions (e.g., ISAC, vendor advisories) | **QW** |

| 8.10-8.12, 5.33, 5.34 | Deletion, masking, DLP, records, privacy | Retention and deletion not enforced | Retention schedule, S3 lifecycle rules, deletion logs, DLP rules on email and cloud, privacy register | **PRJ** |
| 5.35 | Independent review | None | Internal audit by an independent person or an external consultant | **PRJ** (ties to Cl. 9) |

---

## Suggested sequencing

**Weeks 0-6 (quick wins):** Define scope, name an ISMS owner, secure management sign-off, build the legal register, supplier register, data classification scheme, and approved policy set, enforce MFA, formalize vulnerability SLAs, and write the IR plan.

**Months 2-5 (core projects):** Run the risk assessment and produce the SoA, clean up access (PIM, reviews), improve asset inventory and supplier due diligence, and run a restore test and an IR tabletop. Add SDLC security gates to CI.

**Months 5-8 (proving it works):** Run internal audit and management review, close nonconformities, and engage a certification body for Stage 1, followed by Stage 2.

Most organizations your size need roughly 6-12 months, mainly because the ISMS needs to show a period of operation (records of reviews, audits, and exercises actually happening).

---

## Practical tips

- **Keep scope tight at first.** Scoping to the payments platform and supporting corporate IT is more manageable than "the whole company."
- **Your MSPs are in scope as suppliers.** Auditors will ask for contracts, SLAs, and evidence you monitor them.
- **Automate evidence.** Terraform, Jira, Datadog, and Entra reports can generate most of what auditors request. Consider a compliance automation tool if you want continuous collection, though it isn't required.
- **Align with PCI DSS and your regulator** in one control framework to avoid triple the work.

**Effort key:** **QW** = quick win (documentation or config, roughly 1 to 6 weeks), **M** = medium (1 to 3 months), **L** = long project (3+ months)

## Part 1: Management system clauses (4-10)

Annex A gets the attention, but missing clauses 4-10 are the most common reason first audits fail. Your PCI and SOX programs probably cover little of this.

| Clause | Requirement | Likely status | Action | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | Context, interested parties, ISMS scope | Gap | Define scope (see note below), list interested parties (regulators, card brands, auditors, customers) | QW |
| 5 | Leadership commitment, policy, roles | Partial | Sign an ISMS policy, name an ISMS owner, record management commitment | QW |
| 6.1.2-6.1.3 | Risk assessment and treatment, SoA | Gap | Choose a methodology, build a risk register, write a treatment plan, produce the SoA | M |

| 10 | Nonconformity and corrective action, continual improvement | Partial | Corrective-action log (your ITIL problem and CSI processes can be adapted) | QW |

**Scoping note:** Your scope decision drives total effort. Options are (a) the whole company, (b) the payment platform and supporting infrastructure, or (c) the full production environment. | Phase | Actions | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **Now (weeks 1 to 4)** | Inventory all privileged accounts (AWS root and IAM, domain admin, vCenter, DBs, network, SaaS admin). Enforce MFA on all admin access (PCI 8.4.1). Remove shared and standing admin accounts where possible, and secure and test AWS root and break-glass accounts | QW |
| **Next (months 1 to 3)** | Move AWS admins to IAM Identity Center with least-privilege permission sets and time-bound elevation. Create separate admin accounts for on-prem. Add a documented privileged access request and approval flow in your ITIL tooling. Log privileged activity centrally | QW / M |
| **Later (3 to 9 months)** | Select and deploy a PAM tool with credential vaulting, session recording, and just-in-time access across AWS and VMware. Start with CDE and domain-admin access, then expand | **L** |

For the ISO audit, the interim controls plus a risk-justified PAM roadmap are usually acceptable. Auditors want to see that the risk is understood and being treated, not that every tool is already deployed.

### 2. Vulnerability management (8.8)

| Step | Action | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Write a short vulnerability management standard with severity-based SLAs. A common starting point is critical within 7 to 14 days and high within 30. PCI requires critical patches within one month at minimum | QW |
| 2 | Enable Amazon Inspector for EC2, ECR, and Lambda, and deploy a scanner for on-prem VMware assets. Run authenticated scans | QW / M |
| 3 | Schedule internal scans at least quarterly and after significant change (PCI 11.3.1), plus external ASV scans quarterly (PCI 11.3.2) | QW |
| 4 | Assign every finding an owner (via the CMDB), track it as a ticket, and move patching to **monthly plus out-of-cycle for critical or KEV-listed issues** | M |
| 5 | Add an exception and risk-acceptance process with expiry dates | QW |
| 6 | Report metrics monthly: mean time to remediate, SLA compliance, and aging backlog. Use them as ISMS objectives (Clause 6.2) | QW |

Your current quarterly patching cadence is probably the **single most likely audit finding**, for both ISO and PCI, so it deserves the earliest attention.

### 3. Access reviews (5.15, 5.18, 8.2)

| Step | Action | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reuse the SOX access review process as the base, then extend scope to all in-scope systems: AWS, VMware, CDE apps, databases, and key SaaS | QW |
| 2 | Review standard users at least every six months (PCI 7.2.4) and **privileged users quarterly** | QW |
| 3 | Make reviewers system or data owners, not IT admins reviewing their own access. Record approvals and removals with timestamps | QW |
| 4 | Tie joiner/mover/leaver events to HR triggers, and test that leavers are disabled within your target (for example, 24 hours) | QW / M |
| 5 | Review service accounts, API keys, and IAM roles, which are often missed | M |

1. **Weeks 1 to 6:** scope, ISMS policy, risk methodology, privileged account inventory and MFA, vulnerability SLAs, scanner enablement, expanded access reviews
2. **Months 2 to 4:** risk assessment and SoA, centralized logging, monthly patching, BIA and DR test, supplier inventory, IR playbooks
3. **Months 4 to 9:** PAM tool, monitoring and detection maturity, SDLC security tooling, internal audit and management review, then Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits

# Part 2: Vulnerability Management Standard

**Document ID:** `[SEC-STD-VM-001]` | **Version:** `[0.1]` | **Owner:** ITO | **Approver:** `[CISO/EXEC]` | **Review:** annually
**Maps to:** ISO 27001 A.8.8, 8.9, 5.7 | PCI DSS 6.3.1, 6.3.3, 11.3.1, 11.3.2

## 1. Purpose and scope
This standard defines how vulnerabilities are identified, prioritized, remediated, and reported. It covers all in-scope assets: AWS workloads (EC2, containers, Lambda), on-prem VMware hosts and VMs, network devices, endpoints, and the payment platform's application code and dependencies.

## 2. Roles
- **ITO:** runs scanning and patch cycles, and reports metrics.
- **Asset owners (CLD/ENG/ITO):** remediate findings in their SLA.
- **ISMS:** approves exceptions, reviews metrics, and triages threat intelligence.
- **EXEC:** approves high-risk exceptions.

## 3. Requirements
1. **Asset coverage:** every in-scope asset in the CMDB has an owner and is scanned. Unscanned assets are tracked as findings.
2. **Scanning cadence:**
   - Authenticated internal scans: **at least monthly** (the PCI minimum is quarterly and after significant change).
   - Cloud and container image scanning: continuous or on each build.
   - External ASV scans: quarterly and after significant change.
   - Code and dependency scans (SAST/SCA): on every merge to main.
3. **Prioritization:** rate by CVSS, then adjust for exploitability (CISA KEV, active exploitation), asset criticality (CDE or internet-facing), and compensating controls.
4. **Intelligence:** ISMS reviews CISA KEV and vendor advisories (AWS, VMware, OS, key libraries) at least weekly.
5. **Verification:** closure requires a rescan or other evidence.
6. **Patching:** monthly cycle, plus out-of-cycle for critical, KEV-listed, or actively exploited issues. All patches go through change management.

## 4. Remediation SLAs

| Severity | Standard asset | CDE or internet-facing | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** (or KEV-listed or actively exploited) | 14 days | **7 days** | KEV items: 7 days maximum, with emergency change if needed |
| **High** | 30 days | **14 days** | PCI 6.3.3: no later than one month |
| **Medium** | 60 days | 45 days | |
| **Low** | 90 days or next cycle | 90 days | Track, and fix opportunistically |

- **Clock start:** when the vendor patch is released or the finding is validated, whichever is later.
- **Beyond SLA:** the finding needs an approved exception (see section 5) or it is reported as an SLA breach.
- **Targets:** these SLAs are a starting proposal. Check them against your risk appetite and QSA guidance.

## 5. Exception and risk acceptance process
1. **Request:** the asset owner raises a ticket with the finding ID, asset, business reason, and why the patch can't be applied in SLA.
2. **Compensating controls:** the request must describe them (network isolation, WAF rule, disabled service, added monitoring).
3. **Risk rating:** ISMS assesses residual risk.
4. **Approval:**
   - Medium or Low: ISMS.
   - High: ISMS plus the asset owner's director.
   - Critical, or any CDE asset: EXEC.
5. **Expiry:** maximum 90 days, renewable only with fresh review. No open-ended exceptions.
6. **Register:** all exceptions are logged in a central register and reviewed monthly, with a summary in management review.
7. **PCI note:** exceptions on CDE assets still need to satisfy PCI's patch timeline unless the QSA accepts the compensating controls. Check this with the QSA before approving.

## 6. Metrics and reporting
Report monthly to the ISMS owner, and quarterly in management review:
- % of in-scope assets scanned
- Open findings by severity and age
- SLA compliance %
- Mean time to remediate (by severity)
- Active exceptions and expiry dates
- Count of KEV findings and time to close

Suggested ISMS objectives (Clause 6.2): 95% scan coverage, 90% SLA compliance for Critical and High, zero expired exceptions.

## 7. Records
Scan reports, ticket history, change records, exception register, and monthly metric reports. Retain for `[12 months minimum / per retention schedule]`.

## 8. Compliance
Breaches of this standard are reported to ISMS, and persistent non-compliance is escalated to EXEC.

# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Gap Analysis and Roadmap

## Corrections to my earlier notes
- **ITIL access management:** I listed "Access management" as an ITIL 4 practice. ITIL 4 has no standalone practice by that name (it was an ITIL v3 process). Access is handled through **Information security management** and **Service request management**. The mapping below uses those.
- **Stage 1 audit:** I called it a "readiness assessment." Stage 1 is a formal part of certification, a documentation and readiness review that can raise findings. If you want a non-binding dry run, ask the certification body (CB) for a separate pre-assessment, or use a consultant.

## Assumptions
- Ratings below are inferred from your summary, not from an audit. Treat them as hypotheses to validate.
- **Regulator is unknown.** For a regional financial firm (GLBA/FFIEC/NYDFS, PCI DSS, or non-US equivalents), your legal and regulatory register (5.31) must reflect it, and some regulatory controls may outrank ISO priorities.
- Physical security, HR processes, and secure development weren't described, so I've marked them "unknown."
- Scope: the whole organization's IT services (Azure, VMware, SaaS, legacy apps). Narrowing scope can save time but is hard to justify for a 250-person firm.

Your draft is a good start. Five changes will help it survive a Stage 1 review:

## Risk register template

Build this as a spreadsheet or GRC tool table with dropdowns. Suggested tabs: **Register**, **Scales** (likelihood, impact, bands), **Treatment actions**, and **Acceptances**. ISO 27001 Clauses 6.1.2 and 6.1.3 expect identified risks, owners, analysis, evaluation against criteria, treatment decisions, and owner approval of the plan and residual risk.

### Suggested scales (illustrative; set yours in the approved methodology)

| Score | Likelihood | Impact (use the highest dimension) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare (less than once per 5+ years) | Negligible: no data exposure, no service impact |
| 2 | Unlikely (once per 3-5 years) | Minor: small internal impact, no regulatory implication |
| 3 | Possible (once per 1-3 years) | Moderate: limited data exposure or a day of disruption |
| 4 | Likely (about once per year) | Major: PII/financial data breach, regulatory notification required, multi-day outage |
| 5 | Almost certain (multiple times per year) | Severe: large-scale breach, regulatory action, loss of customer trust |

**Score = Likelihood × Impact.** Bands: **Low 1-4, Medium 5-9, High 10-16, Critical 20-25**. Define who may accept each band. For example, Low and Medium by the risk owner, High by the executive sponsor, and Critical not accepted without a funded remediation plan.

## 2. Risk methodology (copy into your policy doc)

**Information Security Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology**
Version 0.1 | Owner: ISMS Lead | Approver: Steering Committee | Review: annually

**2.1 Purpose and scope**
This methodology defines how [Company] identifies, analyzes, evaluates, treats, and accepts information security risks across the ISMS scope, in line with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clauses 6.1.2, 6.1.3, and 8.2-8.3. It applies to all risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information assets.

**2.2 Roles**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Executive Sponsor | Accepts High risks. Sets risk appetite with the steering committee. |
| CEO | Accepts Critical risks (funded plan required). |
| Steering Committee | Approves this methodology. Reviews High and Critical risks. |
| ISMS Lead | Maintains the register and process. Verifies the methodology was followed. |
| Risk Owner | Accountable for the risk and its treatment. Accepts Low and Medium risks. |
| Asset Owner | Confirms business impact and service constraints. |

**2.3 Process**
Identify (by asset or service, using threat and vulnerability) → analyze (inherent likelihood × impact) → evaluate against the bands → choose treatment (mitigate, accept, transfer, avoid) → score residual risk after treatment → obtain approval at the required authority level → monitor and review.

**2.4 Likelihood scale**

| Score | Level | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | Less than once in 5+ years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Once in 3-5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Once in 1-3 years |
| 4 | Likely | About once a year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Multiple times a year |

**2.5 Impact scale (score by the highest applicable dimension)**

| Score | Data / regulatory | Financial [set with Finance] | Operational | Reputation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Negligible | No exposure | < [$X] | No service impact | None |
| 2 Minor | Internal data only, no notification | [$X-$Y] | < 4 hours, non-critical service | Internal awareness only |
| 3 Moderate | Limited non-sensitive exposure | [$Y-$Z] | Up to 1 business day, or a critical service degraded | Limited customer complaints |
| 4 Major | PII/financial exposure, regulator notification required | [$Z-$W] | Multi-day outage of a critical service | Local media or notable customer loss |
| 5 Severe | Large-scale breach, regulatory action or sanction | > [$W] | Extended outage, inability to operate | Loss of trust, significant customer attrition |

**2.6 Scoring and bands**
Score = Likelihood × Impact.

| Band | Score | Treatment expectation | Acceptance authority | Max acceptance period | Review |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 1-4 | Accept or monitor | Risk Owner | 12 months | Annually |
| Medium | 5-9 | Treat where cost-effective | Risk Owner, ISMS Lead informed | 12 months | Every 6 months |
| High | 10-16 | Treatment plan required | Executive Sponsor | 12 months | Quarterly |
| Critical | 20-25 | Immediate action and funded plan | CEO | 6 months | Monthly |

A High or Critical impact score of 4 or 5 on the data/regulatory dimension must also be referred to Legal/Compliance to check notification obligations.

**2.7 Risk appetite statements**
1. [Company] has **very low appetite** for unauthorized disclosure, loss, or alteration of Restricted data (PII and financial data).
2. [Company] has **no appetite** for unmanaged risk. Every risk above Medium must have an owner and a documented decision.
3. **Critical risks are not accepted** unless a funded remediation plan exists, and then only for up to 6 months.
4. [Company] has **low appetite** for prolonged outages of critical financial services beyond the RTOs set in the BIA.
5. Legacy or unsupported systems handling Restricted data are tolerated only with documented compensating controls, a replacement plan, and time-limited acceptance.
6. [Company] will meet all legal and regulatory notification obligations. This is not subject to risk acceptance.

**2.8 Review triggers**
Review the full register at least annually. Also review after any significant incident, major change (new system, supplier, or acquisition), change in law or regulation, or a failed control test. Overdue treatment actions must be re-dated with a recorded reason.

# PART 2: PACKING, DECLUTTER, AND ROOM-BY-ROOM

**Packing timeline:** Start with storage/garage/attic (T-8 to T-4), then guest room, decor, books, off-season (T-5 to T-3), living room and bedrooms (T-2), bathrooms (T-1), kitchen last (final week).

**Declutter tips**
- Movers charge by weight or space, so every item cut saves money. Ask whether you'd buy it again today.
- Remove personal photos and thin out closets, since buyers need to picture themselves in the house.
- Sell large items locally. Donate the rest. Skip moving cheap, bulky items.
- Set a hard deadline: everything leaving the house by T-3 weeks.
- Don't move hazmat (propane, paint, fuel, pesticides). Movers won't take it. Dispose of it through county household hazardous waste programs.

**Room-by-room**
- [ ] **Attic:** Empty completely. Sort keep/sell/toss. Check for forgotten items behind insulation areas.
- [ ] **Garage:** Sort tools, seasonal gear, and paint. Sweep. Address oil stains. Collect openers and remotes.
- [ ] **Living room:** Pack decor and media first. Photograph how electronics are wired.
- [ ] **Bedrooms:** Keep a week of clothes out. Use wardrobe boxes or bags for hanging clothes.
- [ ] **Bathrooms:** Pack medications separately and keep them with you. Seal liquids in bags.
- [ ] **Kitchen:** Use paper plates for a few days. Label knives. Pack a "first-night" box.
- [ ] **Office:** Back up computers. Keep laptops, chargers, and important papers with you.
- [ ] **Basement/laundry:** Empty the washer and dryer lines. Check the mover's appliance prep requirements.
- [ ] **Every box:** Label with room and contents. Put heavy items in small boxes.

## 2. Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

### Packing timeline
| When | What to pack |
|---|---|
| Weeks 6-5 | Storage, garage, off-season clothes, books, decor, extra linens |
| Weeks 4-3 | Guest room, office, dining room, wall art, most of the kitchen |
| Weeks 2-1 | Living room, bedrooms, bathroom backups, pantry |
| Final 2-3 days | Daily-use items, bathroom, bedding, remaining kitchen |

**General rules:** Label every box on the **top and two sides** with room + contents. Number boxes and keep a running inventory. Put heavy items in small boxes and light ones in large. Keep one "do not pack" area for the open-first box and document folder.

### Kitchen
- [ ] Declutter: duplicate utensils, mismatched containers, expired spices and pantry items
- [ ] Wrap dishes vertically, with padding between each
- [ ] Glasses and stemware in dividers or wrapped individually
- [ ] Knives sheathed and labeled "SHARP"
- [ ] Use up or donate perishables and open liquids
- [ ] Keep out: 2 plates/bowls/mugs, a pan, a knife, coffee supplies
- [ ] Movers generally won't take open food, cleaning chemicals, or aerosols. Ask your mover for the exact list.

### Living Room
- [ ] Pad and wrap TV/electronics; photograph cable connections before unplugging
- [ ] Bag cords, label them, and tape them to the device
- [ ] Wrap lamps separately; pack shades in boxes
- [ ] Bubble-wrap or blanket artwork and mirrors; use mirror boxes
- [ ] Books in small boxes only

### Bedrooms
- [ ] Declutter closets: donate anything unworn in a year
- [ ] Keep clothes on hangers in wardrobe boxes if your mover supplies them, or use trash bags over hangers
- [ ] Dresser drawers: remove breakables; light clothes can stay if the mover allows it
- [ ] Disassemble beds; bag and label hardware, taped to the frame
- [ ] Keep out: 1 week of clothes, bedding, toiletries, chargers

### Bathrooms
- [ ] Toss expired meds, cosmetics, and half-empty bottles
- [ ] Seal liquids in zip bags
- [ ] Pack towels as padding
- [ ] Keep out: toiletries, TP, medications, shower curtain

### Office
- [ ] Back up computers; carry laptops yourself
- [ ] Shred old paperwork; scan and keep key documents digitally
- [ ] Photograph desktop setups before unplugging
- [ ] Keep out: laptops, hard drives, important documents

### Garage / Basement / Storage
- [ ] Declutter first. This is where the most money and weight is saved.
- [ ] Drain gas and oil from mowers and trimmers
- [ ] Dispose of paint, propane, chemicals, and batteries per local rules; movers usually can't carry hazmat
- [ ] Bundle tools and label them
- [ ] Check whether large items (grill, bikes, ladders) are worth the shipping weight

### Dog items
- [ ] Pack what you can't buy fast: bed, crate, toys, medications, food
- [ ] Keep the dog's gear in your car, not the truck

### Declutter tips
- **Weight is money.** Movers charge by weight or space. Every box you skip saves cash.
- **The one-year rule:** if you haven't used it in a year, sell or donate it.
- **Replace vs. move:** cheap furniture, old mattresses, and bulky low-value items often cost more to ship than to replace.
- **Sell early:** list larger items 4-6 weeks out. Use Facebook Marketplace or local groups. Donate the rest by week 2.
- **Donation pickups** book up in summer, so schedule them by week 3. Ask for receipts.
- **Hazardous items:** dispose of these before packing day.
- **Photograph high-value items** and keep their serial numbers.

## DIY truck vs hybrid vs full-service

Estimates for 1-2 bedrooms, one dog, and your own car driven. Get live quotes.

| | **DIY truck** | **Hybrid (container or labor-only)** | **Full-service movers** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Total cost** | ~$4,000-7,500 | ~$5,000-9,000 | ~$7,500-14,000+ |
| **Your effort** | Highest: pack, load, drive, unload | Medium: pack and sometimes load or unload | Lowest |
| **Driving** | Two drivers, two vehicles (truck and car) | Just your car | Just your car |
| **Dog** | Dog rides in the car, so you need a second driver | Easiest | Easiest |
| **Timing risk** | Truck is slower, so add buffer. Book early, since July is peak | Containers can take 1-2+ weeks to deliver | Delivery is often 1-3 weeks after pickup, so you may arrive before your stuff |
| **Damage risk and coverage** | You carry the risk. Insurance is optional | Moderate. Check container coverage | Best with Full Value Protection ($200-500) |

**How to choose:**
- If you have a tight budget, a small load, and can both drive, go with the DIY truck.
- If you want to avoid driving a truck but keep costs down, go hybrid.
- If your time or physical capacity is limited, or you have a lot of furniture, go full-service.

Terms vary by company, so confirm each one in writing.

| When | What | Typical amount |
|---|---|---|

Ask about **cancellation and rescheduling fees**, how many **free loading and unloading days** you get, and what **storage** costs if you arrive before your place is ready.

## PACKING BY ROOM: KEEP VS SELL

**Rule of thumb:** long-distance containers cost roughly $0.60-$1.50 per cubic foot of space. If an item costs less to replace than to ship, sell it.

| Room | Keep and ship | Sell or donate | Carry with you (not in container) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Living room** | Good sofa, TV, quality shelves, art | Worn furniture, cheap entertainment centers, old cables | Laptops, remotes, router |
| **Kitchen** | Daily dishes, good cookware, knives, small appliances you use weekly | Duplicates, chipped items, rarely used gadgets, half-used pantry | 1 pan, 2 plates, utensils, kettle for the first few days |
| **Bedrooms** | Mattress (bagged), dressers worth keeping, seasonal clothes | Particle-board furniture, worn bedding, outgrown clothes | 3-5 days of clothes, bedding bag, toiletries |
| **Bathrooms** | Towels, good shower items | Expired products, half-empty bottles | Toiletry kit and medications |
| **Office** | Desk if sturdy, monitors, files you need | Old cords, unused electronics, old paperwork (shred) | Laptops, hard drives, passports and documents |
| **Garage** | Quality tools, bikes, camping gear | Paint, chemicals, propane, clutter | Basic tool kit for the car |
| **Dog** | Large crate if you won't use it in the car, extra toys | Worn bedding and old toys | Bed, bowls, food, leash, meds, records, 3+ days of supplies |
| **Decor and misc.** | Sentimental items, photos | Anything you haven't used in a year | Valuables and jewelry |

**Container loading tips:** Disassemble beds and tables. Wrap furniture in blankets. Heavy boxes go low, light ones high. Leave no gaps. Don't pack liquids, hazmat, perishables, plants, firearms, or ammunition. Label with room and contents, and keep a numbered inventory.

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

**Timeline rule of thumb:** Start with the rooms you use least, and pack the kitchen and bathroom last. For a 1-2 bedroom home, expect roughly 20-40 hours of total packing time, plus extra if you're also decluttering.

## Kitchen (pack last; allow 4-6 hrs)
- [ ] Keep out: 1 pot, 1 pan, 2 plates, bowls, cups, utensils, a knife, a can opener, and coffee supplies
- [ ] Wrap plates vertically and pack them in small boxes; use dish-pack boxes for glassware
- [ ] Use towels and dish cloths as padding
- [ ] Toss expired pantry items; donate unopened non-perishables
- [ ] Don't pack open liquids, aerosols, or cleaning chemicals (most movers refuse them)
- [ ] Label: "Kitchen, fragile" and "Kitchen, heavy"

## Living room (2-3 hrs)
- [ ] Wrap art and mirrors, and use picture boxes
- [ ] Photograph the electronics wiring before unplugging
- [ ] Label cables with tape or bags
- [ ] Pack books in small boxes only, because they get heavy quickly
- [ ] Remove lamp shades and pack them separately

## Bedrooms (3-4 hrs each)
- [ ] Use wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes
- [ ] Keep a week's clothes and bedding for the road and the first night
- [ ] Disassemble bed frames and bag the hardware, taped to the frame
- [ ] Vacuum-bag off-season clothes and linens
- [ ] Pack jewelry and valuables yourself; carry them with you

## Bathrooms (1-2 hrs)
- [ ] Use a toiletry bag for the essentials
- [ ] Seal liquids in plastic bags
- [ ] Toss expired medications and cosmetics
- [ ] Carry prescriptions with you, never in the truck
- [ ] Pack towels last

## Home office (2-3 hrs)
- [ ] Back up all computers to the cloud and an external drive
- [ ] Carry laptops, hard drives, and important documents with you
- [ ] Shred what you don't need to keep
- [ ] Photograph the monitor and printer setup

## Garage, storage, and outdoor (3-6 hrs)
- [ ] Drain gas and oil from mowers and tools; movers won't take fuel
- [ ] Dispose of paint, propane, and chemicals through local hazardous waste
- [ ] Decide what's worth moving: cheap tools and old yard items often cost more to ship than to replace
- [ ] Bag the hardware from anything you take apart

## Closets and linens (1-2 hrs)
- [ ] Donate anything you haven't worn in a year
- [ ] Use linens as padding for fragile items
- [ ] Keep a set of sheets and towels for each person in the first-night box

## Dog items
- [ ] Pack a separate dog bag that rides in the car: food, bowls, meds, records, leash, waste bags, bed, toys
- [ ] Keep the crate out until the very last moment
- [ ] Don't pack the dog's bed or favorite toy in the truck

## "Open First" box (per room)
- [ ] Box cutter, scissors, tape, trash bags
- [ ] Toilet paper, soap, hand towels, paper towels
- [ ] Sheets, pillows, phone chargers
- [ ] Basic tools, light bulbs, and a flashlight
- [ ] Coffee maker, snacks, paper plates

---

# Declutter Tips

1. **Do it by category, not by room.** Clothes, books, kitchen, and papers go faster when you tackle them together.
2. **Use the cost test.** Movers charge by weight or space, and a $40 item costs more than that to move 2,400 miles.
3. **Sort into four piles:** keep, sell, donate, trash. Anything you can't decide on after 30 seconds goes in a "maybe" box with a date. If you haven't opened it by T-2 weeks, let it go.
4. **Sell early.** List big furniture by T-6 weeks. Anything unsold by T-2 weeks gets donated.
5. **Think about the Oregon space.** Measure your new rooms and check that large furniture fits through the doors.
6. **Ask what you'd buy again.** If you wouldn't repurchase it today, it probably doesn't need to ride across the country.
7. **Don't declutter sentimental items last.** Do them mid-way, when you're not exhausted.
8. **Schedule donation pickups early.** Many charities book 2-3 weeks out in summer.
9. **Digitize papers.** Scan what you can, and shred the rest.
10. **Keep a "leaving" corner** by the door, so donation boxes are already staged.

# Dog Checklist and Services Timeline

**Correction first:** Earlier I said a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) is only needed if you fly. That was too simple. Many states technically require a CVI or health certificate for dogs entering by car, though it's rarely checked. Ask your vet, and check the Oregon Department of Agriculture's pet import page. If one is required, it's usually valid for about 30 days, so time it close to departure. (T = Thursday, July 16, 2026.)

---

# Consolidated Dog Checklist

## T-10 to T-8 weeks: Health and planning
- [ ] **M** Book the vet check-up (check-up, vaccines, heartworm and flea/tick prevention up to date). *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Request full records: rabies certificate, vaccine history, microchip number, medication list, and any surgery or condition notes. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Ask the vet whether a CVI is needed for Oregon, and when to schedule it.
- [ ] **M** Discuss travel anxiety, motion sickness, and heat tolerance. Ask about anti-nausea or calming medication and **trial any new medication before the trip**, not on the road.
- [ ] **M** Decide drive vs. fly for the dog (see the flying section). Driving is usually less stressful for a dog.
- [ ] **M** Confirm the microchip is registered and the contact info is current.

## T-8 to T-5 weeks: Booking and conditioning
- [ ] **M** Book dog-friendly lodging for every road night. Get each pet policy and fee in writing. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Confirm the temporary Oregon housing allows dogs. Check breed or size limits and the pet deposit.
- [ ] **M** Buy a crash-tested harness or a well-secured, ventilated crate for the car. *(MED, $40–$200)*
- [ ] **M** Do crate or harness practice and 30-minute test drives, building to 1–2 hours.
- [ ] **M** Identify emergency vets along the route and near the destination. Save the numbers.
- [ ] **M** Find an Oregon vet and ask for a records transfer. Book a visit for T+3 days or so.
- [ ] **M** Look up your Oregon county or city dog license rules. Most require proof of rabies vaccination.
- [ ] **M** Check your new rental's pet policy: pet rent, deposit, and any documentation required.

## T-4 to T-2 weeks: Prep
- [ ] **M** Order a new ID tag with your new phone number and, if possible, a destination address. *(MED)*
- [ ] **M** Arrange dog care for loading day: sitter, boarding, or a friend's home. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Get a 30-day extra supply of medications and preventatives.
- [ ] **M** Get the CVI if needed, timed to the vet's guidance.
- [ ] **M** Take a clear current photo of the dog (for lost-pet posters, just in case).
- [ ] **M** Reconfirm all lodging dog policies before the July 4 weekend.

## T-1 week: Packing the dog kit (rides in the car, never the truck)
- [ ] Food for the trip plus 1 week extra, in a sealed container. Keep the same brand to avoid stomach upset.
- [ ] Water jug (bring water from home at first, then mix in new water gradually if your dog is sensitive)
- [ ] Collapsible bowls, leash, backup leash, harness
- [ ] Waste bags, paper towels, enzyme cleaner, and old towels (for accidents or car sickness)
- [ ] Medications, preventatives, and calming aids
- [ ] Records folder: rabies certificate, vet contact, CVI, microchip number
- [ ] Bed or blanket and favorite toys, with an unwashed item that smells like home
- [ ] Crate, with a cover or sunshade for the car windows
- [ ] First-aid basics: gauze, vet wrap, tweezers (ticks), and your vet's after-hours number
- [ ] Chews or a stuffed toy for hotel evenings

## Moving day
- [ ] **M** Dog is with the sitter, or in a closed room or crate with a "DO NOT OPEN" sign on the door.
- [ ] **M** Light meal the morning of travel, not a heavy one. Walk and exercise before getting in the car.
- [ ] **M** Collar, tag, and leash on the dog before any door opens.
- [ ] **M** Never leave the dog in a parked car, even for a few minutes. In July, interior temperatures can become dangerous within minutes.
- [ ] **M** Plan a break every 2–3 hours for water and a walk. Check pavement temperature with your hand, since hot asphalt burns paws.
- [ ] **M** Drive early or late in the day to avoid the worst heat through the Plains and Mountain West.

## Overnight arrangements

- [ ] Call ahead to confirm the pet policy, since some chains vary by location.
- [ ] Don't leave the dog alone in a room unless the hotel allows it. If you do, crate them and put out a "dog in room" sign.
- [ ] Bring the crate in for the night so the dog has a familiar space.
- [ ] Walk the dog before bed and first thing in the morning.
- [ ] Keep a towel to wipe paws and a sheet to cover hotel bedding if needed.

## Arrival and first two weeks

- [ ] **M** Check the yard and fences for gaps. Walk the perimeter before letting the dog off leash.
- [ ] **M** Keep the dog on a leash for the first few days in unfamiliar territory.
- [ ] **M** Keep feeding and walking times as routine as possible.
- [ ] **M** Update the microchip registry with the new address. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Get the Oregon dog license. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** First Oregon vet visit, with records transferred. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Look up local leash laws, dog parks, and any rental restrictions.
- [ ] **M** Watch for signs of stress (not eating, hiding, accidents). Call the vet if it lasts more than a few days.

---

# Pet-Fee Ballpark Costs

Fees vary widely and change often. Treat these as planning numbers and confirm with each property.

| Lodging type | Typical pet fee | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mainstream hotels | $0–$100 per stay, or $25–$75 per night | Some chains charge per night, some per stay. |
| Pet-friendly boutique or upscale hotels | $50–$150 per stay | Some offer dog beds and treats. |
| Extended-stay hotels | $75–$200 flat per stay, or $15–$25 per night | Often capped for long stays. |
| Motels | $10–$30 per night | Quality varies. Check reviews carefully. |
| Airbnb or VRBO | $20–$75 per stay, sometimes per night | Hosts set their own fees. Some add a cleaning fee. Always disclose the dog. |
| Rental deposit (Oregon apartment) | $200–$500 refundable, plus $25–$75 monthly pet rent | Landlords can't charge pet fees for service animals or assistance animals. |

**Budget for a typical trip:** 3 road nights at $25–$75 = **about $75–$225**. Add **$75–$200** for temporary housing. Total: roughly **$150–$425**. A few hotel brands waive fees, so it's worth checking.

---

# If You End Up Flying the Dog

Summer is the hardest season to fly a dog. Weigh it carefully.

## Option 1: In the cabin
- **Size limit:** The dog and carrier must fit under the seat. Most airlines cap combined weight at about 20 lb, but it varies. The dog has to be able to stand and turn around.
- **Cost:** About **$95–$150 each way**, plus the airline's carrier requirements.
- **Limits:** Airlines cap the number of pets per flight, so book early. Pets can't sit in exit rows.
- **Paperwork:** Airlines generally want a rabies certificate. Some want a CVI dated within 10 days of travel. Check the specific airline.
- **Prep:** Get the dog used to the carrier for weeks. Book direct flights when possible.

## Option 2: As cargo or checked pet
- **Many major airlines have restricted or stopped this**, so check each one's current policy. Alaska Airlines serves Portland and has handled pets in cargo, but verify.
- **Heat embargoes:** In summer, most airlines refuse checked pets when temperatures at the origin, destination, or any connection exceed a threshold (often about 85°F). A July cross-country flight can easily trigger this.
- **Breed limits:** Flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds like bulldogs, pugs, and boxers are often banned or restricted because of breathing risks.
- **Cost:** Often **$200–$1,000+**, depending on size and airline.
- **Crate:** It must be airline-approved (IATA-compliant), large enough for the dog to stand and turn, with secure latches and food and water dishes.
- **Paperwork:** A CVI within 10 days of travel is typical, plus a rabies certificate. Some carriers want signed acclimation or live animal forms.

## Option 3: Professional ground pet transport
- A specialist drives your dog cross-country, often in climate-controlled vehicles.
- **Cost:** Roughly **$1,000–$3,000+**, depending on distance and service.
- Vet the company carefully: check licensing, reviews, and how often the dog gets breaks.

## Flying tips
- **Avoid sedation** unless your vet specifically recommends it. Airlines and veterinary groups generally discourage it because of breathing and heart risks at altitude.
- Book early morning or late evening flights in summer.
- Put an ID tag on the dog and the carrier, with your destination address and phone number.
- Carry a photo of the dog, plus the vet records.
- Book pet-friendly lodging at the destination for the arrival night.
- Check **the airline's own page**, since policies change often and sometimes without notice.

**Bottom line:** For a July move, driving the dog with you is usually the safest and cheapest choice. Fly only if the dog is small enough for the cabin or you have a firm reason.

---

# Services and Subscriptions Timeline

**Golden rule:** Never end a service until its replacement is confirmed, and keep a one-day overlap. Take photos of final meter readings.

## T-8 to T-6 weeks (May 21–June 4): Research and book long-lead items
- [ ] **J** **Internet (Oregon):** Book the install now. Installation can take 2+ weeks, and summer moves compete for slots. Ask whether you need to be home. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **J** **Oregon utilities:** Identify providers by address. Electric is typically PGE or Pacific Power, depending on location. Gas is often NW Natural, and water and trash are usually local or city. Ask about deposits and lead times.
- [ ] **M** **Health insurance:** If you have an employer plan, check network coverage in Oregon. If you buy on the marketplace, a move to a new area generally opens a Special Enrollment Period (usually 60 days), but verify the rules and don't let coverage lapse.
- [ ] **P** **Employer:** Confirm payroll address, state withholding changes (Ohio → Oregon), and benefits.
- [ ] **J** **Gym, lawn service, cleaning service, meal kits:** Check each cancellation notice period. Many gyms require 30 days' written notice.

- [ ] **J** **Ohio utilities (electric, gas, water, trash):** Schedule stop dates for **T+1 day (July 17)**. Ask about final bills and deposit refunds.
- [ ] **J** **Oregon utilities:** Schedule starts for **one or two days before arrival** so power and water are on when you get there. Get confirmation in writing.
- [ ] **M** **Auto insurance:** Call your insurer and ask about Oregon coverage and a new quote. **Don't cancel the old policy until the new one is active.** Oregon requires liability insurance to register.
- [ ] **J** **Renter's or homeowner's insurance:** Cancel the old policy for T+1 and start the new one for the day you get keys.
- [ ] **J** **Prescriptions:** Ask for refills, and transfer them to a national pharmacy chain or an Oregon branch.

- [ ] **J** **Employer HR or payroll:** Update address and withholding.
- [ ] **J** **Social Security Administration, IRS (Form 8822), and other federal accounts:** Update your address. You can file Form 8822 or update accounts directly with each agency.

- [ ] **J** Confirm the forwarding address with the landlord for the deposit refund.

# Budget Totals and Moving-Day One-Pager

**Adjustments to earlier numbers:**
- **Hybrid** now means a portable container (PODS or U-Pack) plus hired loading and unloading labor. The earlier "partial service, $2,500-$5,000" row was too optimistic for 2,400 miles.
- **DMV costs** are widened to $200-$500, since title, registration, and two licenses can exceed my earlier range. Verify at the Oregon DMV site.
- **Meals and tolls** are raised to $300-$500, since $200-$400 was lean for two people over 3-4 days.
- Everything is a 2024-25 ballpark, not live pricing. Summer 2026 prices may be higher, so treat the top of each range as more plausible than the bottom.

**Assumptions:** 2 adults, 1 dog, 1 car, a 1-2 bedroom household, about 2,400 miles. You drive the car and the dog rides with you. Tell me if any of that is wrong and I'll rerun the numbers.

---

# Part 1: Budget

## Costs common to all three options

| Line item | Range | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Car fuel (~30 mpg) | $250-$350 | High |
| Road lodging, 3 nights | $300-$600 | Medium |
| Dog fees on the road (see pet-fee table) | $75-$225 | Medium |
| Meals and tolls | $300-$500 | Medium |
| Utility deposits and setup | $100-$400 | Medium |
| Oregon DMV (title, registration, 2 licenses) | $200-$500 | Medium |
| DEQ emissions test (only if Portland or Medford area) | $0-$60 | High |
| Vet visit, records, dog license | $150-$300 | Medium |
| Dog travel gear (harness or crate, etc.) | $100-$300 | Medium |

Ranking each row with a single unique number is simpler than stacking tie-breaks inside one formula. Because the row number is part of the number, no two rows can tie, which is what was leaving SUPERSEDED blank.

## Paste-ready formulas (row 2, fill down to 421)

**Q: Completeness score** (counts non-blank, non-whitespace cells in Name, Email, JoinedBefore, Phone, PreferredPark)
```
=SUMPRODUCT(--(LEN(TRIM(B2:F2))>0))
```
I used this instead of `COUNTA`, which counts cells containing only a space.

**S: Group key** (the email, only if it looks valid; otherwise blank, so junk emails don't group together)
```
=IF(REGEXMATCH(K2,"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$"),K2,"")
```
This assumes K is still `=LOWER(TRIM(C2))` from before.

**R: Rank key** (higher = better row to keep; priority is completeness, then latest timestamp, then higher row number)
```
=Q2*1E14 + ROUND(IF(ISNUMBER(I2),I2,0)*86400)*1E4 + ROW()
```
Timestamps are converted to whole seconds, and the row number goes in the lowest digits. This works for sheets up to 9,999 rows.

**O: SUPERSEDED** (replaces the old formula)
```
=IF(S2="","",IF(SUMPRODUCT(($S$2:$S$421=S2)*($R$2:$R$421>R2))>0,"SUPERSEDED",""))
```
A row is superseded if any other row with the same email has a higher rank key. I used `SUMPRODUCT` rather than `COUNTIFS` because `COUNTIFS` with `">"&R2` can mangle very large numbers when it converts them to text.

Both changes below assume the Q, R, K, L, G, H, I and J columns are as before.

## 1) Revised group key (column S)

Rows with a valid email group by email. Other rows group by name plus an anchor timestamp: the earliest same-name submission within ±10 minutes of the row.

```
=IF(REGEXMATCH(K2,"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$"),"E:"&K2,
  IF(AND(L2<>"",ISNUMBER(I2)),

2. **7-digit recovery from elsewhere in the sheet.** If a 7-digit number matches the last 7 digits of exactly one valid 10-digit number, borrow that area code. This is a guess, so it gets flagged.

Group-level recovery (another row of the same person has a good phone) is already handled by the merge.

## Step 1: Helper column Z (per-row best phone)

I'm using a helper column because the salvage has to run on every row in a group, not just the current row. A single formula in X would need a `MAP` over the group, which is much harder to debug.

**Z2** (fill down):
```
=IF(H2<>"REVIEW",H2,
  IFERROR(LET(
    main, REGEXREPLACE(LOWER(TRIM(E2)),"\s*(x|ext\.?|extension|#).*$",""),
    d,    REGEXREPLACE(main,"\D",""),
    n,    IF(AND(LEN(d)=11,LEFT(d,1)="1"),RIGHT(d,10),d),
    IF(LEN(n)=10, n,
      IF(LEN(n)=7,
         LET(m, UNIQUE(FILTER($H$2:$H, REGEXMATCH($H$2:$H&"","^\d{3}"&n&"$"))),
             IF(ROWS(m)=1, INDEX(m,1), "REVIEW")),
         "REVIEW"))),
  "REVIEW"))
```
- If H is valid, it's used as-is.
- Otherwise it strips extensions, strips non-digits, drops a leading 1, and accepts 10 digits.
- A 7-digit number is completed only if exactly one distinct valid 10-digit number in the sheet ends with those 7 digits. Zero or multiple matches give `REVIEW`.
- If you don't want the 7-digit guess, delete the `IF(LEN(n)=7, ...)` branch and keep `"REVIEW"`.

**AA2: recovery flag** (so guesses get a human look):
```
=IF(AND(H2="REVIEW",Z2<>"REVIEW"),"RECOVERED","")
```
Spot-check these rows before trusting them. An inferred area code can be wrong if two people share the same last 7 digits.

## Step 2: Final Phone merge (X2, fill down)

```
=IF(S2="",Z2,
  LET(best, MAXIFS($R$2:$R,$S$2:$S,S2,$Z$2:$Z,"<>REVIEW"),
      IF(best=0,"REVIEW",INDEX($Z$2:$Z,MATCH(best,$R$2:$R,0)))))
```
- With no group key (`S` blank), it returns the row's own Z.
- Within a group, it takes the Z value from the highest-ranked row that isn't `REVIEW`. Since Z prefers H, a valid H wins over a salvaged E.
- The open-ended ranges (`$R$2:$R`, etc.) pick up new rows automatically. The ranges are dynamic, but the formulas themselves still need to be filled down for new rows.

## Optional: remove the 421 elsewhere

If you want the rest of the sheet dynamic too, replace `$421` with nothing in the O, T, U, V, W and Y formulas (for example, `$S$2:$S$421` becomes `$S$2:$S`). They should keep working, just slightly slower.

Update the review flag in P to include recoveries if you want them checked:
```
=IF(OR(W2="REVIEW",X2="REVIEW",Y2="REVIEW",I2="REVIEW",T2="CONFLICT",AA2="RECOVERED"),"REVIEW",
  IF(O2="SUPERSEDED","DROP","OK"))
```

**Goal 1: DNA structure and the central dogma (HS-LS1-1)**
*Scope note: mutation is excluded here and addressed in Goal 4.*
*"I can" check:* Given a DNA sequence, I can write the complementary strand, the mRNA, and the amino acid sequence using a codon table. I can explain how replication produces two identical copies of DNA, and how the amino acid sequence determines a protein's shape and function.

**Goal 3: Statistical analysis of inheritance data (HS-LS3-3)**
*"I can" check:* I can explain how segregation and independent assortment during meiosis produce the expected ratios for a cross. I can calculate expected values, compute χ², compare it to a critical value, and explain whether variation in results reflects chance or a flaw in the model.

**Goal 4: Mutations, gene expression, meiosis, and phenotype (HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1)**
*"I can" check:* I can compare a normal and a mutated sequence, predict the effect on the protein, and reason about whether the change is harmful, neutral, or beneficial. I can explain how meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) and mutation each create inheritable variation. I can also explain whether a given mutation can be passed to offspring, depending on whether it occurs in germline or somatic cells.

---

## 2. Updated 3-Week Sequence

| Week | Focus | Goals | Checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation. **Plus one day on meiosis** (how it halves chromosome number and generates new allele combinations through crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilization) | 1, 5 (meiosis supports 2 and 4) | **Assessment 1** (central dogma model, no mutation) |
| 2 | Mendelian genetics, pedigrees, probability, chi-square (connect ratios back to meiosis) | 2, 3, 5 | **Assessment 2** (inheritance investigation) |
| 3 | Mutation types and effects, gene expression, sources of variation (meiosis vs. replication errors vs. environmental mutagens), germline vs. somatic, genetic testing and gene-editing ethics | 4, 6, 5 | **Assessment 3** (gene editing analysis and policy brief) |

*Teaching tip for the meiosis day:* HS-LS3-2's assessment boundary excludes memorizing the phases of meiosis. Focus on outcomes (what meiosis produces and why offspring differ from parents and siblings) rather than prophase I vs. metaphase II.

---

## 3. Revised Assessments

### Assessment 1: Central Dogma Model (HS-LS1-1)
**Task:** Students receive a short DNA sequence for a hypothetical enzyme or a real gene segment. They build a physical or digital model that traces the information through replication, transcription, and translation, showing how the nucleotide sequence determines the amino acid sequence and, in turn, the protein's function.

**Deliverables:**
- Annotated model with labeled template and complementary strands, mRNA, codons, and amino acids
- A short written explanation (claim-evidence-reasoning) of how the sequence of this gene leads to the protein's structure and function
- A one-to-two sentence explanation of why replication must occur before a cell divides, and how it preserves the sequence

**Scoring focus:** Accuracy of base pairing and codon reading, a logical link from sequence to protein to function, and correct description of replication's role.

---

### Assessment 3: Gene Editing Analysis and Policy Brief (HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1, ETS1.B, SEP: Obtaining/Evaluating/Communicating)

**Case:** Students receive a case study of a gene-editing application, such as base editing to correct the sickle cell mutation in *HBB* (GAG → GTG at codon 6) or a fictional equivalent. The packet includes the target sequence, the intended edit, a hypothetical off-target edit in a second gene, efficacy and off-target data, and perspectives from at least three stakeholders.

*Note:* The approved CRISPR sickle cell therapy edits a regulatory region (*BCL11A*), not the *HBB* coding sequence. If you use a real therapy, make sure students aren't conflating the two. A simplified or fictional gene avoids this.

**Part A: Tracing introduced mutations**
- Trace the intended edit through transcription and translation, and classify the resulting change (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift).
- Trace the off-target edit the same way and predict its effect on that gene's protein and the cell's function.
- Compare the two outcomes and explain how an edit meant to fix one protein could create a new problem.

**Part B: Germline vs. somatic**
- Identify whether the application edits somatic cells (such as blood stem cells) or germline cells (embryos, eggs, sperm).
- Explain who would carry the edit and whether it could be inherited.
- Explain how an off-target edit would differ in consequence depending on cell type. A somatic off-target edit affects only the patient, while a germline one could be passed to future generations and appear in every cell of the offspring.

**Part C: Policy brief (1–2 pages)**
- A clear claim about whether and how the technology should be used or regulated
- Evidence from at least two provided sources, including at least one piece of quantitative data
- Integration of Parts A and B as scientific evidence (mutation effects, off-target risk, heritability)
- A counterargument and rebuttal, with consideration of accuracy, access, consent, and stakeholder trade-offs

**Scoring focus:** Accuracy of the mutation tracing and classification, correct distinction between germline and somatic consequences, quality of evidence, and reasoning that connects the science to the policy claim.

---

# Split Assessment 1

## Task 1A (Week 1): Central Dogma Model
**Standards:** HS-LS1-1, SEP: Developing and Using Models

**Task:** Students get the template strand of a short real gene segment (the start of the human *HBB* gene, which codes for part of hemoglobin):

`3'-TAC CAC GTA GAC TGA GGA CTC CTC TTC-5'`

They build a physical or digital model that shows:
1. Replication of the segment (both new strands, with base pairing)
2. Transcription into mRNA: `5'-AUG GUG CAU CUG ACU CCU GAG GAG AAG-3'`
3. Translation into the amino acid chain: Met-Val-His-Leu-Thr-Pro-Glu-Glu-Lys

**Written piece (3-4 sentences):** Explain how the order of nucleotides determines the order of amino acids, and why the amino acid order matters for the protein's shape and function.

### Rubric 1A

| Criterion | 3: Meets | 2: Approaching | 1: Beginning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Replication** | Both strands correctly paired; notes each new DNA molecule has one original and one new strand | Pairing mostly correct, with 1-2 errors, or semiconservative idea missing | Frequent pairing errors or confuses replication with transcription |
| **Transcription** | mRNA correct (U for T), correct direction, labeled | 1-2 errors or missing labels | Copies DNA instead of RNA, or uses the wrong strand throughout |
| **Translation** | Codons read correctly with the codon table; amino acid sequence accurate | 1-2 codon reading errors | Reads bases individually or can't use the table |
| **Structure → function explanation** | Links nucleotide order → amino acid order → protein shape → function, using evidence from the model | Describes the sequence of steps but not why it matters for function | Restates the steps without a causal link |

---

## Task 1B (Week 3): Mutation Extension
**Standards:** HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1

**Task:** Students return to their Week 1 model and revise it. Assign or let them choose one mutation, such as:
- **Substitution (missense):** codon 7 `GAG → GTG` (Glu → Val; this is the sickle cell mutation)
- **Substitution (silent):** `GAG → GAA`
- **Substitution (nonsense):** `GAG → TAG`
- **Deletion or insertion:** removal or addition of one base early in the segment (frameshift)

They trace the change through transcription and translation, then write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) paragraph about the likely effect on the protein and phenotype. They also answer: *Could this mutation be passed to offspring? Under what conditions?* (Germline vs. somatic.)

### Rubric 1B

| Criterion | 3: Meets | 2: Approaching | 1: Beginning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tracing the mutation** | Revised mRNA and amino acid chain correct; mutation type correctly named | Tracing mostly correct, or type misnamed | Can't trace the change through the steps |
| **Claim and evidence** | Claim about protein/phenotype effect is supported by specific sequence evidence (which amino acids changed, where) | Claim is reasonable but evidence is vague | Claim is unsupported or contradicts the model |
| **Reasoning** | Explains why this change does or doesn't affect protein function (e.g., the chemical difference of Val vs. Glu, or a premature stop) | Partial reasoning | No link between protein change and phenotype |
| **Heritability** | Correctly distinguishes germline from somatic mutations and says which can be inherited | Partially correct | Incorrect or missing |
| **Model revision** | Notes at least one limitation of the model (e.g., it ignores regulation or environment) | Limitation is vague | No reflection |

---

# Week 1 Lesson Outline (55 minutes)

**Title:** From Gene to Protein: How DNA's Sequence Becomes a Protein
**Standards:** HS-LS1-1
**Assumes:** Students already know the basic structure of DNA (nucleotides, base pairing, double helix). If not, spend 5 minutes reviewing this in the opening.

**Objective:** Students can describe replication, transcription, and translation, use base-pairing rules and the codon table to move from DNA to mRNA to amino acids, and explain why sequence matters for protein function.

**Materials:** Codon table (one per student), whiteboards or scratch paper, the *HBB* sequence on a slide, strips of paper or colored beads for modeling (optional), Task 1A handout.

### Timeline

| Time | Segment | Teacher moves |
|---|---|---|
| **0-5** | **Hook** | Show a photo of normal and sickled red blood cells. Ask: *"One protein, hemoglobin, is built differently. How could instructions in DNA lead to a physical change in a cell?"* Collect 2-3 ideas without correcting. Preview that today they will trace the path from gene to protein. |
| **5-16** | **Replication** (7 min instruction/activity, 4 min check) | Briefly show how helicase unwinds DNA and polymerase builds new strands using base pairing. Students complete a strand on whiteboards: given `3'-TAC CAC GTA-5'`, build the new strand. Emphasize each daughter molecule keeps one old strand (semiconservative). **→ Formative Check 1** |
| **16-27** | **Transcription** (7 min instruction/activity, 4 min check) | Explain that DNA stays in the nucleus, so a mobile RNA copy is made. Contrast DNA and RNA (U instead of T, single-stranded). Model transcription of the template strand into mRNA, step by step with the *HBB* segment. **→ Formative Check 2** |
| **27-44** | **Translation** (12 min instruction/activity, 5 min check) | Introduce codons, start (AUG) and stop codons, ribosomes, and tRNA at a basic level. Do the first two codons together using the codon table, then students translate the rest in pairs. Briefly connect to function: amino acid order determines how the chain folds, and shape determines function. **→ Formative Check 3 (see below)** |
| **44-52** | **Synthesis** | Students sketch a 3-box flow diagram (DNA → mRNA → protein) and label where each process happens and what it uses. Pairs compare. |
| **52-55** | **Launch Task 1A** | Hand out Task 1A and rubric. Return to the hook: *"What do you think could change in this chain to make a sickled cell?"* Tell them they'll test their ideas in Week 3. |

### Formative Checks

1. **After replication (whiteboard, ~2 min):** Show a template strand and have students hold up the complementary strand. Scan for A/T and C/G pairing errors. Follow-up question: *"If this molecule replicates, how many original strands are in each new DNA molecule?"* (One.)

2. **After transcription (error detection, ~2 min):** Display a flawed mRNA, such as one containing thymine or one that copies the template strand rather than complementing it. Students identify the error(s) with a thumbs signal, then explain to a partner. This catches the most common mistakes: T in RNA and copying instead of complementing.

3. **After translation (exit-style, ~3 min):** On a half sheet, students (a) translate the codons `AUG GAG UAA`, and (b) answer in one sentence: *"Why would changing one amino acid in a protein sometimes change what the protein does?"* Sort responses into three piles (got both / translation only / neither) to plan the next day's reteaching.

### Common Misconceptions to Watch For
- **Replication and transcription mixed up:** Students may think transcription copies the whole DNA molecule. Reinforce that it copies one gene, and into RNA.
- **Reading codons as single bases or in the wrong frame:** Use a physical reading frame (a paper strip with three-base windows).
- **"The mRNA is a copy of the coding strand" vs. "complement of the template":** Pick one convention for the unit and state it explicitly. The task above uses the template strand, so mRNA matches the coding strand with U for T.
- **Proteins as "just chains":** Keep returning to shape and function so the sequence has meaning.

### Differentiation
- **Support:** Provide partially filled sequence organizers and a color-coded codon table.
- **Extension:** Ask what would happen if a stop codon appeared early, or have students predict how a redundant codon (e.g., GAG vs. GAA) might affect the protein. This previews Week 3.

---

**One scheduling note:** With the mutation extension now in Week 3 alongside Goal 4 and the policy brief, that week is the heaviest. If it feels tight, you could run the mutation extension as a 20-30 minute in-class task and give students the policy brief's research stage as homework, or cut the policy brief to a one-page version.

# 2-Day Reteach Plan: "Translation Only" Students

**Target gap:** These students can read codons but can't explain why one amino acid change can alter a protein's function.

## Day 1 (45-50 min): Why Amino Acid Order Matters

**Objectives:** Students can (1) explain that amino acid order determines folding, shape, and function, and (2) use sentence frames to write that chain of reasoning.

| Time | Activity | Details |
|---|---|---|
| 0-12 | **Mini-lesson** | Use a paper chain or pipe cleaner with colored beads or sticky dots (different colors = different amino acids). Show that the same chain folds differently when one bead is swapped. Introduce the chain on the board: **order → folding → shape → function**. Use a lock-and-key analogy: a changed shape means the key no longer fits. |
| 12-30 | **Guided practice** | Work through the sickle cell example together. Translate `GAG` → Glu and `GUG` → Val. Explain simply that Glu likes water and Val does not, so the changed hemoglobin sticks together and bends the red blood cell. Students complete the frames with you: *"The order of ___ decides the order of ___. A different amino acid can change the ___. The shape decides the ___."* |
| 30-45 | **Small-group work** | Groups get 3 cards, each with a one-amino-acid change and a scenario (for example, an enzyme whose shape no longer fits its substrate). They use the frames to write a 2-sentence explanation per card, then swap with another group and check the reasoning chain. |

Students will construct an explanation, using a model, of how DNA sequence is copied in replication and transcribed into mRNA, and how mRNA codons determine the amino acid sequence, and therefore the structure and function, of a protein.

Students will explain how meiosis distributes chromosomes, and the alleles on them, into gametes, and how crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilization generate new genetic combinations in offspring.
*"I can":* I can trace a pair of alleles through meiosis, state which gametes are possible, and explain why siblings from the same parents differ genetically.

Students will ask questions about how traits pass from parents to offspring, predict genotypic and phenotypic ratios for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, and infer the most likely inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked) from a pedigree. *"I can":* I can build a Punnett square whose gametes reflect meiosis, calculate probabilities, and justify an inheritance pattern from pedigree evidence.

Students will make and defend a claim, based on sequence evidence, about how inheritable variation arises from (a) meiosis, (b) viable replication errors, and/or (c) environmental mutagens, and how a specific mutation (substitution, insertion, deletion, frameshift) alters a protein and phenotype. ## Teacher Note on the Codon Table

- Give students a standard **mRNA codon table** (RNA codons, not DNA). Allow it on Questions 5 and 8, or throughout if you prefer.
- Students most often go wrong on Question 8 by reading the template strand as if it were the mRNA, by writing T instead of U, or by reading the table with DNA codons. If you want to check direction separately from table skills, give half credit for correct complementary pairing even when the table lookup is wrong.
- Codons needed to key this quiz: AUG = Met, GCA = Ala, AAC = Asn, CUG = Leu, UAA = Stop, GUA = Val.
- Question 8's template is written 3′ to 5′ so that students can read it left to right. Point out that mRNA is antiparallel to the template, so the mRNA's 5′ end pairs with the template's 3′ end.

## Answer Key

**Part A**

| Q | Answer | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **B** | A-T and G-C |
| 2 | **C** | Semiconservative replication |
| 3 | **B** | Nucleus; mRNA |
| 4 | **C** | RNA has uracil and ribose |
| 5 | **A** | Codon definition |
| 6 | **C** | Four genetically different haploid cells |

**Q7 (3 pts). Model answer:**
"A protein's amino acid sequence determines how it folds into its 3D shape. If one amino acid is replaced by another with different chemical properties, the folding or the active site can change. Since a protein's shape determines its function, the protein may work poorly or not at all. (Example: in sickle cell disease, one amino acid change in hemoglobin causes it to clump.)"

*Scoring:* 1 pt for sequence determines shape, 1 pt for shape determines function, 1 pt for explaining how the substitution changes the shape or function (a correct example counts).

**Q8 (8 pts)**

**(a) mRNA (3 pts):**
**5′ – AUG GCA AAC CUG UAA – 3′**

Template to mRNA by codon: TAC→AUG, CGT→GCA, TTG→AAC, GAC→CUG, ATT→UAA.
*Scoring:* 3 = all correct with U (not T) and ends labeled; 2 = one or two wrong bases, or ends not labeled; 1 = paired as DNA (T instead of U) or direction is clearly confused; 0 = not attempted or unrelated.

**(b) Amino acids (3 pts):**
**Met – Ala – Asn – Leu – Stop**

*Scoring:* 3 = all five correct; 2 = one error; 1 = two or three errors; 0 = otherwise. Give **consequential credit** if the translation is correct for the student's own (incorrect) mRNA.

**(c) Mutation (2 pts):**
Template CGT→CAT changes the mRNA codon GCA to **GUA**, which codes for **Val** (valine). Ala is replaced by Val, so it is a **missense** mutation.
*Scoring:* 1 pt for the correct codon and amino acid, 1 pt for "missense."

**Q9 (3 pts). Model answer:**
(a) Half the gametes carry **A** and half carry **a** (1:1, or 50% each).
(b) The homologous chromosomes separate (segregate) during meiosis I, so each gamete receives only one allele.

*Scoring:* 1 pt for naming both A and a, 1 pt for the 1:1 / 50% ratio, 1 pt for homologs separating in meiosis I.

**Q10 (4 pts). Model answer (any two):**
- **Crossing over:** Homologous chromosomes swap segments during meiosis I, creating chromosomes with new combinations of alleles.
- **Independent assortment:** Each homologous pair lines up and separates independently of the others, so gametes get different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
- **Random fertilization:** Any sperm can fuse with any egg, so each sibling comes from a different pairing of gametes.

*Scoring:* 2 pts per process (1 pt for naming it, 1 pt for an accurate description of how it creates new combinations). Do not give credit for "mutation" alone, since the question asks about processes of meiosis and fertilization.

# Revised Genetics Unit (~3 Weeks)

Mutations are now introduced and assessed only in Week 3. Changes from the previous version are marked **[Revised]** or **[New]**.

## Goals

**1. DNA structure and the central dogma [Revised] (HS-LS1-1)**
Students will explain, using a model, how the nucleotide sequence of a *normal* gene is copied during replication, transcribed into mRNA, and translated into a protein, and how the amino acid sequence determines the protein's shape and function.

*"I can" check:* Given a DNA sequence, I can write the complementary strand, the mRNA, and the amino acid sequence, and explain why sequence order matters for the protein's function.

**2. Mendelian inheritance and pedigrees (HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3)** *(unchanged)*
Students will ask questions about how alleles are passed from parents to offspring, predict genotypic and phenotypic ratios for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, and determine the most likely inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked) from a pedigree, with at least 80% accuracy on the unit assessment.

**3. Statistical analysis of inheritance data (HS-LS3-3)** *(unchanged)*
Students will calculate expected and observed ratios from class-generated data and apply a chi-square test to decide whether the data support a proposed model of inheritance.

**4. Mutations, gene expression, and phenotype [Revised] (HS-LS3-2, HS-LS1-1)**
Building on the Week 1 model of a normal gene, students will construct and defend a claim about how a specific mutation (substitution, insertion, deletion, or frameshift) alters a protein and the resulting phenotype, citing sequence evidence. They will also explain how mutations arising during replication or from environmental factors can produce inheritable variation (and when they are not inherited), and how changes in gene expression can alter phenotype without changing the DNA sequence.

*"I can" check:* I can compare a normal and a mutated sequence, predict the effect on the protein, classify the mutation as harmful, neutral, or beneficial with reasoning, and say whether it could be passed to offspring.

**5. Genotype-to-phenotype modeling [Revised] (SEP: Developing and Using Models; HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-1)**
Students will build a model in Week 1 showing how a normal gene leads to a functional protein and trait, then revise it in Weeks 2 and 3 (adding allele combinations, then mutations and expression changes), identifying its strengths and limitations each time.

**6. Ethics of genetic technologies (ETS1.B; SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information)** *(unchanged)*
Students will evaluate the evidence and societal trade-offs of one genetic testing or gene-editing application and communicate a defensible position that accounts for accuracy, access, consent, and unintended consequences.

### Assessment 1: Central Dogma Trace [Revised] (Week 1; HS-LS1-1)

**Task:** Students receive a short normal DNA sequence for a hypothetical enzyme or a real gene segment. | Criterion | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |

| Protein-to-phenotype claim (CER) | Claim, sequence evidence, and reasoning about protein function are all present and linked | One element is weak | Claim without evidence, or evidence without reasoning | Missing or incorrect |

### Predicted phenotype and heritability

- **A (missense):** The Glu → Val change matches the sickle cell mutation. It makes hemoglobin more likely to clump in low oxygen, so the red blood cells sickle. **Heritability:** If the mutation is in egg or sperm cells (germline), it can be passed on. The sickle allele is recessive, so a child with two copies has sickle cell disease and a child with one copy has sickle cell trait.
- **B (silent):** The protein is identical, so there is no change in phenotype. **Heritability:** It can still be inherited if it is in the germline, but it has no effect on the trait.
- **C (frameshift):** Every codon after the deletion changes, so the protein is very likely nonfunctional. Real *HBB* frameshifts are associated with beta-thalassemia. **Heritability:** Only a germline mutation can be passed on. A somatic mutation would affect only the cells descended from the mutated cell.

### Notes for grading
- **Numbering:** In the standard clinical numbering of *HBB*, the sickle site is "position 6" because the starting Met is not counted. In this 36-nt segment, it is amino acid 7. Tell students this if they search online.
- **Variant C deletion:** The deleted base is the A in the 5th triplet (TGA → TG). Accept a student's answer if they regroup correctly and get the frameshifted mRNA above. The partial last codon (UU) is not translated.
